Deputy Commissioner of ) Income Tax – 1(3)1, Aayakar Bhavan ) M. K. Road, ) Mumbai – 400 020. ) ) 3. Additional Commissioner of ) Income Tax – 1(3), Aayakar Bhavan, ) M. K. Road, ) Mumbai – 400
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the statutory requirements of section 245 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 when trying to adjust Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against alleged outstanding tax demands. Tata Communications, a telecom company, had filed its AY 2019–20 return showing total income of Rs. 638.05 crore, tax liability of Rs. 220.63 crore, TDS/TCS credit of Rs. 425.84 crore, and had claimed a refund of Rs. 205.21 crore. In an earlier writ petition, the Court had already directed the Department on 11 January 2021 to release the refund with interest within two weeks of receipt of that order, and Tata Communications sent that order to the Department on 14 January 2021 asking for compliance.

Instead of simply releasing the refund, the Department issued an intimation under section 143(1) on 17 January 2021 stating that a refund with interest of about Rs. 227.27 crore was payable, but also saying there were outstanding demands for AY 2007–08 (Rs. 153.91 crore) and AY 2008–09 (Rs. 138.26 crore), and that a separate section 245 intimation had been sent proposing to adjust those demands against the refund. The petitioner said it had never actually received any notice under section 245, despite the 143(1) intimation referring to one, and the Court found the Department’s approach unacceptable.

The Court criticized the Department’s stance that the earlier High Court order would not cover or operate over matters/orders passed by the ITAT merely because the Union of India was not a party in that matter. It described this justification as not fit for a State department that is supposed to act as a “model litigant.” The operative consequence is that before adjusting a refund against earlier demands, the Department must strictly follow section 245 procedure, including proper notice and compliance with the statutory requirements; it cannot withhold or offset the refund on the basis of uncommunicated or procedurally defective adjustment actions. The case is specifically relevant to tax refund processing and stay/adjustment of demand, and it concerns AY 2019–20 for the refund and earlier AY 2007–08 and AY 2008–09 for the alleged outstanding demands.

Mistri, Madhur Agrawal, Shyam Walve DATE: April 9, 2021 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: April 24, 2021 (Date of publication) AY: 2012-13 FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: Article 226/ s. 147: (i) A Writ Petition can be filed in the Bombay High Court against an order passed in Delhi if the assessee is based in Mumbai. The litigant has the right to go to ‘a Court’ where part of cause of action arises. (ii) A s. 148 notice & s. 147 reassessment order passed against an amalgamated (non-existing) company is without jurisdiction. The defect cannot be treated as procedural defect. Mere participation of the assessee in the assessment proceedings is of no effect as there is no estoppel against law. rows.summary:
This Bombay High Court decision holds that an income-tax reassessment initiated and completed in the name of a company that had already ceased to exist after amalgamation is without jurisdiction and cannot be cured as a mere procedural defect. Tecnovate Esolutions Pvt. Ltd. had amalgamated with Intelnet Global Services Pvt. Ltd. effective 1 April 2010 (approved by order dated 11 February 2011), so Tecnovate ceased to exist well before the reassessment notice dated 30 March 2019 under section 148 and the reassessment order dated 31 December 2019 under sections 144/147 were issued; the Court held those proceedings were invalid because they were directed against a non-existent entity. The Court further rejected the Revenue’s attempt to rely on section 292B, holding that a notice/order issued to a dead or amalgamated company is a jurisdictional defect, not an irregularity, and the assessee’s participation in the assessment process does not create estoppel against law.  

The case also addressed forum/jurisdiction: the Court held that a writ petition was maintainable in the Bombay High Court even though the impugned notice/order had been issued from Delhi, because the assessee was based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arose there. The assessed year involved was AY 2012–13, and the Court’s reasoning is important for compliance because any tax notice, reassessment, or assessment order issued in the name of a company after its merger/amalgamation or dissolution is vulnerable to being quashed as void ab initio. For corporate groups that have undergone mergers, name changes, or succession, the practical obligation is to ensure tax authorities are promptly informed of the legal successor entity and that all future proceedings are correctly addressed to the surviving company, since participation in proceedings will not validate a notice issued to the wrong legal person.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). The so-called excess value of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be notionally termed as premium over the face value for the purposes of the deeming provision (AS-14 issued by the ICAI & CBDT Circular No 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012 referred) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Income from other sources DCIT v. Facts: The assessee company filed its return of income for AY 2013-14 in question which was subjected to scrutiny assessment. In the course of assessment proceedings, it was gathered by the AO that one M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL) amalgamated with the assessee company under the scheme of amalgamation.
rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held in **DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.** that **section 56(2)(viib)**, which taxes excessive share premium received by a private company when it issues shares above fair value, **does not apply to shares issued under a court-approved amalgamation scheme**. In this case, **Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. merged into Ozone India Ltd.** under a scheme approved by the **Gujarat High Court on 7 September 2012**, effective **1 April 2012**; under that scheme, Ozone issued equity shares to KEPL’s shareholders in exchange for KEPL’s assets and liabilities. The Assessing Officer had treated the difference between the net assets received and the face value of shares issued as taxable income under section 56(2)(viib), because Ozone received assets of **Rs. 60,26,55,864** and liabilities of **Rs. 6,05,39,708**, resulting in net assets of **Rs. 54,21,16,156**, while the corresponding shares issued had face value of **Rs. 15,00,00,000**; the alleged excess of **Rs. 39,21,16,156** was credited as **capital reserve**.

The Tribunal rejected the assessment approach and held that the statutory anti-abuse rule in section 56(2)(viib) is aimed at **unjustified share premium in ordinary share issuances by private companies**, not at share allotments made as consideration in a **legally sanctioned amalgamation**. It specifically noted that the transaction was accounted for under the **pooling of interest method under AS-14**, and that the excess of net assets over share value arising from the merger cannot be notionally treated as “premium” or deemed income under this provision. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that **court-approved amalgamation share issuances are outside the sweep of section 56(2)(viib)** on these facts, even where the accounting results in a large capital reserve or an apparent mismatch between net assets transferred and the face value of shares issued.

This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns application of section 50C of the Income-tax Act to a property sale by a non-resident assessee in AY 2011-12. The assessee sold a flat, and the stamp duty valuation exceeded the stated sale consideration by 6.55%; the dispute was whether this difference was small enough to avoid a section 50C substitution of deemed sale value. The Tribunal noted that the third proviso to section 50C(1), inserted by the Finance Act 2018, provides a tolerance band so that section 50C does not apply if the gap between actual consideration and stamp duty value does not exceed 5%, and that the Finance Act 2020 increased this tolerance band to 10%.

Although the Revenue argued that the 2018 proviso was effective only from 1 April 2019 and the 10% tolerance only from 1 April 2021, the Tribunal held these changes are curative in nature and therefore relate back to the original insertion of section 50C on 1 April 2003. On that reasoning, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the 10% threshold even for this earlier assessment year, because a 6.55% variation falls within the permitted band. The practical compliance impact is that where stamp duty valuation exceeds the declared sale consideration by 10% or less, the declared consideration should be accepted and section 50C anti-avoidance substitution should not be triggered, even for earlier years, according to this ruling.

S. 18 of the Limitation Act, which extends the period of limitation depending upon an acknowledgement of debt made in writing and signed by the corporate debtor, is also applicable to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code since s. 238A uses the expression “as far as may be” governing the applicability of the Limitation Act. The notes annexed to or forming part of the balance sheet, or the auditor’s report, must be read along with the balance sheet. (V. Padmakumar v. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CIVIL APP
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to insolvency proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 through Section 238A, which uses the phrase “as far as may be,” and therefore the general rule that time begins to run and cannot be stopped except by a process known to law continues to govern IBC claims. The Court specifically ruled that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies in IBC cases, so a written and signed acknowledgment of debt by the corporate debtor can extend the limitation period for filing a Section 7 insolvency application. It further held that entries in the corporate debtor’s books of account, including balance sheets, can constitute an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18, and that the notes to the balance sheet and the auditor’s report must be read together with the balance sheet when determining whether there has been such an acknowledgment.

On the facts, Corporate Power Ltd. had borrowed from a consortium of lenders, its account was classified as an NPA by SBI on 31 July 2013, SBI issued a loan recall notice on 27 March 2015, and several lenders assigned their debts to Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited on 31 March 2015. ARCIL issued a SARFAESI notice on 20 June 2015 and took physical possession of the project assets on 1 June 2016. ARCIL then filed its Section 7 IBC application on 26 December 2018 claiming default of Rs. 5,997,80,02,973, and later filed a supplementary affidavit on 8 November 2019 adding the date of default and balance sheets allegedly showing repeated acknowledgment of debt; the NCLT admitted the case on 19 February 2020, but the NCLAT Full Bench precedent in V. Padmakumar, which had treated balance-sheet entries differently, was reversed by the Supreme Court.

For compliance purposes, the ruling means that companies cannot assume insolvency limitation has expired merely because the original loan default is old: every written acknowledgment of the liability by the corporate debtor, if signed and properly recorded in documents such as balance sheets, may restart or extend the limitation clock under Section 18. The decision applies directly to creditors, resolution applicants, and corporate debtors involved in IBC Section 7 proceedings, and it emphasizes the need to preserve and review board-approved financial statements, notes, and audit materials because those documents may later be used to prove acknowledgment of debt. The Court’s decision was delivered on 15 April 2021 and published on 17 April 2021.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that, under the Direct Tax Vivad Se Vishwas Act, 2020 (DTVSV), the Designated Authority cannot reject a valid declaration filed under section 4(1) merely because it believes there is no “disputed income” so long as the case involves “disputed tax” and the declarant otherwise falls within the Act’s eligibility rules. The court emphasized that the scheme is aimed at resolving disputed tax liability, not disputed income, and found that the authority was required to issue Form 3 under section 5(1) specifying the amount payable under section 3 rather than summarily marking the declaration as “Rejected.” The petitioners had filed eleven writ petitions relating to assessment years 1988-89 to 1998-99 after the Pr. CIT/Designated Authority rejected their DTVSV declarations without any justification, despite their ongoing tax dispute history and pending rectification/revision proceedings.

On the facts, the taxpayer’s earlier assessments for AYs 1987-88 to 1995-96 had been reopened under section 147 and completed under section 143(3) read with section 147, while AYs 1996-97 to 1998-99 were completed under section 143(3) with substantial demand. The additions were challenged before the CIT(A), then before the ITAT, which set aside the CIT(A)’s order and directed relief; meanwhile, recovery proceedings were initiated and the taxpayer paid Rs. 12,43,000 via cheques, but the TRO incorrectly applied all challans only to AY 1986-87. As a result, when the ITAT order was given effect, credit for the taxes recovered was wrongly reflected only in AY 1987-88, producing a refund for that year but leaving large tax and interest demands in AYs 1988-89 to 1998-99; the taxpayer therefore sought rectification under section 154, which was rejected, and then filed a revision petition under section 264 for AYs 1987-88 to 1998-99, with that revision pending when he opted into DTVSV.

The High Court found that the petitioner was an “eligible appellant” because his application under section 264 was pending on the specified date, which brings him within section 2(1)(a)(v) of the DTVSV framework, and that he was not shown to be disqualified under section 4(6) or any exception under section 9. It therefore quashed the rejection order and directed the Designated Authority to act on the Form 1 declaration in accordance with law within two weeks from the date of the order dated 09.04.2021. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that under DTVSV a pending section 264 revision can make a taxpayer eligible to file a declaration, and the authority must apply the statute to the existence of “disputed tax” rather than insisting on a particular characterization of “disputed income” before issuing the statutory payment form.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **DCIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd.** held that the **third proviso to section 254(2A) of the Income-tax Act** cannot operate to **automatically vacate a stay of demand merely because 365 days have expired**. The Court found that, as originally worded, the proviso was **discriminatory and manifestly arbitrary** because it required vacation of stay even where the **delay in disposal of the appeal was not attributable to the assessee**, including cases where the **Appellate Tribunal could not hear the appeal in time for reasons beyond the assessee’s control** or where **the revenue itself caused the delay**.  

To cure that constitutional defect, the Court directed that the third proviso to section 254(2A) be **read down by deleting the word “even” and the words “is not” after the phrase “delay in disposing of the appeal”**. As a result, a stay granted by the ITAT will now **stand vacated after the statutory period or periods only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. In practical compliance terms, this means taxpayers who have obtained a stay of demand before the Tribunal should monitor whether any adjournment or delay is being recorded as attributable to them, because only taxpayer-caused delay can now trigger automatic vacation of the stay under this provision.  

This decision applies to **ITAT stay-of-demand orders under section 254(2A)** and is important for any taxpayer litigating income-tax appeals where a stay of recovery has been granted. The judgment is dated **April 6, 2021** (pronounced) and published on **April 7, 2021**.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court dealt with a charity/tax exemption issue concerning educational trusts that had missed the filing deadline for Form No. 10B for AY 2018-19. The petitioners, charitable societies running schools, had filed their return of income on 25.07.2018 declaring nil income, but due to a mistake by their chartered accountant/accountant they uploaded Form No. 10BB instead of Form No. 10B; later, on 06.11.2019, they uploaded Form No. 10B and sought condonation of delay. Because the return was processed under section 143(1), CPC raised a demand of Rs. 1,46,01,489 by denying exemption under sections 11 and 12.  

The specific compliance issue was the CBDT’s Circular No. 2/2020 dated 03.01.2020, which delegated to the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions) the power to condone late filing of Form No. 10B only up to 365 days for AY 2018-19 onwards. The Bombay High Court held that this 365-day limit was not arbitrary or irrational, so the Commissioner’s refusal to condone delay beyond that period was not wrong merely because the filing exceeded one year. However, the Court also held that section 119(2)(b) still permits the CBDT to pass a special order in an individual case even beyond the general 365-day cap, so the CBDT can consider a further condonation request on the merits.  

As a result, the Court directed the petitioners to approach the CBDT under section 119(2)(b) within three weeks from the date of the judgment, and the CBDT was directed to decide the application within four weeks from receipt, with due intimation to the petitioners. For compliance teams, the key point is that for AY 2018-19 and onward, late Form No. 10B filings can generally be condoned only up to 365 days by the CIT(E) under Circular No. 2/2020, but delays beyond that are not automatically barred if a special order is sought from the CBDT under section 119(2)(b). The decision confirms that exemption under sections 11 and 12 may be denied where Form No. 10B is not filed on time, but also that entities should pursue CBDT-level relief where the delay exceeds the delegated 365-day window.

PCIT WP No. 79 of 2021 dated March 25, 2021( Bom) (HC) The Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020 – Wilful attempt to ev
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court in **Macrotech Developers Limited v. PCIT** held that the CBDT’s clarification in **Question 73 of Circular No. 21/2020 dated 4 December 2020** under the **Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020 (VSV Act)** was inconsistent with the statute and therefore was **set aside/quashed**. The issue arose because, for **AY 2015-16**, the taxpayer had an appeal pending before the ITAT on certain disallowances, but there was also a separate **prosecution under section 276C(2)** for alleged wilful attempt to evade tax due to **delayed payment of self-assessment tax**. CBDT’s answer to Q73 had taken the position that if prosecution had been initiated for that assessment year, the taxpayer would be **ineligible to file a declaration under the VSV Act even for unrelated disputed issues** in appeal for that same year.

The Court rejected that reading and held that **section 9(a)(ii)** disqualifies a declaration only where **prosecution has been instituted in respect of the tax arrear relating to that assessment year** as of the date of filing the declaration. In other words, the prosecution must relate to the same **tax arrear/issue** that is sought to be settled under VSV; a prosecution for a different issue in the same year does **not** bar settlement of appeal issues unrelated to that prosecution. The Court found CBDT’s broader interpretation to be **illogical, irrational, and contrary to the legislative intent** of the scheme, which was to **reduce direct tax disputes**.

For compliance purposes, the decision materially narrows the prosecution-based ineligibility under the VSV Act: a taxpayer is not automatically excluded from the scheme merely because any prosecution exists for that assessment year. The relevant check is whether, **on the date of filing the declaration**, there is a prosecution **in respect of the same tax arrear** covered by the declaration; if prosecution exists only on a separate matter, that should not by itself prevent settlement under the VSV scheme. The judgment is dated **25 March 2021** and was published on **27 March 2021**.

Muralidhar J SECTION(S): 68 GENRE: Domestic Tax CATCH WORDS: Accomodation entries, cash credit, peak credit, unexplained cash credit COUNSEL: Dr. Rakesh Gupta DATE: August 4, 2017 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: August 16, 2017 (Date of publication) AY: 1995-96 FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: S. 68 "Peak Credits": An accommodation entry provider wanting to avail the benefit of the 'peak credit' has to make a clean breast of all the facts within his knowledge concerning the credit entries in the accounts. He has to explain with sufficient detail the source of all the deposits in his accounts as well as the corresponding destination of all payments from the accounts. The assessee should be able to show that money has been transferred through banking channels from the bank account of creditors to the bank account of the assessee, the identity of the creditors and that the money paid from the accounts of the assessee has returned to the bank accounts of the creditors. The assessee has to discharge the primary onus of disclosure in this regard (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); (i) There have been numerous cases before the AO, CIT (A), the ITAT and for that matter even before this Court, where the question involved concerns the treatment of ‘accommodation entries’. Basically, what an accommodation entry provider does is to accept cash from an Assessee and arranges to have a cheque issued from his own account or some other account, usually of ‘paper’ or fake entities, to make it
rows.summary:
This Delhi High Court decision under Section 68 addresses when an assessee involved in accommodation entries can claim the benefit of “peak credit.” The court explains that an accommodation entry provider is someone who takes cash from an assessee and arranges cheques from his own or other paper/fake entities so the money appears to be a loan or share-capital investment, typically charging an upfront commission; where the assessee cannot prove the identity of the credit provider, the provider’s creditworthiness, and the genuineness of the transaction, the credit is treated as unexplained income under Section 68. If, however, the assessee first produces full particulars such as incorporation details, PAN, income-tax returns, bank accounts, and director details, the burden shifts to the revenue to investigate and rebut those facts, and failure by the Assessing Officer to make proper enquiry can justify deletion of additions in ordinary cases.

The key holding here is that the assessee in this case did not deny being an accommodation entry operator and accepted that he had floated or owned paper companies for that purpose, while also admitting that he could not explain the source of all deposits or the destination of all outflows in his accounts. Against that factual background, the court rejected the claim that he should automatically be taxed only on a composite peak-credit basis. The court emphasized that peak credit is an accounting-based relief that depends on a factual foundation being laid by the assessee, including ownership of all cash credits and a demonstrated linkage showing that deposits and withdrawals are squared up with the same person; the assessee must make a “clean breast” of all facts within his knowledge and explain the source of every deposit and the destination of every payment.

The judgment further notes that peak credit cannot be claimed merely by pointing to some cheque transactions and asking for a combined peak while excluding cash transactions; the assessee had argued that it was illogical to treat cheque and cash entries differently or compute separate peaks, but the court stressed that the foundational requirement is full disclosure and ownership of all credit entries. The citation specifically references the principle from Bhaiyalal Shyam Bihari v. CIT that peak-credit relief is available only where the assessee owns all cash credits in the books, and only then can the question of peak be raised. For compliance purposes, the decision is a warning that entities engaged in entry operations or routing funds through paper companies cannot rely on peak-credit theory unless they can substantiate every source and corresponding use of funds; absent that, the full unexplained amounts may be assessable under Section 68.

Ganesh DATE: October 24, 2017 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: October 25, 2017 (Date of publication) AY: - FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: Permanent Establishment (PE) under Article 5 of DTAA: Entire law on concept of “fixed place of business”, “service PE” and “agency PE” explained. The fact that there is close association and dependence between the US company and the Indian companies is irrelevant. The functions performed, assets used and risk assumed, is not a proper and appropriate test to determine whether there is a location PE (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The assessing authority decided that the assessees had a permanent establishment (hereinafter referred to as PE) as they had a fixed place where they carried on their own business in Delhi, and that, consequently, Article 5 of the India U.S. Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement of 1990 (hereinafter referred to as DTAA) was attracted. Consequently, the assessees were liable to pay tax in respect of what they earned from the aforesaid fixed place PE in India. The CIT (Appeals) dismissed the appeals of the assessees holding that Article 5 was attracted, not only because there was a fixed place where the assessees carried on their business, but also because they were “service PEs” and “agency PEs” under Article 5. In an appea
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **ADIT v. e-Funds IT Solution Inc.** held that the US parent companies were **not taxable in India on business profits** under the India–US DTAA because the Revenue failed to prove that they had a **permanent establishment (PE) in India**. The Court emphasized that the concept of PE is **not found in the Indian Income-tax Act itself**; it arises only under **Article 5 of the DTAA**, and under **Article 7(1)** a US enterprise is taxable in India only to the extent its business profits are attributable to an Indian PE. The Court identified the relevant PE tests as **fixed place PE** under Article 5(1) and 5(2)(a)–(k), **service PE** under Article 5(2)(l), and **agency PE** under Article 5(4), and stated that the **initial burden is on the Revenue** to prove that a foreign enterprise has such a PE in India.

On the facts, the lower authorities had taken different views: the Assessing Officer treated the assessees as having a **fixed place PE in Delhi**; the CIT(A) also held that they had **fixed place, service, and agency PEs**; and the ITAT agreed there was a **fixed place PE and service PE**, though it said nothing on agency PE because that argument was not pressed before it. The Delhi High Court reversed those findings, and the Supreme Court agreed, dismissing the Revenue’s appeal. The Court reiterated that for a **fixed place PE**, the key requirement is that the premises be **“at the disposal” of the foreign enterprise**—mere access to a place for performing a project is not enough, and ownership or lease is not required, but the place must be available for the enterprise’s business in a meaningful way.

A major compliance takeaway is that the Court rejected the idea that **close association, dependence, common group relationships, or outsourced support functions** between the US company and Indian affiliates automatically create a PE. It also rejected the notion that **functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed** by the Indian entities is, by itself, the correct test for determining a location PE. In short, where an Indian affiliate performs support services for a foreign group company, that alone does not establish taxable presence unless the statutory and treaty conditions for a PE are actually met.

The decision is important for multinational groups using Indian subsidiaries for back-office, IT, or support functions: the group should still assess whether any Indian premises are truly **at the disposal** of the foreign entity, whether employees or dependent agents in India satisfy the treaty’s **service PE or agency PE thresholds/conditions**, and whether any portion of profits can properly be attributed to an established PE. No new filing deadline or rate change was announced in this judgment; the ruling is instead a substantive interpretation of **Article 5 and Article 7 of the India–US DTAA** that narrows the circumstances in which foreign companies are exposed to Indian business-income taxation.

rows.summary: This Government of India order extends the deadline for filing the transitional credit declaration in **FORM GST TRAN-1** under **rule 117 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**, using the authority of **section 168 of the CGST Act, 2017** and based on the GST Council’s recommendation. The change applies to taxpayers required to submit TRAN-1 to carry forward transitional matters under the GST regime; it does not create a new filing obligation, but it **extends the existing submission period**. The new final date for filing **FORM GST TRAN-1** is **31 October 2017**. rows.summary:
This Government of India order extends the deadline for filing the transitional credit declaration in **FORM GST TRAN-1** under **rule 120A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**, which is the form used to report and transition eligible pre-GST credits into the GST regime. Acting under the authority of **section 168 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017**, the Commissioner, on the recommendation of the GST Council, has **extended the time limit for submitting FORM GST TRAN-1 until 31 October 2017**.

For compliance purposes, the key change is purely a **deadline extension**; the document does not change the substantive content of the declaration or add new eligibility rules, thresholds, or rates. It affects taxpayers/businesses required to submit TRAN-1 under the GST transition framework, and the practical obligation is to ensure the declaration is filed by the new cutoff date of **31-10-2017** rather than the earlier deadline. No other procedural amendments are stated in the order.

System based reconciliation of information furnished in FORM
                            GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 with FORM GSTR-3B - regarding

No. 349/164/2017/-GST Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Central Board of Excise and Customs GST Policy Wing New Delhi, Dated the 01 st September, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/ Commissioners of Central Tax (All) The Principal Director Generals/ Director Generals (All) Subject: System based reconciliation of information furnished in FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 with FORM GSTR-3B - regarding Sections 37, 38 and section 39 of the CGST Act, 2017(hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’) read with rules 59, 60 and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017(hereinafter referred to as ‘the Rules’) require every registered person to furnish details of outward supplies made in a month in FORM GSTR-1, details of inward supplies received in a month in FORM GSTR-2 and a return in FORM GSTR-3 by the 10 th , 15 th and 20 th of the next month respectively. Keeping in view that taxpayers may face certain issues in the initial days after the introduction of GST, the GST Council extended the date for filing of FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 for the months of July and August, 2017 and approved the filing of a simplified return in FORM GSTR-3Bfor these two months by the notified due dates after making the due payment of tax. 2. Registered persons opting to utilize transitional credit available under section 140 of the Act read with the rules made there under for discharging the tax liability for the month of July, 2017 were required to file FORM GST TRAN -1 on or before 28 th August,2017. This transitional credit was to be credited to the electronic credit ledger and be available for discharging the tax liability. 3. As per the provisions of sub-rule (5) of rule 61 of the Rules, the return in FORM GSTR-3B was required to be furnished when the due dates for filing of FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 have been extended. After the return in FORM GSTR-3B has been furnished, the process of recon
rows.summary:
This circular explains how GST returns for the initial months after GST rollout would be reconciled when the normal filing timetable was disrupted. Because the GST Council extended the due dates for FORM GSTR-1 and FORM GSTR-2 for July and August 2017, taxpayers were allowed to file the simplified interim return FORM GSTR-3B for those months by the notified due dates after paying tax, instead of filing the full return sequence on the standard schedule. It also notes that taxpayers using transitional credit under section 140 of the CGST Act for July 2017 had to file FORM GST TRAN-1 on or before 28 August 2017, and that this credit would be posted to the electronic credit ledger and used to pay tax liability.

The circular then sets out the reconciliation mechanism under rule 61 of the CGST Rules. Once FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-1 are filed, outward supplies reported in FORM GSTR-1 flow into the recipient’s auto-drafted FORM GSTR-2A, which is described as a replica of GSTR-2 containing supplier-reported details only. The recipient must use GSTR-2A to complete FORM GSTR-2 by adding, deleting, or modifying invoice-level details; adding items not present in GSTR-2A such as imports, reverse-charge inward supplies, supplies from composition taxpayers, exempt/nil-rated/non-GST inward supplies, advances paid on reverse charge supplies and related adjustments; reporting any ITC reversals required under rules 37, 39, 42, and 43; and providing HSN-wise summaries of inward supplies.

The circular also makes clear that errors or mismatches in FORM GSTR-3B are not corrected in GSTR-3B itself, but instead through the monthly GSTR-1 or GSTR-2, depending on whether the error relates to outward supplies or inward supplies/input tax credit. If outward supplies were under-reported or over-reported in GSTR-3B, the corrected figures should be reflected in GSTR-1; if inward supplies or eligible ITC were under-reported or over-reported, the correction should be made in GSTR-2. Those corrected figures then determine the revised output tax liability or eligible ITC.

After the registered person files FORM GSTR-2 by the extended due date, the common portal will auto-draft Part A of FORM GSTR-3 for that month using the information from GSTR-1 and GSTR-2. In short, the document establishes a system-based reconciliation workflow between supplier and recipient return data and the interim GSTR-3B, while assigning taxpayers the obligation to reconcile, correct, and complete the detailed return information through GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 rather than relying on GSTR-3B as the final record.

rows.title:
CGST dated 27.08.2017 is issued to clarify classification and GST
                            rate on lottery
rows.desc: Circular No.06/06/2017-CGST F. No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular dated 27 August 2017 clarifies how lottery tickets are to be treated under GST because the rate notifications showed the classification entry as “-”, which had caused confusion in return filing and tax payment. The government confirms that supply of lottery is treated as a **supply of goods** under the CGST Act, 2017, and although the return-filing process is linked to the notified tax rate rather than the tariff code, taxpayers had reported difficulties because lottery was defined as goods while the code appeared under services.

The key clarification is that, for purposes of the CGST, IGST, UTGST, and SGST rate notifications, lottery must be classified under **“Any Chapter” of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975**. This means the earlier “-” entry is to be read as covering any chapter, removing the classification mismatch. The circular also confirms that tax on lottery must be paid at the applicable notified rate, specifically **12% or 28% as the case may be**, depending on the relevant lottery category under the GST rate notifications.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that entities supplying lottery tickets must ensure their GST return filing and tax payment systems reflect this clarification so that returns can be uploaded and tax deposited on time without classification errors. The circular is effective from its issuance date, **27 August 2017**, and applies to all persons dealing with lottery supplies under the listed GST notifications.

Therefore, in exercise of powers conferred under section 168 (1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, for the purpose of uniformity in the implementation of the Act, following issues are being clarified hereunder: a. Eligibility to export under LUT: Notification No. 16/2017 – Central Tax dated 7 th July, 2017 specifies conditions to be fulfilled for export under Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in place of bond. In the extant Central Excise provisions, LUTs were limited to manufacturer exporters only. The intent of the said notification is to liberalize the facility of LUT and extend it to all kind of suppliers. It is hereby clarified that any registered person who has received a minimum foreign inward remittance of 10% of export turnover in the preceding financial year is eligible for availing the facility of LUT provided that the amount received as foreign inward remittance is not less than Page 2 of 5 Rs. one crore. This means that only such exporters are eligible to LUT facilities who have received a remittance of Rs. one crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is a higher amount, in the previous financial
rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 11 August 2017 by the Central Board of Excise and Customs under section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, clarifies how exporters may furnish a Bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT) for exports without payment of integrated tax (IGST), in response to inconsistent field interpretations of Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 7 July 2017 and earlier circulars. The key compliance change is that the LUT facility is not limited to manufacturer exporters; it is extended to any registered person, but only if the person received foreign inward remittances in the preceding financial year of at least 10% of export turnover and at least Rs. 1 crore, meaning the higher of those two thresholds must be met. The circular gives examples showing that an exporter with Rs. 15 crore prior-year export turnover needs at least Rs. 1.5 crore remittance, while an exporter with Rs. 5 crore turnover needs at least Rs. 1 crore; an exporter with Rs. 2 crore turnover and Rs. 80 lakh remittance is not eligible because the remittance is below Rs. 1 crore, and an exporter with Rs. 40 crore turnover and Rs. 2 crore remittance is also not eligible because the remittance is below 10% of turnover. Status holders under paragraphs 3.20 and 3.21 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-2020 are exempt from these eligibility thresholds and may use LUT regardless of remittance amount.

The circular also specifies the form and processing requirements: bonds must be furnished on non-judicial stamp paper, while LUTs are generally submitted on the exporter’s letterhead with the signature and seal of the person concerned or an authorized person. Because an LUT or bond is a prerequisite for export, including supplies to SEZ developers or SEZ units, tax officers are instructed to process and accept complete LUT/bond submissions within three working days from the date of filing with all required documents. This creates a procedural expectation for both taxpayers and the department and should be tracked for timely filing and escalation if approvals are delayed beyond the three-working-day window.

Two substantive clarifications restrict zero-rating treatment. First, the old Central Excise-era CT-1 form for merchant exporter purchases from manufacturers has no relevance under GST; supplies from a manufacturer to a merchant exporter remain taxable supplies under GST and are not exempt merely because the merchant exporter furnishes an LUT or bond. Zero-rating applies only to the supply by the actual exporter under LUT/bond or on payment of IGST. Second, supplies to Export Oriented Units (EOUs) are not zero-rated and there is no special dispensation for them; such supplies are taxable under GST like any other taxable supply. The circular adds that EOUs themselves remain eligible for zero rating only for their own exports, not for inward procurements.

Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters that difficulties are being faced in complying with the procedure prescribed for making exports of goods and services without payment of integrated tax with respect to furnishing of bonds/Letter of Undertaking. Therefore, in exercise of powers conferred under section 168 (1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, for the purpose of uniformity in the implementation of the Act, these issues are being clarified hereunder. 2. As per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 ( The CGST Rules), any registered person exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax is required to furnisha bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in FORM GST RFD-11. 3. Attention is invited to notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 01-07-2017vide which the category of exporters who are eligible to export under LUT has been specified along with the conditions and safeguards. All exporters, not covered by the said notification, would submit bond. The procedure for submission and acceptance of bond has already been prescribed vide circular No. 2/2/2017-GSTdated 4 th July, 2017.The bond shall be furnished on non-judicial stamp paper of the value as applicable in the State in which bond is being furnished. Page 2 of 3 4. A clarification has been soughtas to whether bond to be furnished for exports is a running bond (with debit / credit facility) or a one-time bond (separate bond for each consignment / export). It is observed consign
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the GST compliance process for exporters making exports of goods or services **without payment of integrated tax (IGST)** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**, using either a **Bond** or a **Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** in **FORM GST RFD-11**. It was issued because exporters and field offices reported difficulty complying with the earlier procedure, and the Central Board of Excise and Customs issued the instructions under **section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017** to ensure uniform implementation.

For exporters **eligible under Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 1 July 2017**, LUT may be used subject to the prescribed conditions and safeguards; **all exporters not covered by that notification must furnish a bond**. The circular confirms that the bond must be submitted on **non-judicial stamp paper of the applicable State value**, and it clarifies an important operational point: the bond is to be a **running bond**, not a separate bond for each shipment. The running bond should cover the exporter’s **estimated tax liability** on exports, and the exporter must ensure the **outstanding export tax liability remains within the bond amount**; if the existing bond amount becomes insufficient for pending exports, a **fresh bond** must be furnished.

The circular also addresses the security requirement for the bond. Although **FORM RFD-11** contemplates a **bank guarantee**, the **jurisdictional Commissioner** is given discretion to decide the amount based on the exporter’s track record. If the Commissioner is satisfied with the exporter’s track record, the bond may be accepted **without any bank guarantee**; otherwise, the bank guarantee should **normally not exceed 15% of the bond amount**. For LUTs, the circular states that an LUT will be **valid for 12 months**, and if the exporter later fails to comply with LUT conditions, the exporter can be required to furnish a bond.

On timing, the circular states that exports may continue under the **existing LUTs/Bonds only up to 31 July 2017**, and exporters must file the **revised format** of LUT/bond **by 31 July 2017**. The instructions apply to **exports on or after 1 July 2017**. In terms of filing authority, the **Bond/LUT is to be accepted by the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner** having jurisdiction over the exporter’s **principal place of business**; until the taxpayer-assignment mechanism is implemented, the exporter may file with either Central Tax or State Tax authorities, and if the State Commissioner issues a general direction, the Bond/LUT in all cases must be accepted by the **Central tax officer** until that mechanism is operational. Finally, the circular cross-references customs guidance and notes that the existing practice of **container sealing under Central Excise supervision or otherwise** would continue only until **1 September 2017**, with sealing done under the officer having physical jurisdiction over the place of business and a copy of the sealing report sent to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner.

This circular, dated 5 July 2017, designates the “proper officers” for administering GST provisions other than registration and composition under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, read with section 20 of the IGST Act and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act. In practical terms, it is an internal jurisdiction/allocation order that tells officers which rank is empowered to exercise specific statutory functions under the CGST rules and sections, so compliance actions, notices, assessments, inspections, recoveries, refunds, and related proceedings must be handled by the officer rank listed for that power.

For Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax, the assigned functions are limited to section 67(7) and the proviso to section 78. For Additional/Joint Commissioners, the circular assigns powers under sections 67(1), (2), (5), and (9); sections 71(1) and (2); the proviso to section 81; the proviso to section 129(6); and rule 139(1)–(4) and rule 140(2). For Deputy/Assistant Commissioners, the circular assigns a broad set of powers including refund-related powers under section 54(5), (6), (7), and (10); scrutiny/verification and determination powers under sections 60(1)–(3), 63, 64(1), 65(6), 74(1), (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (9), and (10), 76(2), (3), (6), and (8), 79(1), 123, 127, 129(3), 130(6) and (7), and 142(1); and numerous rule-based powers including rule 82(2), rule 86(4) and its explanation, rule 87(11) and Explanation 2, rules 90(2)-(3), 91(2)-(3), 92(1)-(5), rule 93 Explanation, rule 94, rule 96(6), rule 97(2), rule 98(2)-(5) and (7), rule 100(2), rule 101(2)-(5), rules 143-146, rule 147(1)-(3), (5)-(8), (10)-(12), (14), (15), rules 151(1)-(3), and rules 152-156. For Superintendents, the assigned powers include section 35(6), sections 61(1) and (3), 62(1), 65(7), 66(6), 67(11), 70(1), sections 73(1), (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (9), (10), rule 56(6), rule 99(1)-(3), rule 132(1), rule 142(1), (2), (3), (7), and rule 150. For Inspectors, the assigned powers are section 68(3), rule 56(17), and rule 58(5).

From a compliance standpoint, the key point is that these assignments determine which officer rank is authorized to issue or act on particular GST proceedings; if a notice, order, inspection, recovery, refund, detention, or other action is issued by an officer outside the assigned rank, the company may have grounds to question whether the action was taken by the proper officer. The circular also directs field formations to issue suitable trade notices to publicize these officer allocations, and it asks that any implementation difficulties be reported to the Board. rows.summary:
This circular addresses the practical process for exporters who want to supply goods or services **without payment of integrated tax** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. The key compliance point is that, before export, a registered person opting for export without IGST must furnish a **Bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** in **FORM GST RFD-11**. Although the rules refer to furnishing the bond/LUT to the jurisdictional Commissioner, the circular relaxes the operational process by stating that **acceptance will be done by the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner**, which is intended to reduce hardship for exporters who may be located far from the Commissioner’s office.

Because the **RFD-11 functionality was not yet available on the GST common portal** at the time, the circular permits exporters to **furnish FORM GST RFD-11 manually** to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner **in the prescribed format** until the online module becomes available. Exporters are instructed to **download FORM GST RFD-11 from the CBEC website (www.cbec.gov.in)**, complete it, and submit it manually rather than waiting for the portal-based process. This means compliance teams needed to ensure their export documentation process included the manual LUT/bond submission step and did not rely on the portal for initial implementation.

The circular applies to **all applications filed on or after 1 July 2017**. It also notes that **Circular No. 26/2017-Customs dated 1 July 2017** had already clarified that the rule 96A procedure applies to export of goods from that date. For compliance purposes, the operative requirement is that any export without payment of IGST after 1 July 2017 must be supported by a valid bond/LUT, and the submission/acceptance route is through the **jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner**, with manual filing allowed until the RFD-11 online module is live.

The circular closes by asking field offices to issue **trade notices** to publicize these instructions and invites reports of any implementation difficulties to the Board. In practical terms, this is an administrative guidance document that does not change the substantive export exemption conditions, but it does change the **filing and acceptance workflow** for LUT/bond submissions and confirms the date from which the process applies.

rows.summary:
This circular amends Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST (as earlier amended by Circular No. 169/01/2022-GST) to update how show cause notices issued by the Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI) are adjudicated when multiple noticees are involved or when related notices involve noticees whose principal places of business fall in different Central Tax Commissionerates. The change follows Notification No. 02/2022-Central Tax dated 11 March 2022, which inserted para 3A into Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax to give specified Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax all-India jurisdiction for adjudicating DGGI-issued show cause notices, and Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax dated 25 November 2024, which expanded that panel by substituting Table V in the 2017 notification. Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax took effect on 1 December 2024, and this circular is dated 4 December 2024.

The revised para 7.1 states that where DGGI issues a show cause notice either to multiple noticees with the same or different PANs, or issues multiple show cause notices on the same issue to multiple noticees having the same PAN, and those noticees’ principal places of business are located in more than one Central Tax Commissionerate, adjudication may be done by one of the Additional/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax who has all-India jurisdiction under the above notifications. The important operational point is that adjudication is permitted regardless of the amount involved in the notice(s); there is no monetary threshold for these all-India jurisdiction adjudications. Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of the specified Central Tax Commissionerates must allocate the adjudication charge for DGGI cases to one or more Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners posted in their commissionerates, and DGGI must make the notice answerable to the concerned officer accordingly.

The circular further clarifies the routing rule for selecting the adjudicating commissionerate: where the principal place of business of the noticee with the highest tax demand in the notice(s) falls within one of the listed zones/commissionerates, the corresponding Additional/Joint Commissioner shown in the table below adjudicates the matter. The mapping specified is: Ahmedabad Zone → Ahmedabad South; Vadodara Zone → Surat; Bhopal Zone → Bhopal; Nagpur Zone → Nagpur-II; Chandigarh Zone → Chandigarh; Panchkula Zone → Faridabad; Chennai Zone → Chennai South; Bengaluru Zone → Bengaluru East; Thiruvananthapuram Zone → Thiruvananthapuram; Delhi North and Delhi East Commissionerates of Delhi Zone → Delhi North; Delhi West and Delhi South Commissionerates of Delhi Zone → Delhi West; Jaipur Zone → Jaipur; Guwahati Zone → Guwahati; Hyderabad Zone → Rangareddy; and Visakhapatnam (Amaravathi) Zone → Visakhapatnam.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that DGGI notices involving multiple noticees or multi-jurisdictional PAN-linked issues must now be tracked for the location of the noticee with the highest tax demand, because that determines the adjudicating commissionerate under the all-India jurisdiction mechanism. Entities receiving such notices should expect adjudication by the designated Additional/Joint Commissioner of Central Tax in the mapped commissionerate even if the case spans multiple jurisdictions or the tax amount is large or small.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court (Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri) dealt with a writ petition by Umen Chandra Roy challenging rejection of a rectification application related to Input Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 39 of the CGST Act read with Section 16(5). The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the Court noted was within the statutory cut-off contemplated under Section 16(5), but later filed a rectification application on January 12, 2026 seeking the ITC benefit. The revenue rejected that application by order dated April 8, 2026, relying on departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024 and another circular dated October 15, 2024, on the ground that the application was not filed within the prescribed period; the judgment initially referred to that period as “six weeks,” but a later correction order dated August 21, 2026 amended this to “six months” and also corrected “communication” to “circular.”

On the merits of the legal issue, the Court held that Section 16(5) confers a substantive right to seek rectification for availing ITC, and that the statute itself does not prescribe any filing deadline for such a rectification application. Because the time limit was created only through executive circulars/notifications, the Court treated those timelines as directory guidelines rather than mandatory rules, and held they cannot override the substantive statutory entitlement under the Act. The Court further said it may, on the facts of a case and unless there is exceptional delay, use its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to extend the period prescribed by such executive instruments. As a result, the Court quashed the April 8, 2026 rejection order and directed the jurisdictional authority to reconsider the rectification application already on record, strictly in accordance with law, and to pass a reasoned order within eight weeks from communication of the judgment.

The Court did not decide whether the petitioner is actually entitled to the ITC relief on the merits, and expressly left the authority free to decide the application independently according to law. It also stated that the judgment would not create any equitable entitlement if the petitioner is ultimately found not eligible. The Court noted that no affidavits had been called for, so the allegations in the writ petition were not deemed admitted by the respondents, and the writ petition was disposed of without costs. The correction order further records that, by consent of the parties, the judgment’s references to “six weeks,” “communication,” the advocate’s name, “notification,” and “section” were corrected as stated above, and that the rest of the judgment remained unchanged.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs ECA Infrastructure India Pvt Ltd (Bombay High Court) Summary: The Bombay High Court rejected the Revenue’s appeal under Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, concerning Assessment Year 2015-16 and the allowability of a provision for major repairs made by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt Ltd. The Revenue challenged the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai order dated 8 February 2023, which had dismissed the Revenue’s appeal against the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Pune order dated 23 March 2022. The assessee was a special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis and collection of toll. For AY 2015-16, it returned a book loss of Rs.4,48,91,467/- and an income-tax loss of Rs.8,46,64,672/-. The Assessing Officer made an addition of Rs.7,47,00,000/- by disallowing the provision for major repairs. The assessee relied upon its BOT agreement with the Government of Maharashtra, under which it had a 30-year concession and was contractually required to undertake major repairs during the concession period. The first major repair was to be undertaken after seven years, i.e. during the eighth year, while the last major repair was required in the 30th year. The assessee contended that the liability accrued over the period and that the expenditure could be provided for on the basis of reliable estimates. It also relied upon CBDT Circular No. 9/2014 concerning expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT agreements. The CIT(Appeals) examined the Concession Agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38 and 39, and
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court upheld the tax deduction claimed by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. for a provision made toward major repairs on its BOT road project, rejecting the Revenue’s Section 260A appeal for AY 2015-16. The Assessing Officer had disallowed the provision and added Rs. 7,47,00,000, but the Court agreed with the CIT(A) and the Tribunal that the liability was not contingent: under the Government of Maharashtra concession agreement, the SPV had a 30-year concession period and a contractual obligation to perform major repairs, with the first such repair due in the 8th year (after seven years) and the last in the 30th year.  

For compliance/tax purposes, the key holding is that a provision for future repair expenditure can be deductible when the obligation has already arisen under the contract and the amount is estimated on a scientific and reasonable basis, even if the cash outflow happens later. The Court specifically accepted the assessee’s detailed working using quantities of bitumen, concrete, and thermoplastic compound, and the estimated major repair cost of Rs. 22,26,47,178. It also noted factual support for reasonableness from later actual spend: in FY 2019-20, the assessee incurred Rs. 17,89,48,545 toward major repairs against an opening provision of Rs. 16,19,64,943, and similar provisions in later years were not disallowed in scrutiny assessments.  

The CIT(A) had examined Articles 17, 37, 38, and 39 of the concession agreement and the project maintenance manual, finding that failure to meet maintenance and safety obligations could lead to termination and retention of corresponding amounts by the Government, which reinforced that the liability was present and enforceable rather than speculative. The assessee also relied on CBDT Circular No. 9/2014 relating to expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT agreements, and the Tribunal and High Court relied on Supreme Court authorities such as Bharat Earth Movers and Rotork Controls to confirm that a definite business liability may be deducted even before payment if it can be estimated with reasonable certainty.  

The practical takeaway is that infrastructure companies operating BOT road/toll projects should ensure that repair/maintenance provisions are tightly tied to contractual obligations, supported by detailed technical estimates and documentation, and consistent with actual maintenance patterns and prior-year treatment. The High Court found no substantial question of law and dismissed the Revenue’s appeal without costs, so the allowance stands on these facts.

The Appellant/Applicant submitted that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in APL-01 and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, stating that the Department was undertaking recovery proceedings. The Respondent-State Government drew the Bench’s attention to its submissions dated 28.07.2026 and, particularly, to APL-02, which had been rejected on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, being the First Appellate Authority. The Registry raised a defect because the GSTAT appeal had been filed before the rejection order of the First Appellate Authority came into existence. After hearing both sides and examining the records, the Bench found that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 had been filed on 19.03.2026, whereas no order under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 was then in existence because the First Appellate Authority had not yet passed its order. The central question before the Bench was whether an aggrieved person could approach GSTAT under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 in the absence of an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108. The Bench reproduced the substance of Section 112(1), under which an aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order passed unde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that a GSTAT appeal is **not maintainable if filed before the First Appellate Authority has passed an order** under Section 107 or Section 108 of the CGST Act, 2017. In this case, Pankajam Plastics filed GSTAT Filing No. **2026133/10100/0064** on **19.03.2026** in **APL-05**, while also stating that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in **APL-01** because the department had begun recovery proceedings. The Tribunal found that on **19.03.2026** no order from the First Appellate Authority existed yet; the relevant **APL-02 rejection order** from the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, was issued only later on **24.06.2026**.

The Bench applied **Section 112(1)**, which allows an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal only by a person aggrieved by an order passed under **Section 107 or Section 108**. Because the GSTAT appeal was filed before any such first-appellate order existed, the Tribunal held the filing was **not in accordance with Section 112(1)** and answered the maintainability question **against the applicant/appellant**. As a result, the appeal was **dismissed as not maintainable**. However, the Tribunal expressly granted liberty to the appellant to **file a fresh GSTAT appeal, if desired, in accordance with law**.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Finds Nil Profiteering as Cost Escalation Offsets GST ITC Benefit
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12635 Case Name DGAP Vs Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. (GSTAT) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT, National Anti-Profiteering Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DGAP Vs Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. (GSTAT) The proceedings arose from an application filed by Sh. Abhilash Mohanty alleging that M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. had failed to pass on the benefit of Input Tax Credit (ITC) to homebuyers in its “Vertex Panache” project following the introduction of GST from 01.07.2017, thereby contravening Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering referred the matter to the DGAP, which initially reported profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, comprising a base profiteered amount of Rs. 65,17,866/- and GST of Rs. 7,82,144/-, allegedly required to be passed on to 140 eligible homebuyers. The Respondent contended that substantial escalation in construction costs had materially offset the additional ITC benefit. The budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/-, whereas actual expenditure amounted to Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, resulting in an overall cost increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost. The Respondent specifically identified increases of 19.87% in Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), 62.98% in Sand and 73.17% in Bricks. Based on actual quantities consumed and costs incurred, the additional expenditure attributable to these major inputs was stated to be Rs. 3,49,87,499/-. The Respondent relied upon the Delhi High Court judgment in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, particularly paragraph 118, concerning price increases based on genuine commercial factors despite reduction in tax or availability of ITC. The Respondent also produced a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co.
rows.summary:
This GST anti-profiteering matter involved a complaint by a homebuyer in Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd.’s “Vertex Panache” project alleging that, after GST became effective on 01.07.2017, the developer failed to pass on the benefit of additional input tax credit (ITC) by reducing unit prices as required under Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee referred the matter to the DGAP, whose original investigation had found profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/- in total, made up of Rs. 65,17,866/- as base profiteered amount plus Rs. 7,82,144/- GST, said to be due to 140 eligible homebuyers.  

Vertex Homes defended the pricing by showing that construction costs had risen substantially and had more than offset the ITC benefit. It stated that budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/-, while actual expenditure was Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, an increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost, and it specifically pointed to increases of 19.87% in Ready-Mix Concrete, 62.98% in sand, and 73.17% in bricks; based on actual consumption, the additional expenditure attributable to these major inputs was Rs. 3,49,87,499/-. The company supported this with a Chartered Accountant’s certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co. LLP and relied on the Delhi High Court’s decision in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (especially paragraph 118), for the principle that genuine commercial cost increases can justify prices not falling even where tax incidence decreases.  

In its clarification dated 30.07.2026, the DGAP verified the cost-escalation claim using the CA certificate and sample invoices, accepted the additional expenditure of Rs. 3,49,87,499/-, and revised the anti-profiteering computation. The revised calculation showed total ITC-related savings of Rs. 2,47,02,175/-, but these were fully outweighed by the proven cost escalation of Rs. 3,49,87,499/-, resulting in negative net savings of Rs. 1,02,85,324/-. On that basis, the DGAP concluded that the profiteered amount was Nil.  

The Tribunal accepted the revised DGAP analysis and held that the developer had demonstrated genuine and substantial escalation in construction costs, supported by independent certification and DGAP verification, so the extra ITC benefit had been entirely offset. It found the revised methodology—subtracting proven cost escalation from ITC savings—to be legally sound, relied on the reasoning in Reckitt Benckiser, and held that M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. had not contravened Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The earlier DGAP report dated 27.08.2025, as clarified on 30.07.2026, was accepted, the anti-profiteering allegation failed, and the matter was disposed of with no profiteered amount payable to homebuyers.
