rows.summary:
This GSTAT ruling arose from an anti-profiteering complaint against M/s Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd. alleging it did not pass on the benefit of the GST rate cut on “MI LED Television 4A 80 cm” from 28% to 18%, effective 01.01.2019 under Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31.12.2018. The DGAP examined pre-rate-cut supplies from 01.11.2018 to 31.12.2018 and post-rate-cut supplies from 01.01.2019 to 31.12.2019, initially determining profiteering at ₹7,79,947, later reducing it to ₹5,58,891 after accepting credit notes worth ₹2,21,056 issued to 174 customers whose orders were cancelled or goods were returned. The key dispute was whether the remaining benefit had been validly passed on through Electronic Gift Vouchers (EGVs): the respondent showed EGVs totaling ₹5,48,650 issued to 488 customers, of which ₹3,17,965 had already been used by 291 customers and ₹2,30,685 remained in customer e-wallets, while the DGAP had objected that the vouchers were allegedly conditional, time-bound, and masked under the system label “Offers and cash back.”  

The Tribunal held that activated EGVs credited to customer wallets without expiry and usable across the platform were a valid and direct transfer of GST benefit under Section 171 of the CGST Act, because they represented monetary value standing to the customer’s credit and were not restricted to a particular product or category. It also held that the system-generated description “Offers and cashback” did not matter because the credits were traceable to specific orders, invoices, dates, prices, and the incremental amount attributable to the GST reduction; in other words, substance controlled over nomenclature. The Tribunal distinguished the Delhi High Court’s Reckitt Benckiser decision and rejected the argument that only a cash refund or a festival-style discount would satisfy anti-profiteering requirements.  

On the final reconciliation, the Tribunal found the respondent had substantially complied but could not account for a residual difference of ₹10,241 between the DGAP’s revised profiteering figure of ₹5,58,891 and the EGVs issued of ₹5,48,650. Because that amount could not be linked to any identifiable customer or invoice, the Tribunal directed it to be deposited into the Central Consumer Welfare Fund. It also ordered interest at 18% under Rule 133(3)(c) of the CGST Rules from the date the higher amount was collected until the date of deposit. For compliance purposes, the decision confirms that documented, unconditional, and traceable EGV credits can be accepted as valid pass-through of GST rate-reduction benefits, but any unreconciled balance must be deposited with statutory interest.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the restriction of input tax credit under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act on works contract services, goods and services used for constructing immovable property, and the statutory exceptions for plant and machinery and construction not undertaken on a taxable person’s own account. It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. Table of Contents▸ Background: Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Comments: What is immovable property? Movable vs immovable property test-various judgements The principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Bharti Airtel Limited v The Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune Eligibility to Input tax credit and immovable property under GST Way ahead and conclusion Possible issues when there is a Single contract for construction of building and supply of machineries, other moveable goods: ACTION POINTS FOR ITC OPTIMISATION: Show all 10 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background: It is being observed that the assesses are receiving notices requiring to reverse/pay back ITC availed pertaining to newly constructed building projects used for business operations[such as factory premise/warehouses], alleging such credit is restricted being of nature of “immovable property”. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of
rows.summary:
This article explains that, although a taxpayer may otherwise satisfy the general input tax credit conditions under Section 16 of the CGST Act, Section 17(5) overrides those rules and blocks ITC for certain construction-related expenditures even when they are used in the course or furtherance of business. In particular, Section 17(5)(c) denies credit on works contract services used for construction of an immovable property other than plant and machinery, with “construction” expressly covering reconstruction, renovation, additions, alterations, or repairs to the extent those costs are capitalized to the immovable property. It also defines works contract service as a material-plus-labour contract for building, construction, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, renovation, or alteration of immovable property involving transfer of property in goods during execution, and defines plant and machinery as apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support and used for making outward supplies, while excluding land, buildings or other civil structures, telecommunication towers, and pipelines laid outside factory premises.

The article notes two key exceptions to the Section 17(5)(c) block: ITC is available where the works contract service is received for construction of “plant and machinery” as defined in the Act, and where the works contract service is itself an input service for the further supply of works contract service. The example given is a developer constructing mall units for onward sale during construction, where credit may be available to the extent attributable to units sold during the construction period. For Section 17(5)(d), the article states that credit is blocked on goods or services used by a taxable person for construction of an immovable property other than plant and machinery on the taxpayer’s own account, including where the property is used in business, if the cost is capitalized.

A specific statutory change is highlighted: the phrase in Section 17(5)(d) was replaced from “plant or machinery” to “plant and machinery” with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017 through Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17.09.2025. The article also emphasizes that “immovable property” is interpreted using the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act, and judicial tests focusing on the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency, and marketability of annexation, which is important because the ITC outcome depends on whether an installation is viewed as immovable or movable.

For compliance purposes, the document warns that businesses are receiving notices requiring reversal or repayment of ITC claimed on newly constructed factory premises, warehouses, and similar business facilities on the ground that the credit relates to immovable property. It specifically discusses installations such as electrical fittings, cabling, sewage treatment plants, security systems, fire-fighting systems, HVAC systems, and machinery, noting that some of these may qualify as movable equipment or plant and machinery depending on the facts and legal tests. The practical recommendation is to structure projects with separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods to reduce the risk that eligible credit is denied because the entire project is characterized as immovable property.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. Table of Contents▸ Background of the Case What the Company Argued What the Department Argued What the Supreme Court Held Key Takeaways for Practitioners Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background of the Case This case deals with a Show Cause Notice (SCN) iss
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended five-year limitation under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by using the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts” in a generic or conclusory way. In this case, the department issued an SCN on 13.06.2025 against a Ratlam-based infrastructure company for FY 2018–19, proposing a demand of Rs. 1,52,56,431 under Section 74 of the CGST/MPGST regime, even though the company argued that the normal Section 73 limitation had already expired on 28.02.2025. The Supreme Court agreed that if the department wants to proceed beyond the ordinary limitation period, the notice itself must set out the foundational facts showing how fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression was committed and how it was detected; a bare reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” is not enough. The Court also noted that the SCN’s use of the word “or” between fraud and concealment reflected uncertainty about the actual basis of the allegation, which further undermined the notice.

The Court refused to let the department cure these defects through explanations first provided later in its counter affidavit, reaffirming that the legal validity of a notice must be judged from the notice itself and that jurisdictional defects cannot be repaired after the fact in litigation. As a result, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order and quashed the SCN, and it restrained the department from proceeding further on that notice. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where a GST notice seeks to apply Section 74 rather than Section 73, the notice must contain concrete factual allegations and reasoning supporting fraud/suppression; a vague or mechanical invocation of Section 74 is vulnerable to challenge, especially where the ordinary limitation period has already run.

The vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018. The E-Way Bill was not available with the driver at the time of interception. Tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- were imposed under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017. The first appellate authority, however, set aside the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018. The Department contended that transportation without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that subsequent production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns and proof of tax payment could not retrospectively cure the statutory violation. It further argued that the interception of the vehicle, nature of the goods, route and subsequent production of documents cumulatively indicated an intention to evade tax. The authorised representative also submitted that an E-Way
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench, held that movement of goods without an E-Way Bill can justify detention and penalty under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 where the surrounding facts indicate an intention to evade tax. The dispute arose from transport of 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly, under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the driver did not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception. On that basis, the Proper Officer imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3), but the first appellate authority later set aside both amounts by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018.

The Department argued that the missing E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that later production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment did not undo the statutory breach. It further argued that the combination of interception, the nature of the goods, the route, and the later production of documents showed intent to evade tax; the representative also emphasized that an E-Way Bill is generated online while invoices are manually issued, creating scope for later manipulation if the bill is not produced at the time of movement. No one appeared for the respondent before the Tribunal despite opportunity. The Tribunal reviewed the precedents cited by the first appellate authority—Sarva Shri Singh Tire, Shri KL Industries, Harley Foods Products, M/s Modern Traders, and M/s Rai Prexim India—and distinguished them on the facts.

The Tribunal specifically found that non-generation/non-production of the E-Way Bill was not a mere technical lapse in this case, because the goods were being moved from Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh to Kichha, Uttarakhand, a short distance of about 25 km, and the absence of the E-Way Bill, coupled with the interception and the nature of the goods, supported an inference of evasion. It also relied on its own later order dated 20.08.2026 in Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026, Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, involving the same kind of goods, the same destination, and a similar pattern where the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception, treating the repetition as significant. On that reasoning, the Tribunal held that the first appellate authority wrongly interfered with the Section 129(3) detention order.

As a result, the Department’s appeal was allowed, the first appellate authority’s order dated 24.09.2021 was set aside, and the original order dated 09.03.2018 imposing tax and penalty was restored. For compliance purposes, the decision underscores that transport of goods without a valid E-Way Bill can lead to full Section 129(3) tax and penalty exposure even where invoices, returns, and tax payment records are later produced, if the facts suggest possible tax evasion.

The appellants were issued show cause notices alleging short-payment of service tax under Commercial or Industrial Construction Services. After 1.6.2007, though they discharged service tax under works contract services under the composition scheme, for three of their four projects namely Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, Surya Skanda, the department was of the view that such payment is not proper for the reason that the services cannot be classified as Works Contract Service and also because appellants have not exercised their opt
rows.summary:
This Tribunal order addresses three appeals by real estate developers in Chennai/Coimbatore who were taxed by the department on amounts received for construction of residential and commercial projects. The core dispute was whether their activities should be treated as taxable construction/commercial construction services under the pre-1.6.2007 regime, or as “works contract” services after 1.6.2007; the department also argued that the appellants could not use the works contract composition scheme because they had not separately intimated their option to the department as required by the Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service Tax) Rules, 2007. For Real Value Promoters Pvt. Ltd., two show cause notices covered the period 1.4.2007 to 31.3.2008 and alleged short-payment of service tax totaling Rs. 2,06,20,252, broken down among projects for amounts received from buyers and landowners: PRGT commercial project Rs. 34,38,337, residential projects The Lords/Sananda Brindavan/Sujeet/Surya Skanda Rs. 1,07,33,392, PRGT Amarasri Rs. 48,98,579, and Sai Brindavan Rs. 15,49,944; the notices also proposed interest and penalties under sections 76 and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994. A separate notice dated 20.10.2009 for the period 1.4.2008 to 31.3.2008 proposed an additional Rs. 1,05,99,978 on PRGT, again on the theory that amounts received for apartment/commercial complex construction were taxable under section 65(105)(zzzh) or section 65(105)(zzq). The common adjudication order dated 16.8.2010 confirmed the full demands with interest, imposed a penalty equal to the tax demand of Rs. 2,06,20,252 under section 78, and also imposed penalties under sections 76 and 77; these findings were appealed.

The third appeal, by Prime Developers, involved a joint development agreement dated 17.1.2005 with Prime Textiles Ltd. for construction of a residential complex of 432 apartments, with units sold under separate agreements to end buyers. A notice dated 10.8.2009 for January 2005 to August 2008 proposed service tax under Construction of Complex Service, and the original authority confirmed Rs. 1,16,42,448, holding that for the period before 1.6.2007 the appellant was liable under construction of complex service rather than any works contract treatment. Overall, the compliance issue raised by the case is that the department treated these developers’ agreements with buyers and landowners as separately taxable construction services, challenged their post-1.6.2007 reclassification as works contracts, and enforced not only tax and interest but also substantial penalties where no composition-option intimation was filed.

rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in Case Crime No. 539 of 2025, arising from allegations of GST fraud linked to a purportedly non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries. The prosecution case was registered under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut. The applicant argued that he was not named in the FIR, had no connection with the alleged fraud, was not the owner of the firm, and was not a beneficiary; his name allegedly emerged only from the statement of Sakeel Khan. He also pointed out that the firm had already been declared bogus in November 2021, while the FIR was lodged much later, on 04.11.2025, and that he had been in jail since 05.04.2026 with no other criminal history.  

After considering the record, allegations, and submissions of both the State/GST Department and the defense, the Court held that the applicant was entitled to bail during the pendency of trial, without expressing any opinion on the merits. The Court ordered release on execution of a personal bond and furnishing two sureties of like amount, subject to standard anti-tampering and non-interference conditions: he must not tamper with evidence, intimidate or pressurize prosecution witnesses, commit any similar offence, or make inducements/threats/promises to persons acquainted with the facts of the case to prevent disclosure to the Court or police. He must appear before the trial court on all dates fixed unless exempted, and the trial court was directed to verify the identity, status, and residence proof of the sureties before accepting them. The Court also stated that any breach of conditions would allow the trial court to cancel bail, and that the order’s observations are limited to the bail issue and will not affect the merits of the trial.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Holds Municipal Hoarding Space Taxable, But Quashes Extended-Period Service Tax Demand
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12629 Case Name Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi considered whether a municipality was liable to service tax on two activities: providing space for display of advertisements through hoardings and renting/licensing its immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons and traders. The disputed period was 2009-10 to 2014-15, covering both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The appellant had received Rs. 3,06,738/- from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974/- as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. On advertisement receipts, the appellant maintained that it merely collected statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than selling advertisin
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Delhi held that a municipality’s activities relating to hoarding space and certain immovable-property rentals could fall within service tax, but it materially limited the Department’s recovery by quashing the extended-period demand. For the period **before 1 July 2012**, the Tribunal found that granting space for hoardings was taxable under **section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994** as “sale of space or time for advertisement,” because the statutory explanation expressly covered providing space for display, advertising, or showcasing products/services on billboards and public places. It therefore upheld taxability on the hoarding receipts of **Rs. 3,06,738** received from **April 2009 to June 2012**.

On the property-rental issue, the Tribunal rejected the municipality’s argument that the phrase **“any other person”** in the renting provision excluded the owner from being the service provider, and it also rejected the claim that **vacant land** used for market places was outside the taxable definition. For the **pre-1 July 2012** regime, it held under **sections 65(90a) and 65(105)(zzzz)** that the land/property was being put to **commercial use**, so rent/license income from those immovable properties was taxable. The Tribunal also noted the municipality’s contention that some arrears had been taxed at an incorrect rate, though the summary outcome is that the activity was still held taxable.

For the period **from 1 July 2012 onward**, the Tribunal applied the negative-list regime under **section 65B(44)** and **section 66D** and held that the municipality’s renting/licensing of immovable property, including vacant land used for **“Flee Markets,”** remained taxable because it was provided **for consideration to traders/business entities** and was a commercial activity rather than a sovereign/statutory function. The Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court’s distinction in **Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, New Mandi Yard, Alwar** between mandatory governmental functions and activities undertaken for consideration, and concluded that the municipality’s conduct fell on the taxable side of that line.

The Department had demanded **Rs. 39,22,945** in service tax, along with **interest, penalties, and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns**, for the dispute period **2009-10 to 2014-15**. The Tribunal upheld taxability on the substantive activities, but on limitation it found no evidence of a **positive act of suppression with intent to evade tax**, emphasizing that mere non-payment or non-declaration is not enough to invoke the **extended limitation period**. As a result, the **extended-period demand was set aside**, the demand was sustained only for the **normal period**, and the penalty was **reduced proportionately**; the appeal was therefore **partly allowed**.

The background was that in an earlier writ petition (W.P. No. 1242 of 2026), the Court had on 09.02.2026 directed the petitioner to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and to respond to the section 148 notice; the petitioner stated that she complied in part by depositing Rs. 5 lakhs, but could not upload the return because of technical problems on the income-tax e-filing portal. In support, she produced proof of the Rs. 5 lakh deposit, other documents she had filed, and a screenshot showing the portal upload failure.

The Court accepted that the portal issue prevented compliance and held that, in the interests of justice, the petitioner should be given an opportunity to file the return. It therefore set aside the impugned demand notice dated 16.07.2026 and directed the Revenue to take necessary steps to provide access to the income-tax portal so the petitioner could upload the return for AY 2015-16. The petitioner was directed to file the return within three weeks from receipt of the order, and the Assessing Officer/Rsvenue was directed to complete the assessment by issuing an assessment order within six weeks from receipt of the return, after giving the petitioner a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The connected miscellaneous petitions were closed, and there was no order as to costs.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the Court treated documented technical inability to upload a return on the tax portal as a valid basis to preserve filing rights and require the department to facilitate portal access, rather than enforce the demand notice immediately. The decision reinforces that where a taxpayer can substantiate attempted compliance—here via a screenshot and proof of partial compliance such as the Rs. 5 lakh deposit—the authorities may be compelled to reopen the practical ability to file and must then proceed quickly with assessment within the court-imposed timelines.

Chessman Impex Private Limited Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017, holding that the customs duty demand of Rs.2,16,93,068/- against Chessman Impex Pvt. Ltd., consequential interest, penalties of Rs.20 lakh each under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 and penalties imposed on the co-appellants could not be sustained in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence. Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 permitting duty-free import of 5350 MTs of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against export obligation of 5000 MTs of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue alleged that the imported scrap was diverted in the domestic market and maize was fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the stipulated steel products. The Tribunal found material support for the appellant’s case in the special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realisation of export proceeds and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. Significantly, the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report recording that the available evidence indicated that
rows.summary:
CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017 in full. The Customs demand of Rs. 2,16,93,068, along with consequential interest, and the penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each imposed on Chessman Impex under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties imposed on the co-noticees, were all quashed because the Tribunal found the Revenue’s case was not supported by reliable, corroborative evidence.

The underlying allegation was that Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 allowing duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods, but instead diverted the imported goods into the domestic market and fraudulently exported maize to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export. The Tribunal rejected this theory, emphasizing that the record actually contained supporting material for the appellant: special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification on AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai confirmation that the goods were manufactured by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realization of export proceeds, and an Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority.

A particularly important point for compliance purposes is that the CBI had already investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report stating that the available evidence indicated the exports to Bangladesh had actually taken place, and that report had been accepted by the criminal court. The Tribunal noted that the adjudicating authority did not produce any additional material beyond what CBI had already considered, and also failed to show independent evidence such as identified domestic buyers of the allegedly diverted material, a cash trail, procurement or transport evidence for maize, seizure of offending goods, or proof of domestic disposal. The Tribunal held that suspicion, inconsistencies, or “grey areas” cannot replace the cogent evidence required for penal action under Sections 112 and 114 of the Customs Act.

The Tribunal also held that the adjudicating authority had gone beyond the Show Cause Notice by introducing new issues, including the classification of CTD bars, availability of 16 mm bars, and amendment of the DEEC licence, which could not be used to sustain the demand. It found material discrepancies in the statements relied on by Revenue, noted that some had been retracted, and observed that statements recorded under Section 108 were relied upon without proper compliance with Section 138B. Since the allegations against the principal noticee failed, the related allegations of connivance or abetment against the co-appellants also failed, and all appeals were allowed with consequential relief.

rows.title: Custom Duty | SC Sets Aside ₹425 Crore Customs Penalty Due to Fake AI-Generated Case Laws
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12622 Case Name Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya Vs Union of India & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya Vs Union of India & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court of India set aside a customs penalty order because the adjudicating officer had relied on case law and articles that the Court found were either fabricated, had fake citations, or were misrepresented as supporting propositions they did not actually contain. The underlying Order-in-Original dated 8 October 2025, issued by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat, had imposed a penalty of ₹425,27,99,100 under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962 on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya for allegedly misdeclaring a consignment of natural diamonds as lab-grown diamonds to obtain a lower tariff. The Gujarat High Court had already dismissed the appellant’s challenge on 20 January 2026, but the Supreme Court interfered without deciding the substantive customs issue because the adjudication itself was tainted by suspected AI-generated “hallucinated” material.

The Court independently checked the authorities cited in the customs order and concluded that the second respondent had relied on nonexistent or false precedents, and on some actual cases that did not stand for the legal rules attributed to them. The Court treated this as a serious integrity problem in adjudication and expressly relied on its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., which adopts a zero-tolerance approach toward producing, citing, or relying on artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. It reiterated that AI may be used only as an assistive tool and not as a substitute for judicial or quasi-judicial decision-making, using the analogy that AI may be “training wheels” but cannot occupy the “pilot’s seat.”

As a result, the Supreme Court set aside both the Gujarat High Court’s order and the Order-in-Original dated 8 October 2025, revived the proceedings before the customs authority for fresh adjudication, and required that the matter be heard by an officer of the same rank other than the officer who issued the original order. The civil appeal was allowed, pending applications were disposed of, and the Court left it to the appointing authority to decide whether to take any action against the author of the original order in accordance with law. The judgment also notes that the Supreme Court had recently released draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026 and invited comments, signaling that while AI may be used in courts in a supportive role, unverified AI-derived legal material is unacceptable and can invalidate a decision.

In W.P.No.20655 of 2024, the petitioner challenged the impugned order/reply dated 29.05.2024 relating to the tax period 2019-2020. In W.P.No.20652 of 2024, the petitioner challenged Notification No.9 of 2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the consequential Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the respective GST enactments extending the period of limitation. TaxGuru has separately published the text and details of Notification No. 09/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023. rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three connected writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited concerning GST matters for the tax period 2019–2020. One petition challenged a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 dated 31.05.2024, another challenged an order/reply dated 29.05.2024, and the third challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the related State/Government orders issued under Section 168A of the GST laws that extended limitation periods. The limitation-extension issue was the key compliance point in the case, but the Court did not rule on the substantive validity of that notification or on the underlying tax dispute.

At admission, the Court had granted interim protection on 13.08.2024. After that, the jurisdictional State Tax Officer submitted a detailed report dated 27.01.2026, and the Court recorded that the report’s conclusion prima facie supported the petitioner’s position. Based on that report and the subsequent developments, the petitioner stated that no further adjudication was necessary for the DRC-01 challenge, and the Court accepted that position.

As a result, the Court held that the challenge in W.P. No. 20657 of 2024 no longer required adjudication, and the challenges in W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 had become academic. The Court therefore closed W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 and disposed of W.P. No. 20657 of 2024. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is procedural rather than substantive: this order does not create a new GST rule or invalidate the limitation-extension notifications on the merits, but it shows that limitation-related GST challenges can be rendered moot by later departmental developments and officer reports. Entities facing GST notices for older tax periods, especially where limitation extension under Section 168A and Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax is involved, should note the dates involved here—31.03.2023 for the notification, 29.05.2024 for the order/reply, 31.05.2024 for the DRC-01, 13.08.2024 for interim protection, and 27.01.2026 for the officer’s report—because the court treated those later developments as decisive in closing the litigation.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rajasthan HC Allows Delayed GST Appeal Citing Medical Reasons Beyond Taxpayer’s Control
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12616 Case Name Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd and set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026, which had rejected the petitioner’s GST appeal on limitation. The Court directed the Appellate Authority to consider and decide the appeal on its own merits, subject to the petitioner firm depositing late fees, penalty and other statutory deposits as admissible. The petitioner had sought quashing of the order dated 07.02.2024 and restoration of its GST registration, besides setting aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026 and a direction for adjudication of the appeal on merits. The petitioner relied principally on the Rajasthan High Court’s Division Bench judgment in M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided on 28.07.2026. In that case, the Court had condoned a 99-day delay after granting relaxation of 120 days under Section 107 of the CGST Act and directed the Appellate Authority to entertain the appeal and adjudicate it on merits if filed within 30 days. The petitioner also relied upon M/s. Molana Construction Company Vs. Central Goods and Service Tax Department & Ors., Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, Central Goods and Services Tax Department & Ors., and the two decisions in RPC PSIPL JV Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors. The petitioner additionally referred to M/s. Kakar Automobiles Vs. Union of India & Ors. The respondents relied upon S
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST appeal should not be rejected solely as time-barred where the delay was caused by medical circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control. In this case, Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. challenged the rejection of its GST appeal by the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, and also sought quashing of the underlying order dated 07.02.2024 as well as restoration of its GST registration. The Court set aside the appellate authority’s limitation-based rejection and directed that the appeal be entertained and decided on its merits in accordance with law.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Court recognized that although appellate authorities remain bound by the limitation rules under Section 107 of the Rajasthan/CGST GST framework, writ jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 may be used in exceptional cases where strict adherence to limitation would cause grave prejudice and the delay arose from reasons outside the taxpayer’s control. The judgment relied on prior Rajasthan High Court cases, especially M/s. Pratap Power Spares, where a 99-day delay was condoned after the Court granted relaxation of the 120-day statutory appeal window under Section 107 and directed the appeal to be heard if filed within 30 days. The Court also referred to other decisions supporting delayed GST appeals in exceptional circumstances, while acknowledging the general rule that writ jurisdiction should not be used to bypass statutory limitation.

The relief was not unconditional: the Court made it subject to the petitioner depositing the late fee, penalty, and other statutory amounts required for entertaining the appeal, “as admissible.” The appellate authority must now consider the appeal on merits rather than refuse it on limitation alone. All pending applications were disposed of. From a compliance perspective, this decision underscores that delayed GST appeals may still be pursued where there is documented, compelling hardship such as medical incapacity, but the taxpayer should expect to satisfy all statutory deposit requirements and should not assume that ordinary limitation deadlines will be excused absent exceptional facts.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rule 86A Safeguards Mandatory for ITC Blocking: Rajasthan HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12615 Case Name Jagdish Prasad Agrawal Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Jagdish Prasad Agrawal Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The petitioner, M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, approached the Rajasthan High Court under Article 226 challenging the blocking of Input Tax Credit (ITC) in its Electronic Credit Ledger. The reliefs sought included a declaration that the blocking of IGST ITC with negative balance was illegal, inoperative and void, a direction to re-credit the Electronic Credit Ledger for any ITC unlawfully set off against the impugned demand, and other appropriate relief. At the hearing, the petitioner submitted that the blocking had already ceased to operate by operation of the statute on expiry of one year and that the Electronic Credit Ledger had consequently been reactivated with the credit. The surviving issue, according to the petitioner, was whether the respondents could have blocked the ITC without complying with the mandatory requirements of Rule 86A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017. The respondents fairly conceded that the Electronic Credit Ledger was operational, but were unable to demonstrate compliance with Rule 86A before the ITC was blocked. In response to the Court’s query as to why the Rule had not been complied with, the respondents submitted that it was a bona fide mistake. They further acknowledged that, although the concerned authority had reasons for taking the action, no proper and reasoned order had been passed and no opportunity of hearing had been afforded to the petitioner before the blocking. The respondents undertook that any future blocking would be
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition by M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, challenging the blocking of Input Tax Credit (ITC) in its Electronic Credit Ledger, specifically an IGST ITC block shown with a negative balance. The petitioner asked for the blocking action to be declared illegal, inoperative, and void, for the ledger to be re-credited with any ITC that had been wrongly set off against the disputed demand, and for other appropriate relief. By the time of hearing, the blocking had already automatically ceased to operate because the statutory one-year period had expired, and the Electronic Credit Ledger had been reactivated; as a result, the live dispute narrowed to whether the ITC could have been blocked at all without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017.

The respondents conceded that the ledger was operational again, but they could not show that the mandatory preconditions under Rule 86A had been satisfied before the block was imposed. The Court noted that Rule 86A requires the competent authority to have “reasons to believe” that ITC was fraudulently availed or was ineligible, and then, for reasons recorded in writing, to disallow debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for payment of tax liability under section 49 or for refund of unutilised credit; the Court also specifically referred to Rule 86A(1)(d). The respondents admitted the omission was a bona fide mistake, acknowledged that no proper reasoned order had been passed, and conceded that the petitioner had not been given an opportunity of hearing before the blocking. They undertook that any future blocking would be done only by the competent authority through a proper, reasoned order and strictly in accordance with Rule 86A, and an unconditional apology was tendered on behalf of the concerned officer.

Although the Court found on the record that the mandatory requirements of Rule 86A had not been complied with, it treated the matter as exceptional because the restriction had already lapsed and the ledger had been restored. The writ petition was therefore disposed of rather than decided on broader merits, and pending applications were also disposed of. Importantly for compliance purposes, the Court issued a clear warning that if the respondents in future block ITC without due compliance with Rule 86A, they may be liable to pay appropriate compensation to the aggrieved party. The practical compliance takeaway is that any ITC-blocking action under Rule 86A must be supported by recorded reasons, based on the statutory “reasons to believe” standard, and carried out by the proper authority with a reasoned order; otherwise, the action risks being treated as non-compliant and exposing the department to compensation claims.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Allows CENVAT Refund Where Credit Was Not Challenged Under Rule 14
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12614 Case Name Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd Vs Commissioner of Central Goods & Service Tax (CESTAT Chandigarh) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Chandigarh Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd Vs Commissioner of Central Goods & Service Tax (CESTAT Chandigarh) Summary: The Chandigarh Bench of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of M/s Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The appellant was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas entities under specific service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Refund of ₹78,79,939 was rejected in respect of General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the ground that the services lacked nexus with exported output services. Before the Tribunal, the appellant contended that availment of CENVAT credit, its utilisation and its refund were distinct aspects and that, where the Department had not challenged availment under Rule 14, refund could not subsequently be denied under Rule 5 by questioning the credit’s eligibility. It further submitted that the disputed services fell within the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l), relying on numerous judicial decisions, and that direct nexus with the final output services was not n
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh held that M/s Agilent Technologies International Pvt. Ltd., a 100% export-oriented service provider, was entitled to refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The company provided Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas clients under service agreements and exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. The specific refund claim rejected by the department was ₹78,79,939, and the rejection related only to credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services on the theory that those services lacked nexus with the exported output services.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that where the Department has not first challenged the availment of CENVAT credit under Rule 14, it cannot later deny refund of the accumulated credit under Rule 5 by questioning whether the credit was eligible in the first place. The Tribunal treated availment, utilisation, and refund of credit as distinct issues and relied on prior case law to conclude that refund proceedings are not the proper stage to re-litigate the underlying eligibility of credit that was never put in dispute under Rule 14. It also reaffirmed that, during the relevant period, the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l) was broad/exhaustive enough to cover General Insurance Service, Commercial or Industrial Construction Service, and Works Contract Service, and that a strict direct nexus with the exported output service was not required.

The Tribunal specifically relied on Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and the decision in Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd. for the proposition that direct one-to-one linkage between each input service and the exported output service is not necessary for refund eligibility. Accordingly, the impugned order rejecting the refund was set aside and the appeal was allowed with consequential relief, if any, as per law. The practical compliance takeaway is that exporters claiming Rule 5 refunds should ensure credits are properly availed and documented as input services, but if the department intends to dispute eligibility, it should do so at the credit-availment stage under Rule 14; otherwise, a later refund denial on nexus grounds is vulnerable.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Hyderabad Sets Aside Tax on Pharma Regulatory Approval Support Services
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12613 Case Name Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020,
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad allowed Aurobindo Pharma Ltd.’s appeal and set aside service tax, interest, and penalties confirmed by the Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 for the periods 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The dispute involved two categories of alleged taxability: first, deductions made by foreign/intermediary banks from export remittances received by the company from overseas buyers; and second, payments to overseas/regulatory consultancy vendors M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban for preparing clinical/non-clinical overviews and regulatory documents to obtain foreign pharmaceutical product approvals. For the bank charges, the Tribunal held that Aurobindo was not the recipient of “Banking and Other Financial Services” merely because the banks’ fees reduced the net remittance amount; there was no evidence of any contract, engagement, or obligation by Aurobindo to pay those foreign banks, so reverse charge liability did not arise.

For the regulatory documentation work, the Tribunal rejected Revenue’s attempt to classify the services as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.” It found that the consultants were mainly compiling existing data, published materials, and dossier/form submissions for regulatory filings, not performing independent scientific research, experimentation, technical studies, or giving advice in a scientific discipline. The Tribunal emphasized that classification must be based on the actual nature of the work performed, not simply on the scientific/technical background of the personnel doing it, and held that services rendered to obtain overseas registrations/permissions do not become scientific or technical consultancy just because they relate to regulated pharma approvals. It also relied on Aurobindo’s own earlier favorable order (Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020) and on the IPCA Laboratories line of cases, noting that no material change in facts or service nature had been shown.

A further point important for compliance is that Aurobindo had already discharged service tax on these consultancy payments under “Management or Business Consultant Service,” and the Department had appropriated that amount in the impugned order while simultaneously reclassifying the same services under another taxable head; once the reclassification failed, the demand could not stand. Because the underlying tax demands were set aside, the related interest and penalties were also cancelled. The Tribunal did not separately decide the appellant’s argument about penalty computation under Section 76 of the Finance Act, 1994, in light of the amendment effective 08.04.2011, because that issue became moot after the substantive liabilities were deleted. For compliance teams, the case reinforces that export-remittance bank deductions are not automatically reverse-charge taxable absent a direct service relationship, and that pharma regulatory dossier preparation/compilation for foreign approvals is not, by itself, scientific or technical consultancy.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Mumbai Deletes Section 112(a) Penalty on Customs Hawaldar for Lack of Proof
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12612 Case Name Ranjita Rajendra Bane Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ranjita Rajendra Bane Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Mumbai) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai considered the appeal filed by Ranjita Rajendra Bane, widow and successor in interest of deceased Rajendra Bane, challenging personal penalties of ₹2,50,000/- and ₹1,00,000/- imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. Rajendra Bane had been serving as a Customs Hawaldar. The penalties arose from an investigation into smuggled gold recovered from the gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport after passengers travelled from Dubai by Spice Jet Flight No. SG 52 on 16.08.2018. The allegation was that although Rajendra Bane was on sanctioned leave and staying at his native place near Ratnagiri, he had facilitated the smuggling of gold and assisted the smugglers. The material relied upon against him included statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962, particularly statements of co-accused/accomplices, call records received from the telephone operator, and recovery of gold from the airport toilet and from a passenger. The defence completely denied involvement. It admitted that Rajendra Bane was on leave and at his native place on the relevant day, but contended that the seizure had actually followed information transmitted by him to the Superintendent on duty at Pune International Airport. The defence claimed that the information involved privileged communication with an informer and therefore its source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected this explanation. He considered the statement
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai deleted the personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 on the deceased Customs Hawaldar, Rajendra Bane, whose widow carried the appeal. The penalties had been imposed on the theory that he had aided a gold-smuggling operation connected to passengers arriving from Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52 on 16.08.2018, but the Tribunal found that the Department had not established his involvement with reliable evidence. In particular, the Tribunal held that he could not be implicated solely on the basis of co-accused/accomplice statements recorded under Section 108, especially where nothing incriminating—including the allegedly relevant SIM card—had been seized from him, and the factual context differed from the Supreme Court decision in Naresh J. Sukhwani on which the Commissioner (Appeals) had relied.

The Tribunal gave significant weight to the call evidence and the sequence of events around the seizure at about 05:15 A.M. It noted that the Superintendent, Shri D.G. Nandanwar, had called Rajendra Bane back and was told that gold brought on the SpiceJet flight had been dumped in the gent’s lavatory of the Immigration Hall, and it also examined the call detail record showing multiple calls between 03:04:03 A.M. and 05:33 A.M. from the mobile number of Rajendra Bane’s son, Prathmesh Rajendra Bane. The Tribunal found it material that the CDR shown to the Superintendent for the 5 A.M. to 6 A.M. period did not reflect that number, and it treated this as supporting the view that the Department’s theory of prior intelligence/connivance was not proved.

The Department’s case was that Rajendra Bane, while on sanctioned leave at his native place near Ratnagiri, had facilitated the smuggling and later tried to camouflage his role by making a phone call to the Superintendent; the Tribunal rejected that as unproven. It also rejected the adverse inference drawn by the Commissioner (Appeals) from the fact that Rajendra Bane allegedly did not contact another officer after the Superintendent did not answer the first call. On the Tribunal’s assessment, the surrounding circumstances were more consistent with Rajendra Bane acting as an informer whose tip led to recovery of more than 13 kg of smuggled gold, including 10 kg placed in the dustbin of the gent’s toilet, rather than as a participant in the smuggling.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that Section 112(a) personal penalty cannot be sustained on conjecture, accomplice statements alone, or inferred involvement where there is no direct incriminating seizure from the person concerned and the call/electronic evidence does not clearly establish participation. The case also shows that authorities must reconcile call detail records and other documentary evidence with the alleged timeline of interception before treating a call to customs officers as an “afterthought” or using silence/failure to contact another officer as proof of culpability.

rows.summary:
The Patna High Court did **not** finally decide whether Nukkad Natak services are exempt from GST; instead, it sent the issue back to the appellate authority for a merits decision. The petitioner, **M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal**, is a **GST-registered entity** that performs **Nukkad Natak (street plays)** for government public-awareness programmes, and the tax dispute arose for **FY 2022–23** based on **gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100** received from the **District Public Relations Officer, Gaya**. An adjudication order dated **20.08.2025** had imposed **tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452**, after a notice was issued under **Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017**.  

The petitioner appealed under **Section 107(1)**, but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on **28.02.2026** solely because it was filed **21 days late**. Before the High Court, the petitioner argued that a later government communication, **Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025**, stated that **GST was not applicable to receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak** and that **Nukkad Natak teams comprising 4, 6, 8, or 10 members were exempt from GST**; the State objected that this memo did not cite any statutory basis or GST Council decision and that the appeal was time-barred. The High Court held that the exemption question went to the root of the tax demand and that the Appellate Authority should have decided that substantive issue rather than disposing of the matter only on limitation.  

Accordingly, the Court **set aside the appellate order dated 28.02.2026** and **remitted the matter to the Appellate Authority** to decide, in accordance with law, whether the petitioner as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak is exempt from GST liability. Procedurally, the petitioner must **produce a copy of the High Court’s order and appear before the Appellate Authority within one week** for fixing a hearing date, and the Appellate Authority must then provide a **personal hearing** and **dispose of the appeal within two months** from receipt/production of the High Court order. For compliance purposes, the decision means the demand remains under challenge and the key open issue is whether the asserted Nukkad Natak exemption has any lawful basis under GST law; the High Court expressly did **not** affirm the exemption, only required a proper adjudication of it.
