Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, allowed the appeal of M/s. N. R. Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, contended that the apparent mismatch between FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-2A did not represent excess ITC. According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The Show Cause Notice itself recorded the date, time and venue of personal hearing as “NA”. The Proper Officer subsequently confirmed the entire demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices.
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the case of **M/s. N. R. Builders v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes** for fresh adjudication after finding that the alleged **ITC mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A** for **FY 2018–19** had not been properly verified. The disputed ITC was **₹2,33,502** in total, split equally into **CGST ₹1,16,751** and **SGST ₹1,16,751**; the department had also levied **interest of ₹2,03,730** and **penalty of ₹23,350**, making the total demand **₹4,60,582**. The taxpayer, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, argued that the credit related to **FY 2017–18 invoices** but was lawfully availed in **FY 2018–19** within the time allowed under **Section 16(4)**, so the mismatch did not automatically mean excess or inadmissible ITC.

On procedure, the Tribunal found a serious **natural justice defect** because the **show-cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024** recorded the personal hearing as **“NA”**, and there was no evidence that any hearing was actually granted; this violated **Section 75(4)**, which requires an opportunity of hearing when an adverse order is contemplated. The proceedings had begun with a **pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024**, followed by the Section 73 notice, and the Proper Officer ultimately confirmed the demand **ex parte**. However, the Tribunal rejected the argument that the absence of **FORM GST ASMT-10** invalidated the case, holding that **Section 61 scrutiny and Section 73 adjudication are independent**, and if the matter is directly assigned under Section 73, ASMT-10 is not a precondition.

Substantively, the Tribunal held that a mismatch between **GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A** cannot be summarily treated as inadmissible ITC without **invoice-wise verification** of the taxpayer’s explanation. It relied on **CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST**, which specifically deals with GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A differences for **FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19** and requires verification rather than automatic disallowance. The Tribunal noted that the mere fact that invoices did not appear in GSTR-2A for FY 2018–19 did not, by itself, prove that the suppliers had not paid tax, and it faulted the lower authorities for not checking the taxpayer’s claim that the invoices belonged to FY 2017–18 but were availed within the permissible extended period.

The Tribunal also distinguished the precedents relied upon by the department/first appellate authority—**Mahalakshmi Cotton Ginning Processing and Oil Industries v. State of Maharashtra**, **ALD Automotive Private Limited v. CTO**, and **Microqual Techno Ltd. v. State of Karnataka**—because those cases involved different statutory settings and factual situations, including the absence here of any finding that the underlying purchases were non-genuine. It therefore set aside both the **Order-in-Original dated 20.04.2024** and the **Order-in-Appeal dated 07.11.2024**, and remanded the matter for **de novo adjudication**. The Proper Officer must now verify the reconciliation **invoice by invoice** with reference to **FY 2017–18 GSTR-2A, suppliers’ GSTR-1 returns, the assessee’s ITC register, books of account, and GSTR-9/GSTR-9C returns for FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19**; the Tribunal also observed that the final position on **interest and penalty** will depend on the fresh determination of the principal tax liability.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative and Judicial Developments – Period covered: September 2025 to September 2026 Summary: The period from September 2025 to September 2026 witnessed substantial changes in India’s GST framework across legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies and judicial interpretation. The Finance Act, 2026 amended provisions governing post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds and appellate arrangements, while omitting Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act concerning intermediary services. Commencement differs across provisions, and the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 of the CGST Act await notification. Rate rationalisation was completed through the withdrawal of compensation cess and migration of specified tobacco and pan masala products to the 40 per cent slab. Risk-based provisional refunds were expanded, GSTAT benches became operational and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals. The return architecture increasingly requires verification and reconciliation before filing, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and the Invoice Management System. Judicial developments clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, statutory timelines for detention orders and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. With the 57th GST Council meeting scheduled for 12 September 2026, further proposals concerning ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds and small-business compliance remain under consideration but cannot be treated as operative law until formally implemented. The twelve months preceding the 57th meeting of the GST Council have produced the densest concentration of change since the levy was introduced in July 2017. Three distinct layers moved at once. The rate architecture recommended by the 56th Council was completed with the withdrawal of compensation cess and the migration of tobacco and pan mas
rows.summary:
This document reviews major GST developments in India from September 2025 to September 2026 and is especially relevant for businesses dealing with discounting, refunds, exports, intermediary services, appellate litigation, and return compliance. The most important legislative change is the Finance Act, 2026, which received Presidential assent on 30 March 2026 and made five GST-related changes: it rewrote Section 15(3)(b) of the CGST Act so that post-supply discounts can be excluded from transaction value only if a credit note is issued and the recipient reverses the related input tax credit; it amended Section 34(1) so such discounts are now an express basis for issuing a credit note; it expanded Section 54 to allow 90% provisional refund in inverted duty structure cases and removed the minimum threshold for refunds on exports made with payment of tax; it inserted Section 101A(1A) to allow the Central Government to authorise an existing tribunal to hear appeals until the National Appellate Authority is set up; and it omitted Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act, which had deemed intermediary services to be supplied at the supplier’s location.  

The commencement dates are not uniform and are critical for compliance: Sections 2 to 129, clause (b) of Section 152, and Section 156 came into force on 1 April 2026, but the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 do not automatically apply until the Central Government notifies them; Section 157 is treated separately and, as described in the document, the deletion of Section 13(8)(b) is in force through that provision’s commencement mechanism. In practical terms, companies should not assume the amended discount and refund rules apply until the relevant notification is issued, while the intermediary-service position must be reassessed because the old place-of-supply deeming rule has been removed.  

On rates, the GST Council completed the long-running rate rationalisation by withdrawing compensation cess and moving specified tobacco and pan masala products into the 40% GST slab. The document treats this as a completed change to the rate architecture, so affected manufacturers, distributors, and importers of those products need to update pricing, classification, invoicing, and tax computations accordingly.  

Refund and appellate processes also changed materially. Administratively, risk-based provisional refunds were expanded ahead of the statutory amendment, so taxpayers seeking refunds should expect greater use of system-driven checks, especially where claims are linked to inverted duty structure or exports. The GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), which had been dormant for eight years, became operational and started issuing orders, and the document notes that revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals; importantly, a relaxation date of 31 December 2026 is not a general extension of limitation, so old appeals still need to be checked against the specific rules rather than treated as broadly revived.  

The return and portal architecture is becoming more verification-heavy before filing. The document highlights the growing role of GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System in pre-filing reconciliation and matching, meaning businesses should tighten vendor data review and internal controls before filing returns. Judicially, the courts clarified that buyers can remain exposed when suppliers fail to deposit tax, that detention orders must meet statutory timelines, and that penalty-related pre-deposit rules apply prospectively rather than retroactively. Finally, the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026, with proposals under discussion on ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance, but none of those proposals are operative until formally implemented.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. Section 76, however, independently empowers the GST department to recover tax collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, together with applicable interest and penalty. Despite this direct remedy, enforcement action is frequently taken against compliant buyers because they are easier to trace, possess identifiable assets and remain active within the GST system, whereas defaulting suppliers may have closed operations, disappeared or operated through shell entities. Automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch identification also makes buyer-side proceedings administratively easier than investigation and recovery against sellers. The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), recognising ITC as a statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions, including supplier payment of tax. Nevertheless, questions of fairness and enforcement sequencing remain. A balanced approach would prioritise recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for transactions involving collusion, fraud or failure to establish genuineness. Until legislation or binding precedent clarifies the sequencing of these provisions, buyers should maintain comprehensive evidence of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport records, banking payments and return reconciliation. Anyone who has dealt with a GST department notice in the las
rows.summary:
The document explains that under **Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act**, a buyer’s right to claim **Input Tax Credit (ITC)** depends on the supplier having **actually paid the tax to the government**; as a result, even a bona fide purchaser who has a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the full amount including GST, and files returns correctly can still be forced to **reverse ITC** if the supplier defaults. It contrasts this with **Section 76**, which gives the GST department a **direct recovery route against the person who collected tax but failed to deposit it**, allowing recovery of the unpaid tax **plus interest and penalty** from the defaulting seller itself. The article’s core point is that, despite Section 76, the department often proceeds against the buyer because buyers are usually easier to find, still active in the GST system, and have identifiable assets, while defaulting suppliers may have shut down, vanished, or operated through shell entities; automated **GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch** checks also make buyer-side action simpler and more routine than tracing and enforcing against sellers.

The document notes that the Supreme Court in **Bhandari Scrap Traders** upheld the constitutional validity of **Section 16(2)(c)**, treating ITC as a **statutory benefit rather than an absolute right** and accepting that Parliament can condition ITC on the supplier’s payment of tax. At the same time, the article criticizes the fairness of routinely shifting the loss to compliant buyers and argues that enforcement should, as a matter of policy, **prioritize recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier** and reserve ITC denial for cases involving **collusion, fraud, or failure to prove the genuineness of the transaction**. There is **no new statutory deadline or rate change** stated in the document, but the practical compliance message is clear: until the law or binding precedent clarifies sequencing, buyers should preserve strong evidence of due diligence and transaction genuineness, including **supplier verification records, tax invoices, proof of receipt of goods/services, e-way bills, transport documents, banking/payment records, and GST return reconciliations** to defend against notices requiring ITC reversal.

The High Court noted that the matter was already seized of by the National Company Law Tribunal and that the assets of both companies were in the custody of the Tribunal. rows.summary:
This Karnataka High Court decision does not create a new corporate rule; rather, it deals with a dispute during ongoing insolvency proceedings over whether certain assets at the IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru, belonged to Byju’s K3 Education Private Limited or were being wrongfully treated as assets of Think and Learn Private Limited. The petitioner, who is the Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3, challenged an NCLT Bengaluru order dated 13.08.2026 in I.A. No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025, and also sought to quash a public announcement dated 02.08.2026 issued under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations for sale of the disputed assets. The petitioner alleged that the Resolution Professional of Think and Learn Private Limited was attempting to sell property at the warehouse site—specifically the premises at IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, 2nd Floor, Plot Nos. 183 to 187 and 254 to 258, Bommasandra Jigani Link Road, Bengaluru, Karnataka 562106—despite the assets allegedly belonging to Byju’s K3, and asked for a halt to any sale, cancellation of any sale already completed, a joint physical verification of the warehouse, access to open cartons and server rooms, and a joint inventory.

The High Court declined to entertain the writ petition as a parallel proceeding, emphasizing that the NCLT was already seized of the insolvency matter and that the relevant assets were under the Tribunal’s custody. The Court held that disputes of this kind, especially disputes between two Resolution Professionals over assets connected with a corporate insolvency resolution process, should be pursued before the Adjudicating Authority rather than through separate writ proceedings in the High Court. It therefore disposed of the petition while granting liberty to the petitioner to pursue the pending proceedings before the NCLT on 20.08.2026 and to file additional applications and documents before that forum, including documents that came into his possession after the writ filing and a copy of the writ petition itself.

Importantly for compliance teams handling CIRP asset sales, the High Court directed the NCLT to take up the dispute and pass appropriate orders as expeditiously as possible, and in any event within 15 days from the following day. The Court also noted that the NCLT could, if necessary, exercise its discretion to protect the companies’ assets in whatever manner it considered appropriate. The practical takeaway is that where there is an asset-title or ownership dispute within an ongoing CIRP, especially between resolution professionals, the forum already supervising the insolvency should be approached immediately, and sale actions should not be assumed to be beyond challenge until the NCLT resolves the matter.

rows.title: Service Tax | STPI’s SOFTEX Certification Charges Taxable as Business Support Service: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12593 Case Name Software Technology Park of India Vs Pr. Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The two appeals concern a common dispute regarding the levy of Service Tax on charges collected by M/s Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) towards certification of SOFTEX forms and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs). The Department classified these activities under “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In appeal no. ST/20226/2014, the dispute covered the period from 2007-08 to 2011-12 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 5,15,53,520/- along with interest and penalties. Appeal no. ST/30531/2016 concerned the period April 2012 to June 2012 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 2,06,792/- along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner (Appeals), in the latter appeal, upheld the demand while extending cum-tax benefit. STPI contended that it is an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and functioning under the administrative control of the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India. It was established, inter alia, to administer and facilitate implementation of the Software Technology Park Scheme. STPI was separately registered with the Service Tax Department and admittedly paid Service Tax on various services including renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services and project consultancy. The controversy was confined to charges connected with activities under the STP Scheme, particularly SOFTEX certification and issuance of NoCs. The appellan
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that charges collected by Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for certifying SOFTEX forms and issuing No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are taxable under Service Tax as “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994, rather than being treated as exempt sovereign/statutory functions. The dispute covered two appeal periods: 2007-08 to 2011-12, involving Service Tax demand of Rs. 5,15,53,520 plus interest and penalties, and April 2012 to June 2012, involving Service Tax demand of Rs. 2,06,792 plus interest and penalties; in the later matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) had already upheld the demand while granting cum-tax benefit. STPI argued that it is an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, operating under the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, and that SOFTEX certification/NoC issuance were statutory functions under the Foreign Trade Policy, FEMA, and RBI circulars, so they should not be taxed; it relied on Board Circulars No. 89/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006 and No. 96/07/2007-ST dated 23.08.2007, which it claimed exempted statutory-fee activities performed by public authorities. The Department countered that STPI is not a Central Government department, that the charges were collected from STP units as consideration for facilitating their export business, and that the amounts were retained by STPI and used for administrative and establishment expenses rather than being collected as a compulsory statutory levy paid into the Government treasury or a consultation fund.

The Tribunal accepted the Department’s position and emphasized that merely because an activity is regulated by law or an organization is authorized by the Government does not make every such activity a sovereign function. It distinguished between truly sovereign acts that only the State can perform and services provided by an autonomous body to support business operations; it found that SOFTEX certification, NoCs, and related assistance are directly connected with software exporters’ business, foreign exchange realization, and regulatory compliance. On that basis, the Tribunal concluded STPI was providing business facilitation/support to STP units and that the resulting charges were taxable as Business Support Service. Practically, the ruling means STPI’s SOFTEX certification and NoC charges for the relevant periods remain liable to Service Tax, along with the associated interest and penalties, and the earlier cum-tax relief in the 2012 period did not alter the underlying taxability finding.

rows.summary:
The Revenue appealed an Order-in-Original dated 18.12.2019 that had confirmed service tax only for the normal limitation period and had dropped the demand for the extended period. The underlying dispute arose from Show Cause Notice No. 20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018, issued to Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd., which sells mobile phones through retail outlets in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, alleging non-payment of service tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers during the period 2013-14 through June 2018. The Commissioner ultimately confirmed service tax of Rs. 1,43,75,615/- only for the normal period and granted consequential relief by rejecting the extended-period allegation.

After that adjudication, the taxpayer opted into the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019 (SVLDRS). Its declaration was accepted, the determined amount was paid, and Form SVLDRS-4 was issued on 10.02.2020 as a discharge certificate signifying full and final settlement. The CESTAT held that once a discharge certificate is issued under Section 127 of the Finance Act, 2019, Section 129 gives finality to the dispute for the period covered by the declaration, so the Department cannot continue pursuing an appeal on the same dispute; the Tribunal relied on Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for that proposition. Independently, the Tribunal also agreed with the Commissioner on limitation: this was the fifth show-cause notice on substantially the same issue, earlier notices had already been adjudicated, and the Department therefore already knew the relevant facts about the company’s accounting method, collection of insurance charges, and service-tax treatment. Because those facts were already within the Department’s knowledge, the Tribunal applied the Supreme Court’s ruling in Nizam Sugar Factory to hold that suppression could not be alleged again to invoke the extended period. On both grounds—the SVLDRS discharge certificate and the merits of the limitation finding—the Revenue’s appeal was dismissed.

rows.summary: The Patna High Court granted regular bail to Jaswant Singh @ Rolly Babu in Complaint Case No. 49 of 2026, arising from allegations under Section 132(1)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the CGST Act, 2017. The prosecution alleged a GST evasion scheme involving issuance of tax invoices without actual movement or supply of goods, fraudulent availment of input tax credit without receipt of goods or services and without corresponding e-way bills, falsification of accounts and financial records, and operation of shell entities by controlling GST credentials, banking operations, passwords, and compliance activities; the alleged revenue implication was approximately ₹73.75 crore. The petitioner denied wrongdoing and challenged the arrest as lacking the required “reason to believe” under Section 69 of the CGST Act, arguing that the arrest memo and authorization did not disclose the monetary threshold or the basis for arrest, that the evidence largely consisted of statements of proprietors/co-accused without cross-examination, and that no incriminating material was found at his residence; he also pointed out that filing work had been handled by his accountant and that investigation of the relevant IP address would be needed before attributing electronic filings to him. He relied on Supreme Court authorities such as Arnesh Kumar and Satender Kumar Antil to argue that arrest and continued detention must be justified by necessity and proper judicial scrutiny, and noted that the investigation was complete, the charge sheet had been filed, there was no risk of tampering with evidence, and he had been in judicial custody since 26.05.2026. The Union of India opposed bail, emphasizing that this was an economic offence requiring strict treatment and arguing that under Section 132, where wrongly availed/utilised input tax credit or refund exceeds ₹5 crore, the punishment may extend to five years. The Court ultimately leaned in favor of bail and ordered release upon furnishing a bail bond of ₹10,000 with two sureties of the like amount each to the satisfaction of the Special Judge, Economic Offence, Patna/concerned court; the order is limited to pre-trial release and does not decide the merits of the alleged fake invoicing, ITC fraud, record falsification, or shell-entity allegations.

rows.summary:
This Calcutta High Court decision concerns GST adjudication and appeal proceedings under Section 107 of the West Bengal GST Act and the Central GST Act, 2017. The petitioner challenged an adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 and an appellate order dated 29.05.2025, after the appeal was rejected solely as time-barred. The underlying dispute began with a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 No. ZD190524017416E dated 12.05.2024, proposing tax, interest, and penalty; the petitioner argued that the notice was uploaded only in the GST portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” tab and no separate intimation was sent, so it was never seen in time and no reply could be filed. The court accepted that this portal-only upload, without separate notice, prevented a response and amounted to a violation of natural justice, and it noted that the appellate authority had not examined the merits at all, but had dismissed the appeal only on limitation.

As a result, the High Court quashed both the appellate order dated 29.05.2025 and the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024, and also set aside the consequential bank attachment. The matter was sent back to respondent no. 1 to reconsider the case on the merits of the grounds raised in the appeal, give the petitioner an opportunity of hearing, and pass a fresh reasoned adjudication order in accordance with law within 12 weeks. The court further directed that the decision be communicated to the petitioner within one week after the fresh order is passed. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that GST notices placed only in the portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” section, without effective intimation, may be vulnerable to challenge on natural justice grounds, especially where the taxpayer is deprived of any chance to respond before adjudication.

The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder and adjudication order bore neither digital nor physical signatures. Examining Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017, the Court held that electronic issuance and authentication are distinct and cumulative requirements and that mere generation of a document on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number cannot substitute authentication by signature. A signature authenticates the document, fixes accountability on the issuing officer and safeguards against arbitrariness by evidencing application of mind. Consequently, an unsigned show-cause notice or order is no notice or order in the eyes of law, and the defect is not a curable irregularity but goes to the root of the authority to proceed. The Court further noted that the documents had been uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders”, the petitioner learnt about the demand only upon bank recovery proceedings, and no effective personal hearing had been afforded contrary to Section 75(4). The plea of alternative remedy was therefore rejected. The show-cause notice, consequential order dated 15.10.2024
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show-cause notice and adjudication order issued under Section 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 are invalid if they are not authenticated by signature. In this case, M/s Mayur Timber challenged a show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024 and the consequential order dated 15.10.2024 confirming GST demand of Rs. 3,13,894, interest of Rs. 4,26,002, and penalty of Rs. 3,13,894, all based on the allegation that the taxpayer had wrongly availed ITC of Rs. 3,13,894 without actual receipt of goods. The Court found that the show-cause notice, reminder, and order bore neither digital nor physical signatures; under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, electronic issuance and authentication are separate and cumulative requirements, so mere upload on the GST portal or allotment of a reference number does not amount to lawful authentication. Because a signature is what shows the issuing officer applied mind and takes responsibility for the document, the Court treated an unsigned notice or order as no notice or order in law, not a curable technical defect.

The Court also noted serious service and hearing defects: the order was uploaded only under “Additional Notices and Orders,” not the normal “Notices and Orders” section; it was never manually served; and the taxpayer first learned of it only when its bank informed it on 21.08.2025 that recovery had been initiated. The department had issued FORM GST DRC-13 on 20.08.2025 under Section 79(1)(c) to Kotak Mahindra Bank, directing recovery of Rs. 9,00,820 from the taxpayer’s account, and the bank account was provisionally attached before being released after the taxpayer filed an affidavit dated 22.08.2025. The Court further held that no effective personal hearing had been granted, contrary to Section 75(4), so the alternative-remedy objection was rejected. As a result, the Court set aside the show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024, the order dated 15.10.2024, and the recovery notice in FORM GST DRC-13 dated 20.08.2025, but it expressly allowed the department to start again with a duly authenticated show-cause notice and by giving an effective opportunity of hearing; the merits of the alleged tax demand were left open.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax Payment: SC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12577 Case Name Saudi Arabian Airlines Vs Union of India & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Saudi Arabian Airlines Vs Union of India & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment.
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) by a carrier is **not the same as non-payment or failure to pay tax** for purposes of **Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979**. In this case, Saudi Arabian Airlines had six delayed remittances of collected FTT: in five instances the delay was only **1 to 11 days** and the demand drafts had been purchased before the due dates but could not be deposited because of security restrictions; in the sixth instance, relating to **December 1995**, the delay was **63 days** because the relevant employee was on emergency leave. An initial penalty of **Rs. 12,000** was later drastically enhanced after remand to **Rs. 71,29,140**, but the Supreme Court set aside the penalty and allowed the airline’s appeal.

The Court interpreted the statutory language in Section 38(3) — “**fails to pay the foreign travel tax**” and “**the amount of the tax not so paid**” — to mean **actual non-payment**, not mere late payment. It held that if Parliament intended delayed payment to be covered by Section 38(3), it would have used express language to that effect, and courts cannot expand fiscal penalty provisions by implication. Instead, the Court said delayed deposit falls within **Section 38(4)** read with the **Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979**, which specifically address delayed compliance and allow flexibility.

Under **Rule 4**, collected FTT had to be deposited **within 30 days from the end of the month**, but the **Collector of Customs** could extend that period on **sufficient cause** and having regard to the carrier’s accounting system. **Rule 9** similarly required monthly returns within the prescribed time but also allowed extension. The Court emphasized that this framework shows the deadlines are **not inflexible**; where delay is explained and condoned under the rules, the situation is not one of punishable non-payment. The Court further stated that payment made **before a show-cause notice is issued** is to be treated as **delayed payment**, not failure to pay.

On penalty, the Court relied on **Rule 12**, which requires a **written show-cause notice**, an opportunity to make a **representation**, and a **reasonable opportunity of hearing** before any penalty can be imposed. That procedural structure means the authority must exercise **discretion**; penalty is **not automatic** merely because a deadline was missed. The Court distinguished between cases where mens rea is not required and cases where penalty still remains discretionary, and it reaffirmed the principle from **Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa** that penalty for breach of a statutory obligation depends on the facts and surrounding circumstances. The decision therefore protects carriers and other entities subject to the FTT regime from automatic penalty exposure for late deposit where the tax was in fact collected and the delay is explainable or otherwise dealt with under the rules.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the assessee’s appeal concerning the allowability of Portfolio Management Service (PMS) charges while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal arose from the order of the Ld. CIT(A), dated 28.08.2025, which had sustained the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2011-12. The assessee had returned total income of Rs. 72,26,297/- from salary, short term capital gain and income from other sources. In computing capital gains, the assessee claimed Rs. 8,42,360/- towards fees and charges paid to Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. for portfolio management services. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount on the ground that the expenditure could not be regarded as expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer of the capital asset within the meaning of section 48. The CIT(A) sustained the disallowance, relying principally upon the Mumbai Tribunal decision in ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah, where PMS fees and performance-linked charges had been held not deductible under section 48. Before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the issue was unsettled because different coordinate Benches had adopted divergent views. Reliance was placed upon KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, where PMS fees were allowed as a deduction while computing capital gains. The assessee also submitted that although the Revenue had challenged KRA Holding and Trading before the Bombay High Court, th
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that Portfolio Management Service (PMS) fees are deductible while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, at least on the facts of this case, where the assessee had paid **Rs. 8,42,360** to **Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd.** for PMS. The assessee, **Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey**, had returned **total income of Rs. 72,26,297** for **Assessment Year 2011-12**, comprising salary, short-term capital gains, and income from other sources; the Assessing Officer disallowed the PMS charges in a **section 143(3)** assessment on the ground that they were not expenditure incurred “wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer” of capital assets under section 48. The **CIT(A) order dated 28.08.2025** upheld that disallowance, relying mainly on **ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah**, where the Mumbai Bench had held PMS fees and performance-linked charges not deductible under section 48.

On appeal, the assessee argued that the law was unsettled because different ITAT Benches had taken different views, citing **KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT** (Pune ITAT), **Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO** (Mumbai ITAT), and **ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd.** (Delhi ITAT), all of which had accepted deduction of PMS-related expenses in the circumstances before them. The assessee also pointed out that although the Revenue had challenged **KRA Holding** before the Bombay High Court, the substantial question there concerned whether the income was taxable as **capital gains** or **business income**; it did **not** specifically raise the deductibility of PMS charges under section 48. The Revenue maintained that PMS charges were composite advisory/management/consultancy fees and not directly linked to the acquisition or transfer of any particular security, so they should not qualify under section 48.

The Tribunal noted the existence of divergent coordinate Bench rulings and found no binding judgment of either the **Bombay High Court** or the **Supreme Court** squarely holding that PMS charges are not deductible under section 48. Applying the Supreme Court’s rule in **CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. (88 ITR 192)**—that where two reasonable interpretations of a taxing provision exist, the interpretation favorable to the assessee should be adopted—the Tribunal chose the assessee-favouring view. It therefore **allowed the deduction of Rs. 8,42,360 as PMS charges** in computing capital gains, **set aside the revenue authorities’ orders on this issue, and directed the Assessing Officer to allow the claim**. The appeal was consequently allowed.

Vs Union of India (Kerala High Court) Summary: The Kerala High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by AVT McCormick Ingredients Pvt. Ltd. challenging an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 to the extent it disallowed refund of input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger under the head SGST credit. The petitioner, engaged in export of spice extracts and oleoresins, was earlier registered under the Kerala Value Added Tax Act, 2003 and had filed Form GST TRAN-1 for transitioning excess input tax credit from its VAT ledger to its Electronic Credit Ledger. According to the petitioner, TRAN-1 was filed in November 2017 and the transitional credit was reflected in the Electronic Credit Ledger on 27.12.2017. For November 2017, the petitioner sought refund of ITC. The Department rejected the claim on the ground that transitional credit was not credit earned during the relevant period and therefore did not qualify as “Net ITC” under Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No.37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018. The respondents also objected to maintainability of the writ petition because the petitioner had not exhausted the statutory remedy and had approached the High Court after expiry of the limitation period for appeal. The petitioner argued that an appeal would be futile because the adjudicating authority had acted on a departmental circular that would also bind the appellate authority. It relied upon Filterco and another v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, Madhya Pradesh and another. On merits, reliance
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court dismissed AVT McCormick Ingredients Pvt. Ltd.’s writ challenge to an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 that had disallowed its GST refund claim to the extent of SGST input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger. The company, an exporter of spice extracts and oleoresins, had earlier been registered under the Kerala VAT regime and had filed Form GST TRAN-1 in November 2017 to transition excess pre-GST input tax credit into the GST Electronic Credit Ledger; it claimed that this transitional credit was reflected in the ledger on 27.12.2017 and used that balance to support a refund claim for November 2017. The Department rejected the refund on the ground that transitional credit is not “Net ITC” for purposes of Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018, and therefore could not be included in the refund computation.

On the legal position, the Court accepted that Section 140 of the CGST Act and Rule 117 of the CGST Rules permit eligible closing credit under the pre-GST regime as on 30.06.2017 to be carried forward into the Electronic Credit Ledger on 01.07.2017, so that unutilised ITC under the earlier regime could form the opening balance under GST. However, the petitioner failed on proof: it did not produce a copy of the TRAN-1 declaration filed within the prescribed period and did not produce satisfactory evidence showing the credit standing in its Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. The Court held that refund could be allowed only if the claimant proves that the amount claimed was actually credited in the ledger as of 01.07.2017, and in the absence of such material, there was no basis to interfere with the adjudication order.

The Court also rejected the writ petition on maintainability grounds because the company had not exhausted statutory remedies and had approached the High Court only after the limitation period for appeal had expired. It noted that Sections 107 and 108 of the CGST Act provide appeal and revision mechanisms against adjudication orders, and that a taxpayer cannot let the statutory appeal period lapse and then use that lapse as a basis to invoke Article 226. The Court relied on Supreme Court authority, including A.V. Venkateswaran, Rikhab Chand Jain, and Glaxo Smith Kline Consumer Health Care, to emphasize that writ jurisdiction must be exercised promptly and consistently with the legislative scheme; it also noted that the petitioner’s reliance on Moriroku UT India was undermined because that High Court decision had been set aside by the Supreme Court. In practical compliance terms, the decision underscores that refund claims based on transitional credit must be supported by timely filed TRAN-1 documentation and evidence of the exact ledger position as on 01.07.2017, and that missed statutory appeal deadlines are unlikely to be cured by later filing a writ petition.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12570 Case Name Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The CESTAT Hyderabad partly allowed the appeal of Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. against an Order-in-Original confirming service tax of Rs.1,63,15,458/- with interest under “Club or Association Service”, besides penalties under Sections 76, 77 and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994 and smaller demands under Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service and Renting of Immovable Property Service. The appellant operated Lahari Resorts and had introduced a Time Share Holiday Scheme under which customers acquired a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for one week every year for 12 years against predetermined consideration. The Tribunal examined whether persons enrolled under the Time Share Scheme could be regarded as “members” of a club or association merely because the agreement used that terminology. It held that taxability must depend upon the real legal and commercial character of the arrangement rather than nomenclature. The customers acquired no proprietary, voting, management or shareholding rights in the appellant company. Their relationship with the appellant remained that of customer and service provider, and they merely purchased accommodation rights for specified periods. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and that the time-share customers did not become members of the company in accordance with that Act. They neither subscribed to the memorandum, became shareholders, nor had the
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd.’s time-share holiday scheme was **not taxable as “Club or Association Service”** under the Finance Act, 1994, because the customers were not actually members of a club or association in the legal sense. The company operated Lahari Resorts and offered customers a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for **one week every year for 12 years** in exchange for predetermined consideration; although the agreement used “member”-type language, the Tribunal said taxability depends on the **real legal and commercial substance**, not labels.

The Tribunal emphasized that the time-share customers had **no proprietary, voting, management, or shareholding rights** in the company and did not become members of the company under the Companies Act, 1956. They did not subscribe to the memorandum, become shareholders, or have their names entered in the register of members, so the legal basis for treating them as “members” of a club/association was absent. The relationship was therefore one of **customer and service provider**, not members of a mutual club or association, and the dominant object of the scheme was **accommodation**, not club privileges, sports, recreation, or similar facilities.

A significant point in the decision was the Tribunal’s reliance on the later introduction of **“Short Term Accommodation Service” under Section 65(105)(zzzzw)** of the Finance Act, 1994, effective **1 May 2011**. The Tribunal viewed this as supporting the conclusion that hotel/resort accommodation was not meant to be taxed earlier under the “Club or Association Service” head merely because it involved a membership-style arrangement. It also relied on the Supreme Court’s reasoning in **State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd.** and on prior hospitality-sector cases such as **Bharat Hotels Ltd.** and **Adarsh Realty & Hotel Pvt. Ltd.**, which treated similar membership/loyalty arrangements as commercial hospitality transactions rather than club services.

On the tax demand side, the original order had confirmed **service tax of Rs. 1,63,15,458/-** along with interest under “Club or Association Service,” plus smaller demands under **Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service, and Renting of Immovable Property Service**, and penalties under **Sections 76, 77, and 78** of the Finance Act, 1994. The Tribunal set aside the entire **Club or Association Service** demand, but upheld the view that the smaller category-wise liabilities had already been **voluntarily paid in full along with applicable interest before the show-cause notice was issued**. Because the Department did not dispute the payment or quantum, and there was no evidence of fraud, wilful suppression, or clandestine conduct, the Tribunal held the appellant was entitled to the protection of **Section 73(3)**, and therefore the penalties under Sections 76, 77, and 78 were not sustainable. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant had maintained regular books, the time-share receipts were disclosed in audited financial statements, and the Department’s case was built on the appellant’s own records, showing that the dispute was about **classification and interpretation**, not concealment.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12569 Case Name Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed a writ petition challenging the prolonged detention and subsequent seizure of a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan. The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that customs authorities cannot keep imported goods—here, a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan—under indefinite “detention” through a Panchnama and then much later issue a seizure memo under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 in an attempt to restart the limitation clock for notice and confiscation proceedings. In this case, the importer filed Bill of Entry No. 7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs. 99,78,795; out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. The DRI searched the importer’s residence on 07.02.2025, recorded a Panchnama, and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle, but did not contemporaneously pass a seizure order; only on 17.04.2026 did it issue a seizure memo, followed by a show-cause notice on 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4).

The Court emphasized the legal distinction between detention and seizure: a Panchnama restraining the owner from dealing with the goods is not, by itself, a valid Section 110 seizure, and if seizure is intended the proper officer must record “reasons to believe” that the goods are liable to confiscation. The Court relied on Supreme Court authority in Union of India v. Jatin Ahuja, reiterating that where goods are seized under Section 110(1), notice under Section 124(a) must be issued within six months, extendable by another six months under Section 110(2), and absent timely notice the goods must be released. It also relied on Worldline Tradex Pvt. Ltd. and Instruction No. 01/2017-Cus. dated 08.02.2017, which require an actual seizure memo/order in addition to the Panchnama and require that, where immediate seizure is impracticable, an appropriate statutory order restricting dealings be served and the investigation fast-tracked.

The Court rejected the Department’s argument that pendency of the writ petition prevented it from initiating proper Section 110 action, noting that the record showed no court order restraining investigation; instead, the Court had repeatedly directed completion of the investigation. It treated the Department’s claim as a bald assertion and found that the delay was attributable to the Department’s own inaction. Critically, the Court held that customs cannot hold goods indefinitely and then issue a Section 110(1) seizure later merely to reset the six-month period under Section 110(2); time ran from the actual detention under the 07.02.2025 Panchnama, so the 17.04.2026 seizure memo could not validate the later notice.

The Court also set aside the provisional release order dated 18.05.2026 because it required a bond of Rs. 85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs. 1.20 crore based on paragraph 2 of Circular No. 35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017, which the Delhi High Court had already struck down in Shanus Impex to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated continued departmental reliance on that paragraph and held the provisional release conditions unlawful. In practical compliance terms, the decision warns customs officers that if imported goods are to be restrained or seized, the statutory seizure process must be followed promptly and cannot be backfilled later to extend limitation periods; for importers, it strengthens the position that prolonged detention without a valid seizure order is challengeable and that release conditions must have a lawful statutory basis.

(CESTAT Kolkata) Summary: CESTAT Kolkata allowed the appeal filed by Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. and set aside the demand for reversal of CENVAT credit of Rs.83,839. The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. In these circumstances, the Tribunal held that the Revenue had failed to establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The demand was accordingly set as
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Kolkata held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the seller’s commercial chain involved a party that did not hold dealer registration, so long as the invoice on which credit is taken satisfies the Rule 9 requirements and the goods were actually received by the assessee. In this case, Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. had taken CENVAT credit of **Rs. 83,839** based on **three invoices**—**two from 2011** and **one dated 22.01.2014**—and the department demanded reversal after alleging the goods were purchased through **M/s Ashis Enterprise**, which allegedly lacked dealer registration. The Tribunal found that the invoice issued by **M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal** specifically named the appellant as the **consignee**, while **Ashis Enterprise** was shown as the buyer; it also accepted the appellant’s explanation that Ashis Enterprise issued a separate commercial invoice only to facilitate payment and that this invoice could be correlated to the main seller’s invoice.

The key compliance point is that the Tribunal treated the main seller’s invoice as valid for credit because it contained all particulars required under **Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004**, and there was **no allegation that the goods were not actually received** by the appellant. The appellant also had the goods recorded in **RG 23A Part I** after receipt at its factory, which supported the legitimacy of the credit. Because the Revenue could not establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, the Tribunal **set aside the confirmed demand** and allowed the appeal.

For compliance teams, the case reinforces that when taking credit on third-party procurement arrangements, companies should preserve invoice chains that clearly show the consignee, buyer, and correlation between commercial documents and the tax invoice, and should maintain contemporaneous receipt records such as RG 23A Part I or equivalent inventory/credit records. The decision does **not** create a new deadline or procedural filing requirement, but it underscores the importance of being able to prove actual receipt of goods and documentary compliance under Rule 9 if credit is challenged. The appellant was also held eligible for **consequential relief, if any, in accordance with law**.

The appellant had executed EPC/works contracts relating to construction of dams, reservoirs, canals and allied structures for the Government of Andhra Pradesh during June 2007 to March 2012. A show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 demanded service tax of Rs.43,86,471/- under Works Contract Service, which was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant challenged the order and sought waiver of pre-deposit. The Commissioner (Appeals) fixed the stay application for hearing on 12.06.2014; although the appellant sought an adjournment, the request was declined and, by order dated 13.06.2014, it was directed to deposit 50% of the service tax demand. The appellant subsequently requested a speaking order considering its legal submissions and precedents, but did not comply with the pre-deposit condition. Its appeal was consequently dismissed on 23.07.2014. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that its appeal had been dismissed without adjudication on merits and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had failed to consider its prima facie case, balance of convenience and financial hardship. It relied, inter alia, upon Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya P
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that a service tax appeal can be dismissed for non-compliance with a pre-deposit condition, and it upheld the Commissioner (Appeals)’ dismissal of ECI BJCL JV’s appeal on that basis. The underlying dispute arose from EPC/works contracts for construction of dams, reservoirs, canals, and related structures executed for the Government of Andhra Pradesh during June 2007 to March 2012; a show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 proposed service tax of Rs. 43,86,471 under Works Contract Service, and the demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant appealed and sought waiver of pre-deposit, but after a hearing date of 12.06.2014 and a rejected adjournment request, the Commissioner (Appeals) issued an order on 13.06.2014 directing deposit of 50% of the adjudged service tax demand; when the appellant did not comply, the appeal was dismissed on 23.07.2014.

Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that the appeal had been thrown out without merits consideration and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not properly evaluated prima facie case, balance of convenience, or financial hardship; it relied on several cited decisions, including Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya Pharmaceutical Ltd., B. Rama Rao & Company, and Thermopads Pvt. Ltd. The Revenue responded that the appellant had been given an opportunity to be heard, the adjournment request was considered and denied for recorded reasons, and failure to make the required deposit justified dismissal. The Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position, finding that the Commissioner (Appeals) had exercised discretion judicially, had recorded reasons for requiring a 50% pre-deposit, and had not acted mechanically or in violation of natural justice.

A key legal point in the ruling was that the amended Section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944, which introduced a mandatory 10% pre-deposit, came into force only on 06.08.2014 and applied prospectively. Because the appellate order under challenge was passed before that amendment, the Tribunal held that the parties’ rights and obligations were governed by the unamended law, under which the Commissioner (Appeals) could insist on a pre-deposit as a condition for stay/waiver. The Tribunal specifically held that a later deposit of 10% could not cure the earlier failure to comply with the 50% condition, and that subsequent compliance with the new statutory regime could not revive an appeal already dismissed under the old one. For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that when an appellate authority imposes a conditional pre-deposit under the applicable statutory framework, the appellant must either comply with that condition or seek relief from a competent forum; failure to do so can result in dismissal of the appeal without a merits ruling.

The petitions stated that the refunds had remained unpaid for about two years even after orders of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and subsequent orders passed by the Assessing Officer giving effect to those appellate decisions. For AY 2012-13, the Tribunal’s order dated 05.06.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 30.10.2024, with refund quantified by the assessee at Rs.11,06,37,172; the Form 26B applications dated 25.04.2025 were rejected. For AY 2013-14, the Tribunal’s order dated 30.04.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 14.10.2024, with refund quantified at Rs.7,57,50,048; the Form 26B application dated 01.02.2025 was rejected. For AYs 2003-04 and 2008-09 to 2011-12, the relevant Tribunal orders were dated 26.11.2024 and 03.02.2025, followed by an appeal-effect order dated 15.05.2026, with refund quantified at Rs.34,45,69,250. The total amount found payable by the Assessing Officer was Rs.53,09,56,470. The petitioner argued that Section 200A, Section 201, Rule 31A and Form 26B address the processing of TDS statements and refunds arising from excess or incorrect deduction/deposit. According to the petitioner, they do not govern a refund that crystallises after an assessment under Section 201 or after an appellate order. The respondents relied on departmental practice and the Standard Operating Pr
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court has ordered the income-tax department to refund **₹53.09 crore of TDS** to the taxpayer **with interest**, and held that **Form 26B** and **Rule 31A** could not be used to deny the refund once a **Section 201 assessment** had already been completed. The core compliance point is that, in this case, the court treated the matter as one where the tax liability and TDS position had already been adjudicated under Section 201, so the department could not insist on a separate procedural filing in Form 26B as a condition for issuing the refund.

For corporate taxpayers and withholding agents, the decision is significant because it limits the tax department’s ability to impose additional procedural hurdles after a Section 201 determination has settled the issue. The ruling implies that where excess TDS has been deposited and the taxpayer’s entitlement is established through assessment, the refund should follow along with applicable interest, rather than being withheld for non-submission of Form 26B. Compliance teams should therefore note that refund claims tied to TDS may turn on the status of the Section 201 proceedings and the court’s view that procedural forms cannot override a completed assessment.

rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs has issued the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026 by notification S.O. 4870(E) dated 2 September 2026, under clauses (aa) and (ab) of section 46(2) of the FEMA, 1999. These rules amend the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 and take effect immediately on publication in the Official Gazette.

The substantive change is the insertion of new serial number 15.2.5 into Schedule I of the 2019 NDI Rules. Under this new provision, an “e-commerce entity” is now expressly permitted to use an inventory-based e-commerce model solely for exporting goods or products that are manufactured or produced in India, provided the activity is carried out in accordance with the Foreign Trade Policy 2023, the Handbook of Procedures (HBP), and the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015. This is a targeted export permission, not a general relaxation for domestic e-commerce or broader inventory-based selling.

The amendment also carves this export activity out from the existing restrictions in serial numbers 15.2.1 to 15.2.4: the B2C restrictions and the restrictions on the inventory-based model of e-commerce in those earlier provisions do not apply to exports of goods or products through e-commerce that are permitted under the new clause 15.2.5. For compliance purposes, companies operating e-commerce export models should confirm that their products are India-manufactured/produced, that the model is exclusively for export, and that their operations align with the FTP 2023, HBP, and the 2015 export regulations rather than treating this as a blanket exemption from FEMA e-commerce restrictions.

The notification also notes the historical context that the principal NDI Rules were originally published on 17 October 2019 and have been amended multiple times, most recently by S.O. 3030(E) dated 12 June 2026 before this Fourth Amendment.

ECLGS 5.0 is a Government-backed credit guarantee scheme approved on 5 May 2026 and implemented by NCGTC to help businesses facing external disruptions by enabling Member Lending Institutions (MLIs) to extend additional working capital credit with reduced risk. The scheme’s stated target is to facilitate up to ₹2.55 lakh crore of additional credit flow, and it is operational until 31 March 2027 or until guarantees totaling ₹2.55 lakh crore are issued, whichever happens first. It is aimed at three borrower groups: MSMEs, eligible non-MSME business borrowers, and scheduled passenger airline companies.

For MSMEs and eligible non-MSMEs, the scheme generally permits additional credit up to 20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding during Q4 FY 2025–26, subject to a maximum of ₹100 crore per borrower. These loans carry a five-year tenure, including a one-year moratorium. Coverage is 100% for eligible MSMEs and 90% for eligible non-MSMEs. For scheduled passenger airlines, the scheme allows additional credit up to 100% subject to a cap of ₹1,500 crore per borrower, with a specific equity requirement applying for amounts above ₹1,000 crore; airline loans have a seven-year tenure including a two-year moratorium and receive 90% guarantee coverage.

As of 20 August 2026, the scheme had issued 6,73,979 guarantees covering ₹2,50,024 crore. MSMEs accounted for 97.3% of guarantees by number and 80.79% of the guaranteed amount, indicating that the scheme has been used primarily by MSME borrowers. The document also notes that access is supported through the Jan Samarth Portal and through outreach by participating banks and financial institutions, which is relevant for monitoring how eligible borrowers are identified, onboarded, and documented.

From a compliance perspective, the key operational obligations are to verify borrower eligibility within the defined categories, apply the correct guarantee coverage percentage, ensure the credit amount stays within the relevant cap and formula, and observe the applicable tenure and moratorium terms. The scheme is framed as a response to supply-chain disruption, logistics cost increases, and liquidity stress, so lenders using it should expect ongoing documentation and monitoring around end-use, eligibility, and guarantee issuance within the scheme’s time and amount limits.

rows.title: Corporate Law | CCPA Imposes ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Dial4Trade for Online Listing and Sale of Ammonium Nitrate Without Mandatory Safeguards
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a ₹10 lakh penalty on Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited for facilitating the online listing, hosting, advertising and sale of Ammonium Nitrate without mandatory regulatory safeguards. The CCPA also directed Dial4Trade to immediately discontinue listing, hosting, advertising or facilitating the sale of Ammonium Nitrate or any other substance classified as an explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884. During its examination, the Authority found that the platform did not adequately disclose the seller’s valid PESO licence details, verify the buyer’s identity and licensed status, provide mechanisms for transaction traceability under the Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012, or caution users regarding legal restrictions and consequences of unauthorised possession. The listing also carried imagery depicting explosions and blast effects. The CCPA held that a product listing communicated to the public over the internet falls within the definition of an “advertisement” under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and that presenting a regulated explosive substance like an ordinary consumer product without required licensing disclosures constitutes a misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice. The Authority rejected Dial4Trade’s B2B marketplace and intermediary safe-harbour contentions, holding that marketplace e-commerce entities remain subject to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and prescribed due-diligence requirements. The action forms part of a sector-wide examination of online platforms dealing with hazardous chemicals and explosive substances. rows.summary:
The CCPA has imposed a ₹10 lakh penalty on Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited for enabling the online listing, hosting, advertising, and sale of Ammonium Nitrate on its e-commerce platform without the safeguards required for a regulated explosive substance. In its final order, passed under Sections 10, 20, and 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Authority also directed Dial4Trade to stop immediately listing, hosting, advertising, or otherwise facilitating the sale of Ammonium Nitrate, and more broadly any substance classified as an explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884. The order was issued and publicly posted on 02 Sep 2026 and forms part of a broader sector-wide scrutiny of online platforms dealing with hazardous chemicals and explosive materials.

The CCPA found that the platform allowed the product to be offered for purchase without disclosing the seller’s valid PESO (Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation) licence details, without verifying the buyer’s identity and licensed status before purchase, and without transaction-traceability mechanisms required under the Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012. It also found no adequate warning to users about the legal restrictions on possession and use of Ammonium Nitrate or the consequences of unauthorized possession. The listing was accompanied by explosion/blast imagery, which the Authority said drew attention to the product rather than signaling its hazardous and regulated status.

A key legal finding was that a product listing on a digital marketplace, when communicated over the internet, is an “advertisement” under Section 2(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. On that basis, the CCPA held that presenting a regulated explosive as if it were an ordinary consumer product, without clearly stating that lawful purchase requires the prescribed licence, amounts to a misleading advertisement and an unfair trade practice under Sections 2(28) and 2(47). The Authority rejected Dial4Trade’s argument that it was merely a B2B marketplace intermediary and therefore not responsible for third-party listings.

For compliance purposes, the decision makes clear that marketplace e-commerce entities cannot rely on intermediary status to avoid due-diligence obligations where regulated hazardous or explosive substances are involved. The CCPA specifically noted that Dial4Trade allowed purchases as low as a single unit and lacked minimum order-quantity controls or institutional-buyer verification features that would be expected in a true B2B model, and it reaffirmed that the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 apply to such platforms.
