Ministry of Labour & Employment
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Labour & Employment has introduced a one-time amnesty under the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) Scheme 2026 to allow retrospective regularisation of the exempt status of Provident Fund (PF) trusts that were recognized under the Income Tax Act, 1961 but never obtained a formal exemption order under section 17 of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions (EPF&MP) Act, 1952 or section 143 of the Code on Social Security (CoSS), 2020. The scheme was notified on 29 June 2026, and the operational circular setting out the application process and procedural requirements was issued on 11 July 2026. The amnesty window is open for six months from notification and closes on 28 December 2026, so affected trusts need to apply within that period if they want to regularize past exemption status.

The main compliance benefit is that qualifying PF trusts may obtain retrospective regularisation and, in addition, may receive waivers of certain CoSS, 2020 requirements that would otherwise apply, specifically the minimum employee headcount requirement, the corpus size requirement, and the three-year compliance rule. After regularisation on a retrospective basis, the establishment is not locked into one compliance model and may choose either exempt or unexempt status going forward. The document indicates that the amnesty is intended as a transitional measure and applies only to the narrow population of PF trusts with Income Tax Act recognition but without a corresponding EPFO exemption order.

EPFO is actively publicizing the scheme through field offices and stakeholder outreach, including seminars/workshops and engagement with the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), because chartered accountants may be able to identify establishments eligible for the amnesty during statutory or income-tax audits. EPFO has also contacted the Income Tax Department to obtain details of PF trusts recognized under the Income Tax Act and to coordinate verification of whether the relevant establishment is covered or exempt under the EPF&MP Act, 1952 or the CoSS, 2020 before recognition is granted, and to withdraw recognition where a PF trust lacks the required formal exemption order. Compliance teams overseeing PF trusts should review whether they fall into this category and, if so, submit an application in line with the EPFO circular dated 11 July 2026 before the 28 December 2026 deadline.

rows.title: Corporate Law | EPFO VISHWAS 2026 Scheme Offers Reduced EPF Damages for Long-Pending Disputes
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Government of India has launched VISHWAS, 2026, a one-time settlement scheme enabling eligible employers to resolve long-pending disputes relating to damages for delayed Provident Fund contributions at substantially reduced rates. The Scheme remains open until 28 December 2026, and employers have been encouraged to apply before the closing date, which will not be extended. Under the Scheme, damages for delays of up to two months are payable at 0.25% per month, delays from two to four months at 0.50% per month, and delays beyond four months at 1% per month, compared with the normal penalty that may reach 37% per year. The Scheme may cover delayed PF contribution cases arising before 14 June 2024 where specified conditions are met, including proceedings pending before courts or tribunals, penalty orders passed by the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) where recovery remains pending, penalty notices issued without final orders, and recorded payment delays where no penalty notice has yet been issued. The Bombay High Court (Pune Bench), Madras High Court and Kerala High Court have issued directions encouraging or requiring eligible establishments to avail the Scheme in specified proceedings. Employers must first clear outstanding interest on delayed PF contributions and then apply online through the EPFO Employer Portal using the VISHWAS, 2026 module. The system calculates the revised damages, and eligible employers are given 15 days for payment, with a further automatic 15-day extension where required. Upon payment confirmation, EPFO issues a digitally signed Settlement Certificate, after which the concerned court or tribunal proceedings stand closed. EPFO has established dedicated VISHWAS Cells and Helpdesks at its 153 Regional Offices. rows.summary:
The Government of India has introduced **VISHWAS, 2026**, a **one-time settlement scheme** for employers to close long-pending disputes over **damages/penalties for delayed Provident Fund (PF) contributions** at sharply reduced rates. The scheme is open **until 28 December 2026**, and the document says the closing date **will not be extended**, so eligible employers are being urged to apply before that deadline.

Under the scheme, the reduced damage rates depend on the length of the delay: **0.25% per month** for delays of **up to 2 months**, **0.50% per month** for delays of **more than 2 months and up to 4 months**, and **1% per month** for delays **beyond 4 months**. This is presented as a major concession compared with the normal penalty regime, which can be as high as **37% per year**.

The scheme can be used for **delayed PF contribution cases arising before 14 June 2024**, but only where the employer falls into one of the covered procedural categories: cases with **penalty proceedings pending before a court or tribunal**, cases where EPFO has already passed a **penalty order but recovery is still pending in whole or part**, cases where EPFO has issued a **penalty notice but no final order yet**, and cases where EPFO records show PF payment delays but **no penalty notice has been issued**. Before applying, employers must **first clear all outstanding interest on the delayed PF contributions**.

The process is now fully **online through the EPFO Employer Portal** at **https://unifiedportal-emp.epfindia.gov.in** using the **VISHWAS, 2026 module**. Employers must select the applicable category, upload the required documents, and complete digital authentication; the system then **automatically calculates the revised damages**. After that, the employer gets **15 days to pay**, with an **automatic additional 15-day extension where required**. Once payment is confirmed, EPFO issues a **digitally signed Settlement Certificate**, and the relevant court or tribunal proceedings are treated as **closed**.

The document also notes judicial encouragement and mandatory directions in specific matters: the **Bombay High Court (Pune Bench)** in **WP No. 4246 of 2018** directed an employer to apply under VISHWAS, 2026 **within two weeks**, modified the tribunal order, and disposed of the writ petition; the **Madras High Court** disposed of **WP No. 38008 of 2024** when the employer said it would avail the scheme, closing the writ and related tribunal proceedings; and the **Kerala High Court (Ernakulam Bench)** issued similar directions in **nineteen separate cases**, instructing those establishments to approach EPFO and settle under the scheme. EPFO has also set up **dedicated VISHWAS Cells and Helpdesks at its 153 Regional Offices** to support applications.

For registering or tracking insurance grievances, the public is directed to use only the official Bima Bharosa portal. IRDAI further advises the public to verify the authenticity of IRDAI-related websites and warns that it will not be responsible for losses, disclosure of information or other consequences arising from interaction with unauthorised or fraudulent websites impersonating IRDAI. rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued Public Notice No. IRDAI/PPGR/BB/2026-27/25 dated 4 September 2026 warning the public, policyholders, and other stakeholders about a fraudulent website, **igmsirdai.online**, including its complaint-registration page **igmsirdai.online/register-complaint**, which is falsely presenting itself as an IRDAI-related insurance grievance/complaint platform. Anyone who has already shared personal, policy, or financial information through the suspected website is advised to take precautionary steps immediately and, where necessary, report the incident to the relevant cybercrime or law-enforcement authorities. IRDAI also states that it will **not be responsible for any loss, disclosure of information, or other consequences** arising from interaction with unauthorized or fraudulent websites impersonating IRDAI, and the notice is issued for public protection and the protection of policyholders’ interests.

It highlights the rise in India’s Financial Inclusion Index, wider account ownership, the role of Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Aadhaar-enabled services, UPI, digital payments, insurance, pensions and investment avenues. The message stresses that financial literacy must extend beyond saving and banking to encompass planning, protection, credit, investment, taxation, financial planning and digital safety, particularly in the face of phishing, impersonation, fraudulent investment schemes, misinformation and AI-enabled manipulation. ICAI’s initiatives including Vittiya Gyan, Investor Awareness Programmes, Project Vanijya and outreach to rural and tribal communities are presented as part of a sustained financial-literacy mission. ICAI President’s Message – September 2026 Institute of Chartered Accountants of India Dear Professional Colleagues, India stands at the inflection point in the realm of i
rows.summary:
The message says India’s financial system has moved beyond basic access to a stage where citizens are increasingly expected to participate meaningfully in formal finance, invest, borrow, insure, and plan, with the long-term goal of financial empowerment. It cites the country’s Financial Inclusion Index rising to 70 in March 2026, up 27% from 2017, and notes the World Bank’s Global Findex Database 2025 showing account ownership at 89% since 2011. It also highlights major enablers of this shift: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Aadhaar-enabled financial services under the JAM Trinity, expanded mobile connectivity, and the rapid adoption of UPI and digital payments, alongside broader access to insurance, pensions, and investment products.

A key compliance-oriented theme is that financial literacy is no longer limited to basic saving and banking; it must now cover planning, protection, credit, investment, taxation, financial planning, and digital safety. The message explicitly warns of newer risks that organizations and professionals must guard against, including phishing, impersonation, fraudulent investment schemes, misinformation, and AI-enabled manipulation. It emphasizes that financial inclusion alone is not sufficient for lasting financial well-being unless it is paired with awareness, prudence, and financial discipline, and that people need the ability to make informed, sustainable, risk-aware decisions.

The document also provides a concrete data point on government financial-disbursement scale: direct benefit transfer has reached INR 52 lakh crore across 320 government schemes as of 10 August 2026. This is presented as evidence of the breadth of India’s digitized welfare and financial infrastructure, and as part of the broader environment in which compliance teams should expect continued growth in digital transactions, formal financial products, and public-sector financial interfaces.

ICAI is positioning itself as a major participant in this financial-literacy and empowerment agenda through initiatives such as Vittiya Gyan, Investor Awareness Programmes, Project Vanijya, and outreach to rural and tribal communities. The message also references ICAI’s wider professional and international engagement, including the IFAC Board Meeting in India, the ICAI International Conference – ASEAN, professional pathways with ISCA, WOFA 2026, public-finance workshops, new IFSCA-related certificate courses, an MoU with the Department of Higher Education of the Government of Madhya Pradesh, the All India Leadership Summit, financial reporting and audit-quality initiatives, the revised Guidance Note on Tax Audit under Section 44AB, the I-Kar Pe Charcha mobile application, ICAI’s strategy meeting, and regional conferences. There are no new statutory obligations or filing deadlines announced in the text itself, but the message is a clear directive that the profession should treat financial literacy, digital-security awareness, and public outreach as ongoing responsibilities in support of a confident and resilient “Viksit Bharat.”

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); R Ramesha Vs Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (Karnataka High Court) When Compensation Arrives Six Years Late, the Return Cannot Travel Back in Time: Karnataka HC Directs Consideration of Condonation u/s 119(2)(b) for Refund of TDS on Exempt Land-Acquisition Compensation The Karnataka High Court has directed the PCIT, Bengaluru-3, to examine & decide the assessee’s application u/s 119(2)(b) seeking condonation of delay in filing the revised return for AY 2019-20, where compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land was actually received only in the year 2025 after resolution of a prolonged title dispute. The assessee claimed that the compensation was exempt from income tax u/s 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 & consequently sought refund of the TDS deducted by the KIADB. Background of the dispute The petitioner claimed title, as legal heir of the original owners, over land measuring 3 acres and 20 guntas situated in Survey Nos.87/3 & 87/4 of Kothanur Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bengaluru South Taluk. The lands, along with surrounding properties, had been acquired by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board – KIADB under the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966. However, payment of compensation was delayed because of a dispute concerning the petitioner’s title to the acquired lands. According to the petitioner, the title dispute was ultimately resolved by a civil court decree in his favour. It was only thereafter that the KIADB deposited the acq
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court in **R Ramesha v. Chief Commissioner of Income Tax** did **not** grant the refund outright, but it **directed the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax (PCIT), Bengaluru-3, to examine and decide the assessee’s request for condonation of delay under section 119(2)(b)**. The underlying issue was that the petitioner had already filed his **original return for AY 2019-20**, but the **compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land** was allegedly received only in **2025**, after a **civil title dispute** was resolved in his favor by court decree; because the statutory time for filing a revised return had expired by then, he could not simply amend the return as of right.

The land in question measured **3 acres and 20 guntas** in **Survey Nos. 87/3 and 87/4, Kothanur Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bengaluru South Taluk**, and had been acquired by the **Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB)** under the **Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966**. The petitioner argued that the compensation was exempt from income tax under **section 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013**, and therefore the **TDS deducted by KIADB** should be refunded, along with applicable interest, because retaining tax on exempt compensation would cause genuine hardship.

Procedurally, the **jurisdictional Assessing Officer (AO)** had already communicated on **27.01.2026** that the petitioner’s **application dated 12.01.2026** and supporting documents were forwarded to the PCIT, Bengaluru-3. The High Court noted that a separate condonation application may not have been directly filed before the PCIT, but since the AO had forwarded the request, the Court held that the matter should still be considered on its merits rather than rejected on a technicality.

The Court therefore gave the petitioner liberty to submit a **certified copy of the order** to the PCIT, and specifically instructed the PCIT to **verify the forwarded application, consider the “peculiar circumstances” of the case, and decide the request for condonation of delay in filing the revised return for AY 2019-20**. In deciding the request, the PCIT was told to take into account that the petitioner claimed title through a **civil court decree** and that the compensation allegedly became receivable only in **2025** after the dispute ended. The PCIT must **communicate the decision within three months from receipt** of the certified copy/order.

rows.title: Company Law | Annual ROC Compliance 2026: Beyond AOC-4 and MGT-7
rows.desc: Summary: Annual ROC compliance for FY 2025-26 should be approached as a complete corporate compliance closure exercise rather than merely filing AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. The process covers finalisation and audit of financial statements, Board approval, Board’s Report, AGM, annual financial-statement and annual-return filings, auditor-related filings, DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital, charges, related-party transactions and other event-based compliances. The FY 2025-26 cycle is particularly significant because the small-company thresholds were enhanced with effect from 1 December 2025 to ₹10 crore paid-up capital and ₹100 crore turnover, while the director KYC framework moved from annual compliance to a three-year cycle effective 31 March 2026. Companies should therefore reassess MGT-7/MGT-7A applicability, XBRL applicability, MGT-8 requirements and the applicable DIR-3 KYC cycle rather than relying on older checklists. AOC-4 should reconcile with the signed financial statements, while MGT-7/MGT-7A should agree with statutory registers, share capital records and MCA master data. Similar reconciliations should be undertaken for borrowings and DPT-3, MSME dues and MSME-1, related-party transactions, charges, CSR and share capital. The article also highlights the distinction between additional filing fees and statutory penalties, potential director-disqualification consequences, the continuing obligations of companies with no business activity, and the increasing importance of consistency between books, GST returns, Income-tax filings and MCA records. The recommended professional approach is Review → Reconcile → Identify Exceptions → Rectify → Approve → File, ensuring that annual ROC filings are the final output of a broader annual corporate compliance review. rows.summary:
This document says annual ROC compliance for FY 2025-26 should be treated as a full corporate compliance closure process, not just the filing of AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. It starts with finalising and auditing the financial statements, obtaining Board approval, preparing the Board’s Report, holding the AGM, and then filing the financial statements and annual return with the ROC; the same annual review should also cover auditor filings, DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital, charges, related-party transactions, loans/guarantees/investments, and other event-based filings. The document specifically warns that the FY 2025-26 cycle is more complex because MCA has raised the small-company thresholds effective 1 December 2025 to paid-up capital of ₹10 crore and turnover of ₹100 crore, which means companies should re-test whether they qualify for MGT-7A, XBRL exemptions/applicability, and whether MGT-8 certification applies, rather than relying on prior-year checklists.

A major change highlighted is director KYC: from FY 2025-26 onward, the framework moves from annual compliance to a three-year cycle, effective 31 March 2026. Companies therefore need to determine which directors are due for DIR-3 KYC under the new cycle and cannot assume annual filing for all directors as before. The document also emphasizes that AOC-4 must reconcile exactly with the signed financial statements, while MGT-7/MGT-7A must agree with statutory registers, share capital records, and MCA master data; similar reconciliations should be done for borrowings against DPT-3, MSME dues against MSME-1, related-party transactions, charges, CSR spend/obligations, and share capital changes.

The compliance approach recommended is to perform a structured annual review using the sequence: Review → Reconcile → Identify Exceptions → Rectify → Approve → File. The article stresses that annual ROC filings are only the final output of that broader review, and that companies should also check consistency across books of account, GST returns, Income-tax filings, and MCA records because discrepancies are increasingly being scrutinized through MCA21 V3 and data matching. It further notes that companies with no business activity still have ongoing ROC obligations, and that being a small company does not eliminate compliance requirements, only changes some filing forms and thresholds.

The document also distinguishes between additional filing fees and statutory penalties, and warns that certain defaults can create more serious consequences such as director disqualification. In practical terms, compliance officers should use this as a directive to reassess the company’s filing obligations for FY 2025-26 in light of the new small-company limits, the new DIR-3 KYC cycle, and the need for end-to-end reconciliation before AGM-related and ROC filings are signed off.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Calcutta HC Allows Extension of ITC Rectification Time Under Section 16(5)
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12643 Case Name Umen Chandra Roy Vs Union of India (Calcutta High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Calcutta High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Umen Chandra Roy Vs Union of India (Calcutta High Court) Summary: The Calcutta High Court, Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri, considered a writ petition concerning the petitioner’s claim to avail Input Tax Credit under Section 39 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with Sub-Section 5 to Section 16. The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the Court noted was within the statutory cut-off contemplated under Section 16(5). The petitioner thereafter filed a rectification application on January 12, 2026 concerning the benefit of the ITC facility. The judgment records that the petitioner’s rectification application was rejected by the revenue authority by order dated April 8, 2026. The rejection proceeded on the basis that the application had not been filed within the stipulated period referred to in the departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024 read with the circular dated October 15, 2024. The judgment itself records the applicable period in paragraph 3 as “six weeks”; however, the subsequent correction order dated August 21, 2026 expressly states that this expression was to be corrected to “six months” and that “communication” was to be corrected as “circular”. The petitioner argued that the prescribed period could be extended because Sub-Section 5 to Section 16 did not itself prescribe a time limit for filing the rectification application. The revenue, on the other hand, submitted that the order in original dated March 6, 2024 had been served upon the petitioner on the same day by post and therefore disputed statemen
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court (Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri) held that a taxpayer’s right under Section 16(5) of the CGST Act to seek rectification for availing Input Tax Credit is a substantive statutory right, and that the provision itself does **not** prescribe a filing deadline for the rectification application. The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to **30 November 2021** and later submitted a rectification application on **12 January 2026**; the revenue rejected that application by order dated **8 April 2026**, relying on timing limits said to arise from a departmental circular/notification dated **8 April 2024** read with a circular dated **15 October 2024**. The Court found that those executive time limits could not override the statute, characterized the departmental timeline as **directory rather than mandatory**, and held that—depending on the facts and absent exceptional delay—the High Court can use its **Article 226** writ jurisdiction to extend the period where Section 16(5) does not itself impose one.

As a result, the Court **quashed and set aside** the rejection order dated **8 April 2026** and directed the appropriate jurisdictional authority to **reconsider the already-filed rectification application** strictly in accordance with law and pass a **reasoned order within eight weeks** of receiving the judgment. The Court expressly said it was **not deciding the merits** of the taxpayer’s ITC claim, and that the authority remained free to reject or allow the application on its own merits; it also cautioned that the order did **not create any equitable right** if the taxpayer is ultimately not entitled to relief under law. The judgment was disposed of **without costs**.

A later correction order, issued by consent of the parties, amended the original judgment dated **17 August 2026** by changing “**six weeks**” to “**six months**,” “**communication**” to “**circular**,” correcting the advocate’s name in paragraph 5 to **Dhiraj Lakhotia**, replacing references to “**notification**” with “**circular**” in paragraph 5, and changing “**section**” to “**Article**” in paragraph 10; the correction order stated that the rest of the judgment remained unchanged. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that where Section 16(5) creates a rectification-based pathway to claim ITC but does not specify a deadline, the Court treated departmental circular-based timing constraints as non-absolute and capable of extension on a case-by-case basis, so taxpayers facing similar ITC rectification issues should preserve the underlying statutory eligibility, documentary record, and service/communication history and be prepared to justify delayed filings if relying on this ruling.

Year: 2007-08 : iii.Whether the Appellate Tribunal is correct in holding that deemed dividend has to be assessed only in t
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court’s 27 March 2017 judgment concerned Revenue appeals under Section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 against a common ITAT order dated 12 May 2016 for Assessment Years 2007–08 and 2010–11. The Court held that the Revenue’s questions on deduction under Section 80IA(4) for a Container Freight Station were not admissible, because identical issues had already been decided against the Revenue in earlier Madras High Court rulings in *CIT v. A.L. Logistics Pvt. Ltd.* and had also followed the Delhi High Court’s view in *Container Corporation of India Ltd. v. ACIT*; the Revenue’s argument that the Delhi case was under Supreme Court appeal did not change that result. In practical terms, for entities claiming 80IA(4) infrastructure-facility deductions for Container Freight Station operations, the Court reaffirmed the existing favorable position and declined to reopen the issue in these appeals.

The second issue, applicable to AY 2007–08, involved whether a capital advance of Rs. 1,09,50,000 received by the assessee-company from Indev Logistics Pvt. Ltd. could be taxed as deemed dividend because the two companies had common shareholders. The Court recited the shareholding pattern: in the assessee-company, Mr. Xavier Britto held 50% and Smt. Vimalarani Britto held 50%; in Indev Logistics Pvt. Ltd., Mr. Xavier Britto held 60% and Smt. Vimalarani Britto held 40%. The Revenue’s theory was that the advance was effectively for the benefit of common shareholders holding more than 10% in both companies, and therefore should be assessed as deemed dividend, even though the assessee-company itself was not the registered shareholder of the lending company. The document excerpt ends while stating the Revenue’s position, so the final outcome on Questions 3 and 4 is not shown in the provided text.

rows.summary:
The Chartered Accountants Association, Jalandhar has made a representation to the Finance Minister requesting an extension of filing deadlines for AY 2026-27, specifically for Tax Audit Reports (TAR), Forms 10B/10BB, other audit-related reports/forms, and the corresponding income-tax return deadlines for audit cases. The association says it supports the newly introduced separate due date of 31 August 2026 for business taxpayers not liable to audit, but argues that this has compressed the compliance window for taxpayers and professionals handling audit cases because August and September are now overloaded with overlapping filing work.

The document states the current due dates for AY 2026-27 as: 31 August 2026 for business non-audit ITRs, 30 September 2026 for Tax Audit Reports, 31 October 2026 for audit ITRs other than transfer pricing cases, and 30 November 2026 for ITRs with TP reports. It also highlights that this structure leaves only one month between the Tax Audit Report deadline and the audit-case ITR deadline, while audit and reporting workloads have increased. A key factual basis for the request is the delayed release of ITR forms and utilities in the current year: ITR-3 on 18 June 2026, ITR-5 on 7 July 2026, ITR-7 on 9 July 2026, and ITR-6 only on 4 August 2026, with online utilities following 15–20 days later, further shortening the practical time available for compliance.

The association additionally says non-corporate assessees now face a mandatory, more detailed financial-statement format implemented by ICAI, similar to corporate reporting, which requires substantially more granular disclosures and also verification/authentication by Chartered Accountants. According to the representation, this has significantly increased the time needed for compilation, reconciliation, and professional review during an already tight audit season. On that basis, the association asks for three forms of relief: moving the Tax Audit Report due date from 30 September 2026 to 31 October 2026, extending Forms 10B/10BB and other audit-related report deadlines correspondingly, or alternatively aligning the Tax Audit Report and audit-case ITR due dates at 31 October 2026. The request expressly says it is not intended to delay tax payment or obtain any undue benefit, but only to allow accurate completion of statutory filings after proper audit and verification.

rows.title: Income Tax | Bombay HC Upholds Deduction for Scientifically Estimated Major Repairs Provision
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12641 Case Name PCIT Vs ECA Infrastructure India Pvt Ltd (Bombay High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Bombay High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs ECA Infrastructure India Pvt Ltd (Bombay High Court) Summary: The Bombay High Court rejected the Revenue’s appeal under Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, concerning Assessment Year 2015-16 and the allowability of a provision for major repairs made by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt Ltd. The Revenue challenged the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai order dated 8 February 2023, which had dismissed the Revenue’s appeal against the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Pune order dated 23 March 2022. The assessee was a special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction on Build Operate Transfer (BOT) basis and collection of toll. For AY 2015-16, it returned a book loss of Rs.4,48,91,467/- and an income-tax loss of Rs.8,46,64,672/-. The Assessing Officer made an addition of Rs.7,47,00,000/- by disallowing the provision for major repairs. The assessee relied upon its BOT agreement with the Government of Maharashtra, under which it had a 30-year concession and was contractually required to undertake major repairs during the concession period. The first major repair was to be undertaken after seven years, i.e. during the eighth year, while the last major repair was required in the 30th year. The assessee contended that the liability accrued over the period and that the expenditure could be provided for on the basis of reliable estimates. It also relied upon CBDT Circular No. 9/2014 concerning expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT agreements. The CIT(Appeals) examined the Concession Agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38 and 39, and
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court upheld the deduction for a provision for major repairs claimed by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. for Assessment Year 2015–16 and dismissed the Revenue’s Section 260A appeal, holding that no substantial question of law arose. The assessee was a special purpose vehicle engaged in BOT road construction and toll collection under a 30-year concession agreement with the Government of Maharashtra, and the agreement required it to carry out major maintenance/repairs during the concession period; the first such repair was due after seven years (in the eighth year) and the last in the 30th year. For AY 2015–16, the company reported a book loss of Rs. 4,48,91,467 and an income-tax loss of Rs. 8,46,64,672, while the Assessing Officer disallowed a provision of Rs. 7,47,00,000 toward major repairs as not actually incurred.  

The Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) had allowed the claim after examining the concession agreement and related maintenance manual, including Articles 17, 37, 38 and 39, and found that the assessee had a present contractual obligation to perform major maintenance, with non-compliance potentially leading to termination and retention of amounts by the Government. The CIT(A) also accepted the assessee’s scientific estimate of the liability, which was based on detailed quantities of materials such as bitumen, concrete and thermoplastic compound, and on an estimated total repair cost of Rs. 22,26,47,178. The Tribunal affirmed this view, relying on Supreme Court precedent such as Bharat Earth Movers and Rotork Controls, and held that a business liability can be deducted when it has definitely arisen and can be estimated with reasonable certainty, even if it will be discharged later.  

The High Court agreed that the liability was not merely contingent but was directly linked to the assessee’s BOT road business and had accrued under the contract, so a realistic and scientifically determined provision could not be disallowed under Section 37 merely because payment would occur in the future. The Court also noted that the assessee later incurred Rs. 17,89,48,545 on major repairs in FY 2019–20 against an opening provision of Rs. 16,19,64,943, and that similar provisions in subsequent assessment years had not been disallowed in scrutiny. Accordingly, the Revenue’s appeal was rejected, the lower orders were sustained, and no costs were awarded. For compliance purposes, the decision supports recognition of a provision for contractually mandated, reasonably estimable future maintenance expenses in BOT road projects where the obligation is already fixed by agreement and supported by a scientific basis, rather than requiring actual cash outflow before deduction is claimed.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12640 Case Name Pankajam Plastics Vs Muthiah Athinarayanan & Ors (GSTAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT, National Anti-Profiteering Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pankajam Plastics Vs Muthiah Athinarayanan & Ors (GSTAT Chennai) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench considered whether Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 filed by Pankajam Plastics was maintainable when the appeal before the First Appellate Authority had not yet resulted in an order. The Appellant/Applicant submitted that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in APL-01 and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, stating that the Department was undertaking recovery proceedings. The Respondent-State Government drew the Bench’s attention to its submissions dated 28.07.2026 and, particularly, to APL-02, which had been rejected on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, being the First Appellate Authority. The Registry raised a defect because the GSTAT appeal had been filed before the rejection order of the First Appellate Authority came into existence. After hearing both sides and examining the records, the Bench found that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 had been filed on 19.03.2026, whereas no order under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 was then in existence because the First Appellate Authority had not yet passed its order. The central question before the Bench was whether an aggrieved person could approach GSTAT under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 in the absence of an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108. The Bench reproduced the substance of Section 112(1), under which an aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order passed unde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that an appeal to GSTAT is **not maintainable if it is filed before the First Appellate Authority has passed an order under Section 107 or 108 of the CGST Act, 2017**. In this case, Pankajam Plastics filed GSTAT Filing No. **2026133/10100/0064** on **19.03.2026**, while also saying it had filed the first appeal (APL-01) the same day because the department had begun recovery proceedings. However, the Tribunal found that **no order of the First Appellate Authority existed on 19.03.2026**, and the relevant APL-02 rejection/order by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals (the First Appellate Authority) was issued only on **24.06.2026**, well after the GSTAT filing.

The Tribunal focused on the wording of **Section 112(1)**, which permits an aggrieved person to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal only against **an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108**. Because the first appellate order had not yet been passed when the GSTAT appeal was filed, the filing was held to be **outside the statutory scheme** and therefore invalid as filed. The Bench therefore answered the maintainability question **against the applicant/appellant**, held the appeal **not maintainable**, and **dismissed** it.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that **GSTAT appeals must be filed only after the relevant first appellate order exists**; filing in anticipation of an adverse order, even if recovery proceedings are underway, will not satisfy Section 112(1). The Tribunal did, however, grant **liberty to the appellant to file an appeal before GSTAT in accordance with law**, meaning a fresh appeal may still be possible once the statutory precondition is met.

According to the petitioner, the credit notes were declared through the e-invoice portal and the corresponding outward tax liability was adjusted against sales effected during previous months/financial years. It contended that this reduced its output tax liability but did not result in any short payment of tax because the liability had ultimately been discharged. The petitioner referred
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court considered a GST recovery dispute involving Best Agrolife Limited and a notice dated 25/03/2025 that required payment of tax and interest within seven days, warning that if payment was not made, recovery proceedings would be started under Section 79 of the Maharashtra GST Act, 2017. Best Agrolife did not pay; instead, it replied by email on 11/04/2025 saying it had issued credit notes under Section 34 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with Rule 53 of the CGST Rules, 2017 for returned goods and rate differences, had declared those credit notes through the e-invoice portal, and had adjusted the corresponding outward tax liability against sales from earlier months/financial years. It argued that this meant there was no actual short payment because the output tax liability had ultimately been discharged, and it supported this with a GSTN “Tax Liability Report” for April 2022 to February 2025 and a “NEGATIVE LIABILITY STATEMENT” for 01/09/2024 to 27/03/2025 showing negative sales/negative liability carried forward and automatically adjusted against later liability. The petitioner also relied on Notification No. 12/2024 – Central Tax dated 10/07/2024, saying the reporting facility from September 2024 onward was intended to improve reconciliation, and complained that the Revenue ignored its representations made in April 2025, May 2025, October 2025, and later in 2025.

The Revenue nonetheless issued recovery notices under Section 79, including a notice to ICICI Bank on 18/07/2025 and later notices to State Bank of India, Akola Branch dated 26/02/2026 and State Bank of India, New Delhi Branch dated 09/03/2026. Best Agrolife sought interim relief from the Court against these recovery actions, but the Court refused it because the petitioner had not acted promptly: the Court held that once the 25/03/2025 notice expressly warned of Section 79 recovery after seven days, the petitioner should have approached the Court in April or May 2025, not much later. The Court therefore rejected interim relief on the ground of unjustified delay, but it did not decide the underlying GST merits or whether the tax demand was correct. At the same time, the Court issued notice to the respondents, returnable on 10/04/2026, and specifically asked the Revenue to explain why the petitioner’s representation was not considered and why recovery action was not taken immediately after the seven-day period expired.

rows.title: Income Tax | Pune ITAT Restores ₹1.73-Crore Penalty U/s 271(1)(c) on Capital Expenditure Claim
rows.desc: IN THE INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL PUNE BENCH “B”, PUNE BEFORE SHRI INTURI RAMA RAO, ACCOUNTANT MEMBER AND SHRI S. S. VISWANETHRA RAVI, JUDICIAL MEMBER . / ITA No.386/PUN/2020 ᭅ ᭅ / Assessment Year : 2014-15 ITO, Ward-7(1), Pune. Vs. M/s. Sarsan Developers, 14A & B, Elephinstone Stone, Opp. East Street Post Office, Camp, Pune- 411001. PAN : ABJFS4506M Appellant Respondent / ORDER PER INTURI RAMA RAO, AM: This is an appeal filed by the Revenue directed against the order of ld. Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals)-8, Pune [‘the CIT(A)’] dated 13.12.2019 for the assessment year 2014-15. 2. Briefly, the facts of the case are that the assessee is a partnership firm engaged in the business of development of lands. The Return of Income for the assessment year 2014-15 was filed on 29.11.2014 declaring Rs.Nil income. Against the said return of income, the assessment was completed by the Income Tax Officer, Revenue by : Shri M. G. Jasnani Assessee by : Shri Kishor Phadke Shir Suhas P. Bora Date of hearing : 08.09.2023 Date of pronouncement : 10.10.2023 ITA No.386/PUN/2020 2 Ward-7(1), Pune (‘the Assessing Officer’) vide order dated 23.12.2016 passed u/s 143(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’) at a total income of Rs.Nil after making addition of Rs.5,60,73,319/- being the amount paid to be retiring partner, namely, Kumar Housing Corporation Limited. The factual background of the case is as under : During the previous year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, the assessee firm debited development expenses of Rs.13,40,50,885/- which includes an amount of Rs.5,60,73,319/- paid to retiring partner, namely, Kumar Housing Corporation Limited. The factual background of the issue was explained by the assessee vide his letter dated 30.11.2016, which is extracted by the Assessing Officer vide para no.4.1 of the assessment order, which reads as under :- “Sarsan Developers Private Limited (SDPL) and Kumar Housing Corporation Limited (KHCL) had entered into an agre
rows.summary:
For assessment year 2014–15, the Pune ITAT in **ITO, Ward-7(1), Pune v. M/s. Sarsan Developers** restored a large disallowance/penalty-related tax consequence arising from the assessee’s claim of a **₹5,60,73,319 payment to an outgoing partner** as deductible business expenditure. The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in land development, had filed its return on **29.11.2014** declaring **nil income**, but in assessment under **section 143(3)** dated **23.12.2016**, the Assessing Officer added the amount paid to the retiring partner, **Kumar Housing Corporation Limited (KHCL)**, and treated it as not allowable under **section 37(1)**, effectively increasing closing work-in-progress rather than allowing an immediate deduction. The factual basis was that Sarsan Developers and KHCL had formed a registered firm, **Sarsan Kumar Developers (SKD)**, on **21.10.2006** to develop a Pune property, but due to a weak market between **2009 and 2013**, the project stalled; under the partnership deed’s **Clause 16**, compensation was payable if a partner exited before project completion at market rate, and the assessee stated it paid **₹10,000** against fixed capital, **₹1,22,25,442** against current capital, **₹78,26,720** for the period **01.04.2013 to 01.08.2013**, and an additional **₹4,99,90,000** as exit/settlement cost, totaling **₹5,60,73,319**. The assessee’s position was that this amount was a project-related settlement cost transferred to capital work-in-progress and should, if not immediately deductible, be amortized/revenue-expensed when sales commenced; it also projected the project would yield about **48,000 sq. ft.** of saleable area and approximately **₹72 crore** in revenue at an average realization of **₹15,000 per sq. ft.**

The **CIT(A)** reversed the Assessing Officer and held that **section 45(4)** did not apply, so the payment should be allowed as **revenue expenditure** rather than being capitalized. On Revenue’s appeal, the ITAT examined the settlement deed and the surrounding facts and ultimately **restored the tax authority’s treatment adverse to the assessee**, concluding that the amount paid in connection with the retiring partner’s exit was not allowable as a current revenue deduction under the assessee’s claimed theory. For compliance purposes, the key point is that amounts paid to remove or settle with a partner in a project-development partnership can be recharacterized as capital/project costs rather than deductible operating expenses, especially where the payment is tied to withdrawal from a development venture and is connected to capital formation or settlement of partnership rights. There were no new procedural filing deadlines announced in the order, but the case underscores the need for careful documentation of partner exit payments, the contractual basis for compensation, and the tax treatment of such amounts in project accounts and returns, because the revenue authorities challenged the deduction and the tribunal sided against the assessee’s revenue-expense characterization.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12642 Case Name Ekviradevi Gramin Bigarsheti Sahakari Patsanstha Maryadit Vs ITO (ITAT, Pune Bench) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Pune Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Following the jurisdictional Bombay High Court decision in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd., the Tribunal held that the AO could not independently assess an altogether different item after abandoning the very issue for which reassessment jurisdiction had been assumed. Reopening Triggered by Cash & Time Deposits The assessee was a co-operative credit society. It had not filed its return of income for AY 2018-19, reportedly because its audit report was not received in time. Information available on the Insight Portal indicated that the assessee had made cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 in The RDCC Urban Bank and had also invested ₹55,50,000 in time deposits. Since no return had been filed, the AO formed the view that these transactions aggregating to ₹1,47,36,100 represented income that had escaped assessment. After issuing a show-cause notice u/s 148A(b), the AO passed an order u/s 148A(d) on 07.04.2022. The AO recorded that the cash deposits & time deposits remained undisclosed and constituted information sug
rows.summary:
The Pune ITAT quashed the reassessment of Ekviradevi Gramin Bigarsheti Sahakari Patsanstha Maryadit for AY 2018-19 because the Assessing Officer (AO) reopened the case only to examine alleged undisclosed cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 and time deposits of ₹55,50,000 in The RDCC Urban Bank, totaling ₹1,47,36,100, but ultimately made no addition on those transactions. The reopening had been initiated through a notice under section 148A(b), followed by an order under section 148A(d) dated 07.04.2022, and then a notice under section 148 on the same date, on the basis that these deposits appeared to be escaped income.  

During the reassessment completed on 20.03.2024 under section 147 read with section 144B, the AO abandoned the original deposit issue and instead disallowed the assessee’s deduction claim of ₹7,06,146 under section 80P(2)(a)(i). The CIT(A)-NFAC upheld that disallowance, but the Tribunal held that this was legally impermissible because the income that formed the recorded basis for reopening was never actually assessed or reassessed.  

Relying on the Bombay High Court’s decision in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd. and supporting authorities such as Ranbaxy Laboratories and Mohmed Juned Dadani, the ITAT reaffirmed that section 147 does not permit a “roving” reassessment on an unrelated issue once the original reason for reopening falls away. In other words, the AO must first assess the very income that justified the reopening; only then can any other escaped income noticed during the proceedings also be brought to tax.  

Because the AO accepted the assessee’s explanation on the cash and time deposits and made no addition on those items, the reassessment lacked jurisdiction once it was used solely to disallow the section 80P deduction instead. The Tribunal therefore quashed the entire reassessment and the resulting addition. This decision is mainly relevant for tax compliance and audit teams of co-operative societies and similar assessees: if a reopening notice is issued for one specific item, the department cannot lawfully complete the reassessment only on a different, unrelated issue unless it first taxes the originally recorded escaped income or starts a fresh reassessment proceeding.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Finds Nil Profiteering as Cost Escalation Offsets GST ITC Benefit
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12635 Case Name DGAP Vs Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. (GSTAT) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT, National Anti-Profiteering Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DGAP Vs Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. (GSTAT) The proceedings arose from an application filed by Sh. Abhilash Mohanty alleging that M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. had failed to pass on the benefit of Input Tax Credit (ITC) to homebuyers in its “Vertex Panache” project following the introduction of GST from 01.07.2017, thereby contravening Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering referred the matter to the DGAP, which initially reported profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, comprising a base profiteered amount of Rs. 65,17,866/- and GST of Rs. 7,82,144/-, allegedly required to be passed on to 140 eligible homebuyers. The Respondent contended that substantial escalation in construction costs had materially offset the additional ITC benefit. The budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/-, whereas actual expenditure amounted to Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, resulting in an overall cost increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost. The Respondent specifically identified increases of 19.87% in Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), 62.98% in Sand and 73.17% in Bricks. Based on actual quantities consumed and costs incurred, the additional expenditure attributable to these major inputs was stated to be Rs. 3,49,87,499/-. The Respondent relied upon the Delhi High Court judgment in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, particularly paragraph 118, concerning price increases based on genuine commercial factors despite reduction in tax or availability of ITC. The Respondent also produced a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co.
rows.summary:
This case concerned an anti-profiteering allegation under Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017, arising from a complaint by a homebuyer in Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd.’s residential project “Vertex Panache” in Kokapet, Hyderabad. The complainant alleged that after GST came into force on 01.07.2017, the developer did not pass on the benefit of additional Input Tax Credit (ITC) through a commensurate price reduction for the unit purchased, which triggered an investigation by the Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering and then the DGAP under Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017.  

The DGAP’s original report dated 27.08.2025 had found profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, made up of Rs. 65,17,866/- as the base profiteered amount and Rs. 7,82,144/- as GST, allegedly attributable to 140 eligible homebuyers. Vertex Homes contested that conclusion by arguing that construction costs had risen substantially and had offset the GST/ITC benefit; it said its budgeted construction cost was Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/- but actual expenditure was Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, an increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- overall including indirect costs. It specifically pointed to sharp increases in key material inputs—RMC up 19.87%, sand up 62.98%, and bricks up 73.17%—and said the additional expenditure attributable to those major inputs alone was Rs. 3,49,87,499/-.  

In support, the respondent relied on a Chartered Accountant’s certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co. LLP and on the Delhi High Court’s reasoning in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, which recognizes that genuine commercial cost increases can affect anti-profiteering calculations. In its clarification dated 30.07.2026, the DGAP accepted the claimed additional expenditure after verifying the certificate and sample invoices, and revised its computation accordingly. On that revised basis, total ITC-related savings were Rs. 2,47,02,175/-, but cost escalation of Rs. 3,49,87,499/- exceeded those savings, producing negative net savings of Rs. 1,02,85,324/- and therefore nil profiteering.  

The Tribunal accepted the DGAP’s revised methodology and concluded that the respondent had demonstrated genuine cost escalation in major construction materials, verified by the DGAP, sufficient to fully absorb the benefit of additional ITC. It held that the revised approach—subtracting proven cost increases from the ITC benefit—was legally sound, found no contravention of Section 171 of the CGST Act, and disposed of the matter with a finding of “Nil” profiteering. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that GST/ITC anti-profiteering exposure in real estate can be negated where a developer can substantiate that bona fide construction cost escalation offset the tax benefit, but that conclusion depended here on documentary support, CA certification, and DGAP verification.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12634 Case Name DGAP Vs Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd. (GSTAT) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT, National Anti-Profiteering Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. (GSTAT) The proceedings arose from a complaint filed by Shri Rohit Kumar Agrawal alleging that M/s Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd. failed to pass on the benefit of reduction in GST rate from 28% to 18% on “MI LED Television 4A 80 cm” with effect from 01.01.2019, pursuant to Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31.12.2018. The matter was referred by the Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering to the DGAP under Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017. The DGAP examined invoices and outward taxable supply details for the pre-rate-reduction period from 01.11.2018 to 31.12.2018 and the post-rate-reduction period from 01.01.2019 to 31.12.2019 and initially determined profiteering of Rs. 7,79,947/-. Following cessation of the National Anti-Profiteering Authority, the matter was transferred through the Competition Commission of India to the GST Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal directed the Respondent to establish that the profiteered amount had been refunded to affected customers. The Respondent submitted Electronic Gift Voucher (EGV) screenshots, an Excel mapping of vouchers to customer orders and invoices, and subsequently credit notes. The DGAP initially objected that the EGVs were conditional, time-bound and restricted and that their system description, “Offers and cash back”, did not establish that the GST benefit had been passed on. The DGAP accepted credit notes of Rs. 2,21,056/- issued to 174 customers whose orders had been cancelled or goods returned. After this adjustment, the profiteering amount was revised to Rs. 5,58,891/-. The Respondent contended th
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal held that Electronic Gift Vouchers (EGVs) can constitute a valid and direct mode of passing on GST rate-reduction benefit under Section 171 of the CGST Act, provided they are credited to customers without expiry, are not tied to purchase of a particular product or category, and can be used broadly across the platform. The case arose from a complaint that Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd. did not pass on the benefit of the GST rate cut on “MI LED Television 4A 80 cm” from 28% to 18%, effective 1 January 2019, under Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31 December 2018; the DGAP had examined invoices and outward supplies for 1 November 2018 to 31 December 2018 versus 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019 and initially quantified profiteering at ₹7,79,947. After the Respondent produced voucher screenshots, order/invoice mapping, and credit notes, the DGAP accepted credit notes of ₹2,21,056 issued to 174 customers for cancelled or returned orders and revised the alleged profiteering to ₹5,58,891.

The Tribunal rejected the DGAP’s argument that the EGVs were ineffective because they were described in the system as “Offers and cash back,” holding that nomenclature does not control where the underlying credits can be traced to specific customer orders, invoices, dates, prices, and the GST-linked differential. It emphasized that the EGVs were activated into customer wallets, had no expiry, were unrestricted in use across the platform, and therefore represented monetary value standing to the customer’s credit; this was treated as a direct and unconditional transfer of the benefit, distinguishable from the Delhi High Court’s Reckitt Benckiser decision because the present case involved actual wallet credits rather than indirect discounting or promotional schemes. The Respondent stated that EGVs totaling ₹5,48,650 had been issued to 488 customers, of which ₹3,17,965 had already been used by 291 customers and ₹2,30,685 remained available in e-wallets.

On reconciliation, the Tribunal found a shortfall of ₹10,241 between the DGAP’s revised profiteering figure of ₹5,58,891 and the EGVs issued of ₹5,48,650. Because the Respondent could not identify any corresponding customer or invoice for that residual amount, it accepted the Respondent’s offer to deposit the difference into the Central Consumer Welfare Fund. The Tribunal therefore directed deposit of ₹10,241 into the Fund and also ordered interest at 18% under Rule 133(3)(c) of the CGST Rules, calculated from the date the higher amount was collected until the date of deposit. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that voucher-based transfers can satisfy anti-profiteering obligations if they are unconditional, traceable, and usable by customers, but any unreconciled balance must still be deposited with statutory interest.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | 57th GST Council Meeting Rescheduled to October 7, 2026: Legal Analysis

The 57th GST Council Meeting, originally notified for September 12, 2026, in New Delhi, has been rescheduled to October 7, 2026, through a formal Office Memorandum issued by the GST Council Secretariat. The Officers’ Meeting will now be held on October 5 and 6, 2026, in New Delhi, while the 57th GST Council Meeting will be convened on October 7, 2026, under the chairpersonship of Union Finance Minister Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman. The postponement has been attributed to India’s hosting of the BRICS Leaders’ Summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, 2026, with the scale of security, protocol, and administrative arrangements making it impracticable to concurrently host the GST Council Meeting. The rescheduling does not alter the Council’s constitutional mandate, composition, or decision-making framework. The forthcoming meeting assumes significance following the 56th GST Council Meeting held on September 3–4, 2025, and the subsequent GST rate restructuring. Issues reported to be under contemplation include simplification of GST registration procedures for businesses that pass on input tax credit exceeding ₹2.5 lakh per month. The postponement does not affect existing statutory compliance obligations, and practitioners are advised to continue monitoring official communications and use the additional time to refine representations and prepare for the October deliberations. rows.summary:
This SEBI adjudication order concerns India Asset Growth Fund (an AIF registered as IN/AIF2/12-13/0037), its manager Essel Finance Advisors and Managers LLP, several key employees, and its trustee Vistra ITCL (India) Limited, after SEBI inspected the fund’s books and records on November 14–15, 2022 for the period April 1, 2021 to March 31, 2022. SEBI sent its inspection findings on October 30, 2023, and the fund responded on December 19, 2023 and March 13, 2024; after review, SEBI concluded there were alleged violations of the AIF Regulations and related circulars, and an adjudicating officer was appointed on May 7, 2024, later transferred to a new officer on November 22, 2024. A show cause notice was issued on June 19, 2024 under Rule 4(1) of the Adjudication Rules and Section 15-I of the SEBI Act, proposing penalties under Section 15EB.

The order states that the fund allegedly failed to disclose key disciplinary and litigation information to investors in its placement memorandum and related disclosures, including the disciplinary history of the sponsor, manager, trustee, their directors/partners/promoters/associates, and a pending matter with the Income Tax Department; SEBI also alleged a failure to disclose disciplinary action history against the trustee. These omissions were treated as non-compliance with Regulations 11(2), 20(1), 20(2), and 20(5) of the AIF Regulations, read with Clause 2(a)(ii) of SEBI circular CIR/IMD/DF/14/2014 dated June 19, 2014 and the Code of Conduct in the Fourth Schedule. SEBI also alleged that the fund, manager, KMPs, and trustee failed to wind up the scheme when required: the scheme continued for 2 years and 5 months beyond the permissible period, despite the regulatory framework allowing only the prescribed extensions of two years in total (described in the order as “1+1”), which SEBI treated as a violation of Regulations 13(4), 20(1), 20(2), 20(5), and 29(1)(a), along with several Code of Conduct provisions.

A further allegation is that the fund used the value of assets owned by portfolio investee companies rather than valuing the securities/units held by the fund itself, indicating a valuation methodology issue for AIF reporting and investor valuation purposes. The excerpt cuts off before the full description of that issue and any final findings or penalties, but the compliance significance is that SEBI viewed these as serious control failures affecting disclosure integrity, valuation accuracy, trustee/manager oversight, and timely winding up of AIF schemes. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaways are that AIFs must ensure full and timely disclosure of disciplinary and litigation history in offering documents and investor communications, must strictly monitor scheme tenure and mandatory winding-up timelines, and must apply the correct valuation basis to fund holdings rather than relying on the underlying investee companies’ asset values.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ravi Kumar Gollapudi Vs DCIT (ITAT, Hyderabad Bench) Interest Paid Today, Interest Received Tomorrow: Cash System u/s 145(1) Cannot Defeat Deduction u/s 57(iii), but Nexus Must Pass the Test—Hyderabad ITAT Remands ₹13.66 Lakh Disallowance The controversy The Hyderabad Bench of the ITAT examined whether interest expenditure incurred on borrowed funds could be disallowed merely because the interest actually received during the year was lower than the interest paid. The assessee contended that he regularly followed the cash system of accounting & had received the balance interest in subsequent years. The Tribunal held that recognition of interest income on actual receipt basis is permissible u/s 145(1). Therefore, a mismatch between interest paid & interest received in a particular year cannot, by itself, justify complete disallowance. However, deduction u/s 57(iii) would be available only after establishing a direct nexus between the borrowed funds, the interest-bearing advance & the corresponding income offered to tax. Interest expenditure against income from other sources The assessee, Shri Ravi Kumar Gollapudi, filed his return for AY 2018-19 declaring a total income of ₹30,33,940. His case was selected for limited scrutiny & notice u/s 143(2) was issued. During assessment proceedings, the AO noticed that the assessee had claimed interest expenditure of ₹65,47,089 against interest income of ₹58,81,505 offered under the head “Income from other sources.” In the preceding year, the assessee had reported interest income of ₹65,26,481, while the interest expend
rows.summary:
The ITAT Hyderabad held that an assessee who regularly follows the cash system of accounting can recognize interest income only on actual receipt under section 145(1), so a year-to-year mismatch between interest paid and interest received does not by itself justify disallowing the interest expense. However, the Tribunal also held that deduction of interest expenditure against “income from other sources” under section 57(iii) is allowed only if the assessee proves that the borrowed money was laid out wholly and exclusively for earning that income, meaning a direct nexus must be shown between the borrowing, the onward advance, and the interest income taxed.

For AY 2018-19, Ravi Kumar Gollapudi had declared total income of ₹30,33,940. In assessment, the AO noted interest expenditure of ₹65,47,089 against interest income of ₹58,81,505, including a fresh loan of ₹3,25,32,284 from M/s IIFL on which interest of ₹13,65,835 was paid; the AO disallowed that ₹13,65,835 because the assessee did not prove that the IIFL loan was used to earn the interest income, and also made an additional addition of ₹7,07,021 merely because interest income had declined compared with the preceding year. The assessment was completed at ₹51,06,796.

The CIT(A) deleted the ₹7,07,021 addition tied to the decline in interest income but sustained the ₹13,65,835 disallowance. Before the Tribunal, the assessee claimed the IIFL funds were advanced to M/s Saket Engineering Pvt. Ltd. on interest, supported by a certificate from Saket Engineering and an Excel statement showing loans obtained, amounts advanced, and interest paid/received for AYs 2018-19 to 2020-21. He said that in AY 2018-19 he received ₹9,25,652 from Saket Engineering and paid ₹13,65,835 to IIFL because of the cash system, with the balance interest received and offered in AYs 2019-20 and 2020-21. The Tribunal accepted the legal proposition that cash-basis recognition of interest income is valid, but remanded the ₹13,65,835 issue because deduction still depends on factual proof of the direct nexus required by section 57(iii).

rows.summary:
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) dealt with a complaint by Smt. Rinima Borah Agarwal under Section 19(1)(a) of the Competition Act, 2002 against Mrs. India Inc., a sole proprietorship run by Smt. Mohini Sharma, alleging violations of Sections 3 and 4. By order dated 02.06.2026 under Section 26(1), the CCI had already directed the Director General (DG) to investigate the matter, and that investigation was still pending when the present interim applications were considered. The complainant’s interim application, IA No. 178A of 2025, sought immediate relief to stay enforcement of specific clauses in the Participant Terms and Conditions dated 23.10.2024 and the Winner’s Terms and Conditions dated 27.10.2024—specifically, clauses xxiii, xxviii, xxix, xxxiii, xxxiv, xxxv, xxxvi, xl, xli, l, lxiv and lxxviii of the Participant Terms, and clauses xiii, xv, xxvii, xx, xxi, xxii, xxiii, xxviii, xxxvii and lii of the Winner’s Terms. She also asked for an order restraining Mrs. India Inc. from sending any communication that would restrict or dissuade her from joining or participating in other competitions while the case was pending.

The CCI rejected the request for interim relief. It held that the reliefs sought were, in substance, final reliefs because granting them at the interim stage would effectively decide issues that were still under DG investigation, especially since the Commission had already formed only a prima facie view and not a final conclusion. Relying on the Supreme Court’s ruling in Competition Commission of India v. Steel Authority of India Ltd. (2010) 10 SCC 744, the CCI found that no case was made out for exercising its power under Section 33, and IA No. 178A of 2025 was disposed of. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that the challenged contractual restrictions remain under investigation but were not stayed by the CCI at this stage, so the order does not itself invalidate the clauses or provide affirmative relief to the complainant.

The CCI also considered IA No. 148 of 2026, dated 14.05.2026, in which the informant sought an opportunity of hearing before the decision on interim relief. The Commission held that Regulation 32 of the Competition Commission of India (General) Regulations, 2024 contemplates a hearing for the party against whom an interim order is made, but does not require a hearing for the informant before an interim-relief application is rejected, particularly where a DG investigation is already underway. That application was also disposed of. The CCI expressly stated that its observations were not a final expression on the merits and would not affect the DG investigation, and directed the Secretary to communicate the order to the informant and the DG.

rows.title: Corporate Law | DNA Evidence Establishes Paternity, Not Consent: Delhi HC Upholds Acquittal
rows.desc: Summary: The Delhi High Court, in KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr., upheld the acquittal of Respondent No. 2 and dismissed the complainant’s appeal. The Court held that a DNA report establishing biological paternity proves the fact of sexual intercourse but does not, by itself, establish whether the relationship was consensual. It considered the allegations of repeated sexual acts, threats, coercion and administration of an intoxicating substance, along with the DNA evidence. The Court examined the Trial Court’s assessment of inconsistencies in the complainant’s testimony, the delay in disclosure and reporting, the surrounding circumstances and the defence of a consensual relationship. Relying on the principles governing appeals against acquittal, including the Supreme Court’s decision in Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors., the Court held that an acquittal should not be disturbed where the Trial Court’s view is reasonably possible. Interference requires patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading or omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons. The Court also cautioned that the conduct of a complainant in a sexual-offence case cannot be assessed through stereotypical assumptions. It ultimately held that the gravity of an accusation cannot substitute the requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt. The Delhi High Court, in **KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.** (CRL.A. 320/2026; CRL.M.A. 10175/2026; Neutral Citation **2026:DHC:7451**), upheld the **acquittal of Respondent No. 2** and dismissed the complainant’s appeal. The appeal was brought by the complainant under **Section 419 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** against the Trial Court’s judgment acquitting the respondent of alleged offences under **Sections 328, 376(2)(n), 377, 506, and 509 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860**. The matter was heard by a **Single Judge Bench of Hon’ble Ms Justice Madhu Jain** in **hybrid mode**.

On the facts, the prosecution alleged that the complainant, who was married and had an adopted child, knew the respondent and that he had physical relations with her against her wishes through **threats, inducements, and coercion**; it was also alleged that on one occasion she was given an **intoxicating substance** before intercourse. She later became pregnant and gave birth to a child. During investigation, DNA samples of the complainant, the respondent, and the child were collected, and the forensic report concluded that the respondent was the child’s **biological father**. The complainant later disclosed the alleged incidents to her husband and family members, her statement was recorded under **Section 164 CrPC**, she was medically examined, and the police filed a charge sheet followed by a **supplementary charge sheet** placing the DNA report on record.

The High Court held that the DNA evidence established **biological paternity** and therefore supported the fact that sexual intercourse occurred, but it **did not by itself prove whether the relationship was consensual or non-consensual**. In reviewing the Trial Court’s decision, the High Court noted that the Trial Court had examined **inconsistencies in the complainant’s testimony, delay in disclosure and reporting, surrounding circumstances, and the defence theory of a consensual relationship**. Applying the settled principles governing interference with an acquittal, including the Supreme Court’s ruling in **Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors.**, the Court reiterated that an appellate court should not disturb an acquittal where the Trial Court’s view is **reasonably possible**; interference is justified only where there is **patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading or omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons**.

The Court also cautioned against assessing a complainant’s conduct in a sexual-offence case through **stereotypical assumptions**, but emphasized that the **gravity of an allegation cannot replace proof beyond reasonable doubt**. On that basis, it found no sufficient ground to overturn the Trial Court’s acquittal and dismissed the appeal.
