rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12636 Case Name Ahmed Altaf Sayeed Vs ITO (ITAT, Hyderabad Bench) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ahmed Altaf Sayeed Vs ITO (ITAT, Hyderabad Bench) Wrong Sanction Sinks Reassessment, Penalty Goes Down With the Ship: Hyderabad ITAT Quashes Penalty u/s 270A Where Notice u/s 148 Lacked Approval of Specified Authority u/s 151 The controversy The Hyderabad Bench of the ITAT dealt with an important question concerning whether an assessee, in an appeal against a penalty order u/s 270A, can challenge the legality of the underlying reassessment proceedings. The Tribunal held that where the reassessment order constitutes the very foundation of the penalty, its validity can be examined even in collateral penalty proceedings. Finding that the notice u/s 148 had been issued with the approval of an incompetent authority, the Tribunal quashed both the reassessment order & the consequential penalty. The assessee, Shri Ahmed Altaf Sayeed, had filed the appeal against the order of the CIT(A) confirming a penalty of ₹2,13,664 u/s 270A for AY 2018-19. Delay caused by professional lapse condoned There was a delay of 110 days in filing the appeal before the Tribunal. The assessee explained that he had entrusted the matter to his Chartered Accountant before travelling to Saudi Arabia for pilgrimage. He genuinely believed that the appeal would be filed within the prescribed period. However, owing to pressure of audit work & return filing, the Chartered Accountant inadvertently lost sight of the limitation date. After returning from Saudi Arabia, the assessee contacted the Chartered Accountant & the appeal was filed immediately. The assessee supported his explanation with an affid
rows.summary:
This Hyderabad ITAT decision concerns AY 2018-19 and holds that a reassessment based on an invalid approval under section 151 cannot support a downstream penalty under section 270A. The assessee had been assessed under section 147 read with section 144B by order dated 28 February 2024, with an addition of ₹5,13,613 on capital gains and total income assessed at ₹9,52,723 because the assessee could not substantiate an alleged cost of improvement claimed to have been incurred in 2003; the AO then levied a penalty of ₹2,13,664 under section 270A, and the CIT(A) upheld it. On appeal, the assessee also challenged the legality of the reassessment itself, arguing that the section 148 notice dated 4 April 2022 was issued more than three years after the end of AY 2018-19, so prior approval had to come from the authority specified in section 151(ii)—the Principal Chief Commissioner or Principal Director General, or if unavailable, the Chief Commissioner or Director General—but the notice had been approved only by the CIT (International Taxation & Transfer Pricing), Hyderabad, which was legally insufficient.

The Tribunal first condoned a 110-day delay in filing the appeal, accepting the assessee’s explanation that he had entrusted the matter to his Chartered Accountant before travelling to Saudi Arabia for pilgrimage, believed the filing would be made in time, and later found that the CA had missed the limitation date because of audit and return-filing pressure; the assessee supported this with an affidavit and passport copy, and the Tribunal applied a liberal, justice-oriented approach consistent with the Supreme Court’s decision in Vidya Shankar Jaiswal v. CIT. The Revenue’s objection that a penalty appeal cannot be used to attack the underlying assessment was rejected: relying on National Thermal Power Co. Ltd. v. CIT and Shri Valley Refractories Ltd. v. DCIT, the Tribunal held that a pure question of law arising from facts already on record can be raised at any stage, and that the validity of the assessment can be examined in penalty proceedings because the assessment is the foundation of the penalty. Because the reassessment notice lacked the approval of the competent “specified authority” under section 151, the Tribunal held the reassessment itself was invalid, and since the penalty under section 270A flowed from that defective assessment, the penalty also could not stand. The practical compliance takeaway is that where reopening occurs beyond the three-year mark, the approving authority must match section 151’s hierarchy exactly; approval from an incorrect officer can nullify the reassessment and any consequential penalty.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the restriction of input tax credit under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act on works contract services, goods and services used for constructing immovable property, and the statutory exceptions for plant and machinery and construction not undertaken on a taxable person’s own account. It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. Table of Contents▸ Background: Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Comments: What is immovable property? Movable vs immovable property test-various judgements The principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Bharti Airtel Limited v The Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune Eligibility to Input tax credit and immovable property under GST Way ahead and conclusion Possible issues when there is a Single contract for construction of building and supply of machineries, other moveable goods: ACTION POINTS FOR ITC OPTIMISATION: Show all 10 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background: It is being observed that the assesses are receiving notices requiring to reverse/pay back ITC availed pertaining to newly constructed building projects used for business operations[such as factory premise/warehouses], alleging such credit is restricted being of nature of “immovable property”. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of
rows.summary:
The document explains that GST input tax credit can be denied even where expenses are otherwise incurred for business if they fall within the blocked-credit rules in Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act. In particular, Section 17(5)(c) blocks credit on works contract services used for the construction of immovable property, except when the same works contract service is taken as an input service for further supply of works contract service; “construction” for this purpose includes reconstruction, renovation, additions, alterations, and repairs to the extent capitalized to the immovable property. The article also clarifies that “plant and machinery” is a key carve-out: it means apparatus, equipment, and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support and used for making outward supplies, including those foundations/supports, but excluding land, buildings or other civil structures, telecommunication towers, and pipelines laid outside factory premises.

A separate exception under Section 17(5)(c) allows ITC where the works contract service is received for construction of “plant and machinery.” The article gives the example of a material-and-labour works contract that results in HVAC plant, stating that such a case can qualify for credit because the contract is tied to plant and machinery rather than blocked civil construction. It also notes the second exception for further supply of works contract service, illustrated by a developer constructing mall units for sale during construction: the developer may take credit to the extent the work relates to units sold during construction.

Section 17(5)(d) is described as blocking credit on goods or services received for construction of immovable property other than plant and machinery when the construction is for the taxpayer’s own account, including use in the course or furtherance of business. The text specifically notes an amendment replacing the phrase “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” retrospectively from 1 July 2017 through Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax dated 17.09.2025. This means compliance teams should treat the plant-and-machinery carve-out as applying consistently back to GST’s start date, and review any prior positions or disputes in light of that retrospective correction.

The article highlights a recurring compliance problem: taxpayers are receiving notices to reverse or repay ITC claimed on newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses, on the theory that the underlying project is immovable property. It emphasizes that such projects often include more than civil construction and may also involve electrical fittings, cabling, sewage treatment plants, security systems, fire-fighting systems, and manufacturing equipment, so the tax treatment depends on whether each component is truly part of blocked immovable property or is separate movable/plant-and-machinery equipment eligible for ITC. The document recommends structuring transactions through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods/services so that eligible credits are less likely to be denied in an audit or notice proceeding.

Finally, the document explains that whether something is “immovable property” is not determined just by attachment to land; the analysis depends on statutory definitions and judicial tests such as the nature of annexation, intention, functionality, permanency, and marketability. It specifically discusses movable-vs-immovable treatment for installations like HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, and other business equipment, implying that compliance teams should assess each item separately rather than assuming all fitters, systems, or equipment embedded in a facility are automatically blocked. The practical takeaway is that businesses constructing operational facilities should document classification carefully, segregate contracts and invoices, and retain evidence showing which items are civil construction, which are plant and machinery, and which are movable business assets to support ITC eligibility.

rows.title: Income Tax | Builder Delay Can Trigger TDS Interest for Homebuyers
rows.desc: How Home Buyers Get Trapped into Paying TDS Interest When Builders Delay Telling Them About TDS on Installments Summary: Homebuyers purchasing property from builders through construction-linked installments may incur substantial interest liability if tax is not deducted at source from each payment. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a buyer acquiring qualifying immovable property from a resident seller must deduct TDS at 1% at the time of payment or credit, whichever is earlier. For transactions governed by the 1961 Act, the buyer must furnish Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction and issue Form 16B to the seller. From 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Problems arise when builders raise installment demands without informing buyers about TDS and communicate the requirement only near possession or final payment. Earlier installments may consequently remain subject to delayed deduction. Interest is then payable from the date on which tax should have been deducted, even if the buyer was unaware of the obligation. Under Section 201(1A) of the 1961 Act, interest applies at 1% per month or part thereof for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part thereof for delayed deposit after deduction. Buyers should independently monitor every installment, deduct TDS within the applicable timeline and complete the prescribed statement and certificate requirements without waiting for instructions from the builder. Table of Contents▸ Introduction What the Law Actually Says Where the Problem Starts Why This Creates an Interest Liability What Buyers Should Actually Do Final Thought Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction Buying a flat or property from a builder is usually done in installments—some amount at booking, some at various construction stages, and the balance near poss
rows.summary:
The document explains that homebuyers purchasing immovable property from builders under construction-linked installment plans can unknowingly trigger TDS default interest if they do not deduct tax on each installment as required. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, where the property is not agricultural land and the purchase price is Rs. 50 lakh or more, the buyer must deduct TDS at 1% from each payment or credit to the resident seller, whichever is earlier; this applies installment by installment, not only at possession or final settlement. After deduction, the buyer must deposit the TDS using Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month in which the deduction was made, and must also issue Form 16B to the seller as evidence of deduction.

The document highlights a change in the governing statute: from 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Substantively, however, the duty remains the same: buyers still must deduct 1% TDS at each installment payment where the transaction value is Rs. 50 lakh or more. If a buyer pays, for example, eight installments over two years, the compliance expectation is eight separate TDS deductions and filings, one for each installment, rather than a single deduction at the end.

The compliance risk arises when builders do not tell buyers about the TDS requirement until late in the project, often near possession or final demand. By then, earlier installments may already have been paid in full without TDS, and the buyer is then forced to make delayed deductions and filings. The document states that ignorance of the obligation does not avoid the tax consequence: interest becomes payable from the date on which TDS should originally have been deducted.

Under Section 201(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the interest rates are 1% per month or part of a month for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part of a month for delayed deposit after deduction. The practical compliance instruction for buyers is to monitor every installment independently, deduct and deposit TDS on time for each payment, and complete the prescribed statement and certificate process without waiting for the builder to prompt them. The key operational issue for corporate compliance teams handling employee housing benefits, real estate payments, or advising customers is that each construction-linked installment is a separate TDS event, and late awareness does not protect against interest exposure.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. Table of Contents▸ Background of the Case What the Company Argued What the Department Argued What the Supreme Court Held Key Takeaways for Practitioners Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background of the Case This case deals with a Show Cause Notice (SCN) iss
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by reciting the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts.” In **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.**, the department had issued an SCN dated **13.06.2025** for **FY 2018-19** demanding **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, and the taxpayer argued that the normal Section 73 limitation had already expired on **28.02.2025** after applying the relevant return-due-date extensions and the COVID-related limitation exclusions. The Court agreed that if the department wants to rely on the **five-year** period under Section 74 instead of the ordinary **three-year** period under Section 73, the notice itself must set out the specific foundational facts showing how fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression occurred; a bare or mechanical reference to those terms is not enough.

The Court rejected the department’s attempt to cure the defect by relying on explanations in its counter affidavit, holding that a notice’s legal validity must be tested on the face of the notice itself and that jurisdictional defects cannot be repaired later in litigation. Here, the SCN contained only a vague reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining what conduct constituted fraud, how concealment was discovered, or why Section 74 was being invoked; the Court also noted that the use of the word “or” suggested uncertainty about the actual allegation. As a result, the Supreme Court set aside the **Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order** and also quashed the **SCN itself**, and it restrained the department from proceeding further on the basis of that notice.

For compliance teams, the key point is procedural and jurisdictional: where the department seeks to use Section 74 rather than Section 73, the SCN must contain concrete facts and reasoning supporting the fraud/suppression allegation at the time of issuance. A notice that simply uses statutory buzzwords without particulars may be vulnerable to challenge, even if the department later supplies details in court filings. This decision reinforces the importance of scrutinizing GST notices for limitation and for whether the jurisdictional basis for invoking the extended period is actually pleaded in the notice itself.

The source order contains a party-description inconsistency: its cause title identifies Santosh Mani Mishra as the appellant and the Islam Trading Company-related party as respondent, while paragraph 1 describes the appellant as Revenue and paragraph 1.2 refers to M/s Islam Trading Company as the appellant. The proceedings arose from transportation of 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly, under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018. The vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018. The E-Way Bill was not available with the driver at the time of interception. Tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- were imposed under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017. The first appellate authority, however, set aside the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018. The Department contended that transportation without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that subsequent production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns and proof of tax payment could not retrospectively cure the statutory violation. It further argued that the interception of the vehicle, nature of the goods, route and subsequent production of documents cumulatively indicated an intention to evade tax. The authorised representative also submitted that an E-Way
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench, restored a detention-cum-penalty order under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017 for movement of iron goods without an E-Way Bill, holding that the facts showed an intention to evade tax rather than a mere technical lapse. The case involved 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods transported by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the driver did not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception. On that basis, the Proper Officer had imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3).  

The First Appellate Authority had later set aside both the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018, but the Department appealed, arguing that transportation without a mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that producing the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment only after interception could not cure the violation. The Department also stressed that the E-Way Bill is generated online while the invoice is manually issued, creating scope for later manipulation of records, and that the route, nature of goods, and post-interception documents together indicated evasion; no one appeared for the respondent despite opportunity.  

The Tribunal accepted the Department’s position and distinguished the precedents relied upon by the first appellate authority, including Sarva Shri Singh Tire, Shri KL Industries, Harley Foods Products, Modern Traders, and Rai Prexim India, on the facts. It specifically noted that the goods were loaded at Baheri, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh for delivery to Kichha, Uttarakhand, about 25 km away, and treated the short-distance movement, the absence of the E-Way Bill, and the interception circumstances as supporting an inference of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal also relied on its own later order dated 20.08.2026 in Appeal No. APL/79/LKC/2026, Om Prakash v. M/s Islam Trading Company, involving the same goods, same destination, and a similar pattern where the E-Way Bill was produced only after interception, and held that the repeated post-interception production of the E-Way Bill showed a recurring modus operandi rather than a harmless procedural lapse.  

As a result, the Tribunal held that the First Appellate Authority erred in interfering with the Section 129(3) detention order, allowed the Revenue’s appeal, set aside the appellate order dated 24.09.2021, and restored the original order dated 09.03.2018 imposing the Rs. 47,844 tax and Rs. 47,844 penalty. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that transporting goods without the E-Way Bill at the time of interception can sustain Section 129 detention and penalty where the authorities infer evasive intent from the surrounding facts, and post-interception production of supporting documents may not be enough to avoid penalty.

Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Chennai Arising out of Order-in-Original No.9/2010 dated 16.8.2010 passed by Commissioner of Central Excise, Chennai – IV ST/350/2010 Ceebros Property Development Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Chennai Arising out of Order-in-Original No.1/2010 dated 6.1.2010 passed by Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Chennai ST/528/2010 Prime Developers Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, Coimbatore Arising out of Order-in-Original No.4/2010 dated 10.5.2010 passed by Commissioner of Customs, Central Excise and Service Tax, Coimbatore – IV Appearance Shri G. The appellant M/s. Real Value Promoters (P) Ltd. are involved in activity of constructing commercial projects PRGT www.taxguru.in 2 and residential projects. The appellants were issued show cause notices alleging short-payment of service tax under Commercial or Industrial Construction Services. After 1.6.2007, though they discharged service tax under works contract services under the composition scheme, for three of their four projects namely Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, Surya Skanda, the department was of the view that such payment is not proper for the reason that the services cannot be classified as Works Contract Service and also because appellants have not exercised their opt
rows.summary:
This common CESTAT Chennai order (pronounced 18.09.2018) disposed of three appeals involving real-estate developers and the levy of service tax on property-construction transactions. The core dispute was whether the appellants’ arrangements should be taxed as “construction of complex / commercial or industrial construction services” under the Finance Act, 1994, or as “works contract service” after 1.6.2007; the department also argued that, even where works contract composition was claimed, the assessees had not validly opted into the composition scheme by notifying the department as required under the Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service Tax) Rules, 2007. In the Real Value Promoters matter, the department issued SCN No. 351/2008 dated 23.10.2008 for the period 1.4.2007 to 31.3.2008, proposing service tax of Rs. 2,06,20,252 plus interest and penalties under sections 76 and 78, split across buyer-facing and landowner-facing development projects: commercial PRGT (Rs. 34,38,337), residential The Lords / Sananda Brindavan / Sujeet / Surya Skanda (Rs. 1,07,33,392), commercial PRGT Amarasri (Rs. 48,98,579), and residential Sai Brindavan (Rs. 15,49,944). A second SCN, No. 570/2009 dated 20.10.2009, covered amounts received for construction of residential apartments and commercial complexes and proposed an additional Rs. 1,05,99,978 on Commercial PRGT for the allegation of non-payment on services provided to buyers.

The adjudicating authority’s common order dated 16.8.2010 confirmed the entire demand raised in those notices, with interest, imposed a penalty equal to Rs. 2,06,20,252 under section 78, and also imposed penalties under sections 76 and 77. In the Prime Developers appeal, the developer had entered into a Joint Development Agreement dated 17.1.2005 with the landowner (Prime Textiles Ltd.) for a 432-apartment residential complex, and sold units to ultimate buyers under separate agreements; SCN dated 10.8.2009 covered the period January 2005 to August 2008 and the original authority confirmed Rs. 1,16,42,448, holding that service tax was payable under CICS at least for the period before 1.6.2007. For compliance teams, the practical issue is that the department treated the construction activity as taxable both where developers contracted with buyers and where they received consideration from landowners in JDA-style structures, and it specifically challenged the availability of works-contract classification and the procedural validity of the composition option. The final outcome of the Tribunal’s legal analysis is not fully shown in the excerpt provided, so the safe compliance takeaway from the document content alone is that these construction/JDA arrangements were under active tax scrutiny for the stated periods, with large confirmed demands, interest exposure, and section 76/77/78 penalty risk, particularly where no documented works-contract composition option had been exercised before the department.

It was also submitted that, considering the heavy pendency of cases, there was no likelihood of an early conclusion of the trial. The prayer for bail was opposed by the learned A.G.A. as well as the counsel appearing for the GST Department. After considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the record, evidence, nature of allegations and submissions of the parties, the Court held that the applicant was entitled to be enlarged on bail during pendency of the trial. Ac
rows.summary:
This is an Allahabad High Court bail order in a criminal prosecution arising out of an alleged GST fraud connected to a non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries, and it does **not** announce any new GST rule, filing requirement, tax rate, or compliance deadline. The underlying case is Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, registered under Sections **420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC**. The applicant, **Waseem Akram @ Monu**, argued that he was not named in the FIR, had no connection with the alleged fraud, was not the owner of the firm, and was not a beneficiary; his name allegedly surfaced only from the statement of **Sakeel Khan**. He also pointed out that the firm had been declared bogus in **November 2021**, while the FIR was filed on **04.11.2025**, and that he had no criminal history apart from this case and had been in custody since **05.04.2026**.

The State and GST Department opposed bail, but the Court held that, based on the record, allegations, and submissions, the applicant was entitled to bail during trial. The Court ordered release on bail upon execution of a **personal bond** and furnishing **two sureties of like amount**, subject to standard compliance conditions: he must not tamper with evidence, threaten or influence prosecution witnesses, commit a similar offence, or make inducements/threats/promises to persons connected with the case to prevent disclosure of facts to the Court or police. He must appear before the trial court on all dates unless exempted, and the trial court must verify the **identity, status, and residence proof** of the sureties before accepting them. If any condition is breached, the trial court may cancel bail. The Court expressly said its observations were limited to the bail decision and would not affect the merits of the case at trial.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Holds Municipal Hoarding Space Taxable, But Quashes Extended-Period Service Tax Demand
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12629 Case Name Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chief Municipal Officer Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi considered whether a municipality was liable to service tax on two activities: providing space for display of advertisements through hoardings and renting/licensing its immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons and traders. The disputed period was 2009-10 to 2014-15, covering both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The appellant had received Rs. 3,06,738/- from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974/- as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. On advertisement receipts, the appellant maintained that it merely collected statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than selling advertisin
rows.summary:
The CESTAT, New Delhi held that a municipality’s activity of giving space on hoardings for advertisements was taxable as “sale of space or time for advertisement services” for the period up to 01.07.2012 under section 65(105)(zzzm) of the Finance Act, 1994, because the statutory explanation expressly covered space used for display, advertising, or showcasing products or services on billboards and in public places. The Tribunal also held that the municipality’s leasing/licensing of immovable property, including vacant land, for commercial use was taxable both before and after 01.07.2012: for the pre-negative-list period, it rejected the argument that “any other person” meant only a person other than the owner and found that the vacant land used as market space was not within the claimed exclusion; for the post-01.07.2012 period, it found the activity fell within the broad definition of “service” in section 65B(44) and was not covered by the negative list because the property was provided to business entities for commercial activities such as “Flee Markets.”

The dispute covered the period 2009-10 to 2014-15. The municipality had received Rs. 3,06,738 from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974 as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department had proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945, along with interest, penalties, and a late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns, and the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals) had upheld the demand before the matter reached the Tribunal.

A key compliance outcome is that the Tribunal accepted the Department’s substantive position on taxability of both revenue streams, including amounts described as “licence fee” rather than rent, because the underlying activity was commercial and for consideration. However, it granted major relief on limitation: because the appellant was a government authority and there was no evidence of a positive act of suppression with intent to evade tax, the extended limitation period could not be invoked. The Tribunal relied on the principle from Anand Nishikawa Co. Ltd. that mere non-payment or non-declaration is not enough to establish wilful suppression; a positive act is required.

For compliance purposes, the practical result is that similar municipal or local-authority monetization of hoardings, advertising space, vacant land, market space, or other immovable property for commercial use can be subject to service tax/GST-era successor analysis depending on the period and facts, especially where the recipient is a trader or business entity and the arrangement is for consideration. In this case, the demand survived only for the normal limitation period, with proportionate reduction in penalty, while the extended-period demand was set aside. The appeal was therefore partly allowed.

rows.title: Income Tax | MEIS Rewards Taxable as Revenue Receipt from AY 2016-17: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12628 Case Name DCIT Vs Aarti Drugs Ltd. (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2016-17 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Aarti Drugs Ltd. (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench was constituted to decide whether the amount received by the assessee under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 is taxable as a revenue receipt in view of the amendment to Section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act by insertion of clause (xviii) with effect from Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee, engaged in manufacturing specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, had initially claimed the MEIS assistance as a revenue receipt, but subsequently contended before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt. The CIT(A) accepted the assessee’s contention for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18, leading to the Revenue’s appeals. The Revenue argued that MEIS constitutes government assistance and falls within the amended definition of income under Section 2(24)(xviii), irrespective of the nomenclature of the benefit as a “reward”. It relied upon the objective of the Foreign Trade Policy, the expression “by whatever name called”, the Supreme Court’s decisions in Sahney Steel Press Works Ltd. and Ponni Sugars & Chemicals Ltd., and various Tribunal decisions. The assessee, on the other hand, contended that MEIS was a reward intended to improve the export competitiveness of the country and did not constitute the forms of assistance contemplated by Section 2(24)(xviii). It relied, among others, upon Ponni Sugars, CIT v. Chaphalkar Brothers, DCIT v. Munjal Auto Industries and Shree Balaji Alloys. The Special Bench first examined the “purpose test” laid down by the Supreme Court. In Sahney S
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench held that incentives received under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 are taxable as revenue receipts and therefore form part of business income, beginning with AY 2016-17, because of the amendment to section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act inserting clause (xviii). The dispute arose in the case of Aarti Drugs Ltd., a manufacturer of specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, which had initially treated the MEIS benefit as revenue receipt, later argued before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt, and succeeded before the CIT(A) for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18; the Revenue appealed. The Revenue’s position was that MEIS is government assistance covered by section 2(24)(xviii), and that the label “reward” does not matter because the statute includes assistance “by whatever name called.”

The Special Bench applied the Supreme Court’s “purpose test” and concluded that MEIS was designed to offset export-related infrastructural inefficiencies and other ordinary export costs, and to improve India’s export competitiveness, not to help set up a new unit, expand capacity, or make capital investment. It noted that MEIS duty credit scrips are freely transferable, can be used to pay various duties and taxes, and do not carry any condition that they be used to acquire capital assets or repay capital borrowings; the benefit is computed with reference to the FOB value of exports and is available to qualifying manufacturer and merchant exporters. On that basis, the Bench held MEIS rewards are revenue in nature and are taxable as business income.

The Bench also held that section 2(24)(xviii) is drafted broadly enough to include assistance in the form of subsidy, grant, cash incentive, duty drawback, waiver, concession, reimbursement, or other similar government assistance “by whatever name called,” and rejected the assessee’s attempt to narrow the provision through ejusdem generis. It specifically found that the term “reward” used under MEIS falls within this broad language and that the MEIS benefit is, in substance, a cash incentive because it is linked to a percentage of FOB exports. The two statutory exclusions in section 2(24)(xviii) did not apply: MEIS was not an amount linked to the actual cost of a depreciable asset, and it was not a corpus donation to a trust or institution.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that, for AY 2016-17 onward, MEIS receipts should be treated as taxable income and included in business income rather than booked as a capital receipt. The decision also signals that exporters and other recipients of similar government export incentives should review their tax positions, accounting treatment, and return disclosures for periods covered by the amended definition of income, particularly where benefits are structured as duty credit scrips or “rewards” rather than explicitly labeled subsidies or grants.

Ltd (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court considered the Revenue’s appeal under section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 arising from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal order dated 12.11.2024 for A.Y. 2009-10. The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing edible and non-edible oil products and byproducts. The original assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 29.12.2011. The source records total income at Rs. 22,55,48,605/- in paragraph 3.1, while paragraph 7 records Rs. 22,55,48,602/-. A notice under section 148 was issued on 09.03.2015 beyond four years from the end of the relevant assessment year. The recorded reasons concerned two matters: an alleged short computation of disallowance under section 14A read with Rule 8D, and an alleged income of Rs.244.98 crores said to have been received from National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL) through so-called paper trade. In reassessment, however, the Assessing Officer made a disallowance of Rs.13,89,08,810/- under section 43(5) read with section 73 and section 40A(2)(b), along with excess disallowance of Rs.1,04,652/- under section 14A. The assessee challenged the reopening before the CIT(Appeals), pointing out that no addition had ultimately been made on either recorded reason. The CIT(Appeals) found that the NSEL figure of Rs.244.98 crores related to an addition in the assessee’s own case for A.Y. 2011-12 and that the assessee had not carried out NSEL transactions in the year under consideration. The CIT(Appeals) also noted that the original section 14A disallowance had been deleted by th
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court dismissed the Revenue’s section 260A appeal in **PCIT v. NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd.** for A.Y. **2009-10**, upholding the Tribunal’s order that had quashed the reassessment as **without jurisdiction**. The reassessment notice under **section 148** had been issued on **09.03.2015**, which was **beyond four years** from the end of the assessment year, so the reopening could stand only if the Revenue could show that income had escaped assessment because of the assessee’s **failure to disclose truly and fully all material facts**. The recorded reasons for reopening were limited to two alleged escapement items: an alleged under-disallowance under **section 14A read with Rule 8D**, and an alleged **Rs. 244.98 crore** receipt from **National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL)** through a supposed paper trade.

The reassessment ultimately did **not** make any addition on either of those recorded reasons. Instead, the Assessing Officer made a different addition of **Rs. 13,89,08,810/-** under **sections 43(5), 73, and 40A(2)(b)**, plus an alleged excess disallowance of **Rs. 1,04,652/-** under **section 14A**. The CIT(A) and Tribunal both held that this could not sustain the reassessment because the NSEL figure related to an addition made in the assessee’s **A.Y. 2011-12** proceedings and the assessee had **not carried out NSEL transactions in the year under review**, while the original section 14A disallowance had already been deleted by the Ahmedabad ITAT on the ground that the assessee had **not earned exempt dividend income**. The Court agreed that the reopening failed at the threshold because the recorded reasons produced **no addition**, there was **no allegation of failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts**, and the Revenue had brought **no new tangible material** on record.

The High Court also rejected the Revenue’s reliance on **Explanation 3 to section 147**, holding that while that Explanation may allow the Assessing Officer, after a **valid** reopening, to assess other income that comes to notice during reassessment, it does **not** override the basic jurisdictional requirements of section 147. The Court applied the principle from **CIT v. Mohmed Juned Dadani** that if the **foundation** for reopening collapses, the reassessment cannot survive; it also reiterated that an Explanation cannot enlarge the scope of the main statutory provision. Practically, the ruling means that where a reassessment is initiated **after four years** and the recorded grounds themselves do not result in any addition, the Revenue cannot salvage the reassessment by making unrelated additions discovered later in the process.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12626 Case Name Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2013-14 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Summary: The appeal concerned levy of penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for failure by a charitable trust to furnish its return of income. The assessee, a charitable trust running an educational institution and registered under section 12A, had not filed its return for AY 2013-14. The Assessing Officer received information that the assessee had deposited cash of Rs. 75,55,200/- into its bank account. Consequently, assessment proceedings were reopened by issuing notice under section 147. In response, the assessee filed a return declaring Nil income after claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). The assessment under section 147 accepted the returned income. Subsequently, penalty proceedings under section 272A(2)(e) were initiated. The assessee explained that the return had not been filed because of a bona fide belief that no return was required where the income was exempt. It also contended that there was no loss to the Revenue and no intention to conceal income. The Assessing Officer rejected these submissions and levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300/-. The CIT(A) confirmed the penalty, holding, among other things, that the assessee had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law was not an acceptable excuse, absence of revenue loss and mens rea was irrelevant, and that the penalty was mandatory in the absence of reasonable cause under section 273B. At the hearing before the Tribunal, the assessee pressed only ground No.8 and did not press the remaining gro
rows.summary:
The Chennai ITAT held that a penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act for failure to furnish a return cannot run indefinitely past the point at which the assessee was still legally able to file a valid voluntary return under section 139(4). The case involved a charitable trust registered under section 12A and running an educational institution, which had not filed its return for AY 2013-14; the Assessing Officer reopened the case under section 147 after finding cash deposits of Rs. 75,55,200 in the trust’s bank account, and the trust then filed a return declaring nil income and claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). Although the assessment was completed on the returned income, the Assessing Officer levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300 under section 272A(2)(e), and the CIT(A) upheld it, taking the view that the trust had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law and absence of revenue loss were irrelevant, and that no relief was available absent “reasonable cause” under section 273B.

Before the Tribunal, the trust pressed only the issue that the penalty period should stop when the time for filing a valid belated return under section 139(4) expired, rather than continuing until the return was actually filed in response to notice under section 148. The Revenue argued that because section 272A(2)(e) applies for every day during which the failure continues, the default should be treated as continuing up to the eventual filing date. The Tribunal rejected that approach, holding that once the section 139(4) deadline passed, the assessee no longer had the statutory ability to voluntarily furnish a valid return, so the failure could not be treated as continuing beyond that point for purposes of section 272A(2)(e).

Relying on Bethany Seva Sangam v. ITO [2023] 155 taxmann.com 352 (Raipur Tribunal) and also noting G. Pulla Reddy v. JCIT (2010) 47 DTR 1 (Hyd.), the Tribunal ruled that the penalty must be restricted to the period up to the last date permitted under section 139(4), and not extended to the date of filing in response to the section 148 notice. It therefore set aside the penalty computation and remanded the matter to the Assessing Officer solely to recompute the penalty by limiting the default period to the section 139(4) window. The appeal was partly allowed.

rows.summary:
This Madras High Court order concerns **AY 2015-16** and a taxpayer, **Sankaran Mekala**, who challenged a **demand communication/order dated 16.07.2026** issued in connection with an earlier reassessment matter under **sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961**. The taxpayer had already filed **W.P. No. 1242 of 2026** against the underlying **assessment order dated 16.01.2024** and **notice dated 12.04.2022**; that earlier writ was disposed of on **09.02.2026** with directions to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and respond to the section 148 notice. The petitioner stated she had complied in part by depositing **Rs. 5 lakhs** pursuant to the earlier order, but could not upload the return because of technical issues on the income-tax e-filing portal, and she produced a **screenshot** evidencing the upload failure along with proof of other filings.

The Court accepted that the portal issue prevented compliance and held that, in the interests of justice, the taxpayer should be given another opportunity to file the return. It therefore **set aside the impugned demand notice dated 16.07.2026** and directed the Revenue to **take necessary steps to provide access to the income-tax portal** so the return for AY 2015-16 could be uploaded. The taxpayer was ordered to **file the return within three weeks from receipt of the order**, and the department was then required to **complete the assessment by issuing an assessment order within six weeks from receipt of the return**, after granting a **reasonable opportunity** to the taxpayer. The connected miscellaneous petitions were closed, and **no costs** were awarded.  

From a compliance perspective, the order is significant because it shows the Court will treat **documented portal/access failures** as a valid basis for relief where the taxpayer has otherwise attempted to comply, and it reinforces that the department must provide a functional means of electronic filing when a court has directed the taxpayer to file a return.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Directs Interest-First Income Tax Refund Adjustment Under Section 244A
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12624 Case Name DCIT-2(1)(1) Vs Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2003-04 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT-2(1)(1) Vs Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s appeals concerning the manner in which refunds payable to M/s. Bank of Baroda were required to be adjusted between the interest component and the principal tax component. The consolidated order covered AYs 2003-04, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, 2016-17 and 2005-06, with ITA No.5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 taken as the lead case. The Revenue challenged the order of the CIT(A), NFAC, contending that where a refund comprised both tax and interest under section 244A, any refund payment should first be appropriated towards the principal tax component rather than the interest component. According to the Revenue, section 244A contained no express provision prescribing that interest should be adjusted first. It was also argued that adjusting the refund against interest would result in further interest liability on the unpaid tax component and would effectively amount to charging interest on interest. The assessee contended that the issue had already been settled by various judicial decisions and by decisions of the Tribunal in its own case. It relied on the principle of consistency and submitted that, in the absence of any change in facts or circumstances, the earlier view should be followed. The assessee also relied upon decisions concerning Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India and Tata Sons Limited, among others. The Tribunal noted that section 244A provides
rows.summary:
The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that, when the Income Tax Department issues a refund that includes both the principal tax amount and interest payable under section 244A, the refund must be adjusted **interest first and principal tax second**. The Revenue had argued the opposite—that the refund should first be appropriated toward the tax component because section 244A does not expressly say interest must be paid first, and that paying interest first could create further interest on the unpaid tax. The Tribunal rejected that position and, relying on the purpose of section 244A, said the provision is meant to compensate the taxpayer for excess payment and delay in refund through **simple interest**, not to leave the interest component unpaid while only the principal is returned.

The ruling was based on prior judicial authorities, especially **India Trade Promotion Organisation v. CIT** and **Sandvik Asia Ltd. v. CIT**, along with other cases including **CIT v. H.E.G. Ltd.** and **Narendra Doshi**, which support the view that the “amount due” on refund is not limited to the principal tax alone and can include the interest element. The Tribunal emphasized that, where later assessment or appellate orders change the refundable tax amount, section 244A contains its own mechanism for adjusting the interest accordingly; however, that does not permit the Department to reverse the order of appropriation so that tax is satisfied before interest. It viewed interest as compensation for the time value of money retained by the government, so paying tax first would undercut the statutory compensation scheme.

This decision arose in the case of **DCIT-2(1)(1) v. Bank of Baroda (ITAT Mumbai)** and covered multiple assessment years: **AY 2003-04, 2005-06, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, and 2016-17**. The Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s lead appeal for **AY 2003-04 (ITA No. 5707/Mum/2025)** and applied the same reasoning to the related appeals, including **ITA Nos. 5709, 5710 and 5711/Mum/2025 and 5659 and 5708/Mum/2025**, so all Revenue appeals were dismissed. For compliance purposes, this means that in refund processing where section 244A interest is part of the amount payable, the Department’s adjustment sequence is expected to prioritize **interest before tax**, and taxpayers receiving such refunds may rely on this precedent in similar Mumbai ITAT matters unless and until a higher court says otherwise.

Ltd., consequential interest, penalties of Rs.20 lakh each under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 and penalties imposed on the co-appellants could not be sustained in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence. Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997-2002 permitting duty-free import of 5350 MTs of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against export obligation of 5000 MTs of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue alleged that the imported scrap was diverted in the domestic market and maize was fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the stipulated steel products. The Tribunal found material support for the appellant’s case in the special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, undisputed realisation of export proceeds and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. rows.summary:
CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017. The adjudication had demanded customs duty of Rs. 2,16,93,068 along with consequential interest and imposed penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each on Chessman Impex under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as penalties on the co-appellants, on the allegation that duty-free DEEC imports were misused and that the export obligation was fraudulently fulfilled through export of maize rather than the permitted steel products.

The Tribunal noted that Chessman Impex had obtained a DEEC licence under the EXIM Policy 1997–2002 for duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue’s theory was that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that maize was exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the required steel goods, but the Tribunal found the record insufficient to support that case. It relied on multiple pieces of evidence supporting the assessee, including special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, Customs examination of export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation that the goods were manufactured by Goyal Ispat Ltd., permission from the foreign buyer to segregate and export unprocessed scrap, realization of export proceeds, and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority.

A key factor was that the CBI had already investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report stating that the available evidence indicated the disputed exports to Bangladesh had actually taken place; that report had been accepted by the competent criminal court. The Tribunal held that the customs adjudicating authority had not brought any additional reliable material beyond what the CBI had examined, and Revenue had produced no independent proof of buyers for the allegedly diverted material, cash trail evidence, procurement or transport of maize, domestic disposal, or seizure of offending goods. It emphasized that suspicion or “grey areas” cannot replace cogent evidence for imposing penalties under Sections 112 and 114 of the Customs Act.

The Tribunal also held that the adjudicating authority went beyond the scope of the Show Cause Notice by raising new issues such as classification of CTD bars, availability of 16 mm bars, and amendment of the DEEC licence. It found discrepancies in the witness statements relied upon by Revenue, noted that some statements had been retracted, and criticized the reliance on Section 108 statements without proper consideration of Section 138B requirements. Because the allegations against the principal noticee failed for lack of reliable and corroborative evidence, the derivative allegations of connivance or abetment against the co-appellants also failed, and all penalties were set aside with consequential relief.

rows.title: Custom Duty | SC Sets Aside ₹425 Crore Customs Penalty Due to Fake AI-Generated Case Laws
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12622 Case Name Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya Vs Union of India & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya Vs Union of India & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court set aside a customs penalty order after finding that the adjudicating officer appears to have relied on fake or AI-generated legal authorities. The underlying Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025, issued by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat, had imposed a penalty of ₹425,27,99,100 under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962 on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya for allegedly misdeclaring a consignment of natural diamonds as lab-grown diamonds in order to pay a lower tariff; the Gujarat High Court had upheld/dismissed the challenge on 20.01.2026, but the Supreme Court reversed that outcome without deciding the substantive customs merits.

The Court said it independently verified the judgments and articles cited in the customs order and found that some were non-existent or carried fake citations, while others existed but did not support the propositions attributed to them. It described the material as appearing to be an AI “hallucination” and relied on its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1258), reaffirming a zero-tolerance approach to producing, citing, or relying on artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification.

On the AI policy issue, the Court observed that it had recently released draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026 and invited comments/suggestions, but those regulations were not yet finalized. The Court acknowledged AI may be used only as an assistive tool to speed decision-making, but emphasized that AI cannot be put in the “pilot’s seat” of adjudication. Because the penalty order was tainted by reliance on dubious and unverified authorities, the Supreme Court held the order unsustainable and set it aside, along with the Gujarat High Court order that had confirmed it.

Procedurally, the Court revived the proceedings before the customs authority for fresh adjudication by another officer of the same rank, expressly requiring that the new officer be different from the one who issued the original order. It allowed the civil appeal, disposed of pending applications, and left it to the appointing authority to decide whether any action should be taken against the author of the original order in accordance with law.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras HC Upholds Negative Blocking of Electronic Credit Ledger Under Section 79
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12621 Case Name Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions Vs Assistant Commissioner Coimbatore (Madras High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Madras High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions Vs Assistant Commissioner Coimbatore (Madras High Court) Summary: The Madras High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/s.Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions challenging the blocking/freezing of its electronic credit ledger pursuant to reference No. BL3302250000152 dated 04.02.2025. The petitioner sought a direction to the respondent to lift the blockage and permit free utilisation of the Input Tax Credit available in the electronic credit ledger. An assessment order dated 17.03.2023 had been issued for the assessment period 2017-2020. Primarily challenging the clubbing of assessments relating to multiple assessment periods, the petitioner had filed W.P.No.41890 of 2025. An interim stay concerning recovery measures was granted on 25.02.2026. The electronic credit ledger, however, had already been blocked on 04.02.2025, and that blocking order was challenged in the present writ petition. The petitioner contended that the blocking could not survive in view of the interim order dated 25.02.2026. It was further argued that the blocking travelled beyond the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act. Comparing Section 79 with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, learned counsel contended that negative blocking was impermissible under Section 79. The Revenue submitted that there was no infirmity in the blocking. It also contended that the interim order dated 25.02.2026 merely directed that recovery proceedings be kept in abeyance and did not affect the earlier blocking order. The Court accepted the Revenue’s inter
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court upheld the blocking of M/s. Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions’ electronic credit ledger and rejected the argument that the blockage had to be lifted because of an interim stay in a related case. The ledger had been blocked by reference No. BL3302250000152 dated 04.02.2025, and the petitioner asked for permission to freely use the input tax credit in that ledger; the Court held that the later interim order dated 25.02.2026 only paused recovery proceedings and did not undo or invalidate the earlier blocking order. The Court also confirmed that the underlying assessment order dated 17.03.2023 covered the assessment period 2017–2020, and that the related writ challenge to clubbing of multiple assessment periods did not change the effect of the blocking order being challenged here.

On the legal issue, the petitioner argued that “negative blocking” of the electronic credit ledger was beyond the power granted by Section 79 of the CGST Act and compared that provision with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The Court disagreed and held that Section 79(1) is broad enough to authorize recovery of amounts payable to the Government through the specified recovery modes in clauses (a) to (f), and that blocking the credit ledger — including negative blocking — falls within that recovery framework. The Court specifically distinguished Rule 86A as a provisional, pre-determination safeguard, whereas Section 79 operates after liability has been determined and permits recovery of dues already payable. As a result, the Court found no legal infirmity in the blocking of the electronic credit ledger, held that amounts in the ledger could not be debited for recovery while the interim stay remained in effect, and disposed of the writ petition with no order as to costs.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kerala HC Remands Medical PG Stipend vs Salary Dispute for Fresh Assessment
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12620 Case Name Nahas Kakkattummal Vs ITO (Kerala High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Kerala High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Nahas Kakkattummal Vs ITO (Kerala High Court) Summary: The appellant approached the Kerala High Court in a writ appeal after the learned Single Judge declined to exercise writ jurisdiction and relegated him to the alternative statutory remedy under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The dispute concerned amounts received by the appellant while pursuing postgraduate medical studies. According to the appellant, the amounts were stipend and not salary. The appellant’s counsel contended that the assessment order had been issued by relying “blindly” on documents supplied by the University where the appellant was studying and drawing stipend, in which the sums were shown as salary. It was submitted that the appellant was admittedly a postgraduate student and that the amount received was stipend statutorily paid under law and in accordance with mandatory guidelines of the National Medical Commission. On that basis, it was argued that the Assessing Authority could not assess the receipts as salary. Alternatively, the appellant sought liberty to produce additional documents before the Assessing Authority. Counsel pointed out that even the University communication relied upon by the Assessing Authority categorically certified that the appellant had been admitted to an MD/MS postgraduate course as a Junior Resident. It was submitted that such students were covered by the regulations of the NMC, which prohibited payment of salary but mandated stipend. The appellant also relied upon Ext.P5, which certified that he was a bona fide PG student of the University, and contended that the letters relied upon by th
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court remanded a tax dispute involving a postgraduate medical student’s receipts, holding that the Assessing Officer had assessed the amounts as “salary” without adequately considering the taxpayer’s claim that they were a statutory stipend paid to an MD/MS junior resident under National Medical Commission (NMC) rules. The assessee argued that the university documents relied on by the department were being read too literally, that a separate government order and certificate showed he was a bona fide postgraduate student, and that under the applicable medical education framework stipend — not salary — is what such students are to receive; he also asked for permission to submit additional records. The Income Tax Department countered that the university had informed it the payment was salary “in lieu of the work tendered,” and that TDS had been deducted and remitted, so the issue was factual and should be pursued through the ordinary statutory remedy rather than writ jurisdiction.

The High Court held that while writ jurisdiction is normally avoided where an effective alternative remedy exists, an exception applies where the assessment order is said to have been made without considering relevant facts and law. Here, the Court found that the Assessing Officer had relied only on certain university letters and had not addressed the taxpayer’s other materials, including Ext. P5 and the government order under which he was admitted to the course; the Court also noted that the assessment order did not deal with the taxpayer’s central contention that stipend paid to students is outside the tax net. The Court emphasized that whether the receipts were actually stipend was a material factual question that should be tested on a complete record, and that the taxpayer should be given a proper opportunity to produce supporting documents before any final adverse conclusion is reached.

As a result, the High Court set aside both the Single Judge’s order and the impugned assessment-related order (Ext. P12), and sent the matter back to the Assessing Officer for fresh consideration. The department was given full liberty to reconsider the issue after allowing the assessee to place all relevant documents and other material, and the Court directed that a new assessment order be passed as expeditiously as possible. The Court expressly did not decide the merits of whether the payments were stipend or salary; it only ruled that the prior decision could not stand because the assessee had not been afforded a fair opportunity to establish his case.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12619 Case Name Sandhya Roy Vs ITO (ITAT Kolkata) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2015-16 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Kolkata Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. rows.summary:
The ITAT Kolkata’s SMC Bench did not finally decide the tax liability in this case; instead, it set aside the CIT(A)’s order and sent the matter back for fresh adjudication on the merits. The dispute arose from AY 2015-16 and concerned a Joint Development Agreement dated 22.01.2015 entered into by Sandhya Roy, under which the Assessing Officer treated the arrangement as a “transfer” of a capital asset under section 2(47) and assessed long-term capital gains of ₹48,68,542, using fair market value plus cash consideration as the sale consideration and taking the cost of acquisition at nil. The reassessment was initiated through a notice under section 148 dated 31.03.2022; the assessee had not filed a return originally or in response to that notice, and the assessment was completed under sections 147, 144 and 144B.

Before the CIT(A), the assessee challenged both the reopening and the capital-gains addition. On limitation, the CIT(A) rejected the challenge, holding that because the section 148 notice was issued before 01.04.2022, it was not one of the notices treated as time-barred in the reassessment transition cases; it applied the Supreme Court’s directions in Union of India vs. Ashish Agarwal and Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajeev Bansal. On merits, the CIT(A) agreed with the Assessing Officer that execution of the JDA extinguished the assessee’s rights and therefore amounted to a transfer, and it held that section 45(5A) did not apply to this assessment year. It also upheld the nil cost basis because, in its view, the assessee had not produced documentary evidence of cost of acquisition.

The Tribunal, however, did not affirm that merits determination. The assessee argued that the valuation report for the properties had never been communicated, that she therefore could not properly respond to the show-cause process, and that the property had been inherited in 1994 from her father along with her mother, so the cost of acquisition should have been taken into account; she also pointed to the father’s purchase deed and explained the agreed allotment of a first-floor flat, car parking space, and monetary consideration under the JDA. The Tribunal accepted that the matter required further factual examination and restored the appeal to the CIT(A) with directions to pass a speaking order after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity of hearing, avoiding unnecessary adjournments, following Rule 46A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 if additional evidence is involved, and giving the Assessing Officer an opportunity to be heard if needed. As a result, the ₹48,68,542 capital-gains addition remains unresolved on the merits and was neither deleted nor sustained by the Tribunal; the appeal was allowed only for statistical purposes.
