Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Summary: The petitioner challenged the order dated May 28, 2022 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The writ petition was filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The petitioner’s registration under the Act had been cancelled on 16.11.2021. Thereafter, the petitioner did not carry on any business. A show cause notice was uploaded on the GST portal and, subsequently, the impugned order was passed under Section 74. The Court held that once the registration had been cancelled, the petitioner was not obligated to check the GST portal. The Court observed that the mode of service of any show cause notice had to be by way of alternative means to the petitioner. The petitioner relied upon the coordinate Bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB. The Court stated that it was essentially in agreement with the principle enunciated by the coordinate Bench. Finding a violation of the principle of natural justice, the Allahabad High Court quashed and set aside the impugned order dated May 28, 2022. The Department was left at liberty to issue a proper notice to the petitioner and act in accordance with law. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT 1. Heard Sri Mukesh Kumar Tewa
rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court quashed a GST demand/order passed under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh GST Act, 2017 because the department served the show-cause notice only by uploading it on the GST portal after the taxpayer’s registration had already been cancelled. In this case, Ved Enterprises Unnao’s registration was cancelled on 16.11.2021, it stopped carrying on business thereafter, and the impugned order was passed on 28.05.2022 by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao. The Court held that once registration is cancelled, the taxpayer is not expected to keep checking the GST portal, so service of notice must be made by an alternative/appropriate means that actually reaches the taxpayer.

The Court agreed with the principle laid down in the coordinate Bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others (Neutral Citation No. 2024:AHC:23697-DB), and found that failure to serve notice properly amounted to a violation of natural justice. As a result, the Section 74 order dated 28.05.2022 was set aside. The department was, however, expressly given liberty to issue a fresh, proper notice and proceed in accordance with law. For compliance teams, the key point is that after GST registration cancellation, portal-only service of show-cause notices may be legally insufficient; tax authorities must use a mode of service that reasonably informs the former registrant before passing adverse orders.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court issued a common order on 24.04.2026 disposing of three interconnected writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited concerning GST proceedings for the tax period 2019–2020. One petition challenged a show cause notice in Form GST DRC-01 dated 31.05.2024; another challenged an order/reply dated 29.05.2024; and the third challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023, along with consequential Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the GST enactments that extended the limitation period. The dispute therefore centered on whether the limitation period for GST actions had been validly extended and whether the resulting notice and related proceedings for 2019–2020 could survive.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Court did not decide the merits of the limitation-extension notification or the underlying GST liability. At admission, the Court had granted interim protection on 13.08.2024, and afterward the jurisdictional State Tax Officer filed a detailed report dated 27.01.2026. The Court recorded that this report prima facie supported the petitioner’s position, and on that basis the petitioner stated that no further adjudication remained necessary in respect of the DRC-01 proceeding.

As a result of those subsequent developments, the Court treated the challenge to the show cause notice as no longer requiring adjudication and held that the challenges to the limitation-extension notification and the related order/reply had also become academic. Accordingly, W.P. Nos. 20652 and 20655 of 2024 were closed, and W.P. No. 20657 of 2024 was disposed of. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed. The practical takeaway is that this order ends this particular litigation pathway without resolving the substantive validity of Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax or establishing a general rule on limitation extension under Section 168A for other taxpayers.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd and set aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026, which had rejected the petitioner’s GST appeal on limitation. The Court directed the Appellate Authority to consider and decide the appeal on its own merits, subject to the petitioner firm depositing late fees, penalty and other statutory deposits as admissible. The petitioner had sought quashing of the order dated 07.02.2024 and restoration of its GST registration, besides setting aside the appellate order dated 27.02.2026 and a direction for adjudication of the appeal on merits. The petitioner relied principally on the Rajasthan High Court’s Division Bench judgment in M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 9882/2024, decided on 28.07.2026. In that case, the Court had condoned a 99-day delay after granting relaxation of 120 days under Section 107 of the CGST Act and directed the Appellate Authority to entertain the appeal and adjudicate it on merits if filed within 30 days. The petitioner also relied upon M/s. Molana Construction Company Vs. Central Goods and Service Tax Department & Ors., Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, Central Goods and Services Tax Department & Ors., and the two decisions in RPC PSIPL JV Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors. The petitioner additionally referred to M/s. Kakar Automobiles Vs. Union of India & Ors. The respondents relied upon S
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST appeal rejected as time-barred could still be revived in exceptional circumstances where the delay was caused by medical reasons beyond the taxpayer’s control. In this case, Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. challenged the order dated 07.02.2024 and also sought restoration of its GST registration; it further sought quashing of the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, which had refused to entertain the GST appeal on limitation grounds. The Court accepted the petitioner’s reliance on prior Rajasthan High Court decisions, including **Pratap Power Spares**, **Molana Construction Company**, **Man Singh Tanwar**, **RPC PSIPL JV**, and **Kakar Automobiles**, and distinguished the respondents’ reliance on **Sharwan Singh Devda**, noting that Article 226/227 relief is not barred after expiry of the statutory appeal period but should be used only in exceptional cases such as natural justice failures or clear lack of jurisdiction.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that although the appellate authority remains bound by the limitation provisions under **Section 107 of the RGST/CGST Act**, the High Court can intervene where the taxpayer shows that non-filing within time resulted from circumstances outside its control, here specifically medical reasons. The Court found that refusing to decide the appeal on merits would cause grave injury and prejudice to the petitioner, so it exercised writ jurisdiction to set aside the appellate order dated **27.02.2026** and ordered the appellate authority to hear and decide the appeal on merits in accordance with law. This relief was not unconditional: the petitioner must first deposit the **late fees, penalty, and other statutory deposits “as admissible”** for the appeal to be entertained. The judgment does not create a general extension of limitation, but it confirms that delayed GST appeals may be considered where a taxpayer can prove exceptional, uncontrollable circumstances, subject to compliance with the monetary/statutory pre-deposit requirements.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition by M/s Jagdish Prasad Agrawal, a partnership firm, challenging the blocking of its Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the Electronic Credit Ledger, including an alleged blocking of IGST ITC with a negative balance. The petitioner asked the Court to declare the blocking illegal, inoperative, and void, to quash it, and to direct re-credit of any ITC unlawfully set off against the disputed demand. By the time of hearing, the blocking had already ceased automatically by operation of law after one year, and the Electronic Credit Ledger had been reactivated, so the dispute had narrowed to whether the ITC could lawfully have been blocked in the first place without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017.

The respondents conceded that the ledger was now operational, but they could not show that the mandatory conditions under Rule 86A had been satisfied before blocking the credit. They admitted that the action was a bona fide mistake and that, although the officer had reasons for action, no proper reasoned order had been passed and the petitioner had not been given an opportunity of hearing before the blockage. The Court specifically noted that Rule 86A requires the competent authority to have “reasons to believe” that ITC has been fraudulently availed or is ineligible, and to record those reasons in writing before disallowing debit of an equivalent amount from the Electronic Credit Ledger for payment of tax liability under section 49 or for a refund of unutilised credit. The Court found, on the record before it, that these mandatory preconditions were not complied with.

Because the restriction had already expired and the ledger had been restored, the Court did not grant further substantive relief in the petition; instead, it disposed of the matter after accepting the unconditional apology tendered on behalf of the concerned officer. However, the Court issued a clear warning for future cases: if the department blocks ITC without due compliance with Rule 86A, it may become liable to pay appropriate compensation to the affected taxpayer. For compliance purposes, the key point is that Rule 86A safeguards are mandatory before ITC blocking—specifically, a recorded written basis and proper legal satisfaction by the competent authority are required, and a failure to follow those steps can expose the department to compensation exposure and judicial censure.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt. Ltd.’s appeal against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Agilent was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers under service agreements and exporting those services without paying service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005; it had claimed refund of accumulated credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The refund amount at issue was ₹78,79,939, which the department had rejected on the ground that credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services allegedly had no nexus with the exported output services.  

The Tribunal held that the department could not deny a Rule 5 refund by re-litigating the eligibility of credit where the availment of that CENVAT credit had never been challenged under Rule 14 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. In other words, the decision treats credit availment, its utilisation, and refund of unutilised credit as distinct issues, and says a refund objection under Rule 5 cannot be used as a substitute for an untimely or absent challenge to credit admissibility itself. The Tribunal also reiterated that, for the relevant period, the definition of “input service” under Rule 2(l) was exhaustive and that the disputed services had been accepted in various precedents as qualifying input services; it further accepted the appellant’s position that direct one-to-one nexus with the exported output services was not necessary, relying on Circular No. 120/1/2010-ST dated 19.01.2010 and case law including Reliance Corporate IT Park Ltd.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that exporters claiming Rule 5 refunds should retain documentation showing that the underlying credits were validly availed and not previously disputed, because the Tribunal emphasized that once the department has not invoked Rule 14 to challenge availment, it cannot later deny refund merely by questioning nexus at the refund stage. The order ultimately set aside the impugned denial and granted the refund with consequential relief, if any, as per law.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Hyderabad Sets Aside Tax on Pharma Regulatory Approval Support Services
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12613 Case Name Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020,
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad set aside the Service Tax demands raised against Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. in an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 for the periods 2011-12 and up to June 2012, along with the related interest and penalties. Two categories of demand were in dispute: first, amounts deducted by foreign/intermediary banks from export remittances before the net proceeds reached the appellant’s Indian bank; and second, payments to overseas regulatory consultants for preparing clinical/non-clinical overviews and other documentation for foreign pharma product approvals.  

On the banking issue, the Tribunal held that Aurobindo was not the recipient of a taxable banking service merely because bank charges were economically borne through reduced export proceeds. The record did not show that the company had contracted with, engaged, or owed consideration to the foreign banks, so the reverse charge demand under “Banking and Other Financial Services” was unsustainable; the Tribunal also relied on its own earlier favourable order for an earlier period and the Eastman Exports decision.  

On the consultancy issue, the Tribunal rejected Revenue’s attempt to classify regulatory dossier preparation and compilation work performed by M/s DADA Consultancy and M/s Pharpe Dr. D.R. Iban as “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.” It held that compiling already available information and published material for regulatory submissions, without independent scientific research, experimentation, technical studies, or actual advice in a scientific/technical discipline, does not become scientific/technical consultancy simply because the service providers have technical expertise or the documentation relates to scientific product particulars. The Tribunal emphasized that the true nature of the activity controls classification, and it followed the appellant’s earlier case and IPCA Laboratories Ltd. for the proposition that services connected with obtaining regulatory approvals/registrations abroad are not automatically taxable under that head.  

The order also noted that Aurobindo had already discharged Service Tax on these consultant payments under “Management or Business Consultant Service,” and the impugned order had appropriated that tax while simultaneously reclassifying the same activity under another taxable heading; once the reclassification failed, the demand could not survive. Because the substantive tax demands were set aside, the associated interest and penalties were also quashed, and the Tribunal did not separately rule on the appellant’s Section 76 penalty-computation argument tied to the amendment effective 08.04.2011.

Rajendra Bane had been serving as a Customs Hawaldar. The penalties arose from an investigation into smuggled gold recovered from the gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport after passengers travelled from Dubai by Spice Jet Flight No. SG 52 on 16.08.2018. The allegation was that although Rajendra Bane was on sanctioned leave and staying at his native place near Ratnagiri, he had facilitated the smuggling of gold and assisted the smugglers. The material relied upon against him included statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962, particularly statements of co-accused/accomplices, call records received from the telephone operator, and recovery of gold from the airport toilet and from a passenger. The defence completely denied involvement. It admitted that Rajendra Bane was on leave and at his native place on the relevant day, but contended that the seizure had actually followed information transmitted by him to the Superintendent on duty at Pune International Airport. The defence claimed that the information involved privileged communication with an informer and therefore its source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected this explanation. He considered the statement
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai set aside the personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 on late Rajendra Bane, a Customs Hawaldar, and deleted the penalties entirely for lack of proof that he knowingly aided the smuggling operation. The case arose from the recovery of smuggled gold from a men’s toilet at Pune International Airport after SpiceJet Flight SG 52 from Dubai arrived on 16.08.2018, with the Department alleging that Bane—though on sanctioned leave and at his native place near Ratnagiri—had facilitated the smuggling through statements of co-accused, call records, and the recovery of gold from the airport and a passenger.  

The Tribunal held that the Department’s case rested too heavily on accomplice/co-accused statements and that, under the evidentiary principle reflected in Section 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act, a person cannot be implicated solely on such statements where no incriminating material was seized from him. It specifically noted that no incriminating article, including the allegedly relevant SIM card, had been recovered from Bane, and it distinguished the Commissioner (Appeals)’ reliance on the Supreme Court’s Naresh J. Sukhwani precedent as being in a materially different factual setting. The Tribunal also found weaknesses in the call-record theory: the Superintendent, Shri D.G. Nandanwar, had called Bane back and was told that the gold had been dumped in the Immigration Hall men’s lavatory, and the investigation showed calls from Bane’s son Prathmesh Rajendra Bane’s number between 03:04:03 A.M. and 05:33 A.M., whereas the CDR produced to the Superintendent for 5:00 A.M. to 6:00 A.M. did not show that number; the seizure itself occurred at 05:15 A.M.  

On the facts, the Tribunal concluded that the Department failed to establish that the later call to the Superintendent was a fabricated afterthought or that Bane was acting in connivance with the smugglers. It also rejected the adverse inference drawn by the lower authority from Bane’s alleged failure to contact another officer when the Superintendent did not answer the first call, finding that such reasoning did not overcome the absence of direct incriminating evidence. The Tribunal viewed the surrounding circumstances as more consistent with Bane having provided an actionable tip that led to recovery of more than 13 kg of smuggled gold, including about 10 kg found in the dustbin of the men’s toilet, rather than with his being part of the smuggling network. As a result, the Section 112(a) penalties were deleted in full.

The dispute arose for the financial year 2022-23. A notice had been issued against the petitioner under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 on the basis of gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100/- received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya. The Adjudicating Authority subsequently imposed a liability of tax, interest and penalty amounting to Rs. 1,63,452/- on 20.08.2025. The petitioner thereafter filed an appeal under Section 107(1) of the CGST Act, 2017. The appeal was dismissed on 28.02.2026 because it was filed with a delay of 21 days. The petitioner, however, relied upon a subsequent memo issued by the Collectorate, Gaya, Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025. According to the petitioner, that communication stated that GST was not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in the profession of Nukkad Natak and that Nukkad Natak teams comprising (4-6-8-10) members were exempted from the GST regime. Before the High Court, the petitioner therefore contended that the underlying issue was not merely
rows.summary:
The Patna High Court did **not** decide the merits of whether Nukkad Natak services are exempt from GST, but it held that the **exemption question must be examined on the merits** rather than being rejected solely as time-barred. The petitioner, **M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal**, is a **GST-registered entity** engaged in **Nukkad Natak (street plays)** for public awareness programs assigned mainly by government departments; for **FY 2022–23**, it received **gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100** from the **District Public Relations Officer, Gaya**, leading to a **Section 73 CGST Act notice** and an adjudication order dated **20.08.2025** imposing **tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452**. The petitioner appealed under **Section 107(1)** of the CGST Act, but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on **28.02.2026** because it was filed **21 days late**.  

The petitioner relied on **Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025**, which allegedly stated that **GST is not applicable to receipts against sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak** and that **Nukkad Natak teams of 4–6–8–10 members are exempt from GST**; however, the State argued that this communication did not identify any statutory exemption provision or GST Council decision and that the appeal was simply out of time. The High Court treated the exemption issue as one going to the **root of tax jurisdiction** and faulted the Appellate Authority for dismissing the appeal on limitation without deciding the substantive claim. Accordingly, the Court **set aside the 28.02.2026 appellate order** and **remitted the matter back to the Appellate Authority** to decide whether the petitioner, as a registered person performing Nukkad Natak, is actually **exempt from GST liability**, in accordance with law.  

For procedure, the petitioner must **produce a copy of the High Court order and appear before the Appellate Authority within one week** for fixation of a hearing date. Upon production, the Appellate Authority must provide a **personal hearing** and dispose of the appeal **within a maximum of two months** from receipt/production of the High Court order. Compliance takeaway: this ruling does **not** create a general GST exemption for Nukkad Natak teams; it only requires the appellate forum to determine the exemption claim on its legal merits in this case.

rows.summary: This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns an AY 2014-15 penalty dispute under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, arising from the assessee’s claim of section 54 capital gains exemption after selling a residential house for Rs.1,35,00,000 and computing long-term capital gain of Rs.72,19,588. The assessee initially claimed exemption for the full capital gain, stating that Rs.68,25,500 had been invested with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers for a proposed residential project and Rs.10,00,000 had been deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme with SBI; when the project stalled, he later entered into a compromise and purchased another residential property for Rs.49,95,000, leaving a shortfall of Rs.24,40,579 that was ultimately admitted to be taxable. The Assessing Officer taxed that Rs.24,40,579 in AY 2014-15 and imposed a penalty of Rs.5,25,923, equal to 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, and the CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the penalty on the theory that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars by claiming excess exemption and had not voluntarily disclosed the shortfall before scrutiny, relying on MAK Data (P.) Ltd. The Tribunal disagreed and held that, under section 54(2), the shortfall could not be taxed in AY 2014-15 because the statutory investment period had not yet expired when the original return was filed, and by the time it became clear that the full investment would not materialize, the time limit for filing a revised return under section 139(5) had already lapsed; the Tribunal also noted that a fresh purchase agreement was entered into on 28.05.2015, relevant to AY 2016-17. Although the proviso to section 54(2) technically applies to unutilised amounts in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme, the Tribunal treated the legislative intent as supporting the view that taxability arises only in the year of expiry of the prescribed period, not immediately in the original assessment year. Because the Rs.24,40,579 was held not taxable in AY 2014-15, the Tribunal found that there was no basis for alleging concealment or furnishing of inaccurate particulars for that year and deleted the entire penalty of Rs.5,25,923; the assessee’s appeal was allowed.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for Fresh Verification
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12609 Case Name N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, allowed the appeal of M/s. N. R. Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, contended that the apparent mismatch between FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-2A did not represent excess ITC. According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The Show Cause Notice itself recorded the date, time and venue of personal hearing as “NA”. The Proper Officer subsequently confirmed the entire demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices.
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded a GST input tax credit dispute involving M/s. N. R. Builders, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, after setting aside both the Order-in-Original dated 20.04.2024 and the Order-in-Appeal dated 07.11.2024. The case involved an alleged excess ITC of ₹2,33,502 for FY 2018–19, split equally into CGST of ₹1,16,751 and SGST of ₹1,16,751, with related interest of ₹2,03,730 and penalty of ₹23,350, taking the total demand to ₹4,60,582. The department had issued a pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024 and then a show cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 on 30.01.2024 under Section 73; the notice recorded the personal hearing details as “NA,” and the Proper Officer confirmed the demand ex parte. The Tribunal held that the dispute could not be resolved merely by pointing to a GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A mismatch, because the assessee’s explanation was that the credit related to FY 2017–18 invoices but was lawfully availed in FY 2018–19 within the period permitted by Section 16(4). It relied on CBIC Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST, which requires verification of such mismatches for FY 2017–18 and 2018–19 instead of automatic disallowance, and specifically found that non-appearance of an invoice in GSTR-2A does not by itself prove that the supplier failed to pay tax.

On facts, the Tribunal concluded that neither the adjudicating authority nor the first appellate authority had conducted the necessary invoice-wise verification of the appellant’s explanation, and therefore the demand could not be sustained on the existing record. It also rejected the first appellate authority’s reliance on Mahalakshmi Cotton Ginning Processing and Oil Industries v. State of Maharashtra, ALD Automotive Private Limited v. CTO, and Microqual Techno Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, holding that those cases were distinguishable because the statutory provisions and factual circumstances differed and there was no finding here that the underlying purchases were non-genuine. On natural justice, the Tribunal found a procedural defect: Section 75(4) requires an opportunity of hearing when an adverse decision is proposed, and since the notice itself showed “NA” for personal hearing and there was no evidence that any hearing was actually granted, the ex parte order was unsustainable. The Tribunal rejected the appellant’s argument that FORM GST ASMT-10 was mandatory, holding that Section 61 scrutiny and Section 73 demand proceedings are independent and that failure to issue ASMT-10 does not invalidate a directly initiated Section 73 proceeding. Interest and penalty were left to follow the outcome of the reassessment, with the Tribunal noting their dependence on the final tax determination and citing the compensatory nature of interest.

For compliance purposes, the remand order requires the Proper Officer to redo the adjudication de novo and specifically verify the ITC invoice-wise against FY 2017–18 GSTR-2A, suppliers’ GSTR-1, the assessee’s ITC register, books of account, and GSTR-9/GSTR-9C for both FY 2017–18 and FY 2018–19. The practical takeaway is that where a taxpayer claims that ITC appearing mismatched in GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A was actually eligible because it related to prior-year invoices booked and availed within the Section 16(4) time limit, the department must examine the underlying invoices and reconciliation before disallowing credit, and must also provide a genuine opportunity of hearing before confirming liability.

(Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court has allowed the writ petition filed by Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar and quashed the order dated 19.11.2020 passed under Section 264 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, rejecting the Trust’s claim for exemption under Section 11(1A) in respect of capital gains reinvested in a fixed deposit. The petitioner, a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007, had sold its immovable property for Rs.4,87,50,000/- under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011. The entire sale proceeds were thereafter invested in a two-year Fixed Deposit Receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, in accordance with the conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the Trust inadvertently failed to claim the exemption under Section 11(1A) for the reinvestment of the capital gains, although the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid. The return was processed under Section 143(1), resulting in a demand of Rs.19,44,180/-. The Trust subsequently invoked Section 264. The High Court relied upon the principles laid down in C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports and S.R. Koshti, holding that revisional jurisdiction under Section 264 is sufficiently wide to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a mistake or omission. The fact that the assessee itself had disclosed the income in the o
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that a charitable trust could obtain exemption under Section 11(1A) of the Income-tax Act even though it had not claimed the exemption in its original return, and it quashed the Commissioner’s rejection of the trust’s Section 264 revision application dated 19.11.2020. The assessee, Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar, was a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and registered under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007; it sold immovable property for Rs. 4,87,50,000 under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011 and then invested the entire sale consideration in a two-year fixed deposit receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, pursuant to conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the trust inadvertently omitted the Section 11(1A) claim in its return, although the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid, and the return was processed under Section 143(1) resulting in a tax demand of Rs. 19,44,180.

The Court accepted that Section 264 revisional jurisdiction is broad enough to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a bona fide omission or mistake, even if the income was already disclosed in the original return. It relied on Gujarat and other precedents, including C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports, S.R. Koshti, and Swaminarayan Mandir Trust, and held that the Commissioner should have examined whether the trust satisfied the substantive conditions for Section 11(1A) relief rather than refusing relief because the claim had not been made at the assessment stage. The Court specifically held that the relevant test was compliance with Section 11(1A) read with CBDT Instruction No. 883 dated 24.09.1975, and that because the sale proceeds were placed in an FDR with a scheduled bank for more than six months, the transaction qualified for the intended exemption treatment.

The Court also rejected the attempt to deny exemption by linking Section 11(1A) with Section 36(1)(a) of the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950, holding that Section 11(1A) is a standalone income-tax provision and cannot be curtailed by that state-law provision. It further held that the Supreme Court’s decision in Goetze (India) Ltd. was not controlling because that case dealt with claims before the Assessing Officer otherwise than by revised return, not the Commissioner’s powers under Section 264. Finding that the trust had acted bona fide, fully disclosed the capital gains, paid the tax, and suppressed nothing material, the Court allowed the Section 264 application, held that the trust was entitled to the Section 11(1A) exemption, and directed refund/payment of excess tax of Rs. 1,00,27,295 for A.Y. 2012-13 together with applicable interest under Section 244A, with consequential orders to be passed within four weeks. From a compliance perspective, the case reinforces that charitable trusts with qualifying reinvestment of sale proceeds should not assume a lost exemption claim is irrecoverable: if the facts and statutory conditions are satisfied, relief may still be available through revision, particularly where the omission was inadvertent and the tax position was otherwise fully disclosed.

rows.title: Income Tax | Bogus Purchases & Sales Cannot Justify Entire Purchase Addition; 5% GP Applied: Delhi ITAT
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12607 Case Name HSB Home Solutions Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2012-13 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); HSB Home Solutions Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Delhi ITAT partly allowed the assessee’s appeal for AY 2012-13. The Tribunal first upheld the validity of reassessment proceedings initiated after four years, holding that the subsequent survey conducted on 30.11.2018 revealed information regarding allegedly bogus transactions which had not been examined in the original assessment. The original assessment order itself recorded that the assessee had no business activity, despite substantial purchases, sales and disclosed profit. The Tribunal therefore found that the reopening was based on subsequent information and was not merely a change of opinion. On merits, however, the Tribunal held that the Assessing Officer could not simply treat the entire purchases of Rs.5,81,57,000/- as undisclosed income when the corresponding sales of Rs.5,94,91,966/- had also been treated as bogus. The Tribunal rejected the assessee’s contention that banking-channel transactions alone established genuineness, since physical movement of goods and existence of the parties had not been established. Considering the totality of circumstances, it directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs.5,94,91,966/-, while giving credit for the profit already disclosed by the assessee. List of Cases Discussed / Relied Upon New Delhi Television Limited v. DCIT, 424 ITR 607 (SC) Phool Chand Bajrang Lal v. ITO, 203 ITR 456 (SC) ITO v. Lakhmani Mewal Das, 103 ITR 437 (SC) High Gain Finvest (P) Ltd., 304 ITR 325 (Delhi) Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. v. ITO, 236 ITR 34 (SC) Sanand Prop
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT dealt with AY 2012-13 in the case of HSB Home Solutions Ltd. and first upheld the validity of reopening under section 148 even though the notice was issued after four years from the end of the assessment year. The Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position that the reassessment was based on fresh information from a survey conducted on 30.11.2018 under section 133A in the case of Shri Ashok Kumar Gupta and others, which allegedly exposed accommodation-entry activity through M/s Gayatri Maa Enterprise; this was not treated as a mere change of opinion because the original assessment had not examined the bogus-transaction issue and the survey material surfaced later. The original assessment record also noted that the assessee had no business activity despite reporting substantial purchases, sales, and profit, which supported the reopening.

On the merits, the Assessing Officer had treated the entire alleged bogus purchases of Rs. 5,81,57,000 as undisclosed income, and the CIT(A) upheld that full addition. The ITAT disagreed with the approach of taxing the entire purchases when the corresponding sales of Rs. 5,94,91,966 were also found to be bogus, holding that the Revenue could not simply select the purchase side for a 100% addition. At the same time, the Tribunal rejected the assessee’s argument that payments through banking channels alone proved genuineness, because the actual movement of goods and even the existence of the parties from whom purchases were allegedly made had not been established.

Instead of sustaining the full purchase disallowance, the ITAT directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs. 5,94,91,966, with credit allowed for profit already disclosed by the assessee. In practical compliance terms, the decision confirms that reassessment after four years can still be sustained where later survey material reveals previously unexamined bogus-entry activity, and it also confirms that in cases where both purchases and sales are treated as non-genuine, the tax addition should be based on a reasonable profit estimate rather than automatically adding the entire purchase figure.

The Assessing Officer/TPO had made an adjustment of Rs. 1,17,72,05,188/-, taking the position that electricity generate
rows.summary:
The Ahmedabad ITAT dismissed both Revenue appeals in **DCIT v. Nirma Limited**, being **ITA Nos. 1569 and 1570/AHD/2026**, which covered **Assessment Years 2018-19 and 2020-21** and arose from CIT(A), Ahmedabad-13 orders dated **09.02.2026** under **Section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**. The Tribunal heard the matters together because they involved substantially identical issues and issued a common order on **21.08.2026**, ultimately confirming the CIT(A)’s relief to the taxpayer on every contested point.

For **AY 2018-19**, the Revenue’s challenge to deletion of **Rs. 4,09,94,465** of depreciation on **goodwill** created on amalgamation of **Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd.** was rejected; the Tribunal accepted that the issue was already covered by earlier Tribunal orders in the assessee’s own case for **AYs 2012-13 to 2016-17**. The Revenue’s challenge to deletion of **Rs. 1,73,64,613** of depreciation on **brands and names** transferred from a demerged unit was also dismissed on the same basis. The major transfer-pricing dispute for this year was the inter-unit sale of **electricity** from a captive power plant, where the AO/TPO had made an adjustment of **Rs. 1,17,72,05,188** by valuing the electricity not at the rate charged to the manufacturing unit, but at the price at which power-generating companies sell to distribution companies; the Tribunal upheld the CIT(A)’s reliance on **CIT v. Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd. (395 ITR 247, Gujarat High Court)** and earlier assessee-favourable decisions, and sustained deletion of the adjustment.

For **AY 2020-21**, the Revenue again failed on depreciation claims: the Tribunal upheld deletion of **Rs. 97,67,598** on **brands and trade marks** transferred under demerger and **Rs. 2,30,59,386** on **goodwill** arising from the amalgamation of Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd., rejecting arguments that the intangible valuation had not attained finality and that the goodwill was artificially created. The Revenue also lost on inter-unit electricity benchmarking, where the CIT(A)’s deletion of **Rs. 20,17,23,105** was affirmed by following the Tribunal’s ruling on the AY 2018-19 issue.

The remaining substantive issue was valuation of **steam** transferred between eligible and non-eligible units for **AY 2020-21**. The AO/TPO had treated steam generated as a by-product of the captive power plant as having **nil arm’s length price** and made an adjustment of **Rs. 1,06,55,75,141**. The CIT(A) rejected that approach, relying on **Vishal Fabrics Ltd.**, **Star Paper Mill Ltd. v. DCIT (134 Taxmann.com 177 (2022))**, and **Gujarat Alkalies & Chemicals Ltd.**, holding that the fact steam is a by-product does not mean it has no cost or market value and that external market prices can be used as a benchmark if reliable data and appropriate adjustments are available. The Tribunal agreed, upheld the CIT(A)’s use of the prevailing market rate approach, and dismissed the Revenue’s ground challenging deletion of the steam adjustment.

In practical compliance terms, the order reinforces that, for this taxpayer and similar transfer-pricing fact patterns, **captive electricity and steam transfers cannot automatically be benchmarked at nil or at a generically higher external supply rate without regard to the actual inter-unit transaction and judicial precedent**, and that depreciation on **goodwill, brands, and trademarks** arising from amalgamation/demerger remains allowable where prior year rulings in the assessee’s own case have already settled the issue. The final outcome is that **both Revenue appeals were dismissed in full**.

rows.title: Income Tax | IBC Resolution Plan Bars Pending Pre-Approval Income Tax Proceedings: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12605 Case Name DCIT Vs Indusind General Insurance Company Limited (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2020-21 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Indusind General Insurance Company Limited (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, disposed of a consolidated batch comprising Revenue’s appeals for Assessment Years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21 and the assessee’s appeals for Assessment Years 2012-13 and 2020-21. The appeals arose from orders of the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) concerning, among other matters, disallowances relating to payments made to motor vehicle dealers. The Tribunal, however, decided the batch on a preliminary legal issue arising from a subsequent insolvency resolution process and did not adjudicate the merits of the individual additions or disallowances. The assessee, now IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited and formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited, was an unlisted subsidiary of Reliance Capital Limited (RCL), which held approximately 99.83% of its equity share capital during the relevant period. RCL was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The NCLT, Mumbai Bench, admitted the insolvency petition on 06.12.2021 and declared a moratorium under Section 14. A Resolution Plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and subsequently approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Income-tax Department had participated in the NCLT proceedings and had raised objections, principally concerning carry forward of losses under Section
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that once an insolvency resolution plan is approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, pending income-tax proceedings relating to periods before the plan’s approval generally cannot be continued if the claims were not preserved in the approved plan. This ruling came in the consolidated appeals of the Revenue and the assessee (IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited, formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited) for Assessment Years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21, but the Tribunal did not decide the underlying merits of the tax additions/disallowances; it disposed of the matters on the legal effect of the approved resolution plan.

The facts the Tribunal relied on were that Reliance Capital Limited, which held about 99.83% of the assessee’s equity, went into CIRP, the NCLT Mumbai admitted the insolvency petition on 06.12.2021 and imposed the Section 14 moratorium, and a resolution plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and then approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the IBC. The Income-tax Department had already participated in the NCLT process and objected mainly on Section 79 loss-carryforward issues, but those objections were considered and rejected. The assessee’s later name change effective 22.09.2025 did not alter the Tribunal’s analysis.

Procedurally, the Tribunal admitted additional grounds raised by the assessee and allowed the Revenue matter to be argued under Rule 27 of the ITAT Rules because the issue was a pure question of law based on undisputed later events, and no fresh fact-finding was needed. Substantively, the Tribunal placed weight on Section 31 of the IBC, which makes an approved resolution plan binding on the corporate debtor and its stakeholders, including governmental authorities, and on Clauses 9.1.8 and 9.1.9 of the approved plan. Clause 9.1.8 specifically addressed pending, threatened, present, or future tax proceedings and other proceedings relating to periods before the approval date for the corporate debtor and related entities, while Clause 9.1.9 barred governmental, judicial, and quasi-judicial authorities from acting contrary to the plan.

The Tribunal also relied on the NCLT’s approval order dated 27.02.2024, its corrective order dated 13.03.2024 clarifying that approval extended to Clauses 9.1.8 through 9.1.13, and the NCLT’s refusal to accept SEBI’s later attempt to limit relief only to Reliance Capital and exclude subsidiaries. Citing the Supreme Court’s decision in Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons and Bombay High Court decisions such as Uttam Value Steels and AMNS Gandhidham, the Tribunal held that claims not included in an approved resolution plan stand extinguished and cannot be pursued afterward. It rejected the Revenue’s reliance on S. V. Kondaskar as distinguishable because that case involved winding-up under the Companies Act, 1956, not the post-approval consequences of an IBC resolution plan. The damaged stock could not be sold as normal guar gum and was processed into Churi/Korma. The assessee contended that it had consistently followed Accounting Standard-2 (AS-2), under which inventories are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. TaxGuru’s publication on AS-2 confirms that inventories are required to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value and explains that the cost may not be recoverable where inventories are damaged or their selling prices have declined. rows.summary:
For Assessment Year 2017–18, the ITAT Jodhpur dismissed the Revenue’s appeal in **ITO v. Varsha Mills** and upheld deletion of two major additions: **₹2,79,03,981** relating to alleged undervaluation of damaged guar gum stock and **₹3,36,49,500** added under **Section 69A** for cash deposits made during the demonetization period. The assessee was in the business of manufacturing and trading agricultural products, mainly guar gum and its by-products Churi and Korma; its Phalodi account had turned into an NPA, the bank took possession of the factory and residential premises on **29.09.2016**, and the stock was allegedly damaged by rain, germs, bacteria, and lack of proper care while in the bank’s possession. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s closing stock valuation and substituted a market-based **net realisable value (NRV) of ₹82.58 per kg** sourced from an internet website, but the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that under **Accounting Standard 2 (AS-2)** inventories are valued at the **lower of cost and NRV**, and that damaged inventory must be written down rather than valued as normal stock. The Tribunal also relied on the fact that the damaged guar gum had actually been processed into **Churi/Korma** and sold for **₹2,02,69,593**, with that amount already offered to tax, so the stock addition was not sustainable.  

On the Section 69A issue, the disputed cash deposits were made in Mumbai bank accounts during **09.11.2016 to 25.11.2016**, and the Revenue objected because the assessee had a Phalodi account and questioned why cash from Phalodi sales was deposited elsewhere. The assessee explained that because the Phalodi account had become an NPA and the premises had been taken over, he and his family had shifted to Mumbai and therefore deposited the cash there instead. The Tribunal accepted this explanation and, importantly for compliance purposes, noted that the cash deposits were already recorded in the audited books as **cash sales**, supported by **sale bills, delivery challans, the sale register, and the stock register** produced before the Assessing Officer. Because the cash receipts had been duly recorded in the regular books and the related income had already been offered to tax, the same money could not be taxed again as unexplained under **Section 69A** absent contrary evidence. The practical takeaway is that properly documented, recorded cash sales—especially in exceptional circumstances like bank possession, relocation, and demonetization-era banking constraints—were sufficient here to defeat an unexplained-money addition, while damaged inventory supported by accounting policy, audit disclosure, and evidence of actual disposal at reduced value was also protected from arbitrary revaluation.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corruption Controls
rows.desc: Summary: Audits are a quiet but essential safeguard for bank deposits, investments, provident funds, companies and cooperative societies. However, the effectiveness of this safeguard is being weakened by declining real audit fees, market concentration and inadequate time for completing complex assignments. Between FY2018 and FY2023, the market value of Nifty 500 companies reportedly increased by about 92%, while their audit fees rose by only 28%. At the same time, six large audit networks handle around two-thirds of Nifty 500 companies, concentrating both influence and systemic risk. The problem is even sharper in cooperative societies, rural branches and local bodies, where auditors may have only a few days to examine cash-heavy, paper-based records. Professional restrictions also affect smaller practitioners: chartered accountants are generally restricted from undertaking business activities without ICAI permission, while the revised tax-audit ceiling treats assignments of widely different sizes as one audit each. Strengthening audit as an anti-corruption mechanism requires disclosure of the actual time available for an audit, scrutiny of abnormally low fees, development of capable mid-sized firms, risk- and complexity-based audit ceilings, and fair remuneration and timelines for rural and cooperative audits. Higher fees alone cannot guarantee quality, but persistent underpricing, rushed work, market concentration and conflicted incentives can collectively weaken independence and reduce the depth of scrutiny. Your savings sit in a fixed deposit, a mutual fund, maybe a cooperative society your family has trusted for years. Your provident fund is invested in companies you have never heard of. The company you work for reports its numbers every year, and your job depends on those numbers be
rows.summary:
The document argues that underpriced audit engagements can undermine anti-corruption controls by reducing audit quality, because very low fees, limited auditor time, and concentration of work in a small market can all weaken the independence, depth, and effectiveness of audits. Its core compliance message is that when audits are priced too cheaply, auditors may not devote sufficient resources to properly test controls, scrutinize transactions, or identify warning signs of corruption and misuse of funds, which in turn increases risk for companies, investors, and depositors. It emphasizes that stronger, better-resourced audits are important for protecting savings and improving India’s broader anti-corruption environment.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical implication is that audit pricing and scope should not be treated as a purely commercial issue: if an audit is materially underpriced, management should consider whether the fee level could impair audit quality or signal that planned procedures may be too shallow to detect control failures. The document does not appear to announce a new legal deadline, filing requirement, numerical threshold, or formal regulatory rule; rather, it is a policy-oriented warning about the compliance risk created by low-fee audit arrangements and market concentration. Organizations using external auditors should therefore ensure the engagement is resourced adequately for the complexity and risk profile of the business, and should be alert to whether budget pressure could compromise the auditor’s ability to perform a credible anti-corruption review.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. Section 76, however, independently empowers the GST department to recover tax collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, together with applicable interest and penalty. Despite this direct remedy, enforcement action is frequently taken against compliant buyers because they are easier to trace, possess identifiable assets and remain active within the GST system, whereas defaulting suppliers may have closed operations, disappeared or operated through shell entities. Automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch identification also makes buyer-side proceedings administratively easier than investigation and recovery against sellers. The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), recognising ITC as a statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions, including supplier payment of tax. Nevertheless, questions of fairness and enforcement sequencing remain. A balanced approach would prioritise recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for transactions involving collusion, fraud or failure to establish genuineness. Until legislation or binding precedent clarifies the sequencing of these provisions, buyers should maintain comprehensive evidence of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport records, banking payments and return reconciliation. rows.summary:
The document is a commentary on a recurring GST compliance issue rather than a new statutory amendment: it examines why bona fide purchasers can be denied input tax credit (ITC) when their suppliers collect GST but fail to deposit it with the government. The discussion focuses on the interaction between Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, which conditions ITC on tax actually being paid to the government, and Section 76, which allows recovery of tax from a person who has collected it but not remitted it. The key compliance message is that, under this framework, the tax department may target the buyer’s ITC claim even where the buyer acted in good faith, if the seller did not discharge the tax liability.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that invoice possession and payment to the vendor are not enough to secure ITC unless the supplier has also properly reported and paid the tax. Businesses therefore need stronger vendor-due-diligence and invoice-validation controls, because the risk of ITC denial can arise from counterparty non-compliance rather than the buyer’s own error. The document’s emphasis is on the policy and legal rationale behind this enforcement approach, namely that GST law prioritizes tax actually reaching the exchequer and gives the department a route to recover from the person who collected the tax but defaulted on payment. No new filing deadline, rate change, or numerical threshold is set out in the excerpt provided.

rows.title: Income Tax | Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS 2026)
rows.desc: Summary: The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS) provides a one-time, time-bound route for eligible taxpayers to declare specified foreign assets and foreign income omitted from earlier returns. The Scheme operates under Chapter IV of the Finance Act, 2026, comprising sections 130 to 144, together with the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers–Disclosure Scheme Rules, 2026. Form 1 may be filed electronically up to 31 December 2026. Section 133 creates two separate declaration routes: Row 1 covers undisclosed foreign assets or foreign income, subject to an aggregate ceiling of ₹1 crore and payment equal to 30% tax plus an amount equal to 100% of that tax, producing an effective burden of 60%; Row 2 covers specified foreign assets acquired from foreign income earned while non-resident or from income already offered to tax but omitted from Schedule FA, subject to a ₹5 crore ceiling and a flat ₹1 lakh fee. Rule 3 prescribes valuation as on 31 March 2026, including special rules for foreign bank accounts, sold assets, reinvestment and currency conversion. Rule 5 operationalises electronic filing and provides a 20% valuation-variance safeguard for assets other than bank accounts. The Scheme also prescribes Forms 2 to 4 for determination, payment intimation and certification. Full and timely payment is essential for immunity under the Black Money Act; false particulars, excluded cases, excess-value declarations and payment defaults may invalidate or bar relief. It therefore could not be treated like an ordinary private public trust requiring registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959. Reliance was placed on section 77 of the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, which provides that the Act does not apply to a public trust administered by an agency acting under the control of the State Government or by a local authority. The Tribunal accepted that the legal character of the assessee was material. It held that before drawing an adverse inference from non-registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, the CIT
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that an assessee’s failure to obtain registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, by itself, cannot be used as a ground to reject renewal of registration under Section 12AB of the Income-tax Act. The case concerned Urban Improvement Trust, Pali, whose Section 12AB renewal application had been rejected; the Tribunal did not finally grant renewal on the merits but directed the tax authorities to conduct a fresh examination of the application.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that renewal under Section 12AB must be evaluated on the statutory income-tax criteria, and a separate state-law registration deficiency cannot automatically defeat the application. Any authority reviewing a Section 12AB renewal request must therefore base its decision on the requirements of the Income-tax Act and the relevant facts of the trust’s activities and eligibility, rather than relying solely on absence of Rajasthan Public Trust Act registration.

rows.title: Income Tax | Corpus Donations Not Taxable Merely Due to Section 10(23C)(vi) Claim: ITAT Jodhpur
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12598 Case Name Mewar University Vs ITO (Exemption) (ITAT Jodhpur) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2017-18 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Jodhpur Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mewar University Vs ITO (Exemption) (ITAT Jodhpur) Summary: The Jodhpur Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by Mewar University for Assessment Year 2017-18 and directed deletion of an addition of ₹26,50,000 representing corpus contributions. The dispute arose because the University had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi), while the Assessing Officer and CIT(A) considered the specific exemption contemplated under section 11(1)(d) unavailable under that provision for the relevant year. Mewar University, Chittorgarh, was constituted under the Mewar University Act, 2009 enacted by the Rajasthan State Legislature. It was registered under section 12AA and also had approval under section 10(23C)(vi). It filed its return for AY 2017-18 declaring nil income. Assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 30.12.2019 determining total income at ₹15,61,58,900 after various additions and disallowances. The CIT(A) granted relief on the other substantive issues, but sustained the addition relating to the corpus contribution of ₹26,50,000. The disputed amount consisted of two donations: ₹1,50,000 received from Shri Ramesh Chandra Baser through NEFT and ₹25,00,000 received from Mundra International through cheque. Confirmations from the donors were furnished and specifically stated that the contributions were towards the corpus of the University. The Assessing Officer took the view that because the assessee had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi), rather than under section 11, there was no question of allowing the corpus contrib
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that corpus donations totaling ₹26.50 lakh cannot be treated as taxable income merely because the recipient institution had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi) of the Income-tax Act. In other words, the tax authority cannot deny corpus-donation treatment or automatically tax these receipts solely on the basis that the entity is claiming a particular exemption provision.  

For compliance purposes, this ruling is relevant to educational or other institutions receiving donations intended to form part of their corpus, because it confirms that the tax characterization of the receipt depends on the nature and purpose of the donation, not just on the fact that the institution has sought exemption under section 10(23C)(vi). The decision does not announce a new filing deadline, rate, or numeric threshold beyond the specific amount involved in the case, but it reinforces that corpus contributions documented as such should not be added to taxable income simply due to the exemption claim.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); International Society for Krishna Consciousness Vs CIT (Exemptions) (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal considered two appeals filed by International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON) against separate orders dated 30.03.2026 passed by the Commissioner of Income-tax (Exemptions), Mumbai, rejecting its applications for renewal of registration under section 12AB and approval under section 80G. The Tribunal treated the section 80G appeal as consequential to the section 12AB appeal and therefore first adjudicated the registration issue. ISKCON had been registered as a charitable institution under section 12A since 11.06.1975 and had enjoyed section 80G approval since 16.01.1971. The Tribunal recorded that its objects and activities had not undergone change and that it operates more than 270 centres across India. Its activities include free food distribution, education, yoga, medical relief, environmental projects, maintenance of goshalas, agricultural and rural-development work, devotional publications, broadcasting and accommodation for spiritual seekers. The CIT(E) treated activities including meditation camps, scriptural courses, devotional books and articles, satvik food distribution, broadcasting and royalty, agriculture and farm operations, and accommodation as falling within the residuary limb of section 2(15), namely advancement of any other object of general public utility. He consequently invoked the proviso to section 2(15), relied upon selected data from the ISKCON Juhu centre,
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai ruled in favor of ISKCON, holding that its charitable activities do not fall within the restrictive proviso to section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, which is often used to deny charitable status where an organization is seen as carrying on “advancement of any other object of general public utility” with commercial elements. As a result, the tribunal set aside the tax authority’s rejection of ISKCON’s registration under section 12AB, meaning ISKCON’s charitable registration should not be denied on that ground. The tribunal also directed renewal of ISKCON’s approval under section 80G, which is the provision that allows donors to claim tax deduction benefits for contributions made to the organization.  

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the tribunal found ISKCON’s activities to remain within the charitable framework and not to be disqualified merely because of the nature of its operations. The decision affects entities with similar religious/charitable structures that seek or rely on section 12AB registration and section 80G approval, especially where the tax department has challenged charitable status by invoking the section 2(15) proviso. No specific monetary thresholds, procedural deadlines, or new filing timelines are mentioned in the document excerpt; the operative change is the appellate relief reversing the rejection of 12AB registration and requiring renewal of 80G approval.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); TPJ Carriers Theppala House Vs State of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court) Summary: The Karnataka High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/s. TPJ Carriers, owner of a 14-wheeler tanker bearing No. KL-40/S-7040, which had been hired by M/s. SVP Petro Products for transporting bulk bitumen. The conveyance was intercepted by the State GST Authorities and proceedings were initiated under Section 129(3) of the CGST/KSGST Act, 2017. A penalty of Rs.23,86,590/- was imposed. The petitioner, being the transporter, contended that it was entitled to release of the conveyance on payment of Rs.1,00,000/-. The Court noted that this was the lesser amount contemplated under the first proviso to Section 129(6), and recorded that the petitioner had paid the said amount. The petitioner’s grievance was that although approximately two and a half months had elapsed after the penalty order, the authorities had taken no action for sale of the seized goods. The respondents submitted that the goods had not been brought to sale because the period for filing an appeal might not have expired. The Court examined Section 129(6), which provides that where the person transporting the goods or the owner fails to pay the penalty within fifteen days from receipt of the order under Section 129(3), the detained or seized goods or conveyance become liable to be sold or otherwise disposed of for recovery of the penalty. The first proviso provides for release of the conveyance upon payment by the transporter of the penalty or one lakh rupees, whichever is less. The second proviso permits re
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that hazardous goods seized under GST enforcement may be sold by the authorities under section 129(6) after the required notice process, rather than being left in custody indefinitely. The case arose after a transporter paid ₹1 lakh, and the court directed the authorities to proceed with sale of the hazardous seized goods in accordance with section 129(6), indicating that the enforcement mechanism can extend to disposal/sale where the goods are hazardous and continued retention would be impractical or unsafe.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that seizure of hazardous goods does not necessarily mean they will remain stored until a prolonged adjudication is completed; instead, authorities may move to sale after issuing notice under the statute. This decision is relevant to taxpayers, transporters, and logistics operators handling hazardous consignments under GST because it underscores the need to respond promptly to detention/seizure notices, address any demanded payment or penalty exposure quickly, and recognize that the goods themselves may be liquidated by the department if statutory procedures are followed. No broader rate, deadline, or industry-wide threshold is stated in the summary beyond the ₹1 lakh payment noted in the case.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); GRP Auto Vs JCIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Delhi Bench “F”, allowed the appeal filed by GRP Auto for Assessment Year 2010-11 and deleted the addition of Rs. 1,08,51,505 made by the Assessing Officer by adopting a differential gross profit rate. The Tribunal also held that rejection of the assessee’s books of account under section 145(3) of the Act was not justified. The assessee, a firm engaged in trading auto parts, filed its return for AY 2010-11 declaring total income of Rs. 4,36,31,310. It belonged to a group of concerns engaged in manufacturing and trading auto parts and had made major purchases from sister concerns, including Swiss Auto Products, Swiss Lamps Pvt. Ltd., Swiss Auto Pvt. Ltd., Swiss Devices (1) and Taruna Auto Pvt. Ltd. A survey under section 133A was conducted at the assessee’s business premises on 21-01-2010. Following discrepancies noticed during the survey, the assessee declared additional income of Rs. 1,15,16,100 towards excess cash, Rs. 1,75,98,542 towards excess stock and Rs. 2,27,29,200 towards undisclosed investment in furniture and fixtures, aggregating to Rs. 5,18,43,842. The assessee incorporated the excess-stock amount of Rs. 1,75,98,542 in its profit and loss account under “Sales and Other Income”. After considering that amount, its gross profit worked out to Rs. 8,42,95,900, or 10.79%. The Assessing Officer, however, treated the excess-stock surrender as income from other sources and excluded it while computing the business gross profit. The resulting gross profit was Rs. 6,66,97,358, representing 8.53% of turnover. T
rows.summary: The ITAT Delhi held that the Assessing Officer could not reject the taxpayer’s books of account under Section 145(3) merely to make a gross profit (“GP”) addition on an ad hoc basis, and it deleted the GP addition made in this case. The key point of the ruling is that a GP rate cannot be mechanically applied as a uniform benchmark across pre-survey and post-survey periods without proper justification and factual support, so an assessment cannot rest solely on a generalized rate comparison. For compliance purposes, this means tax authorities must have a defensible basis before discarding books or imposing estimated profit adjustments, and companies should preserve books, inventory records, and supporting explanations for any margin changes around survey periods to rebut arbitrary GP extrapolations. No new statutory rate, threshold, filing deadline, or procedural change was announced in the document itself; the significance is the limitation it places on ad hoc profit estimation and the need for evidence-based assessments under Section 145(3).

No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025, and quashing of the public announcement dated 02.08.2026 concerning sale of certain assets at IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru. The petitioner apprehended that Respondent No.1, being the Resolution Professional of Think and Learn Private Limited, a subsidiary or related company of Byju’s K3, was proposing to sell properties allegedly belonging to Byju’s K3, which could adversely affect the insolvency resolution process being conducted by the petitioner. The High Court noted that the matter was already seized of by the National Company Law Tribunal and that the assets of both companies were in the custody of the Tribunal. The Court therefore held that the petitioner should pursue the matter before the NCLT and that parallel proceedings could not be initiated before the High Court, particularly when the dispute was between two Resolution Professionals. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of by reserving liberty to the petitioner to move the pending proceedings before the NCLT on 20.08.2026 and directing the NCLT to take up the matter and pass appropriate orders. The High Court further permitted the petitioner to produce documents that subsequently came into his possession
rows.summary:
The document reports a Karnataka High Court order in a corporate insolvency dispute involving Byju’s, where the court declined to continue parallel proceedings against the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and instead directed the NCLT to promptly hear and decide the Resolution Professional’s application concerning the proposed sale of the company’s “K3 assets.” The key issue is whether those assets were already sold under an earlier process or whether the Resolution Professional can lawfully proceed with the proposed sale; the article indicates the assets are “allegedly” subject to dispute, which makes their ownership/status central to any transaction. For compliance purposes, the practical implication is that any contemplated sale, transfer, or related action involving these assets should be treated as legally uncertain until the NCLT rules, because the High Court has pushed the matter back to the insolvency forum rather than adjudicating it itself.

The order does not announce a new statutory rule, threshold, fee, or general compliance deadline. Instead, it imposes a procedural direction: the NCLT must consider the Resolution Professional’s request expeditiously, meaning parties affected by the insolvency proceedings should monitor the tribunal case closely and be prepared for a quick decision that could authorize, restrict, or invalidate a proposed asset sale. If a corporate compliance team is involved with the borrower, resolution process, bidders, or creditors, it should ensure no transaction steps assume clear title to the K3 assets until the tribunal’s decision is issued and any resulting legal constraints are reviewed.
