The Department classified these activities under “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In appeal no. ST/20226/2014, the dispute covered the period from 2007-08 to 2011-12 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 5,15,53,520/- along with interest and penalties. Appeal no. ST/30531/2016 concerned the period April 2012 to June 2012 and involved Service Tax of Rs. 2,06,792/- along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner (Appeals), in the latter appeal, upheld the demand while extending cum-tax benefit. STPI contended that it is an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and functioning under the administrative control of the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India. It was established, inter alia, to administer and facilitate implementation of the Software Technology Park Scheme. STPI was separately registered with the Service Tax Department and admittedly paid Service Tax on various services including renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services and project consultancy. The controversy was confined to charges connected with activities under the STP Scheme, particularly SOFTEX certification and issuance of NoCs. The appellan
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad has held that charges collected by the Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for SOFTEX certification and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are taxable as “Business Support Service” under the Finance Act, 1994. In practical terms, the tribunal treated these services as taxable support services rather than as non-taxable or merely regulatory/administrative charges, meaning the amounts recovered by STPI for these certifications can fall within the service tax net.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the ruling affects entities that pay for or provide such certification-related services in the STPI context, particularly where the charges are linked to business facilitation for software exporters or similar regulated activities. No specific effective date, rate, threshold, exemption, or procedural deadline is stated in the provided text, but the legal consequence is that these SOFTEX certification and NoC fees are characterized as taxable consideration for service tax purposes under the pre-GST regime. Companies dealing with STPI certifications should therefore review whether historical service tax was charged, paid, or accounted for correctly on such fees and assess any exposure for past periods, credits, or disclosures.

rows.title: Income Tax | Madras HC Upholds Deletion of Penny Stock Gains Addition under Section 68
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12592 Case Name CIT Vs Sohanraj Uttamchand (Madras High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Madras High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); CIT Vs Sohanraj Uttamchand (Madras High Court) Summary: The Madras High Court dismissed the Revenue’s appeals in T.C.A.Nos.714 and 721 of 2018 and upheld the Tribunal’s deletion of additions of Rs.32.90 crore and Rs.38.05 crore made under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of gains claimed as exempt Long Term Capital Gains under Section 10(38). The Court held that although the Revenue’s investigation could give rise to strong suspicion regarding manipulation in the prices of PFL Infotech Limited and Risa International Limited shares, suspicion, however grave, could not substitute proof. The Court noted that the shares had been purchased and sold through recognised stock exchanges, Securities Transaction Tax had been paid, sale consideration had been received through banking channels, and there was no positive material establishing that either assessee had paid unaccounted cash to an operator or participated in an arrangement to manipulate share prices. The Court further held that the Tribunal’s findings of fact could not be interfered with under Section 260A in the absence of perversity. The Supreme Court decisions in CIT v. Durga Prasad More and Sumati Dayal v. CIT, dealing with the test of human probabilities, were distinguished on facts. The Court emphasised that the test of human probabilities does not dispense with the requirement of positive material connecting the assessee with an alleged tax-evasion design. Relying also on the principles stated in Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CIT, Omar Salay Mohamed Sait v. CIT and Umacharan Shaw and Brothers v. CIT, the Cour
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court decision affirming the deletion of an income-tax addition made under Section 68 in relation to alleged “penny stock” gains. The court held that the tax authority cannot sustain an addition merely on suspicion or on the general view that the scrip was associated with price manipulation; there must be concrete evidence connecting the specific assessee to the alleged manipulation or to an unexplained credit scheme. In other words, the fact that a stock is low-priced or suspected of being a penny stock is not enough by itself to tax the gains as unexplained income.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is evidentiary: if an assessee has reported gains from share transactions, the Revenue must establish a direct link between that taxpayer and the fraud/manipulation before invoking Section 68. The decision reinforces that documentation of genuine transactions—such as purchase/sale records, contract notes, demat entries, payment trails, and other corroborating records—remains critical in defending against penny-stock related additions. The document does not announce a new statutory amendment, rate change, threshold, filing deadline, or procedural rule; it describes a judicial ruling that narrows the practical basis on which Section 68 additions can be made in penny-stock cases.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12591 Case Name Dhukha Ram Vs ACIT (ITAT Jodhpur) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2016-17 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Jodhpur Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Dhukha Ram Vs ACIT (ITAT Jodhpur) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Jodhpur Bench, allowed the assessee’s appeal concerning the application of the special tax rate under section 115BBE to ₹6,25,000 surrendered during a survey. The appeal arose from the order dated 22.10.2025 passed by the Ld. Addl./JCIT(A)-5, Kolkata, in relation to the assessment framed under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee was an individual engaged in retail trading of medicines and also derived income from operation of a sonography machine. A survey under section 133A was conducted at the business premises on 20.09.2016, during which ₹6,25,000 was surrendered. The assessee subsequently filed a return declaring total income of ₹14,81,960, including the surrendered amount, and paid tax at the normal applicable rate. During assessment, the Assessing Officer issued a show-cause notice proposing application of section 115BBE. The assessee contended that section 115BBE could apply only where the income fell within sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C or 69D, and that none of those deeming provisions applied to the surrendered business income. The AO rejected the explanation and taxed ₹6,25,000 at 30% under section 115BBE. Significantly, the AO did not invoke any particular provision from sections 68 to 69D or record a finding that the statutory requirements of any such provision were satisfied. The CIT(A) upheld the AO’s action, reasoning that the assessee had not explained the exact source of the surrendered income and that the deeming provisions would consequently apply. According to
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that income surrendered during a survey cannot automatically be taxed at the punitive rate under Section 115BBE unless the Revenue first brings that income within one of the deeming provisions in Sections 68 to 69D. In other words, a mere voluntary surrender in a survey does not, by itself, make the amount “deemed income” of the kind that triggers Section 115BBE’s higher tax treatment. The practical compliance point is that taxpayers who disclose income during a survey should not be assumed to face 115BBE taxation unless the tax authority can specifically classify the surrendered amount under the statutory deeming rules for unexplained cash credits, investments, money, bullion, expenditures, etc.

For affected entities, this ruling is relevant to businesses and individuals subject to tax surveys under the Income-tax Act, especially where income is offered to settle survey findings. It signals that the department must establish the legal basis for applying Section 115BBE rather than relying solely on the fact of surrender. There is no new statutory deadline or procedural filing requirement announced here; the key change is interpretive, limiting when the higher 115BBE rate can be imposed on survey-related surrendered income. Compliance teams should still document the source and nature of any surrendered amounts carefully, because if the income does fall within Sections 68 to 69D, Section 115BBE can still apply.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Co-operative Bank Conversion Mid-Recovery: Forum, Composite Notice & Cost of Delay
rows.desc: When a Co-operative Bank Changes Its Registration Midway Through Recovery – The forum, the composite notice and the cost of delay Summary: A State co-operative bank’s conversion into a multi-State co-operative bank during recovery can materially affect the forum, limitation and enforceability of proceedings against borrowers and guarantors. The article examines whether pre-conversion members automatically become members under the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002; whether claims against sureties fall within Section 84; and how the six-year limitation under Section 85 interacts with acknowledgments made only by the principal borrower. It also analyses whether a composite SARFAESI demand notice adequately identifies borrower-wise liabilities and secured assets, and whether prolonged delay after possession can reduce a guarantor’s liability under Sections 139 and 141 of the Contract Act where security loses value. Parallel SARFAESI and arbitration proceedings may be permissible, but multiple references arising from one composite secured transaction require transparent appropriation and consolidated accounts to prevent duplication. Conditional attachment before award must satisfy the statutory requirement of intent to defeat or delay execution, while indiscriminate freezes involving non-parties may exceed arbitral authority. The article further highlights objections concerning the Central Registrar’s appointment power, delegation, tribunal constitution and the distinction between the place and seat of arbitration. It concludes with a practical defence sequence: challenge constitution and membership promptly, raise limitation early, contest attachment within the appeal deadline, demand complete account and valuation records, and obtain independent evidence of security value and sale consideration. Table of Contents▸ Brief Introduction The law as it stands The present position Conversion does not carry the members across Is a claim against a surety arbitrable u
rows.summary:
The document addresses legal and recovery-process implications when a co-operative bank converts during an ongoing enforcement/recovery matter, with a focus on what happens to the proper forum, limitation, guarantor liability, SARFAESI notices, delayed asset sales, and attachment actions after conversion. The core compliance issue is that a bank’s conversion mid-recovery can change the legal characterization of the institution and may affect which authority or court has jurisdiction over the dispute or enforcement action, so recovery teams must confirm the correct forum before proceeding further. It also emphasizes the need to review whether previously issued notices remain valid after conversion, especially composite notices under recovery law and SARFAESI-based demand or enforcement notices, because a procedural defect in notice/service can later be used to challenge the recovery steps.

The document also highlights that guarantor liability remains a material issue in mid-recovery conversion cases, meaning compliance teams should not assume that a change in the bank’s structure automatically extinguishes or weakens enforcement rights against guarantors. Delays in asset sale or attachment are treated as legally significant, and the document suggests that postponement can create additional risk, including arguments about delay, prejudice, or invalidity of the enforcement timeline. In practical terms, the bank or recovery team should document the conversion date, map it against each recovery step already taken, verify whether any fresh or amended notices are needed, and reassess the legal basis for continued SARFAESI action, sale of secured assets, and attachment proceedings after the conversion event.

The assessee was engaged in mobile recharge services for BSNL and was also an authorised dealer of BSNL products. It contended that the difference between the amount reported in Form 26AS and the income recorded in its books represented trade discounts allowed by BSNL on recharge vouchers, which had been netted against the receipts. The Assessing Officer rejected the reconciliation and treated the receipts of ₹76,38,827 reflected in Form 26AS as commission income. After allowing expenses and partner remuneration/interest, the AO made a further addition of ₹48,08,962 and initiated penalty proceedings under section 270A. The CIT(A) upheld the addition, principally observing that the assessee had not produced revised TDS certificates, correction of Form 26AS, confirmation from BSNL or other independent corroborative evidence. The Tribunal, however, noted that the assessee had produced a detailed reconciliation along with invoice-wise details of recharge vouchers showing the face value, discounted purchase price and margin retained. On verification, the Tribunal found that the difference between the gross amount reported in Form 26AS and the commission income disclosed in the books substantially corresponded to the trade di
rows.summary:
The document reports a Chennai Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) ruling in **Sri Balaji Shopping World** in which the Tribunal **deleted an addition of ₹48.09 lakh** made by the tax authorities. The disputed amount related to **receipts from BSNL**, which the Assessing Officer had treated as **commission income** largely because the **gross receipts appeared in Form 26AS**; the ITAT held that **Form 26AS alone is not determinative of the true nature of income**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Tribunal recognized the taxpayer’s position that the BSNL amounts were in the nature of a **trade discount** rather than commission, and it rejected the revenue’s attempt to recharacterize the receipts solely on the basis of tax-reporting data. The ruling reinforces that **third-party reporting in Form 26AS does not by itself establish the legal character of a payment or receipt**; the substance of the underlying arrangement and supporting evidence matter. No new statutory deadline, filing date, or rate change is announced in the document, but the decision is relevant to entities dealing with **BSNL or similar commercial arrangements** where receipts may be reflected in Form 26AS under a label that could later be challenged by tax authorities.

The Court noted that questions relating to guarantee fee, interest on convertible loan, product registration expenditure, trademark registration and patent fee, expenses incurred outside the approved R&D facility under Section 35(2AB), and exclusion of Section 14A disallowance while computing book profit under Section 115JB were already admitted for consideration in Tax Appeal No.590 of 2022. Accordingly, questions A, B, C, D, F and H were admitted. In relation to Section 35(2AB), the Court relied upon its earlier decision in Banco Products India Ltd. Vs DCIT, which had followed the principles laid down in Claris Lifesciences Ltd. and the Delhi High Court decision in Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. Vs Union of India. The Court held that once the prescribed authority grants approval/recognition to the R&D facility, the deduction cannot be denied merely because the approval was granted in a subsequent year. In the present case, the assessee had applied for recognition before the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) on 21 June 2012, and the recognition was approved on 9 Oct
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court decision involving AY 2013-14 in which the Revenue’s appeal was admitted on six tax issues, but the Court rejected the Revenue’s challenge to the taxpayer’s claim of a deduction under Section 35(2AB) of the Income-tax Act. The key holding is that the deduction for in-house research and development expenses cannot be denied merely because DSIR approval was granted later, so long as the underlying claim otherwise satisfies the statutory conditions; in other words, a delayed approval from the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research does not by itself defeat the deduction.  

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that taxpayers claiming Section 35(2AB) relief should still maintain full support for the R&D expenditure, the eligible in-house facility, and the linkage between the spend and the approved scientific research activity, because the court’s ruling addresses timing of DSIR approval rather than eliminating the need for documentation or substantive eligibility. The document does not provide any new monetary threshold, rate change, filing deadline, or procedural amendment; its significance is judicial confirmation that later DSIR approval, by itself, is not a valid basis for disallowance of the deduction for AY 2013-14.

Educate Limited Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Delhi Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal partly allowed the appeals of C L Educate Limited for Assessment Years 2013-14 and 2017-18. In AY 2013-14, the Tribunal deleted the addition of Rs. 3,59,22,304 under section 56(2)(viib), holding that the provision could not apply where shares were allotted as consideration other than cash pursuant to acquisition of a business undertaking. The Tribunal also allowed deduction of Rs. 11,61,86,712 written off as irrecoverable from Career Launcher Education Foundation under section 36(1)(vii), deleted the Rs. 1,41,71,192 disallowance under section 14A in the absence of exempt income, deleted the Rs. 1,88,42,329 addition relating to liabilities no longer required, and allowed Rs. 19,04,795 of loan processing charges as revenue expenditure. The royalty disallowance of Rs. 14,33,356 under section 40(a)(ia) was also deleted because the payee had included the receipt in its taxable income. However, the 100% disallowance of advertisement/business promotion expenses was sustained and the disallowance of prior-period expenses of Rs. 32,87,466 was upheld. For AY 2017-18, the Tribunal deleted the Rs. 34,10,731 ad hoc bad-debt disallowance, holding that the Assessing Officer had no basis to disallow 1/11th of the claim merely on the basis of sample verification. The disallowance of commission to non-executive directors was restricted to 30% under section 40(a)(ia). The issue concerning Rs. 1,18,75,095 provision for expenses was restored to the Assessing Officer for de novo verificati
rows.summary:
The document is a short tax-law update reporting that the ITAT Delhi granted relief to C L Educate Ltd across several income-tax disputes, specifically on share premium, bad debts, Section 14A disallowance, liabilities written back, and loan processing charges. The key point for compliance purposes is the ruling on shares issued as business acquisition consideration: the tribunal held that where shares are issued in connection with acquiring a business, the issue is treated as consideration for the acquisition and falls outside the scope of Section 56(2)(viib), which is the anti–share premium provision often used to tax excessive premium received by closely held companies. In practical terms, this means a company issuing shares as part of a bona fide business acquisition structure should not automatically be taxed under Section 56(2)(viib) merely because the shares are issued at a premium, provided the transaction is genuinely acquisition-linked rather than a disguised capital infusion.

The update does not describe any new statutory amendment, rate change, filing deadline, or numeric threshold; instead, it summarizes a judicial interpretation that may be relied on in similar fact patterns. Compliance teams should therefore focus on whether share issuances in acquisition transactions are properly documented as acquisition consideration, with board approvals, acquisition agreements, valuation support, and transaction records showing commercial substance. The same article also notes the tribunal’s favorable outcome for the taxpayer on the other contested items, but it does not provide the detailed reasoning or operative compliance standards for those issues.

rows.summary:
The ITAT Chennai held that a mere delay in filing an amended trust deed or modifying objects, by itself, cannot be treated as a valid ground to reject applications for registration under Section 12AB or approval under Section 80G. In this matter, the tribunal restored the assessee’s applications and found that the authorities were not justified in denying registration/approval solely because the object modification was filed late, without first examining the merits of the trust’s objects and eligibility under the law.

For compliance teams, the practical point is that charitable or religious entities seeking Section 12AB registration or Section 80G approval should not be denied relief automatically on a procedural timing issue relating to object amendments alone. The tax authority is expected to look at the substance of the application—namely, whether the entity’s stated objects and activities satisfy the statutory requirements—rather than relying only on the timing of the deed modification.

No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or hard filing deadlines are stated in the document excerpt. The key compliance implication is that entities should still keep object clauses, trust deeds, and related amendments properly documented and aligned with their actual activities, but a late amendment, without more, should not by itself defeat a Section 12AB or 80G application.

rows.title: Service Tax | SVLDRS Discharge Certificate Bars Revenue Appeal on Same Dispute: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad dismissed Revenue’s appeal after SVLDRS discharge certificate and also rejected extended limitation in the fifth SCN.The post SVLDRS Discharge Certificate Bars Revenue Appeal on Same
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad decision holding that once a taxpayer has received a valid discharge certificate under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme (SVLDRS), the Revenue cannot continue or revive an appeal on the same settled dispute. In this case, the Tribunal dismissed the Department’s appeal because the underlying tax dispute had already been resolved through SVLDRS, and the discharge certificate operated as final settlement for that matter. For compliance teams, the key point is that an SVLDRS discharge certificate has binding finality with respect to the covered issue, so any later departmental challenge on the same demand should be barred.

The decision also addresses limitation in a fifth show-cause notice (SCN): the Tribunal rejected the Revenue’s attempt to invoke the extended period of limitation for that notice. This means the Department could not justify the additional time window for raising the demand, which is important where allegations depend on suppression, wilful misstatement, or similar grounds typically needed to extend the normal limitation period. Although the summary provided does not include the underlying tax amount, dates, or the exact factual basis for the fifth SCN, the ruling is significant for entities that have concluded disputes under SVLDRS or are facing late-issued service tax notices, because it reinforces both the finality of the SVLDRS settlement and the need for the Department to meet strict legal standards before relying on extended limitation.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 153C Time Limit Runs From Material Receipt: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi holds AYs 2010-11 and 2011-12 outside Section 153C limitation as the block period runs from receipt of seized material by the other person’s AO.The post Section 153C Time Limit Runs From Ma
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi ruling on **Section 153C of the Income-tax Act** concerning the **time limit for completing assessments** in cases involving seized material belonging to “the other person” (i.e., a person other than the one searched). The key holding is that the **limitation period for Section 153C proceedings starts from the date the Assessing Officer (AO) of the other person receives the seized material**, not from the date of the original search or seizure. Based on that rule, the Tribunal held that the assessments for **Assessment Years (AYs) 2010-11 and 2011-12** were **outside the permissible Section 153C limitation period** and therefore could not be sustained.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that when a company or related entity becomes subject to Section 153C proceedings because materials were found in someone else’s search, the department must be able to show **when the receiving AO actually got the seized material**, since that date governs the statutory block-period timeline. If the notice or assessment is issued beyond the limitation calculated from that receipt date, the assessment may be vulnerable to challenge as time-barred. The decision underscores the need to preserve records of the **date of transfer/receipt of seized documents between AOs**, because that date can determine whether the income-tax department’s action is valid.

rows.summary: The document reports that the Patna High Court granted bail in a GST evasion matter involving alleged tax evasion of ₹73.75 crore, and that the court was examining the legality of an arrest made under Sections 69 and 132 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act. From a compliance perspective, the only substantive information provided is that the case concerns a large-scale GST evasion allegation and that enforcement action included arrest powers under those two provisions. No rule change, new compliance obligation, filing deadline, effective date, threshold, or procedural amendment is described in the text. The document therefore functions as a litigation/enforcement update rather than a regulatory change notice, and it does not state any specific operational requirement for businesses beyond highlighting the continued use of arrest provisions in serious GST evasion cases.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Recovery Demand Alone Does Not Require Custodial Interrogation: Bombay HC
rows.desc: Bombay HC confirmed anticipatory bail after investigation was completed and State stated custodial interrogation was no longer required.The post GST Recovery Demand Alone Does Not Require Custodial In
rows.summary: The Bombay High Court held that a GST recovery demand by itself does not justify custodial interrogation, and on that basis it confirmed anticipatory bail for the accused once the investigation had been completed. The State itself stated that custodial interrogation was no longer required, which the Court treated as an important factor in deciding that arrest-related custody was unnecessary. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that a recovery proceeding or demand under GST, standing alone, was not treated here as enough to support custodial detention where the investigative phase had already ended. The decision is relevant to businesses and individuals facing GST enforcement because it indicates that, at least on these facts, coercive custody was not warranted merely because tax recovery was being pursued. No specific monetary threshold, deadline, or new filing procedure is stated in the provided text.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Notice Only Under Additional Notices Tab Violates Natural Justice: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Calcutta HC quashed GST adjudication and appellate orders where SCN was uploaded only under Additional Notice and Orders without separate intimation.The post GST Notice Only Under Additional Notices T
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court held that a GST adjudication order and the related appellate order could not stand where the department uploaded the show cause notice (SCN) only under the “Additional Notices” tab on the GST portal and did not separately intimate the taxpayer. The court found this mode of service violated natural justice because the taxpayer was deprived of a proper and effective opportunity to see and respond to the notice before adverse orders were passed. As a result, the HC quashed both the adjudication order and the appellate order.

For compliance purposes, the key point is procedural: GST authorities cannot rely on a buried portal upload alone if it does not reasonably alert the registered person to the SCN. Taxpayers should therefore monitor the GST portal carefully, including the “Additional Notices” section, and maintain internal controls to detect portal communications promptly. At the same time, if an SCN or order was issued without separate intimation and the taxpayer can show it was not effectively brought to its attention, this decision supports a challenge on natural justice grounds. The document does not state any new tax rate, threshold, or substantive GST liability change; it is a service/procedure ruling affecting how notices and orders must be communicated.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Sports Centre Building Tax Exemption Claim Requires Reconsideration: Kerala HC
rows.desc: Kerala HC directed reconsideration of Sports Centre’s building tax exemption claim based on principal use and charitable activities.The post Sports Centre Building Tax Exemption Claim Requires Reconsi
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court has directed that Sports Centre’s claim for exemption from building tax be reconsidered, focusing on the centre’s **principal use** and whether its activities qualify as **charitable**. The court did not appear to grant the exemption outright in the document provided; instead, it required the relevant authority to re-examine the claim on the merits under the applicable tax-exemption standards.

For compliance purposes, the key issue is that tax exemption entitlement for a building will depend on the **actual dominant use of the premises**, not merely on how the entity describes itself. The decision indicates that if an organization is seeking building tax relief on the basis of charitable status or charitable use, it should be prepared to substantiate that the property is primarily used for that exempt purpose and that its activities genuinely fit within the charitable category recognized by law.

No specific effective date, filing deadline, tax rate, or numerical threshold is stated in the document excerpt. The practical compliance takeaway is that entities claiming building tax exemptions should maintain clear records demonstrating the building’s primary use, the nature of the organization’s activities, and the legal basis for exemption, because authorities may be required to reassess such claims if the factual basis is disputed.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Unsigned GST Show Cause Notice & Order Invalid: Rajasthan High Court
rows.desc: Rajasthan HC quashes unsigned GST SCN and order, holding digital or physical authentication mandatory under Rule 26(3) of CGST Rules.The post Unsigned GST Show Cause Notice & Order Invalid: Rajas
rows.summary: The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show cause notice and the resulting order were invalid because they were unsigned, emphasizing that either digital authentication or physical signature is mandatory under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules. In practical terms, the court found that GST notices/orders issued without proper authentication do not satisfy the legal requirement for validity, so taxpayers can challenge such documents on the ground that they were not duly signed. This ruling directly affects GST-registered entities that receive departmental notices or adjudication orders, because they should verify that any SCN, demand notice, or order is properly authenticated before treating it as enforceable. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is to check every GST communication for valid signature or digital authentication and to preserve a copy of any unsigned document as a potential ground for objection or appeal.

rows.title: Income Tax | Stale Investigation Material Cannot Justify Reassessment: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashes reassessment based on stale material already available in earlier proceedings; Section 151 approval held mechanical.The post Stale Investigation Material Cannot Justify Reassessment
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi decision holding that a reassessment under the Income-tax Act cannot be sustained where it is based on stale investigation material that was already available to the tax department in earlier proceedings. In the case described, the tribunal found that the reassessment was improperly initiated because the “reasons to believe” did not rest on fresh, live information or a valid new basis; instead, the department attempted to reopen an assessment using the same information it had previously possessed and could have acted on earlier.

A key compliance takeaway is that the tribunal also held the approval under Section 151 to be mechanical, meaning the sanctioning authority had not applied independent, meaningful scrutiny before approving the reopening. That matters because reassessments require proper statutory approval, and the decision reinforces that such approval cannot be a rubber-stamp exercise; it must reflect real consideration of the facts and legal basis for reopening.

For companies and tax teams, the practical implication is that if the department issues a reassessment notice relying on old investigation material or information already on record, the notice may be challengeable as invalid, especially if the approval process appears perfunctory. This is not a substantive change in tax rates or filing deadlines, but a procedural ruling affecting the validity of reassessment actions under the Income-tax Act and the standards for Section 151 approval.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Allowed Section 80G Approval as Religious Spending Stayed Within 5% Limit
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi directs grant of Section 80G registration where spiritual and satsang expenditure remained below the permissible 5% limit.The post ITAT Delhi Allowed Section 80G Approval as Religious Spend
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Delhi decision directing the tax authority to grant Section 80G approval/registration to an applicant despite some spiritual or satsang-related expenditure, because that religious spending stayed within the statutory tolerance limit of 5%. The key compliance point is that charitable institutions seeking or maintaining Section 80G status are not disqualified merely because they incur some religious expenditure, so long as that spending does not exceed the permitted threshold. In this case, the Tribunal treated the applicant’s expenditure as acceptable because it was below the 5% cap, and therefore approved the Section 80G registration rather than denying it on the basis of religious use of funds. 

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that organizations applying for or relying on Section 80G recognition should monitor any spending that could be characterized as religious or spiritual and ensure it remains within the 5% limit referenced by the Tribunal. The document does not describe a new rule, effective date, or broader procedural change; it reflects an adjudicated application of the existing Section 80G standard to a specific fact pattern.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax Payment: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court rules delayed Foreign Travel Tax payment is not non-payment under Section 38(3) and penalty cannot be imposed automatically.The post Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax
rows.summary:
The document reports a Supreme Court holding that a **delay in paying Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) does not amount to “non-payment” under Section 38(3)** of the relevant law, and therefore **penalty cannot be imposed automatically solely because the tax was paid late**. In other words, the Court distinguished between **late payment** and **failure to pay**, limiting the automatic use of penalty provisions where the tax was eventually paid rather than wholly omitted.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that entities responsible for collecting/remitting Foreign Travel Tax should still **pay on time to avoid disputes**, but a delayed remittance by itself is **not treated as an outright default equivalent to non-payment** under Section 38(3). Any penalty action must be assessed in light of this ruling rather than assumed to follow mechanically from lateness. The document does not specify any new filing deadline, rate change, or revised procedure; it is primarily a **judicial clarification restricting automatic penalty imposition** for delayed FTT payment.

rows.title: Income Tax | Telangana HC Dismisses ITTA as ₹10 Lakh Tax Effect Falls Below CBDT Monetary Limit
rows.desc: Telangana HC dismissed ITTA No. 4 of 2026 as ₹10 lakh tax effect was below the CBDT monetary limit under Circular No. 5 of 2024.The post Telangana HC Dismisses ITTA as ₹10 Lakh Tax Effect Falls Below
rows.summary: The document reports that the Telangana High Court dismissed Income Tax Appeal (ITTA) No. 4 of 2026 because the tax effect involved was only ₹10 lakh, which is below the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) monetary limit for filing appeals under Circular No. 5 of 2024. The practical compliance point is that the tax authority did not pursue the appeal since the amount in dispute did not meet the minimum threshold set by the CBDT for litigation. This is not a change in substantive tax law, but it confirms the operational effect of the CBDT’s litigation-management policy: appeals should generally not be filed or continued where the tax effect is below the prescribed limit. For corporate taxpayers and tax teams, the key takeaway is that small-value disputes may be vulnerable to dismissal on monetary-limit grounds, so appeal strategy should be reviewed against the current CBDT threshold before proceeding.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Karnataka HC Directs Reimbursement of Differential GST to Government Contractor
rows.desc: Karnataka HC directs PWD to determine and reimburse differential GST to contractor within six weeks, subject to verification of records.The post Karnataka HC Directs Reimbursement of Differential GST
rows.summary:
The document reports that the Karnataka High Court has directed the Public Works Department (PWD) to determine and reimburse the **differential GST** payable to a government contractor. The court’s order requires the PWD to complete this exercise **within six weeks**, and the reimbursement is expressly **subject to verification of the relevant records**, meaning the contractor’s claim is not automatic and must be checked against supporting documentation.

For a compliance team, the key point is that this is a **contractor-specific GST reimbursement direction** arising in a government contracting context, and it creates an immediate administrative obligation for the PWD to review the tax difference and process payment within the court-imposed timeline. The document does not provide the underlying GST rate difference, the contract details, or the amount involved, but it does establish that differential GST claims in such matters may need to be examined and settled based on records rather than denied outright.

rows.title: Income Tax | Madras HC Directs Fresh Section 148 Notice to Legal Representatives of Deceased Assessee
rows.desc: Madras HC directs fresh Section 148 notice to legal representatives where reassessment notice was issued in deceased assessee's name.The post Madras HC Directs Fresh Section 148 Notice to Legal Repres
rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court ruling on reassessment procedure under the Income-tax Act: where the Income Tax Department had issued a Section 148 reassessment notice in the name of a deceased assessee, the court directed that a fresh notice must be issued to the deceased person’s legal representatives instead. The key compliance point is that a notice addressed only to a deceased individual is not sufficient to validly initiate or continue reassessment proceedings; the department must instead serve the legally responsible representatives of the deceased taxpayer.

For taxpayers and their estates, this means reassessment proceedings cannot be pursued mechanically against a dead person’s name, and legal heirs/executors must be properly identified and notified before the reassessment can proceed. The ruling is specifically relevant to notices under Section 148, i.e. notices for income escaping assessment, and it reinforces that procedural validity depends on issuing the notice to the correct legal person. The document does not mention any new monetary thresholds, tax rates, filing deadlines, or substantive tax changes; its significance is procedural and relates to proper service of reassessment notices after a taxpayer’s death.

rows.title: Income Tax | PMS Charges Deductible Under Section 48 Amid Divergent Views: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai allows Rs. 8.42 lakh PMS charges as deduction under Section 48, following the assessee-favouring rule amid divergent Tribunal views.The post PMS Charges Deductible Under Section 48 Amid Di
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai has held that portfolio management service (PMS) charges of Rs. 8.42 lakh are deductible while computing capital gains under Section 48 of the Income-tax Act. In this case, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position and allowed the PMS fees to be treated as an expenditure incurred in connection with the transfer of capital assets, despite the fact that there have been divergent views among different Tribunal decisions on this issue. The practical effect is that taxpayers who have incurred PMS charges in relation to managing investments and then realized capital gains may be able to claim those charges as a deduction from capital gains, reducing taxable gains, subject to the facts of their case and the applicable judicial view.  

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this is a favorable appellate ruling, but it is not described as a statutory amendment or a universal rule change; rather, it reflects a tribunal-level interpretation in a contested area. Entities or individuals using PMS should therefore preserve documentation showing the PMS fees paid, the link between those charges and the management/transfer of capital assets, and the basis on which the deduction is claimed under Section 48, because the deductibility position may still depend on jurisdictional precedent and case-specific facts.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Belated Writ Cannot Revive Time-Barred GST Refund Challenge: Kerala HC
rows.desc: Kerala HC dismissed a belated writ against rejection of transitional ITC refund, holding Article 226 cannot revive a remedy lost by limitation.The post Belated Writ Cannot Revive Time-Barred GST Refun
rows.summary: The Kerala High Court held that a taxpayer cannot use a delayed writ petition under Article 226 to resurrect a GST refund challenge that has already become time-barred. The case involved rejection of a transitional input tax credit (ITC) refund, and the court dismissed the writ on the ground that the claimant had missed the legally available time to pursue the remedy. In practical compliance terms, the decision reinforces that GST refund and transitional credit disputes must be raised within the prescribed limitation period, because courts may refuse to entertain stale challenges even if the underlying grievance concerns tax credit or refund denial. The ruling does not announce a new GST filing requirement or change any statutory deadline, but it is an important procedural warning: once the statutory or otherwise available challenge window closes, Article 226 will generally not be available as a fallback to reopen the matter.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kerala HC Quashes Reassessment Order for Ignoring Taxpayer’s Prior-Year Tax Claim
rows.desc: Kerala HC quashes a Section 148A(3) order for failing to examine the assessee’s claim that the disputed amount was already taxed in AY 2019-20.The post Kerala HC Quashes Reassessment Order for Ignorin
rows.summary: The document reports a Kerala High Court ruling on an income tax reassessment matter in which the court quashed an order passed under Section 148A(3) because the assessing authority did not properly consider the taxpayer’s claim that the disputed amount had already been taxed in Assessment Year (AY) 2019-20. In practical terms, the court held that before initiating or sustaining reassessment proceedings, the department must meaningfully examine the assessee’s explanation and tax history, especially where the taxpayer asserts that the same income has already been offered to tax in an earlier year. The decision appears to affect taxpayers facing reassessment notices under Section 148A and the tax authorities handling them, reinforcing that a reassessment order cannot be sustained if it ignores a material factual contention raised by the assessee. No specific tax rate, monetary threshold, or filing deadline is mentioned in the excerpt, but the compliance takeaway is that companies should preserve and be prepared to produce prior-year tax computations, return disclosures, and supporting records whenever the department questions whether an amount has been taxed already.

rows.title: Service Tax | Time Share Accommodation Not Taxable as Club or Association Service: CESTAT Hyderabad
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad set aside service tax on time-share accommodation, holding customers were not club members and penalties were unsustainable.The post Time Share Accommodation Not Taxable as Club or As
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that service tax could not be levied on time-share accommodation by treating it as a “club or association” service, and it set aside the tax demand. The tribunal’s reasoning was that the customers using the time-share accommodation were not members of a club or association in the legal sense required for that tax category, so the arrangement did not fit the taxable service definition relied on by the department. As a result, the related penalties were also struck down as unsustainable.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this decision narrows the department’s ability to classify time-share accommodation receipts as club/association service merely because customers pay for access or use over time; the legal form of the relationship matters. The ruling indicates that businesses offering time-share accommodation should review how their service is categorized for indirect tax purposes, especially where the tax position was based on the customers being treated as members. No effective date, rate change, or prospective compliance deadline is stated in the text provided; the document reflects a judicial determination on a disputed tax classification and penalty exposure.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs Cannot Indefinitely Detain Imported Car Without Seizure Order: Gujarat HC
rows.desc: Gujarat HC ordered release of an imported Land Cruiser, holding Customs cannot bypass Section 110 limitation by keeping goods under prolonged detention.The post Customs Cannot Indefinitely Detain Impo
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court ruling that Customs authorities cannot avoid the statutory seizure framework under Section 110 of the Customs Act by simply keeping imported goods under prolonged detention without issuing a proper seizure order. The specific case involved an imported Land Cruiser that had been held by Customs, and the court directed its release, indicating that indefinite retention of imported goods is not permissible when Customs has not lawfully completed the seizure process.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that once Customs takes possession or control of imported goods, it must act within the legal limits and cannot continue detaining the property indefinitely as a substitute for seizure. The ruling reinforces that Customs enforcement actions must follow the prescribed statutory procedure, including timely issuance of a seizure order where required, rather than relying on open-ended detention. No specific monetary thresholds, deadlines, or rate changes are mentioned in the provided text, but the decision is significant for importers, customs brokers, and compliance teams handling detained shipments because it strengthens the ability to challenge prolonged detention that is not backed by formal seizure action.

rows.title: Excise Duty | CENVAT Credit Cannot Be Denied When Manufacturer’s Invoice Names Assessee as Consignee: CESTAT Kolkata
rows.desc: CESTAT Kolkata allows CENVAT credit where manufacturer’s invoice named assessee as consignee and goods were received and accounted for.The post CENVAT Credit Cannot Be Denied When Manufacturer’s Invoi
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Kolkata ruling on excise/CENVAT credit, holding that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the manufacturer’s invoice named the assessee as the **consignee**, so long as the goods were actually received by the assessee and properly entered in its records/accounts. In other words, the tribunal recognized that the invoice description and consignee designation were sufficient to support credit when the underlying transaction was genuine and the receipt of goods was evidenced.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that credit eligibility should be evaluated based on **substance and documentation of receipt/use**, not only on rigid invoice-form terminology, where the assessee is clearly identified as the consignee and the goods are traced into inventory or accounting records. The ruling does not announce a new rate, threshold, or filing deadline; it is a judicial interpretation affecting how manufacturers and recipients defend CENVAT credit claims in excise audits or disputes. Firms should still retain invoices, goods receipt evidence, stock/accounting entries, and any supporting transport or inward records to substantiate that the goods were received and accounted for, because those facts were central to the credit being allowed.

The tribunal had ordered a deposit of 50% of the disputed amount under the **unamended Section 35F**, and the appeal was dismissed when that condition was not satisfied. For compliance purposes, the key point is that, at least for appeals governed by the pre-amendment regime, failure to make the required pre-deposit can be a complete bar to appellate relief and can result in dismissal of the case without a merits hearing. The decision reinforces that companies contesting service tax demands must strictly track and meet any court/tribunal-ordered pre-deposit requirement within the prescribed time, because non-compliance can forfeit the appeal.

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC Orders Rs.53 Crore TDS Refund with Interest Without Form 26B
rows.desc: Delhi High Court directs Rs.53.09 crore TDS refund with interest, holding Form 26B and Rule 31A inapplicable after Section 201 assessment.The post Delhi HC Orders Rs.53 Crore TDS Refund with Interest
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court has directed the income tax department to refund **Rs. 53.09 crore of TDS, together with applicable interest**, and held that the department could not insist on **Form 26B** or rely on **Rule 31A** in this situation. The key point is that, **after a Section 201 assessment has already been completed**, the court treated the request as one that did not require the payer to go through the usual Form 26B process for correction or refund processing.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this ruling limits the tax department’s ability to reject or delay a TDS refund merely because **Form 26B was not filed**, where the liability issue has already been determined under **Section 201**. The decision appears to affect **deductors/payers seeking TDS refund after an adverse or completed Section 201 proceeding**, and it reinforces that procedural requirements under **Rule 31A** should not be applied mechanically to defeat a refund once the substantive assessment has been concluded.

The document does not provide any broader statutory amendment, rate change, or general new filing deadline; it is a **court-directed refund order** with interest, based on the facts of the case. Compliance officers should read it as a signal to review refund positions in Section 201 matters, especially where the department may attempt to insist on Form 26B even though the assessment record already resolves the tax position.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has approved Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) to acquire up to 9.99% of ICICI Bank’s paid-up share capital or voting rights, but only for a limited period of one year starting from the date of the RBI’s approval letter, which is dated September 4, 2026. ICICI Bank confirmed it received the RBI communication on September 4, 2026 at 9:09 pm and stated that if LIC does not complete the acquisition within that one-year window, the approval will lapse and stand cancelled. The permission is framed as approval for LIC’s “aggregate holding” in the bank, meaning LIC may build up its total stake only up to the 9.99% ceiling authorized by RBI.

For compliance purposes, this is not an open-ended ownership right and does not itself authorize immediate purchase of the full stake; it only permits LIC to increase its holding over time within the approved limit and subject to market purchases or other acquisition mechanics that still comply with law. ICICI Bank’s filing makes clear that the approval is conditional on compliance with all applicable statutory and regulatory requirements, so any transaction activity will still need to fit the broader rules governing shareholding in regulated banking entities and any other applicable filings or approvals. The approval therefore affects LIC as the prospective acquirer and ICICI Bank as the regulated entity whose ownership profile may change, while also signaling that any future increase in LIC’s stake remains subject to the usual banking-sector ownership constraints.

The filing also notes that this RBI approval follows a similar approval given to LIC for HDFC Bank, where LIC was permitted to acquire up to 9.99% of that bank’s paid-up share capital or voting rights; HDFC Bank disclosed in that August 19 filing that LIC already held 4.11% of its total share capital at that time. Taken together, these approvals show LIC expanding its potential holdings across major private lenders, but the key operative compliance point is that each approval is time-bound, capped at 9.99%, and contingent on adherence to all statutory and regulatory conditions.

The case follows a complaint filed by LICHFL, which has accused Chandra, Pankaj Suroliya, Amish Pandya and Rajeev Dholakia of allegedly cheating the housing finance company and conspiring to secure credit facilities on the basis of disputed financial disclosures.According to the complaint, Chandra submitted a net worth certificate in 2018 declaring his net worth at Rs 59,113 crore. LICHFL has alleged that the certificate was used to obtain loan facilities for M/s Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt Ltd and other companies linked to him.Relying on the financial certificate, LICHFL subsequently extended credit facilities to three companies associated with Chandra, the complaint stated.The housing finance company has now raised objections over Chandra's statements made during subsequent insolvency proceedings, particularly his denial that he had ever possessed a net worth of Rs 50,000 crore, as reflected in the certificates submitted to LICHFL.LICHFL has alleged cheating, criminal breach of trust and conspiracy in its complaint to the investigating agency.The complaint given to the CBI Head Office reads, "A loan facility of Rs. 500 Crores to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt. Ltd. and Pan India Infra projects Pvt. Ltd. (Co-borrower) as a Home Entity Loan (Takeover & Top-up for Business Expansion) under Loan Account No. 610700003341 secured by a Letter of Continuing Guarantee dated 28th March 18 executed by Subhas
rows.summary:
The Central Bureau of Investigation has registered a criminal case against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and three others — Pankaj Suroliya, Amish Pandya, and Rajeev Dholakia — in connection with an alleged fraud exceeding Rs 1,322 crore involving LIC Housing Finance Ltd. The case stems from a complaint by LIC Housing Finance alleging cheating, criminal breach of trust, and conspiracy in relation to credit facilities allegedly obtained using disputed net-worth disclosures.

According to LIC Housing Finance’s complaint, Subhash Chandra submitted a net-worth certificate in 2018 stating his net worth was Rs 59,113 crore (described in the filing as US$ 6,197.62 million as of 31 March 2017), which LICHFL says was used to secure financing for entities linked to him. One facility cited was a Rs 500 crore loan to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt. Ltd. and Pan India Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. as co-borrower, structured as a Home Entity Loan (Takeover & Top-up for Business Expansion) under Loan Account No. 610700003341 and supported by a continuing guarantee dated 28 March 2018 executed by Chandra. Another cited facility was a Rs 480 crore loan to Digital Subscriber Management and Consultancy Services Pvt. Ltd. and Spirit Infra Power and Multi Ventures Pvt. Ltd. as co-borrower, structured as a Rental Discounting facility under the Scheme of Rental Securitization under Loan Account No. 610700003500 and supported by a continuing guarantee dated 10 August 2018 executed by Chandra.

LICHFL says both facilities were extended at least in part on the basis of the net-worth certificates and now alleges that, during later insolvency proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, Chandra denied ever having the net worth shown in those certificates. The complaint says he later stated his net worth in 2024 was Rs 31.79 crore and claimed that even in 2017-18 he did not have a net worth above Rs 40,000 crore, which LICHFL says is inconsistent with the representations made to obtain the loans. The document does not describe any regulatory rule change or new industry-wide obligation; instead, it reflects an enforcement action based on alleged misstatements in financing documentation and guarantor disclosures.

Chandra separately stated on 27 August that he has not borrowed money from any lender and is only a personal guarantor. He said the total claim against him in the personal insolvency proceedings is Rs 3,992 crore from objecting creditors, not Rs 22,000 crore, and that Rs 21,696 crore had been admitted by the Resolution Professional. He also said Rs 620 crore of the objecting creditors’ claim has been settled and that borrower entities have offered another Rs 1,063 crore, while the borrowing entities for which he gave personal guarantees have repaid Rs 43,000 crore to date. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this is a fraud/criminal enforcement matter centered on the accuracy of net-worth certificates, the basis for loan underwriting to related entities, and the exposure created by personal guarantees in insolvency proceedings.

Read Today's Paper var _BL_pg = 0;var competitionClients = ''; var showFullWidthArticle = '1'; var crrArtId = '133755358'; India's balance of payments likely to post $60-65 bn surplus in FY27 despite wider CAD: HDFC BankSECTIONSIndia's balance of payments likely to post $60-65 bn surplus in FY27 despite wider CAD: HDFC BankANILast Updated: Sep 04, 2026, 12:47:00 PM ISTRate StoryFollow usShareFont SizeAbcSmallAbcMediumAbcLargeSavePrintSynopsisIndia’s balance of payments (BoP) is likely to post a $60-65 billion surplus in FY27, despite a widening current account deficit, HDFC Bank said.ANIIndia’s BoP likely to post USD 60-65 bn surplus in FY27 despite wider CAD: HDFC BankNew Delhi [India], September 4 (ANI): India's balance of payments (BoP) is expected to post a surplus of USD 60-65 billion in FY27 despite a widening current account deficit, as strong inflows through special RBI schemes are likely to offset weak capital flows, HDFC Bank said in a report. #sr_widget.onDemand p, #stock_pro.onDemand p{font-size: 14px;line-height: 1.28;} .onDemand .live_stock{left:17px;padding:1px 3px 1px 5px;font-size:12px;font-weight:600;line-height:18px;top:9px} #sr_widget.onDemand .sr_desc{margin:0 auto 0;} #sr_widget.onDemand .live_stock p a{color: #fff;;} #sr_widget.onDemand .sr_desc{color: #024d99;margin-top:10px;} #sr_widget.onDemand .crypto .live_stock .lb-icon{8px 6px 5px 3px !important} #sr_widget.crypto.onDemand a.text{border-bottom:1px solid #ccc;padding-bottom:5px;display:block;width:100%} #sr_widget.onDemand .sr_desc .text p, #stock_pro.onDemand .sr_desc .text p{font-size:12px;font-weight:400;} The bank expects the current account deficit (CAD) to widen to around 1.1-1.3 per cent of GDP
rows.summary:
HDFC Bank’s report says India’s balance of payments is expected to remain in surplus in FY27, with a projected surplus of about USD 60–65 billion, even though the current account deficit is likely to widen. The bank expects the current account deficit to rise to roughly 1.1%–1.3% of GDP in FY27, and to be even higher in the second quarter at about 1.5%–1.7% of GDP. Despite that deterioration in the current account, HDFC Bank says the overall BoP should stay positive because large inflows mobilized through the RBI’s special foreign-currency funding channels are expected to more than offset weaker capital-account flows.

The report specifically points to the RBI’s FCNR(B) deposit scheme and overseas borrowing measures as the main sources of support for the surplus. As of August 31, total foreign exchange inflows under the RBI’s special USD-INR swap facility had reached USD 136.38 billion, broken down into USD 127.23 billion from FCNR(B) deposits, USD 5.26 billion from overseas foreign currency borrowings (OFCBs), and USD 3.89 billion from external commercial borrowings (ECBs). The document also notes that India’s BoP posted a deficit of USD 8.1 billion in the first quarter, versus a surplus of USD 4.5 billion in the same quarter a year earlier.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the relevant RBI special funding channels remain a material source of FX inflows, and entities using FCNR(B), OFCB, or ECB routes should expect continued policy significance of these instruments in supporting external financing conditions. The article does not announce a new rule or deadline, but it indicates that the RBI measures are already being used at scale and are central to the expected FY27 BoP outcome.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) materially tightened system liquidity by absorbing more than ₹6 trillion in a single day after bank liquidity had surged to a record level. Specifically, the RBI received ₹3.53 trillion in bids at an overnight variable reverse repo-style auction and also took in ₹2.59 trillion through a 30-day auction, bringing the total liquidity absorbed to over ₹6 trillion. The article says the RBI had intended to withdraw ₹7 trillion through the 30-day operation, but participation was described by traders as weak; one explanation given was a technical glitch in the auction process, although another source familiar with the matter denied glitches and said all bids were processed through the RBI’s e-Kuber system.  

For compliance and treasury monitoring purposes, the key point is that this is a central-bank liquidity-management action affecting the Indian banking system, not a new rule imposing direct obligations on corporates; however, it can affect funding conditions, short-term rates, and bank balance-sheet liquidity. The article states that India’s banking system liquidity surplus had reached ₹11.6 trillion on September 6, which was nearly 4% of banking system deposits, and this spike appears to be the trigger for the RBI’s absorption operations. No specific filing deadline, effective date, or entity-level compliance requirement is announced in the piece, but banks and other market participants should note the scale of the withdrawal and the RBI’s use of overnight and 30-day auctions as the mechanism.

RBI Deputy Governor Swaminathan J used the 3rd Conference of Registrars of Cooperative Societies (RCSs), organized by the RBI, to call for tighter governance and stronger internal controls in urban cooperative banks (UCBs), along with faster adoption of technology. His remarks specifically urged UCBs to improve oversight and control systems and to strengthen defenses against cyber-enabled frauds and money-mule accounts, indicating a compliance focus not just on traditional prudential controls but also on digital fraud prevention.

He also stressed that effective supervision of UCBs requires closer coordination between the RBI, the Registrars of Cooperative Societies (RCSs), and the Central Registrar of Cooperative Societies (CRCS). The article mentions “Mission SAKSHAM” as an RBI capacity-building initiative, suggesting that the RBI is tying these governance expectations to broader institution-building and supervisory readiness efforts.

No specific regulatory circular, formal rule change, effective date, deadline, numerical threshold, or mandatory reporting requirement is stated in the article. For compliance teams at UCBs or cooperative-sector entities, the practical takeaway is that regulators are signaling heightened expectations around governance, internal controls, cyber-fraud prevention, and coordination with cooperative registrars, but the piece itself does not announce a new enforceable compliance deadline or quantified requirement.

This article is primarily a market update on the Reserve Bank of India’s FCNR-B deposit scheme rather than a new rule or circular, so it does not itself announce a fresh compliance obligation. It reports that the FCNR-B deposit facility has attracted more than **$127 billion**, far exceeding market expectations, and notes that the RBI had earlier introduced supporting measures in **early June 2026** to boost capital inflows into India.

The measures referenced were designed to make FCNR-B deposits more attractive and to support external financing: the RBI offered **hedging cost support for three-year and five-year FCNR-B deposits** and opened a **concessional swap window for public sector entities** raising funds through **external commercial borrowings (ECBs)**. The article does not specify any further deadline, filing requirement, rate, cap, or procedural change beyond those June support measures, and it does not describe a new obligation for corporates beyond the fact that eligible institutions may have been able to access these RBI-backed incentives.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this signals strong inflows and continued RBI support for foreign currency deposits and ECB-related funding channels, which may affect treasury, funding, and hedging strategy. Any institution considering FCNR-B-linked funding or ECB activity should confirm whether it qualified for the June 2026 support windows and whether its hedging or swap arrangements were structured in line with the terms of those facilities.

rows.summary:
The document reports a change in how banks are classifying certain microfinance-related lending: loans connected to microfinance institutions (MFIs) are being treated as **retail credit** rather than as microfinance exposure. The shift is described as being driven largely by banks that are now categorizing **unsecured home loans extended to households earning below ₹3 lakh annually** as retail loans, which has the practical effect of moving this lending out of the microfinance bucket and into the retail lending book.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the affected activity is the origination/classification of loans to lower-income households, specifically **unsecured home loans to borrowers with annual household income below ₹3 lakh**. The document does not set out a new regulatory filing deadline, implementation date, or numeric prudential ratio; it is describing an industry-wide reclassification trend that changes how banks book these exposures for internal reporting, portfolio management, and potentially regulatory capital or sectoral exposure monitoring. Compliance teams should verify how their institution is classifying MFI-originated or MFI-linked loans, confirm whether the bank’s underwriting and product taxonomy now places these loans under retail credit, and ensure internal reporting, risk systems, and portfolio definitions are aligned with that treatment.

rows.title: ARCIL seeing fastest growth in NBFC originated retail bad loans: CEO Phanindranath Kakarla
rows.desc: Articles 5 min read ARCIL seeing fastest growth in NBFC originated retail bad loans: CEO Phanindranath Kakarla Asset Reconstruction Company India Ltd (ARCIL) is seeing the fastest growth in retail assets originated by NBFCs, even as bank originated, corporate and other retail portfolios continue to grow, with CEO Phanindranath Kakarla and CFO Pramod Kumar Gupta saying retail and SME assets are likely to gain a larger share of the portfolio as they grow faster than corporate assets. The company, which is set to become the first standalone asset reconstruction company to list in India, is also open to acquisitions of smaller ARCs. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Sep 6, 2026 at 11:03 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133846109; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook INTERVIEW | ARCIL CEO Phanindranath Kakarla & CFO Pramod Kumar Gupta* ARCIL expects retail and SME assets to gain share as they grow faster than corporate assets.* The fastest growth in ARCIL’s portfolio is currently coming from retail assets originated by NBFCs.* Retail and SME together accounted for a little over 31% of ARCIL’s portfolio in FY26, while corporate assets accounted for around 69%.* ARCIL’s retail and SME portfolio has grown at a CAGR of close to 56% over the last couple of years.* Currently handles around 32 lakh NPA accounts on the retail side and operates across around 24 states.* Resolves close to 25% of its opening AUM every year, supported by low leverage and cash flows generated through resolutions.* Around Rs 5.5 lakh crore of corporate assets written off by banks and NBFCs are returning to the resolution ecosystem.* Sees NARCL as both a competitor and a complement, with NARCL largely focused on very large-ticket stressed assets.* ARCIL is open to acquiring smaller ARCs where there is a willing seller, the right valuation and a strategic fit.Q. W
rows.summary:
ARCIL is describing a strategic shift in the stressed-asset market rather than a new rule, and the key takeaway for compliance is that the company’s portfolio and operating model are becoming more retail- and SME-heavy, especially in NBFC-originated retail bad loans. Management says the fastest growth in ARCIL’s book is now coming from retail assets originated by NBFCs; bank-originated retail assets, corporate assets, and other retail portfolios are also growing, but at a slower pace. ARCIL expects retail and SME assets to keep gaining share because they are growing faster than corporate assets, and in FY26 retail plus SME together made up a little over 31% of the portfolio, versus about 69% corporate, with SME around 8% and the rest retail.

The document gives several operating scale indicators relevant to compliance oversight: ARCIL currently handles around 32 lakh NPA accounts on the retail side and operates across about 24 states. Its retail and SME portfolio has grown at a compound annual growth rate of close to 56% over the last couple of years, and the company says it resolves close to 25% of its opening AUM every year, supported by low leverage and cash flows from resolutions. It also notes that around Rs 5.5 lakh crore of corporate assets written off by banks and NBFCs are returning to the resolution ecosystem, which management views as a continuing source of opportunity.

From a controls and operational risk perspective, management says the increase in smaller-ticket secured and unsecured retail assets is raising the burden on systems, processes, and operating capacity because transaction volumes are much higher than in corporate resolution. ARCIL states it is already using AI in operations, not merely piloting it, and that retail resolution is much more technology-led than corporate resolution. The article also notes ARCIL is set to become the first standalone asset reconstruction company to list in India, and that it is open to acquiring smaller ARCs if there is a willing seller, appropriate valuation, and strategic fit; for compliance teams, that implies potential future M&A and listing-related diligence, governance, and disclosure obligations, although the article does not give a specific listing date or acquisition timetable.

The document also provides market context that may matter for risk assessment: management says banking system NPAs are at decadal lows, but with a credit base of more than Rs 200 lakh crore and roughly 2% of that becoming stressed annually, the absolute opportunity for ARCs remains large; annual incremental lending is around Rs 30 lakh crore. ARCIL says NARCL is both a competitor and a complement, with NARCL mainly focused on very large stressed assets. The article is an interview and does not announce any new regulatory requirement, deadline, or compliance filing obligation; its material import is that ARCIL is scaling into higher-volume retail/SME recoveries, particularly NBFC-originated retail NPAs, and therefore may need tighter governance around technology use, account handling, portfolio acquisition, and any future acquisition or listing-related compliance.

rows.summary:
This article reports a market movement in Indian bank lending benchmarks, not a new regulatory rule or compliance mandate. The key change is that the one-year median marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) for scheduled commercial banks rose to 8.70% in August from 8.60% in July, and above its year-ago level of 8.60% for the first time in 14 months, even though the repo rate stayed unchanged at 5.25%. The increase was not broad-based: it was driven entirely by foreign banks, whose one-year median MCLR increased to 7.33% from 7.20%, while public sector banks stayed at 8.80% and private sector banks stayed at 9.35%.  

The article attributes the move to funding-cost pressures and market conditions rather than any policy action. Bank liquidity improved sharply, with surplus system liquidity rising to about Rs 6.7 lakh crore by August 31 from Rs 2.5 lakh crore at the end of July and Rs 1.4 lakh crore at the end of June, helped largely by conversion of Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits into rupees. Despite that liquidity boost, banks’ fresh spread widened only modestly overall: scheduled commercial banks’ spread increased 8 basis points month-on-month to 2.62%, fresh deposit rates fell 9 basis points to 5.90%, and fresh lending rates stayed roughly flat at 8.52%. Private banks saw a larger spread improvement, with fresh spreads widening 22 basis points to 3.13% as fresh deposit rates fell 25 basis points to 5.96%, while public sector banks’ fresh spreads narrowed 5 basis points to 1.58%.  

From a funding and liquidity management perspective, the article notes reduced reliance on certificates of deposit, with CD issuance falling to about Rs 95,000 crore in July from Rs 1.71 lakh crore in June, and CD/commercial paper rates softening in the second half of July and August as liquidity improved. Credit growth remained stronger than deposit growth: bank credit grew 18.3% year-on-year as of August 15 versus 14.7% deposit growth, leaving a 360 basis point gap, narrower than the roughly 500 basis point gap a month earlier when credit grew 17.7% and deposits 12.7%.  

The improvement may be temporary because the special FCNR(B) deposit mobilisation window closed on August 31, although associated swaps remain available until September 11. The article also highlights that lending-rate transmission is still incomplete: cumulative transmission to fresh lending rates since February 2025 was 80 basis points versus 125 basis points of repo-rate cuts, and outstanding rupee loan rates only edged up to 8.97% in July while outstanding deposit rates were unchanged at 6.58%. For compliance teams at banks, the practical takeaway is to monitor benchmark-linkage effects, deposit competition, and funding-cost pressures—especially for institutions with larger MCLR-linked portfolios, since public sector banks remain more sensitive to MCLR/funding changes while private banks are more insulated because more of their floating-rate loans are linked to external benchmarks.
