This listing shows recent SEBI commodity derivatives regulatory materials and indicates that firms active in the commodity derivatives market need to monitor multiple updates across trading, clearing, settlement, and risk management obligations. The document itself is a search/listing page rather than a full circular, so it does not provide the detailed text of each rule change; however, it identifies the most material current items and their publication dates.

The newest items are a **12 Aug 2026 circular** on the **review of inclusion of historical scenarios in stress testing for the commodity derivatives segment**, and **11 Aug 2026 consultation papers** on both **expanding the scope of the SEBI (Vault Managers) Regulations, 2021** and **FPI participation in exchange traded commodity derivatives (ETCDs)**. These are currently consultation-stage items, meaning they are not yet operative rules, but they are important because they may affect how risk is modeled, how warehoused commodities are handled, and whether foreign portfolio investors can participate in commodity derivative products under revised conditions.

On **19 Jun 2026**, SEBI issued a circular on **clarification regarding the applicability of the benefit of early pay-in in the commodity derivatives segment**. Any exchange member, clearing member, or participant relying on early pay-in treatment should review this because it clarifies when the benefit applies and therefore affects margin, settlement, and operational processing.

On **16 Mar 2026**, SEBI issued a circular on the **coverage of the Settlement Guarantee Fund (SGF) for the commodity derivatives segment**, and on **5 Feb 2026** it released a related **consultation paper on draft circulars covering both historical scenario inclusion in stress testing and SGF coverage**. Together, these items indicate a broader review of default-risk backstops and stress-testing methodology for clearing corporations and commodity derivatives market infrastructure. Compliance teams at clearing corporations and exchanges should treat these as likely to affect risk parameter calibration, default fund coverage, and the documentation used for internal and regulatory risk controls.

The 2024 items are operationally significant and directly relevant to market infrastructure and members. On **30 May 2024**, SEBI issued a circular on **comprehensive guidelines for the Investor Protection Fund (IPF) and Investor Services Fund (ISF) for stock exchanges having a commodity derivatives segment**, and another circular on **revision of eligibility criteria for launching commodity futures contracts**. These affect exchanges that list commodity derivatives and may change the conditions that must be satisfied before a new commodity futures contract can be introduced, as well as the contribution/use framework for investor protection and services funds. On the same date, SEBI also modified the **requirement for inspection of accredited warehouses by clearing corporations**, which affects warehouse accreditation and ongoing supervision over deliverable inventory used in physical settlement.

Also on **27 May 2024**, SEBI issued a **standard operating procedure for handling stock exchange outages and extending trading hours in the commodity derivatives segment**, and a circular setting **eligibility criteria for launching options on commodity futures as underlying** for stock exchanges with commodity derivative segments. These require exchanges and members to have explicit outage-response procedures and could impose conditions on listing new options products, including product-launch controls, risk checks, and operational readiness. On **24 May 2024**, SEBI modified the **staggered delivery period in commodity futures contracts**, which is directly relevant to delivery-cycle planning, warehouse coordination, and member/client settlement processes.

Finally, the listing includes earlier 2024 and 2023 framework items such as **cross-margin benefits for offsetting positions with different expiry dates** (23 Apr 2024), a **notification of goods under the SCRA, 1956** (5 Mar 2024), a **Master Circular for the Commodity Derivatives Segment** (4 Aug 2023), a **revision in computation of the Core Settlement Guarantee Fund** (23 May 2023), and **direct market access (DMA) to SEBI-registered…** (10 May 2023, truncated in the listing). For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that commodity derivatives participants should check whether they are an exchange, clearing corporation, broker, FPI, warehouse/vault operator, or other market intermediary because different updates affect different parts of the market stack, and several of the newest items may still be under consultation rather than final implementation.

These are the core documents a CRA, and in some cases market participants interacting with CRAs, would need to follow.  

The 3 July 2023 Master Circular for Credit Rating Agencies consolidates the regulatory requirements applicable to CRAs; it supersedes or compiles the earlier operational directions into one reference document for ongoing compliance. The 6 January 2023 Operational Circular for Credit Rating Agencies is the more immediate operational instruction set for CRAs and should be read together with the Regulations, because it governs day-to-day compliance implementation.  

A separate 4 September 2023 circular specifically addresses the mechanism for sharing information by CRAs with debenture trustees, meaning CRAs must follow prescribed information-sharing arrangements with DTs where relevant to debt issues and surveillance of instruments. This is directly relevant where a company has rated debt securities backed by a debenture trustee structure, since the circular affects what rating-related information is shared and the process/timing for such exchange.  

The page also lists a 22 May 2024 master circular covering the issue and listing of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, security receipts, municipal debt securities, and commercial paper, and a 18 December 2025 circular on modification of conditions for reduction in denomination of debt securities, plus a 27 February 2026 circular on revised norms for appointment of an independent third-party reviewer/certifier for green debt securities. Those later items are not CRA-specific in the narrow sense, but they matter to entities issuing rated debt or green debt because they affect issuance/listing mechanics and, for green debt, third-party review/certification expectations.  

The document does not contain the substantive text of the requirements, deadlines, fees, thresholds, or detailed procedures; it is essentially a regulatory index showing the current legal/regulatory touchpoints for CRAs. From a compliance standpoint, the actionable takeaway is to monitor the 2023 CRA master/operational circulars and the underlying CRA Regulations as the governing framework, and to review the 4 September 2023 debenture-trustee information-sharing circular if your organization is involved in rated debt securities or trustee reporting.

This document is a SEBI “COVID-19 Measures” listing page, not a single substantive rule text. It shows a sequence of COVID-related circulars, press releases, and relaxation measures issued across 2020–2021, indicating that SEBI repeatedly extended or modified compliance timelines and procedural requirements because of the pandemic. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these were temporary regulatory relief measures affecting multiple market participants, and the firm would need to identify which of these circulars applied to its regulated activities and whether any extended deadlines or relaxed procedural requirements were still operative or had already expired.

The listed measures cover several regulated segments: Investment Advisers, AIFs and VCFs, Debenture Trustees, Debt and Hybrid Securities issuers and related disclosure requirements, issuer/listing procedures, valuation of debt and money market instruments, portfolio segregation, and other general regulatory compliance timelines. The page specifically references “relaxation in timelines for compliance with regulatory requirements” on multiple dates in 2020 and 2021, showing that SEBI continued to defer deadlines as the pandemic evolved. It also references an “addendum” to the April 13, 2020 COVID-19 timeline-relaxation circular, a further extension for “creation of security in issuance of listed debt securities and due diligence by debenture trustee(s),” and a circular on “relaxation from compliance with certain provisions of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 / other applicable circulars,” which signals that both statutory/regulatory obligations and SEBI circular-based obligations were affected.

The page provides specific dated entries that compliance teams should map against internal obligations: May 31, 2021 (AIFs/VCFs relaxation), May 3, 2021 (debenture trustees’ compliance timeline relaxation), April 29, 2021 (general timeline relaxation and addendum), April 29, 2021 (LODR/circular compliance relaxation for debt and hybrid securities), January 19, 2021 (procedural relaxations relating to issues and listing), December 31, 2020 (general timeline relaxation and extension of implementation timeline for creation of security and debenture trustee due diligence), December 1, 2020 (general timeline relaxation), October 1, 2020 (valuation of debt and money market instruments due to COVID-19 and another general timeline relaxation), September 29, 2020 (validity of SEBI observations and revision in issue size), September 18, 2020 (regulatory measures to continue), September 2, 2020 (segregation of portfolio review), and September 30, 2021 (extension of timelines for investment advisers).

Because the content is only a listing index, it does not contain the actual deadline lengths, numeric thresholds, or the precise revised dates in the text shown here. A compliance officer should treat this as an alert to review each linked circular/press release individually, confirm the exact relaxations granted, check whether any requirements were extended again or lapsed, and verify whether the firm had to file, disclose, maintain records, or implement procedures differently during the applicable COVID-19 relief period.

This document is a listing of SEBI materials relevant to **Debenture Trustees** rather than a single rule change. The most recent items show an active regulatory focus on how debenture trustees manage listed debt issuance, security creation, monitoring, defaults, reporting, and the scope of activities they may perform.

The newest listed item is a **circular dated April 28, 2026** titled **“Extension of timeline for compliance with terms and conditions by Debenture Trustees for carrying out activities outside the purview of SEBI.”** Although the underlying text is not provided here, the title indicates SEBI has extended a compliance deadline relating to debenture trustees undertaking activities that are outside SEBI’s regulatory scope, so firms relying on any such permissions or conditional relaxations should verify the revised timeline and ensure their activity set still conforms to the conditions attached to that extension. The listing also includes a **December 18, 2025 circular** on **modification in conditions for reduction in denomination of debt securities**, which would be relevant where listed debt securities are being re-denominated or subdivided and would require compliance with whatever revised conditions SEBI has imposed for that process.

The most operationally important items in the listing are the **2024 master circular** and the **2022/2021/2020 circulars** dealing with **security creation, due diligence, monitoring, and default procedures** for listed debt securities. The **May 22, 2024 Master Circular for issue and listing of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, security receipts, municipal debt securities and commercial paper** consolidates the operative framework for debt-market issuance and listing and would be the primary reference document for ongoing compliance. The **August 4, 2022 circular** introduced **enhanced guidelines for debenture trustees and listed issuers on security creation and initial due diligence**, and the **December 19, 2022 clarification** interprets or supplements that framework; together these require trustees to carry out more robust pre-issuance checks and security-verification steps before relying on the issuance structure. The **May 19, 2022 circular** revised the **format of the security cover certificate** and also changed **monitoring and revision timelines**, so issuers and trustees must use the updated certificate format and meet the revised reporting/monitoring schedule rather than older versions. There is also a **December 31, 2020 circular** extending the implementation timeline for **creation of security in issuance of listed debt securities and due diligence by debenture trustees**, which indicates that SEBI had previously deferred the effective date for those obligations and that compliance teams should confirm whether later circulars have superseded those deadlines.

The list also includes SEBI’s **default-management and investor-protection measures**. The **October 13, 2020 circular** standardized the procedure debenture trustees must follow when an issuer of listed debt securities defaults, meaning trustees must follow a prescribed sequence of actions rather than ad hoc responses when payment or covenant failures occur. The **October 22, 2020 circular** requires issuers of listed or proposed-to-be-listed debt securities to contribute to a **“Recovery Expense Fund,”** which creates a specific funding obligation that needs to be built into issuance documentation and compliance tracking. The **August 13, 2021 circular** on **“Security and Covenant Monitoring” using Distributed Ledger Technology** indicates SEBI approved/encouraged a technology-based monitoring mechanism for covenant and security compliance, so trustees using that framework would need to ensure their systems and reporting processes align with the DLT-based monitoring model.

Several items affect periodic reporting and internal governance. The **December 19, 2011 circular** on **review of regulatory compliance, periodic reporting, and contents of trust deed** implies trustees must maintain an ongoing compliance-review process, submit periodic reports, and ensure the trust deed contains mandated provisions. The **June 20, 2011 circular** addressed **periodical reports and grant of prior approval to debenture trustees**, indicating that some actions require prior regulator approval rather than post-facto reporting. Earlier foundational rules appear as well, including the **SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, 2008**, the **SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993** as amended, and older circulars on **dissemination of information on debentures** and the **simplified listing agreement for debt securities**, all of which remain relevant as the baseline framework unless specifically overridden.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that this page signals a regulatory environment where debenture trustees must stay current on: the **latest master circular**, the **updated security-cover certificate format**, the **enhanced pre-issuance due diligence and security-creation requirements**, the **prescribed default-handling procedure**, any **Recovery Expense Fund contribution requirement**, and any **deadline extensions** granted for activities outside SEBI’s core remit. Because several entries are amendments, clarifications, or extensions, compliance should not rely on legacy processes or old timeline assumptions without confirming the latest circular text and effective dates.

rows.summary:
This document sets out the rights and obligations of a Beneficial Owner (account holder) and a Depository Participant (DP) under the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, SEBI rules/circulars/guidelines, and the relevant depository bye-laws, business rules, operating instructions, and government notifications in force from time to time. A DP may open or activate a demat account only after receiving a complete account-opening form, KYC, and supporting documents as specified by SEBI, and it must keep all beneficial owner information confidential except where disclosure is required by a legal, statutory, or regulatory authority. The beneficial owner must promptly notify the DP in writing of any change in the details originally provided in the account-opening documents.

On costs, the beneficial owner must pay the charges agreed with the DP as reflected in the DP’s tariff sheet for holding and transferring securities in dematerialized form and for depository services, and the document explicitly notes that no charges are payable for opening a demat account. For Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP must follow the charge structure prescribed by SEBI and/or the depository through applicable circulars, directions, or notifications. Any increase in agreed charges or tariff requires at least 30 days’ prior written notice to the beneficial owner.

The beneficial owner has the right to dematerialize securities admitted on the depository, and the DP must maintain separate accounts for each beneficial owner so that securities are segregated and not mixed with other clients’ securities or the DP’s own dematerialized holdings. The DP may not facilitate any pledge, hypothecation, or other encumbrance over securities except in the manner specifically permitted under the Depositories Act, SEBI regulations, and depository rules. Transfers into or out of the demat account can be made only on the basis of a duly authorized order, instruction, direction, or mandate from the beneficial owner, and the DP must preserve the original authorization documents and an audit trail.

For account statements, the DP must provide statements in the format and at the times agreed with the beneficial owner and as required by SEBI or the depository. If there are no transactions during the year, or the balance becomes nil, the DP must send one physical holding statement annually and then restart transaction statements once activity resumes. Electronic statements are allowed if the beneficial owner wants them, and the DP may issue them under its digital signature in accordance with the Information Technology Act, 2000; if the DP lacks electronic statement capability, it must send physical statements instead. For Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP must send transaction statements as specifically mandated by SEBI and/or the depository from time to time.

The excerpt cuts off at the beginning of the “Manner of Closure of Demat account” section, so any closure requirements are incomplete in the provided text and cannot be summarized reliably from this excerpt alone.

Earlier entries also reference position limits for mutual funds in **10-year IRF**, revised position limits for banks trading **USD/INR derivative contracts**, and the introduction of IRFs on **2-year and 5-year Government of India securities**.

The listing also reflects compliance-related operational rules covering **client margin short-collection/non-collection**, **post-trade modification of client codes**, **self-clearing membership in the currency derivatives segment**, **liquidity enhancement schemes for illiquid securities in equity derivatives**, and **physical settlement of stock derivatives**. Other product/eligibility changes shown include **mini index derivatives on Sensex and Nifty**, **revision of eligibility criteria for stocks in the derivatives segment**, **European-style stock options**, **options on USD-INR spot rate**, **index options with tenure up to 5 years**, and **derivative contracts on volatility indices** and **foreign stock indices**.

rows.summary:
The document summarizes stakeholder comments and SEBI’s responses on the proposed **SWAGAT-FI / FPI framework**. On the proposal to require **existing FPIs to prove SWAGAT-FI status**, commenters objected that this would force investors to provide extensive evidence of diversification, fund-manager independence, regulator confirmation, blind-pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios, creating unnecessary paperwork and operational burden. SEBI **disagreed with the objection** and said the verification approach will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry already uses, in order to reduce operational burden while still validating eligibility.

On the proposal to change the **re-KYC cadence and fee-payment periodicity**, commenters argued that the current periodicity should remain unchanged and that existing re-KYC should continue for FPIs, with material changes such as **UBO changes** caught through that process; they also objected that moving to a 10-year payment cycle would reduce SEBI’s flexibility to change annual fees. SEBI **disagreed**, stating that the requirement to report **material changes** will continue and that the earlier removal of additional re-KYC was based on a **risk-versus-convenience assessment**. SEBI clarified that there is **no annual fee requirement today**; rather, the **fee block period is being extended from 3 years to 10 years**, and this change is intended to **coincide with the re-KYC requirement**.

On the proposal relating to a **single demat account for different modes of foreign investment**, commenters warned that combining investment routes would obscure the distinction between **FPI** and **FVCI** holdings, complicate reporting, and create monitoring and compliance problems, especially for **unlisted FVCI investments** recorded in an FPI-tagged account. SEBI **disagreed** with the objection and stated that a **single demat account is optional**, meaning investors may choose it if convenient. SEBI also said that the **operational details** for implementation of the **SWAGAT-FI framework** will be provided in the relevant **notification or Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)**.

The document is a SEBI “Investment Advisers” listings page, not a single substantive rule text, so the material information it provides is a chronological index of advisories, circulars, master circulars, FAQs, and press releases affecting SEBI-registered Investment Advisers (and, in some items, Research Analysts). The most recent listed item is a **March 25, 2026 circular** clarifying the **eligibility of members of the Institute of Cost Accountants of India to conduct the annual audit of Investment Advisers**, which indicates a compliance issue around who may perform the required audit. Another recent item, dated **February 26, 2026**, concerns **Ease of Doing Investment (EoDI)** and requires **SEBI-regulated entities and their agents** to disclose their **registered name and registration number on social media platforms**, which is a specific external disclosure obligation.

The page also shows a **February 6, 2026 Master Circular for Investment Advisers**, which would consolidate existing obligations for IAs, and an earlier **May 21, 2024 Master Circular for Investment Advisers**, plus a **May 7, 2024 circular** on the **periodic reporting format for Investment Advisers**. From that, compliance teams should understand that periodic reporting requirements were formalized/updated and that the reporting format is a specific operational obligation for registered advisers. The page further lists an **October 10, 2023 circular** extending the timeline for compliance with the **qualification and experience requirements under Regulation 7(1) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013**, which is important because it shows SEBI granted additional time to meet adviser qualification/experience norms.

rows.title: Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/251 A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 20 September 02, 2026 To All Authorised Dealer Category-I banks Madam / Sir Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks Please refer to Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of the A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No.92, dated April 4, 2003, in terms of which AD banks were required to: a. Furnish an up-to-date list of all its offices/branches maintaining Rupee accounts of non-resident banks, as at the end of December each year before 15th January of the following year to the Central Office of Reserve Bank, and b. Report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/ correspondents over permissible limit, if not adjusted within five days, to the Central Office of Reserve Bank. 2. On a review, it has been decided to dispense with the above reporting requirements with immediate effect. 3. The directions contained in this circular have been issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (42 of 1999) and are without prejudice to permissions/approvals, if any, required under any other law. Yours faithfully (N. Senthil Kumar) Chief General Manager
rows.summary: The Reserve Bank of India has removed two previously applicable reporting obligations for Authorised Dealer (AD) Category-I banks with immediate effect, under RBI/2026-27/251 dated September 2, 2026. Specifically, banks are no longer required to submit to the RBI Central Office an annual up-to-date list of all offices/branches maintaining rupee accounts of non-resident banks as of December 31 by January 15 of the following year. They are also no longer required to report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/correspondents that exceed the permissible limit if those overdrawals are not adjusted within five days. These changes apply to AD Category-I banks and concern deposits/accounts of non-resident banks; all other permissions or approvals required under any other law remain unaffected. The circular states that the directions are issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.

rows.title: Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half-Yearly Return
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/250 CO.FIDD.FSD.No.S544/05-10-001/2026-27 September 02, 2026 The Chief Executive Officer / Managing Director All Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) All Local Area Banks/ Urban Cooperative Banks/ Rural Cooperative Banks/ Non- Banking Financial Companies / AIFIs Madam / Dear Sir, Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half- Yearly Return The regulatory framework governing the relief measures to be extended by the Regulated Entities (REs) in areas affected by natural calamities has been revised vide the amendment directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets dated April 29, 2026 (list enclosed), which came into effect from July 1, 2026. 2. These directions require REs to submit data relating to relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities through the CIMS portal on a half-yearly basis. Accordingly, in order to align the existing reporting mechanism with the revised regulatory framework, REs shall furnish the required information in the revised reporting format through the CIMS portal. 3. The return shall be submitted within 30 days from the end of each half-year, i.e., by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31. 4. REs shall ensure that the information submitted through the CIMS portal is accurate, complete, and duly validated. Appropriate internal systems and processes may be 2 established to facilitate timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the required information. 5. Further, the existing monthly return which was applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks and excluding Regional Rural Banks) on relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities stands discontinued with effect from July 1, 2026. Yours sincerely, (R Giridharan) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The RBI has updated the reporting framework for relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities, following the amendment directions to the Resolution of Stressed Assets framework issued on April 29, 2026, which became effective on July 1, 2026. Regulated Entities covered by this circular — all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks, as well as Local Area Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, Rural Cooperative Banks, NBFCs, and AIFIs — must now report data on such relief measures through the CIMS portal on a half-yearly basis in the revised format.

The new return must be filed within 30 days after the end of each half-year: by October 30 for the half-year ended September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ended March 31. RBI also requires that the information submitted through CIMS be accurate, complete, and duly validated, and expects REs to put in place internal systems and processes for timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the data.

At the same time, the existing monthly return requirement for relief measures in areas affected by natural calamities has been discontinued effective July 1, 2026. That monthly return had applied to Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks, but excluded Regional Rural Banks; those entities should therefore shift to the new half-yearly CIMS reporting regime instead of the discontinued monthly filing. The circular does not change the substantive relief measures themselves, but it does change the reporting cadence, submission channel, and compliance controls needed to support the new filing obligation.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Second Amendment Directions, 2026 modify Chapter VIII of the 2025 UCB investment portfolio directions to expressly permit urban co-operative banks (UCBs) to invest in equity shares of the Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC), the new central digital payment fraud intelligence platform, for the purpose of acquiring membership. The amendment also updates the existing permission relating to equity investments by UCBs in umbrella organizations of the UCB sector: paragraph 101(5) is replaced so that equity shares of the UCB sector’s Umbrella Organization (UO) and IDPIC are both covered where membership is being acquired.

A second substitution broadens the list of equity investments that may be made when necessary to obtain membership. Under revised paragraph 107(1), UCBs may invest in equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), the UCB sector’s UO, IDPIC, and CCBs/StCBs if such investment is needed to acquire membership of those entities. The directions are issued under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

The amendment takes effect immediately on the date of issue, September 2, 2026, and no delayed implementation date is provided. For compliance purposes, UCBs should treat IDPIC as an expressly permitted membership-related equity investment, and update any internal investment policy, approvals, and portfolio classification/valuation processes to reflect the revised membership-linked permissions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Second Amendment Directions, 2026** under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, with **immediate effect**. This amendment applies to the existing **Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** (updated as of **June 17, 2026**) and shortens the period of a temporary interest-rate relaxation that had been granted from **June 17, 2026 through September 30, 2026**.

Specifically, the RBI has decided to replace the end date **“September 30, 2026”** with **“August 31, 2026”** in the two provisions covering: (1) the **temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors**, and (2) the **restriction on interest rates on NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above, including deposits renewed on maturity**. In practical terms, rural co-operative banks that were relying on this temporary relaxation must now treat it as available only **from June 17, 2026 until August 31, 2026**, not through the end of September.

The amendment makes this change by substituting the date language in **paragraph 24(4) subscript (1)** and **paragraph 29(7) subscript (2)** of the 2025 Directions. For compliance purposes, affected banks should ensure their deposit-pricing systems, product terms, renewal handling, and any customer communications reflect the revised sunset date of **August 31, 2026** immediately.

The Reserve Bank of India has amended the 2025 Directions on interest rates for Urban Co-operative Banks, specifically shortening the duration of a temporary deposit-rate relaxation that had been granted on June 17, 2026. Under the original temporary measure, RBI had withdrawn the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3-5 year tenors and restricted interest rates on NRE deposits of 3 years and above tenors, including renewals upon maturity, for the period ending September 30, 2026; this amendment changes that end date to **August 31, 2026** instead. The amendment is issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Third Amendment Directions, 2026**, and **comes into force immediately** upon its issuance dated **August 25, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the operative change is purely a date revision in the underlying Directions: paragraph **24(4) subscript (1)** and paragraph **29(7) subscript (2)** are both updated so that the temporary relaxation runs **from June 17, 2026 through August 31, 2026** instead of through September 30, 2026. Urban Co-operative Banks that were relying on the temporary flexibility for **fresh FCNR(B) deposits of 3–5 year maturity** and for **NRE deposits of 3 years and above, including renewals**, must treat the relaxation as ending one month earlier than previously stated and ensure deposit pricing, renewals, and any related customer communications or product terms are aligned to the revised cutoff.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits – Third Amendment Directions, 2026** shortens the end date of a temporary deposit-rate relaxation that had already been introduced under the **Directions dated November 28, 2025** (updated June 17, 2026). Specifically, the RBI had temporarily **withdrawn the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and had also **restricted interest rates on NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above, including deposits renewed on maturity**, starting **June 17, 2026**; this relaxation was originally set to run until **September 30, 2026**.

This amendment changes that end date from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**. The change is made in two places in the underlying Directions: **paragraph 26(4)(1)** and **paragraph 31(7)(2)**, each replacing the phrase “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026” with “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until August 31, 2026.”

The amendment is issued by the RBI under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and came into force **immediately on August 25, 2026**. For compliance purposes, any Regional Rural Bank relying on the temporary relaxation for **FCNR(B) 3–5 year deposits** or the related **NRE deposit rate restriction for 3-year-and-above tenors** must treat **August 31, 2026** as the final effective date of the temporary regime, not September 30, 2026, and ensure deposit pricing, renewal treatment, and related internal instructions are updated accordingly.

The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** on **August 25, 2026**, and they take effect **immediately**. The amendment applies to **Local Area Banks** that are subject to the RBI’s **Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025**.

The only substantive change is a **shortening of the temporary relaxation period** that had previously been granted for certain foreign-currency and non-resident deposits. Under the 2025 Directions (as updated on June 17, 2026), RBI had temporarily withdrawn the interest-rate ceiling on **fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and restricted interest rates on **NRE deposits of 3 years and above**, including deposits renewed on maturity, for the period **from June 17, 2026 until September 30, 2026**. This amendment replaces the end date **“September 30, 2026”** with **“August 31, 2026”** in both affected provisions (paragraph **26(4)** and paragraph **31(7)**), meaning the temporary relaxation now ends **one month earlier**.

For compliance purposes, Local Area Banks must ensure that all deposit-pricing systems, product terms, and renewal processes for the affected **FCNR(B)** and **NRE** deposits reflect the revised cutoff date. Any reliance on the temporary flexibility for those deposit categories is limited to the period **June 17, 2026 through August 31, 2026**, and after that date the applicable interest-rate restrictions under the underlying Directions revert to the normal rules.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Third Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the earlier **Directions dated November 28, 2025** (updated as of **June 17, 2026**) by **shortening the duration of a temporary deposit-rate relaxation** for small finance banks. Specifically, the RBI has changed the end date of the temporary measure from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**.

The relaxation being shortened applies to **fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors**, for which the **interest rate ceiling was temporarily withdrawn**, and to **NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above**, including **renewed deposits upon maturity**, for which the applicable interest-rate restriction was temporarily relaxed. The original temporary relief had taken effect on **June 17, 2026**; this amendment preserves that start date but makes clear the relief now runs only **through August 31, 2026**.

The amendment was issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and comes into force **with immediate effect**. Operationally, the amendment makes two textual substitutions in the underlying Directions—at **paragraph 26(4), subscript (1)** and **paragraph 31(7), subscript (2)**—replacing “**with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026**” with “**with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until August 31, 2026**.” For compliance purposes, small finance banks should ensure their deposit pricing, renewal, and tenor-based interest-rate practices for the affected **FCNR(B)** and **NRE** products reflect the revised cutoff date and no longer rely on the temporary relaxation beyond **August 31, 2026**.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Third Amendment Directions, 2026** shortens the period of an existing temporary deposit-rate relaxation. Under the earlier 2025 Directions (as updated on June 17, 2026), commercial banks were allowed, **from June 17, 2026 through September 30, 2026**, to apply a temporary **withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and a temporary **restriction on interest rates for NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above, including renewals on maturity**. This amendment changes the end date of that temporary treatment from **September 30, 2026 to August 31, 2026**.

The amendment is issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and comes into force **immediately** on **August 25, 2026**. It specifically replaces the relevant wording in **paragraph 27(4) footnote 1** and **paragraph 32(7) footnote 2** of the 2025 Directions, so compliance teams at affected **commercial banks** should treat the special FCNR(B) and NRE deposit-rate relief as expiring **one month earlier than previously stated**. Practically, banks should ensure that any pricing, renewal, and system controls relying on the temporary relaxation are updated so that the relaxation applies only **up to August 31, 2026** and not beyond.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** for **rural co-operative banks** revise the earlier **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) Directions, 2025** (updated June 19, 2026) by **shortening the availability window** for certain CRR/SLR exemptions on specified fresh deposits. Specifically, the RBI had previously exempted from CRR and SLR maintenance: **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a minimum tenor of **3 years** and maximum tenor of **5 years** mobilized by banks **between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026**, and **fresh NRE term deposits** with a tenor of **3 years or more** (including deposits renewed on maturity) mobilized **between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026**.

Under this amendment, the end date for both exemption windows is moved earlier from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**. As a result, only deposits mobilized within the amended periods—**June 8, 2026 to August 31, 2026** for FCNR(B) deposits and **June 19, 2026 to August 31, 2026** for NRE term deposits—continue to qualify for the exemption from CRR and SLR maintenance.

The amendment is issued under the RBI’s statutory powers, including **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, and **Sections 18 and 24 read with section 56(AACS) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** and states that it takes effect **immediately** upon issuance, dated **August 25, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, rural co-operative banks must therefore ensure that only deposits meeting the original tenor conditions **and** placed within the revised dates through **August 31, 2026** are treated as exempt for CRR/SLR calculation purposes. Any FCNR(B) or NRE deposits mobilized after **August 31, 2026** will no longer fall within the exemption window created by the 2025 Directions as amended.

The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026**, effective **immediately on August 25, 2026**. This amendment applies to **urban co-operative banks** subject to the RBI’s CRR/SLR framework under the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**.

The only substantive change is a **shortening of the qualifying period** for the existing CRR and SLR exemptions on certain new deposits. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** for **Small Finance Banks’ Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** shortens the eligibility window for certain deposit exemptions. Under the underlying 2025 Directions, RBI had granted **exemption from CRR and SLR maintenance** for **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years** and for **fresh NRE term deposits** with a **tenor of 3 years or more**, including deposits renewed on maturity, if mobilized within specified periods. This amendment changes the end date for those exemption windows from **September 30, 2026** to **August 31, 2026**.

Specifically, the exemption period for the **FCNR(B)** category is now **June 8, 2026 through August 31, 2026** (instead of through September 30, 2026), and the exemption period for the **NRE term deposit** category is now **June 19, 2026 through August 31, 2026** (instead of through September 30, 2026). The change is made by amending paragraphs **20(6)** and **20(7)** of the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**.

The amendment was issued under RBI’s powers, including **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934**, and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It took effect **immediately upon issuance on August 25, 2026**. For compliance purposes, small finance banks should treat **August 31, 2026** as the final date for deposits to qualify for the CRR/SLR exemption under these two categories, and deposits mobilized after that date will not fall within the amended exemption window.

Under the underlying 2025 Directions, fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a minimum tenor of three years and a maximum tenor of five years were exempt from cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio maintenance if mobilized by banks between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and fresh NRE term deposits with a tenor of three years or more were similarly exempt if mobilized (including renewals upon maturity) between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026. On a review, it has been decided to revise the large exposure framework for Infrastructure Debt Fund-Non-Banking Financial Company (IDF-NBFC) in the Upper Layer. 2. The large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFC shall also be applicable to IDF-NBFC that are subject to Upper Layer regulations in terms of paragraph 60A of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 read together with 2 paragraph 18 (4) (i) of the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** on **August 25, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. The amendment was made under the RBI’s statutory powers and specifically revises the **large exposure framework** for **Infrastructure Debt Fund–Non-Banking Financial Companies (IDF-NBFCs)** that fall within the **Upper Layer** regulatory category.  

The sole substantive change is the insertion of a new **paragraph 39A** after paragraph 39 in Chapter IV of the existing **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025**. This new paragraph states that the **large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFCs** will also apply to **IDF-NBFCs subject to Upper Layer regulation**, as determined under **paragraph 60A of the RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**, read with **paragraph 18(4)(i) of the RBI (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**.  

For compliance purposes, this means affected IDF-NBFCs in the Upper Layer must now monitor and comply with the same concentration-risk / large-exposure caps and related controls that already apply to NBFC-IFCs, effective immediately, with no transition period stated in the amendment. The document does not introduce new numeric thresholds in the text itself; instead, it imports the existing NBFC-IFC large exposure limits by reference into the IDF-NBFC Upper Layer framework.

rows.summary:
This RBI circular instructs all regulated entities covered by the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 — including commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban and rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions — to continue enforcing the section 51A UAPA, 1967 obligations that prohibit maintaining accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved terrorist sanctions lists. The specific update being communicated is the UN Security Council press release SC/16435 dated August 18, 2026, which amended 21 entries on the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al‑Qaida Sanctions List under UNSC resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), with those individuals/entities subject to asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo measures under resolution 2734 (2024).

Compliance teams are directed to act immediately in accordance with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025, and to strictly follow the UAPA Order dated February 2, 2021 as amended on April 22, 2024. Practically, this means institutions must screen against the updated UNSC lists, ensure no accounts are held in the names of listed persons/entities, and take appropriate sanctions-response action whenever a match or new listing is identified. RBI also points institutions to the UNSC narrative summaries and sanctions detail pages for identifying information and the scope of the measures/exemptions.

On de-listing, the circular reflects MHA guidance that any delisting request received by a bank must be forwarded electronically to the Joint Secretary (CTCR), Ministry of Home Affairs for consideration. It also notes that listed persons or entities may submit delisting requests to the UN Secretary-General’s independent Ombudsperson. No separate RBI deadline is given for filing actions in this circular, but the operative expectation is immediate and ongoing compliance with the updated UNSC designations and the prescribed UAPA/RBI procedures.

rows.summary:
This RBI amendment revises the Priority Sector Lending (PSL) classification rules so that certain advances made in India against eligible fresh foreign currency/non-resident deposits will be excluded from the calculation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC), which is the base used for computing priority sector lending targets. Specifically, advances against fresh FCNR(B) dollar deposits with a minimum tenor of 3 years and a maximum tenor of 5 years, mobilised or renewed between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and advances against NRE term deposits of 3 years or more, mobilised or renewed between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026, are to be excluded from ANBC. This exclusion is tied to the related CRR/SLR exemption regime introduced by the RBI’s June 8, 2026 and June 19, 2026 directions, meaning the amount excluded from ANBC cannot exceed the amount of fresh FCNR(B)/NRE deposits that actually qualify for CRR/SLR exemption under those circulars.

The amendment changes paragraph 6.1, item VI of the 2025 PSL Directions by replacing the prior language with a narrower rule focused on “incremental fresh FCNR(B) / NRE deposits” that are eligible for CRR/SLR exemption under the listed RBI circulars and amendment directions. It also deletes footnote 3, which had contained the earlier methodology for calculating incremental advances using a comparison to the bank’s outstanding advances on March 7, 2014 (or June 13, 2014 for UCBs) versus the base date of July 26, 2013; that prior formula and zero/negative-difference limitation are removed from the directions. In practical terms, banks should stop using the deleted footnote methodology and instead apply the new exclusion rule only to the eligible incremental deposit-linked advances described in the amended text, subject to the cap that excluded amounts cannot exceed the qualifying deposit base.

The amendment is effective immediately as of August 7, 2026. It applies to advances extended in India by banks that fall within the PSL framework and affects compliance calculations for priority sector target achievement by reducing ANBC to the extent of the eligible exclusions. Banks should ensure their PSL reporting, ANBC computation, and related deposit-linked advance tracking reflect the eligible date windows, tenor requirements, and the direct linkage to CRR/SLR-exempt FCNR(B)/NRE deposits.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** replace the existing HFC-specific recovery-agent guidance in Chapter X (“Fair Practices Code”) of the **RBI (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025**. Specifically, **sub-section A.15 “Guidelines for engaging Recovery Agents” and paragraph 170 are deleted** and replaced with a new provision, **A.15A “Conduct of HFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agents”**, which directs every HFC to comply with **paragraphs 100A.2 to 100AB of Chapter III** of the **RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025**.

The practical effect is that HFCs must now follow the RBI’s broader, comprehensive conduct standards for recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies that apply to NBFCs under the Responsible Business Conduct framework, rather than the prior standalone HFC recovery-agent instructions. rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** overhaul the framework governing **recovery of loan dues and the use of recovery agencies/agents** by NBFCs. The RBI states that it has reviewed the existing recovery-agent instructions and is replacing them with **comprehensive conduct requirements** for all **NBFCs**, except **Mortgage Guarantee Companies, Core Investment Companies, NBFC-Account Aggregators, Standalone Primary Dealers, Non-Operating Financial Holding Companies, and NBFCs with no customer interface**. The amendment is issued under **Sections 45JA, 45L and 45M of the RBI Act, 1934** and **takes effect on January 1, 2027**.

The amendment adds formal definitions that matter for outsourcing governance: a **“recovery agency”** is any entity or individual other than the NBFC’s own employees that is engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **including taking possession of security**; a **“recovery agent”** is the representative of that agency who performs recovery-related activities **at the point of customer interface**. The text makes clear that if an **individual is directly engaged by an NBFC** under an outsourcing arrangement for recovery or possession-related work, then **all rules applicable to both the recovery agency and recovery agent apply to that individual**.

The amendment also removes earlier provisions in the 2025 Directions: **paragraphs 26, 27, and 89 to 97** in Chapter III are deleted, along with the prior **Section I on “Responsibilities of Recovery Agents of the NBFC”** and paragraphs **98 to 100** under it. In their place, RBI inserts a new **Section J: “Conduct of NBFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies”**, which applies to recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default, **including possession of security**. Where explicitly stated, it also applies **mutatis mutandis** to **normal-course collection from non-defaulting borrowers**. The new section also clarifies that it does **not override statutory enforcement rights** or any other recovery-related directions, including special recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

From a compliance standpoint, the new requirements begin with a mandatory **board-/management-level policy** on collection and recovery. Every affected NBFC must have a policy covering recovery by both **its own employees and recovery agents**, and that policy must address: the **triggers for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix**, **codes of conduct** for employees and agents, handling recovery when the **borrower has died**, and a **structured framework for financially distressed customers**, including **documented pre-escalation engagement** and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also set out the NBFC’s standards for **engaging recovery agencies**, including **eligibility and due diligence criteria**, **performance evaluation**, **inspection/audit/control mechanisms** for legal and regulatory compliance, and **procedures and penalties** for non-compliant agencies or agents. The new section continues beyond the excerpt, but the portions shown already make clear that NBFCs must tighten vendor oversight, document escalation and resolution processes, and ensure recovery practices are governed by a formal policy well before the **January 1, 2027** effective date.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Third Amendment Directions, 2026 revise the RBI’s existing “All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct” framework and apply to all All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) from **January 1, 2027**. The key change is that RBI is replacing the prior, narrower instructions on recovery agents with a **comprehensive set of conduct requirements for recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies**, including both collection from defaulting borrowers and, where specifically stated, certain collection activities in the normal course from non-defaulting borrowers.

A new set of definitions is added to the RBI directions. A **“recovery agency”** is defined broadly as any entity or individual, other than the AIFI’s own employees, engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **including taking possession of security**, regardless of the contractual label used. A **“recovery agent”** is a representative of such a recovery agency who interacts with the customer on behalf of the AIFI. The amendment also makes clear that if an individual is directly engaged by the AIFI under outsourcing for recovery or possession-related work, then the rules for both recovery agencies and recovery agents apply to that individual.

Paragraph 32 of Chapter III is deleted and replaced with a new section on **“Conduct of AIFIs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This section applies to recovery from borrowers in default, including possession of security, and—only when expressly stated—also applies mutatis mutandis to certain collection activities from borrowers who are not in default. It is also stated to be **without prejudice to the AIFI’s statutory rights and obligations** relating to enforcement of security under other laws, and without affecting separate provisions on specific recovery actions such as one-time settlements contained in other RBI directions. For this section, “AIFI employees” is expanded to include employees deployed for recovery work, including possession of security.

Every AIFI must now have a **formal policy on collection/recovery of loan dues** by its own employees or recovery agents. That policy must address, at a minimum: when recovery actions are triggered; a **graded escalation matrix** for recovery; a **code of conduct** for employees and recovery agents; procedures for recovery in the event of a borrower’s death; and a **structured framework for financially distressed borrowers**, including documented pre-escalation engagement and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also set out **eligibility and due diligence criteria** for appointing recovery agencies, performance standards, inspection/audit and control mechanisms to ensure statutory and regulatory compliance, and the procedures and penalties to be applied if recovery agencies or their agents are non-compliant.

The policy must further include rules for **compensation to borrowers and guarantors** for losses arising from recovery-related actions by the AIFI or its recovery agencies when those actions are not consistent with the RBI directions. In addition, where an AIFI uses a **technology-based recovery mechanism** under the later-referenced paragraph 32.1S, the institution must incorporate the related requirements and restrictions into this policy as well. Overall, the amendment is intended to make AIFIs responsible not just for appointing recovery intermediaries, but for governing their conduct, monitoring compliance, and remedying harm caused by improper recovery practices.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) – Responsible Business Conduct Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the 2025 Responsible Business Conduct framework specifically to impose a new, more comprehensive regime for **recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies**. The amendment is issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and **takes effect on January 1, 2027**. It replaces the earlier, narrower recovery-agent instructions by inserting a new dedicated section in Chapter VIII and deleting the prior paragraphs **369 to 378**.

A key change is the addition of formal definitions that broaden who is covered. A **“recovery agency”** is defined as any entity or individual, other than the RCB’s own employees, engaged under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a borrower in default, **including taking possession of security**, regardless of the contract label used. The circular expressly states that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related activities on behalf of an RCB is treated as a recovery agency. A **“recovery agent”** is defined as the representative of a recovery agency who performs recovery activities at the point of customer interface; where an individual is directly engaged by the RCB under outsourcing for recovery or possession-related work, the rules applying to both recovery agency and recovery agent apply to that person.

The new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default**, including possession of secured assets, and—where explicitly stated—also to **collection of dues in the normal course from borrowers who are not in default**. It is also made clear that these provisions do **not** override any statutory rights or obligations relating to security enforcement under other laws, and they are separate from other recovery frameworks such as one-time settlement provisions in other Directions. For these purposes, **“RCB employees”** includes employees deployed for recovery activities, including taking possession of security.

Each RCB must now have a **written policy** covering collection and recovery by both its own employees and recovery agents. That policy must at minimum set out: the **trigger(s) for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix**, a **code of conduct** for employees and recovery agents, procedures for recovering dues where the **borrower has died**, and a **structured framework for financially distressed borrowers** that includes documented pre-escalation engagement and guidance on available resolution options. For recovery agencies specifically, the policy must also define **eligibility and due diligence criteria**, performance standards, inspection/audit and control mechanisms to ensure compliance with statutory and regulatory requirements, and the procedures and penalties to be used when a recovery agency or its agents are non-compliant.

The policy must further provide for **compensation to borrowers or guarantors for losses caused by recovery actions that are not consistent with these Directions**. The text also indicates that RCBs using a **technology-based recovery mechanism** must follow separate instructions set out later in paragraph **378S** (the excerpt stops before those details), so compliance teams should expect additional operational controls if such tools are used. Overall, the amendment requires RCBs to formalize governance, due diligence, escalation, conduct, remediation, and compensation arrangements for all recovery activity before the **January 1, 2027** commencement date.

rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** will take effect on **1 January 2027** and materially overhaul the rules governing **loan recovery, collection practices, and the engagement of recovery agents/agencies by Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**. The RBI says the earlier instructions on recovery agents have been reviewed and replaced with **comprehensive conduct requirements** for both recovery of loan dues and the use of recovery agencies. The amendment is issued under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and modifies the existing **SFB Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025**.

A major change is the addition of new definitions. A **“recovery agency”** is now defined broadly to mean any entity or individual, other than the SFB’s own employees, engaged by an SFB under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a defaulting borrower, **including taking possession of security**, regardless of the contractual label used. The RBI explicitly states that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related activities on behalf of an SFB will be treated as a recovery agency for these purposes. A **“recovery agent”** is defined as the representative of a recovery agency who actually interacts with the customer at the point of interface; if an individual is directly hired by the SFB under outsourcing for recovery or possession work, the rules for both recovery agencies and recovery agents apply to that person.

The amendment **deletes paragraphs 408 to 416 and 442 to 454** in Chapter VIII on Responsible Lending Conduct and replaces them with a new section, **“L. Conduct of SFBs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from defaulting borrowers, including taking possession of security**, and it can also apply, where specifically stated, to normal-course collection from borrowers who are not in default. The RBI also clarifies that these provisions do **not** override any statutory enforcement rights or obligations a bank may have under other laws, and they do not displace other RBI directions covering specific recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

Under the new framework, each SFB must adopt a **formal policy** on collection and recovery of loan dues, including possession of security, whether recovery is conducted by the bank’s own employees or by recovery agents. That policy must cover, at a minimum: the **triggers for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix**, a **code of conduct** for employees and agents, procedures for recovery in the event of the **borrower’s death**, and a **structured process for handling financially distressed borrowers**, including **documented pre-escalation engagement** and guidance on available resolution options. Where recovery agencies are used, the policy must also set out **eligibility and due diligence criteria**, **performance evaluation standards**, **inspection/audit mechanisms**, compliance controls to ensure adherence to statutory and regulatory requirements, and the **procedures and penalties** for dealing with non-compliant agencies or agents. The policy must further include rules on **compensation to borrowers or guarantors** for losses caused by recovery actions that are not consistent with the Directions.

The amendment also makes clear that the new section applies to SFB employees involved in recovery and possession work, by defining **“SFB employees”** for this purpose to include employees deployed for those activities. Although the excerpt provided ends partway through paragraph 454G, the document signals that SFBs using a **technology-based mechanism for recovery** under the forthcoming paragraph 454S will need to build that mechanism into their policy as well. For compliance teams, the key implementation task is to ensure that, by **1 January 2027**, all recovery arrangements, BC-related recovery activity, outsourcing contracts, conduct standards, escalation procedures, grievance/compensation processes, and oversight controls are aligned with the new RBI framework.

The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** applies to **all Commercial Banks except Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and Local Area Banks**. It **comes into effect on January 1, 2027** and replaces the earlier piecemeal instructions on recovery agents with a more comprehensive framework governing **recovery of loan dues, possession of security, and engagement of recovery agencies**. The RBI has issued these changes under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

The amendment first introduces two key defined terms into the Directions. A **“recovery agency”** is any entity or individual, other than the bank’s own employees, engaged by a bank under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovering loan dues from a borrower in default, including taking possession of security; the definition explicitly says that a **Business Correspondent (BC)** involved in recovery-related work for a bank is treated as a recovery agency for these purposes. A **“recovery agent”** is the representative of such a recovery agency who interacts directly with customers at the point of customer interface. If an individual is directly engaged by the bank under an outsourcing arrangement for recovery or possession-related work, that person is subject to the requirements applicable to both recovery agencies and recovery agents.

The amendment then **deletes paragraphs 408 to 416 and 442 to 454** of Chapter VIII on Responsible Lending Conduct and inserts a new section titled **“Conduct of Banks in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agencies.”** This new section applies to **recovery of loan dues from borrowers in default, including taking possession of security**, and, where expressly stated, also applies **mutatis mutandis to dues collection from borrowers who are not in default**. It also makes clear that these provisions are **without prejudice to any statutory enforcement rights or obligations under other laws** and do not override other Directions dealing with specific recovery actions such as **one-time settlement**.

Under the new section, a bank must have a formal **policy on collection/recovery of loan dues and possession of security** by both its own employees and recovery agents. That policy must specify, at minimum, the **trigger points for starting recovery**, a **graded escalation matrix** for recovery actions, a **code of conduct** for employees and recovery agents, procedures for cases involving the **death of a borrower**, and a **structured framework for dealing with financial distress**, including documented pre-escalation engagement and guidance on available resolution options. The policy must also cover the **eligibility and due diligence standards** for appointing recovery agencies, their **performance evaluation criteria**, **inspection/audit/control mechanisms** to ensure compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, and the **procedures and penalties** for dealing with non-compliant recovery agencies or their agents.

The amendment further requires the policy to include provisions for **compensating borrowers or guarantors for losses arising from recovery-related actions** of the bank or its recovery agencies that are not in compliance with applicable requirements, and it is clear from the structure of the inserted section that the RBI expects banks to tighten governance over outsourcing, borrower treatment, escalation discipline, and remedy mechanisms. Although the excerpt cuts off before the remainder of paragraph 454F and any additional paragraphs, the material change is already clear: banks will need to review and likely revise their recovery and outsourcing policies, staff and agent conduct rules, due diligence and monitoring processes, and borrower-redress/compensation arrangements so they are compliant by **1 January 2027**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This 2026 RBI Supervisory Directions consolidate and restate the Reserve Bank of India’s expectations for commercial banks on a wide set of operational, conduct, governance, and control matters. They are issued by the Department of Supervision on 31 July 2026 under RBI/DoS/2026-27/416 and apply to commercial banks as covered by the document’s applicability section. The directions span IT system access, monitoring of end-use of funds, Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), interest-charging practices, inoperative and unclaimed accounts, nomination, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, and vigilance governance.

A major theme is tighter control over access, accountability, and monitoring. Banks must ensure controlled access to IT systems and maintain procedures that support traceability and supervision of user activities. They also must implement monitoring of end use of funds, which means they are expected to track whether borrowed or sanctioned funds are actually used for the stated purpose, with heightened controls where misuse risk is present. The PCA chapter establishes RBI’s framework for supervisory escalation when banks’ financial condition deteriorates; affected banks may be placed under corrective actions once specified trigger points are breached, and they must then comply with the RBI-directed restrictions and remediation steps that accompany the framework.

The directions also reinforce customer-protection requirements. Banks must follow the Fair Practices Code on charging of interest, meaning interest must be levied in a transparent, non-exploitative manner and in line with RBI’s fair-lending expectations. For inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits, banks are required to maintain systems and procedures to identify dormant accounts, handle unclaimed balances appropriately, and support claim resolution. The nomination chapter requires banks to provide and administer nomination facilities so depositors and other eligible customers can designate nominees for account balances and related claims.

Fraud prevention is a substantial component of the document and covers multiple scenarios that compliance teams should treat as control requirements. The directions address frauds involving collusion by bank officials, large-value frauds, bulk retail-loan sanctions, frauds using fake title deeds of property, frauds in non-resident accounts, and safekeeping of critical documents. Banks must also manage accounts opened by employees with enhanced scrutiny, maintain a legal compliance certificate and a legal compliance audit process, and carry out forensic scrutiny where needed. The document further addresses the exercise of discretionary powers and sets out a “best practices” code for banks, indicating that internal decision-making authority must be documented, disciplined, and subject to control review rather than left to informal discretion.

The Protected Disclosure Scheme chapter requires banks to provide a protected complaint mechanism for reporting wrongdoing. It covers the scheme’s scope, the procedure for lodging complaints, and the protected disclosure policy, meaning banks must be able to receive complaints confidentially and protect whistleblowers from retaliation while ensuring appropriate inquiry and handling. The vigilance chapter then adds governance expectations for anti-corruption and integrity controls: it introduces vigilance-angle assessment, the role and appointment of a Chief of Internal Vigilance, tenure expectations, restrictions on association with sensitive matters, and reporting/return submission and review requirements. It also requires preventive vigilance measures, staff rotation, and mandatory leave in sensitive roles, plus established complaint-handling and investigation arrangements, including the use of investigation agencies and review of cases entrusted to them.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026**, under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The directions apply to **commercial banks only**—specifically **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**, as well as **corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India**. They define **“Supervisory Returns”** broadly to cover **all periodic and ad hoc data submitted to RBI in prescribed formats**, regardless of the technology platform, frequency, or submission mode, and define **CIMS** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and related data dissemination.

From a governance standpoint, the directions require the **Board and Senior Management** to treat **data quality risk** as part of the bank’s overall risk management framework. The framework must include **ownership/accountability, governance, controls, approvals, and escalation mechanisms** for the preparation and submission of supervisory returns, so compliance is not just a filing exercise but a board-level control responsibility. The document also places responsibility on banks to maintain a **robust data architecture and IT infrastructure** that supports accurate, complete, and timely supervisory reporting, which means banks need systems capable of producing regulatory data reliably and in a controlled manner.

The directions further require banks to ensure the **accuracy and integrity of reporting**, including processes to verify returns before submission and to correct errors when identified. In practice, this means banks must have procedures for **validation, reconciliation, review, and authorization** of supervisory data, with clear internal controls to prevent misreporting. The document also contemplates **operational guidelines, a list of applicable returns, timelines, exceptions, penalties, and other instructions** in Chapter III, indicating that banks will need to monitor the specific return-wise filing calendar and comply with any format- or event-driven reporting obligations prescribed by RBI from time to time.

Finally, the directions include standard legal provisions on **repeal and saving**, application of other laws not barred, and interpretation, meaning these directions sit alongside other applicable statutory and regulatory requirements rather than replacing them wholesale.
