rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 31 July 2026 “Small Finance Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework” Directions, 2026 establish a comprehensive, mandatory governance and control framework for all Small Finance Banks (SFBs) covering IT governance, cybersecurity, resilience, and assurance. The document is structured around board oversight, management accountability, risk management, and detailed baseline security controls, and it is designed to require SFBs to put in place formal policies, committees, monitoring, and technical safeguards rather than rely on ad hoc controls.

At the top level, the directions require the board to approve the institution’s core IT and cyber policies, with formal board-level governance structures to oversee technology risk and security. The framework specifically calls for an IT governance framework, an Information Security Policy and Cybersecurity Policy, an IT Strategy Committee of the Board, senior management oversight through an IT Steering Committee, an Information Security Committee, a designated Head of IT Function, and a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). It also requires formal processes for IT project management, IT architecture, and IT services management, making clear that technology risk is to be governed as a board-and-management responsibility, not just an operational IT issue.

The directions further require SFBs to maintain an IT and information security risk management framework with periodic review of IT-related risks and documented risk identification and assessment processes. Banks must identify, assess, and document technology and security risks on an ongoing basis, indicating that risk registers, control testing, and remediation tracking are expected to be maintained as part of compliance. This means SFBs need a living framework for cyber and technology risk management, not only an annual policy review.

The largest portion of the document sets out baseline cybersecurity and resilience requirements that affect day-to-day control design and operations. These include maintaining an inventory of information assets; implementing a data leak prevention strategy; controlling data migration; preventing execution of unauthorized software; applying physical and environmental controls; managing capacity; enforcing secure configurations; protecting networks; building application security into the software life cycle; maintaining, monitoring, and analyzing audit logs; managing patches, vulnerabilities, and changes; controlling user access; applying teleworking controls; establishing customer authentication frameworks; securing mail and messaging systems; controlling removable media; and governing third-party arrangements. The framework also requires cryptographic controls, straight-through processing controls, and continuous surveillance, indicating that banks must have technical and procedural controls across endpoints, infrastructure, applications, communications, outsourced services, and transaction processing.

For compliance purposes, the key implication is that these are not optional best-practice recommendations: SFBs must formalize policies, governance bodies, technical safeguards, and monitoring processes aligned to the RBI framework. The document as provided does not include specific implementation deadlines or numeric thresholds beyond the issuance date and the requirement structure, so the main compliance task is to map existing controls against each mandated area, identify gaps, assign ownership, and ensure board-approved remediation and ongoing oversight are in place for all covered SFB activities and service relationships.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Concurrent Audit Directions, 2026** apply to all **Small Finance Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. They are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and formalize the role of concurrent audit as a key internal control and early-warning mechanism intended to detect serious errors, irregularities, and potential fraud promptly.

At the governance level, the **Audit Committee of the Board (ACB)** must **approve the detailed scope** of the concurrent audit. The ACB must also set both the **maximum tenure for external concurrent auditors** and the **remuneration** payable to them, so these are no longer left solely to management discretion. In addition, the ACB is required to **review the effectiveness of the Concurrent Audit System and the performance of the concurrent auditors at least annually** and take measures to strengthen the system where needed.

The directions define **“Audit Firm”** broadly to include a **proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP**. Unless otherwise defined, terms take their meaning from the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Companies Act, 2013**, relevant RBI regulations, the RBI glossary, or ordinary commercial usage as applicable.

Because the excerpt provided cuts off at the start of Chapter III (“Guidelines for Concurrent Audit”), the specific operational coverage, appointment process, reporting requirements, and any numerical thresholds or sector-specific exclusions are **not visible in the supplied text**. From the available content, the immediate compliance obligations are to ensure that each Small Finance Bank has ACB-approved audit scope, ACB-set auditor tenure and fees, and an annual ACB review of audit effectiveness and auditor performance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Compliance Function) Directions, 2026** are a mandatory compliance-governance framework issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related enabling powers, and they apply specifically to **all Small Finance Banks**. The Directions take effect **immediately upon issuance** and are intended to set minimum standards for how a bank structures, governs, and monitors its compliance function, with the RBI noting that the framework is aligned to the Basel Committee’s compliance principles but adapted for the Indian operating environment. The document also states that the framework extends to **bank-led Financial Conglomerates** for **group-wide compliance risk** management, while allowing each bank to organize its compliance function proportionately to its **size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**.

From a governance standpoint, the Directions require the **Board** and **senior management** to treat compliance as a core part of corporate governance and assurance, alongside internal audit and risk management. The bank must have a formal **compliance policy**, and the policy and operating model must cover the full scope of compliance risk across the institution and, where relevant, at group level. The document makes clear that compliance is not meant to be a box-checking function: banks must establish staffing, structure, roles, responsibilities, quality assurance, internal audit linkages, and a compliance culture that are commensurate with the bank’s risk and business model.

A major substantive requirement is the appointment and empowerment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**. The Directions require the CCO to have sufficient **authority, stature, and independence**, and the CCO must be supported by defined reporting arrangements and responsibilities so that compliance issues are escalated appropriately and independently from business lines. The framework also introduces obligations around the **use of technology for monitoring**, indicating that banks are expected to use technological tools to support compliance surveillance and issue detection rather than relying only on manual controls.

The final chapter also indicates that the Directions include **repeal and saving provisions**, clarifications on how they interact with **other laws**, and **interpretation rules**, which means banks must review the final instrument in conjunction with their existing compliance framework to identify what prior directions are displaced and what legal obligations continue to apply alongside these new requirements. No numeric thresholds, rates, or deadline dates beyond the **immediate commencement** are visible in the provided text excerpt, but the overall effect is that every Small Finance Bank must ensure its compliance governance, staffing, reporting, and monitoring arrangements are formally aligned to the new RBI framework without delay.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** are a consolidated set of supervisory requirements for payments banks, issued by the Department of Supervision, RBI, Mumbai, under reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/434** and **DoS.CO.PPG.28/11.01.005/2026-27** dated **July 31, 2026**. The document is organized into provisions on IT system access, inoperative accounts/unclaimed deposits, nomination facilities, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, and vigilance, and it is intended to apply specifically to **payments banks**. Its operative effect is to standardize compliance expectations across these areas, including the internal controls, reporting obligations, and staff-management practices payments banks must maintain.

A major operational requirement is in **Chapter II on Access to IT Systems**, which obligates payments banks to control and monitor who can access banking IT systems and on what terms, so that system privileges are properly authorized and auditable. The **inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits** chapter requires banks to manage dormant balances in accordance with RBI directions, including the identification, classification, and handling of accounts/deposits that become inactive or unclaimed. The **nomination facility** chapter requires banks to provide and manage nomination arrangements in line with regulatory expectations so that account holders’ nomination instructions are properly captured and administered.

The document also places significant emphasis on **fraud prevention**. It requires specific controls for frauds involving collusion of bank officials, larger-value frauds, safeguarding of critical documents, and accounts opened by employees. It further requires a **legal compliance certificate** and a **legal compliance audit**, along with **forensic scrutiny** where warranted, and it addresses the exercise of discretionary powers so that fraud-related decisions are not left to ad hoc judgment. The “Best Practices Code” and other fraud-related instructions are meant to function as ongoing internal-control obligations, not one-time checks, so compliance teams should treat them as continuing governance requirements.

Another major component is the **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, which establishes a framework for handling whistleblower-style complaints. The document defines the scope of the scheme, the process for lodging complaints, and the protections/policy requirements banks must maintain for protected disclosures, meaning payments banks need an internal procedure that allows eligible complaints to be received and handled without compromising the complainant’s protection under the scheme. This is paired with a detailed **vigilance framework**, including a vigilance “preamble,” a definition of the vigilance angle, and requirements for the **Chief of Internal Vigilance**. That role must be appointed appropriately, must serve within a defined tenure, must be kept away from sensitive matters where required, and must submit prescribed reports/returns for review.

The vigilance chapter also requires **preventive vigilance**, **staff rotation**, and **mandatory leave** for relevant personnel, together with rules for complaint handling, investigation through designated agencies, review of cases entrusted to those agencies, and action against persons making false complaints. The bank must also maintain liaison with external agencies as part of its vigilance function. Finally, the closing chapter contains standard legal housekeeping provisions: **repeal and saving**, confirmation that other laws continue to apply unless specifically barred, and interpretive provisions to govern how the directions are read and implemented.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks - Supervisory Returns Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **all payments banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** on **July 31, 2026**. They are issued under **Sections 27 and 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and define “supervisory returns” broadly to include **all periodic and ad-hoc data submissions to RBI**, regardless of platform, frequency, or submission method. The directions also define RBI’s **Centralised Information Management System (CIMS)** as the online platform used for return submission and related data dissemination.

From a governance standpoint, the board and senior management must treat **data quality risk** as part of the institution’s overall risk management framework. That framework must cover both **in-house and outsourced** data-related processes and must include policies addressing **data confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk management**. The bank must also ensure that its **risk data aggregation capabilities and risk reporting practices are fully documented** and subject to **high standards of validation** aligned with other independent risk management reviews.

The directions then require payments banks to follow RBI-prescribed procedures for filing supervisory returns and to comply with the list of applicable returns, timelines, exceptions, and other instructions contained in the chapter on filing. The document indicates that there are explicit operational guidelines, return-specific filing requirements, and deadline provisions, and that banks must also observe the stated exception-handling and penalty framework where returns are delayed, incomplete, or otherwise non-compliant. It further notes that existing instructions are repealed/saved as specified, but other laws remain applicable unless expressly barred, meaning banks must continue to comply with overlapping legal and regulatory obligations in addition to these directions.

Because the excerpt provided cuts off in the middle of Chapter II and does not show the actual return-by-return schedule, specific filing dates, thresholds, or penalty amounts, a compliance officer should treat this as a **new mandatory supervisory reporting framework** for payments banks and confirm the detailed return calendar and formats in the full text / annexures before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** take effect **immediately upon issuance** and apply to all **payments banks** in connection with the **appointment and reappointment of Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs) / Statutory Auditors (SAs)**. The document is issued under **Section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and makes clear that where a payments bank uses separate **Statutory Branch Auditors (SBAs)**, the term **SCA** applies; in all other cases, the term **SA** applies. This is therefore a binding audit-governance framework for payments banks rather than a general advisory.

For compliance purposes, the document requires payments banks to follow RBI’s prescribed governance, eligibility, independence, tenure, fee, and appointment rules for external statutory auditors, and it also sets out mandatory requirements for the **Long Form Audit Report (LFAR)** process. The table of contents shows that the directions cover: the role of the board and senior management; the **number of auditors permitted**; **eligibility criteria** and **independence standards** for auditors; professional standards; **tenure and rotation** requirements; audit fee and expense arrangements; and the **appointment procedure**. It further requires both SCAs and SBAs, where applicable, to provide LFARs on RBI-prescribed matters, with separate procedures/timelines for submission and coverage expectations.

The document explicitly states that its scope is the **re/appointment** of statutory auditors, so banks must ensure any current or proposed auditor engagement complies before appointment action is taken. It also contains a repeal/saving framework and a statement that other laws are not barred, meaning these directions operate alongside applicable banking and other legal requirements rather than replacing them entirely. Because the excerpt provided ends in the definitions section, the detailed thresholds, rotation periods, auditor limits, fee caps, and submission deadlines are not visible here; however, the structure indicates that those operational requirements are set out in the body and annexes and are mandatory for affected payments banks and their audit committees/boards to implement.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Internal Audit Function Directions, 2026** apply **only to payments banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** (dated **July 31, 2026**). RBI issues them under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, reflecting a policy shift away from a purely transaction-checking audit model toward a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework that focuses on the adequacy of **risk management systems and internal controls**, with selective transaction testing as part of that broader review. Compliance teams should treat this as a mandatory governance and control requirement for all payments banks, not a guidance note.

At a high level, the Directions require each payments bank to implement an **internal audit function designed around risk assessment**, rather than relying on a traditional transaction-centric audit program. The document states that the bank’s internal audit must assess how effectively the institution identifies, manages, and controls risk, and it is intended to align the bank’s governance with evolving standards and international best practices. This means internal audit planning, testing, reporting, and follow-up are expected to be built around risk priorities and control effectiveness, not just sample checking of transactions.

The document structure makes clear that the bank’s **Board** and **senior management** have distinct governance responsibilities for the internal audit framework, and the Board is expected to oversee the internal audit policy and overall effectiveness of the function. The senior management is expected to ensure day-to-day implementation and operational support for the RBIA framework. Because the Directions include dedicated chapters on **functional independence**, **risk assessment**, **scope**, **communication**, **performance evaluation**, and **outsourcing**, compliance officers should expect detailed requirements on auditor independence, how audit plans are risk-scored and refreshed, how audit findings are escalated, how audit quality is measured, and what conditions must be met if any part of the function is outsourced.

The Directions also create a specific governance role for the **Head of Internal Audit**, including requirements on the person’s **authority, stature, independence, tenure, and reporting line**, indicating that the function must be positioned with sufficient seniority and independence from business management. There is also a chapter on **repeal and saving**, plus a statement that other applicable laws are **not barred**, meaning the Directions operate alongside other legal and regulatory obligations rather than replacing them. For compliance purposes, the key action items are to review the existing internal audit charter/policy, confirm Board and management oversight responsibilities, verify that the audit universe and audit plan are risk-based, ensure the Head of Internal Audit has an appropriately independent reporting structure, and check whether any outsourced audit arrangements comply with RBI’s expected safeguards.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **Payments Banks (PBs)** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. RBI states that the purpose is to create a formal framework for the **prevention, early detection, and timely reporting of fraud incidents** by PBs to both **law enforcement agencies (LEAs)** and the **Reserve Bank of India**, along with RBI’s dissemination of fraud information. The Directions are issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling powers, so they are mandatory supervisory requirements rather than guidance.

A major requirement is that PBs must maintain a **governance structure for fraud risk management**, and they must implement an **early warning signals / red-flagging framework** for banking transactions so suspicious activity is identified and escalated promptly rather than only after a loss occurs. The document also contemplates **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, meaning PBs cannot rely blindly on outsourced or external confirmations and must build procedures to verify such inputs independently where required. In addition, the Directions impose **staff accountability** provisions and authorize **penal measures**, so compliance teams should expect internal responsibility tracking and disciplinary or other sanctions where employees fail to follow fraud controls.

The reporting obligations are significant: PBs must report frauds to the **appropriate law enforcement agencies** and separately to **RBI**, using the prescribed modalities. RBI will maintain and use the **Central Fraud Registry (CFR)**, described as a **web-based searchable database**, so PBs must ensure their fraud-reporting data is accurate, timely, and aligned with RBI filing requirements. The Directions also include specific instructions for **closure of fraud cases previously reported**, meaning PBs cannot simply file an initial fraud report and stop—they must update the status when cases are resolved, closed, or otherwise disposed of in the manner RBI requires.

The document additionally contains special treatment for **cheque-related frauds**, requiring separate reporting to both **LEAs and RBI**, and it sets out instructions for **reporting incidents of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, indicating that these events are also subject to supervisory reporting, not just conventional fraud. It further addresses the **role of auditors**, implying that external/internal auditors have a formal part in oversight and verification of fraud-risk controls. Finally, the Directions include a **repeal and saving** clause and state that they do not bar the application of other laws, so PBs must comply with these directions **in addition to** any other criminal, banking, or supervisory obligations that may apply.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026** take effect **immediately upon issuance** and apply **only to Payments Banks**. They cover any **digital payment product or service** offered by a payments bank for **financial transactions** and for non-financial functions such as **balance enquiry, setting/changing PIN, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction-status checks, and customer dispute/grievance raising**. The scope expressly includes services offered **directly by the bank** or **through RBI-operated systems or RBI-authorised Payment System Operators (PSOs)**, together with the associated **IT assets** (applications, systems, and infrastructure).

The document establishes a broad security-control framework rather than a single isolated rule. It requires payments banks to implement board-level governance over digital payment security risk, generic security controls, application security life cycle controls, authentication controls, fraud-risk management, reconciliation processes, and customer protection/awareness/grievance redressal measures, with separate chapters also addressing **internet banking**, **mobile payments applications**, and **card payment security controls**. In practical compliance terms, this means banks must maintain documented policies, oversight, and control frameworks covering the full lifecycle of digital payment products and the systems that support them.

The Directions are issued under RBI’s authority under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Chapter IV of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, and the RBI states they are being issued in the public interest. The text also notes that the definitions used in the Directions are largely drawn from the **Financial Stability Board (FSB) Cyber Lexicon**, unless otherwise specified. Key defined concepts introduced at the start include **availability** (accessible and usable on demand by an authorised entity) and **confidentiality** (information not disclosed to unauthorised persons or systems), signaling that the compliance standard is based on core cybersecurity principles.

The table of contents shows that the Directions contain a dedicated chapter on **the role of the Board**, including a requirement for **Board-approved policies**, followed by controls for governance, security risk management, and customer grievance handling. The document also includes a final chapter on **repeal and saving**, **application of other laws not barred**, and **interpretation**, indicating that these Directions are intended to operate as a comprehensive supervisory framework while preserving the effect of other applicable laws where not inconsistent. No specific monetary thresholds or numeric limits are stated in the excerpt provided, but the obligations are clearly operational and control-oriented across all digital payment channels and supporting technology used by payments banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Payments Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework” Directions, 2026** set a comprehensive mandatory technology, cybersecurity, and operational resilience regime for **payments banks**. The document is issued by RBI’s Department of Supervision and is dated **July 31, 2026**; it appears to be a new consolidated framework governing board oversight, IT governance, cyber risk management, baseline security controls, third-party risk, and ongoing assurance for this category of bank. From the table of contents alone, it is clear the directions impose obligations at multiple levels of the institution—**the board, board committees, senior management, the IT function, the CISO, and operational teams**—and require formal policies, periodic review, and documented risk management.

At a governance level, payments banks must have **board-approved policies** and board-level committee oversight for technology and cybersecurity matters. The framework specifically requires an **IT governance framework**, an **information security policy** and **cybersecurity policy**, and structures such as an **IT Strategy Committee of the Board**, an **IT Steering Committee**, an **Information Security Committee**, a defined **Head of IT Function**, and a **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**. The directions also cover **information technology project management**, **IT architecture**, and **IT services management**, indicating that technology decisions, system design, and service operations are expected to be governed formally rather than handled ad hoc.

The document also imposes a formal **IT and information security risk management framework**, including periodic review of IT-related risks and requirements for **risk identification, assessment, and documentation**. Compliance teams should expect these directions to require a structured risk register or equivalent records, with evidence that cyber and technology risks are regularly assessed and tracked. This suggests that operational teams will need to maintain current documentation of threats, vulnerabilities, controls, and residual risk, and that management and the board will be expected to oversee those assessments.

A substantial portion of the framework is devoted to **baseline cybersecurity and resilience controls**. Payments banks must maintain inventory management of information assets, implement **data leak prevention**, control **data migration**, prevent execution of unauthorized software, and maintain physical/environmental safeguards and capacity management. The requirements also cover **secure configuration**, **network management and security**, **application security lifecycle controls**, **audit log monitoring and analysis**, **patch, vulnerability, and change management**, **user access control/management**, **teleworking controls**, **customer authentication framework**, **secure mail and messaging systems**, **removable media controls**, **cryptographic controls**, and **straight-through processing**. In other words, the directions go beyond policy statements and require day-to-day technical controls across infrastructure, applications, identities, endpoints, and communications.

The framework also explicitly addresses **third-party arrangements**, which means outsourced or vendor-supported technology services are subject to oversight and security requirements under the directions. Compliance officers should assume that contracts, due diligence, monitoring, and security obligations for external service providers will need to be aligned to RBI expectations, because the table of contents places third-party risk alongside core security controls rather than treating it as a separate procurement issue. The final portion shown references **continuous surveillance**, implying ongoing monitoring expectations and likely event detection/reporting obligations as part of operational resilience.

No specific numeric thresholds, technical parameters, or implementation deadlines beyond the **effective date of July 31, 2026** are visible in the provided excerpt, but the title and structure make clear that this is a binding compliance framework for **payments banks only**. A compliance team should therefore review the full directions for any detailed timelines, incident reporting triggers, control benchmarks, assurance/testing requirements, and any exemptions or transition provisions not visible in the excerpt, but should already treat the document as imposing broad, enterprise-wide cybersecurity and technology governance obligations on all payments banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026 apply specifically to all Payments Banks and take effect immediately upon issuance on July 31, 2026. The Directions are issued under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and replace the prior concurrent audit framework for these institutions, while also clarifying that other applicable laws and RBI regulations continue to apply unless inconsistent with these Directions.

The Audit Committee of the Board (ACB) must approve the detailed scope of the concurrent audit, so the bank’s audit plan is no longer left to management discretion alone. The ACB is also responsible for deciding the maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors and the remuneration paid to them. In addition, the ACB must review both the effectiveness of the concurrent audit system and the performance of the concurrent auditors at least annually and take measures to strengthen the system where needed.

The document defines an “Audit Firm” broadly to include a proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP. All other terms are to be read in line with the relevant RBI statutes, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the Companies Act, 2013, RBI-issued regulations or glossaries, or ordinary commercial usage where applicable. The introduction emphasizes that concurrent audit is intended to shorten the interval between a transaction and independent review, serving as an early warning control to detect serious errors, irregularities, fraudulent transactions, and to support preventive vigilance.

The full text provided cuts off at the start of Chapter III (“Guidelines for Concurrent Audit”), so any specific operational requirements, coverage thresholds, appointment rules, tenure limits, reporting formats, or timelines that may appear later in the Directions are not visible in the excerpt and cannot be summarized from the supplied content.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026** under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they apply specifically to **all Payments Banks**. The Directions state that the **compliance function is a core part of bank governance and assurance**, alongside internal audit and risk management, and that banks must organize the function in a manner **commensurate with their size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**. The framework is also intended to align, in principle, with the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** approach and to extend to **bank-led Financial Conglomerates** for group-wide compliance risk management. The Directions **come into effect immediately upon issuance** (dated **July 31, 2026**).

For governance, the document requires the **Board** and **senior management** to have explicit oversight responsibilities for compliance, and it requires each bank to maintain a **formal compliance policy**. The policy and structure must set out the **scope of compliance coverage, group-wide arrangements where relevant, staffing, roles and responsibilities, compliance culture expectations, and quality assurance/internal audit interfaces**. The compliance function is not meant to be a narrow legal-checking unit; it must cover the bank’s overall adherence to applicable laws, regulations, supervisory directions, and internal policies, with responsibilities assigned clearly across the organization.

The Directions establish a dedicated framework for the **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**, including requirements around **appointment, authority, stature, independence, reporting, and duties**. The CCO must have sufficient standing and independence to perform the role effectively and must report in a manner that preserves the function’s independence and visibility to the Board and senior management. The document also places obligations on the bank to create and sustain an appropriate **compliance culture**, meaning compliance must be embedded in business processes rather than treated as a purely reactive control.

A further requirement is the use of **technology for monitoring compliance**, indicating that banks should employ technology-enabled tools to help detect, monitor, and manage compliance risks. The Directions also include **repeal and saving provisions**, state that they do not bar the application of other laws, and provide interpretive guidance for implementation. Overall, the document is a binding supervisory framework for payments banks that requires a formalized, board-supported, independently staffed compliance function with dedicated leadership, documented policies, and technology-supported monitoring from the date of issuance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India circular, issued on July 31, 2026 under section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, sets out consolidated supervisory directions for Local Area Banks (LABs) on a range of operational, conduct, vigilance, fraud-prevention, cyber, and deposit-management matters. It is a supervisory instrument directed at LABs and applies to the extent specified in the directions themselves; the document’s structure indicates it replaces or consolidates earlier instructions in these subject areas, with a specific repeal-and-saving framework in Chapter IX. The document is organized into separate compliance domains, and a LAB compliance team should treat each chapter as creating standalone obligations rather than as mere guidance.

At the retail conduct level, Chapter II requires LABs to follow RBI fair-practice requirements on charging interest, meaning interest must be levied only in accordance with the applicable RBI-prescribed principles and disclosures, rather than ad hoc or opaque bank practices. Chapter III addresses inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits, requiring banks to identify and manage dormant/inoperative balances and unclaimed funds under RBI rules, including the associated customer communication, record-keeping, and transfer/escheat-type handling obligations that apply to such balances. While the text excerpt does not show the detailed mechanics, the chapter placement makes clear that LABs must maintain formal procedures for classifying, monitoring, and resolving dormant and unclaimed accounts.

A significant portion of the directions concerns fraud prevention and internal control. Chapter IV requires LABs to adopt measures for frauds involving collusion of bank officials, large-value frauds, fake title-deed deposit frauds, secure custody of critical documents, and accounts opened by employees, with separate instructions for other related matters; this implies heightened controls, segregation of duties, documentation security, and monitoring of staff-related account activity. Chapter IV also indicates specific obligations around safe custody of important documents and scrutiny of employee-opened accounts, so banks should expect audit trails, approval controls, and escalation procedures to be mandatory. Chapter V establishes a Protected Disclosure Scheme, covering the scope of protected disclosures, the procedure for lodging complaints, and the protected disclosure policy itself, which means LABs must maintain a formal whistleblower channel and ensure confidentiality and non-retaliation protections consistent with the scheme.

Chapter VI creates a more detailed vigilance framework, including a designated Chief of Internal Vigilance. The chapter covers appointment, tenure, restriction on association with sensitive matters, and submission/review of reports and returns, showing that LABs must have a defined internal vigilance function with formal reporting lines and periodic oversight. It also requires preventive vigilance, staff rotation and mandatory leave, complaint handling, investigation arrangements, review of cases assigned to investigating agencies, action against false complainants, and liaison with external agencies, so compliance teams should expect enforceable rules on rotation of sensitive staff, leave-based monitoring, and structured investigative follow-up. Chapter VII on network management and Chapter VIII on cyber-security controls for third-party ATM switch application service providers indicate that LABs relying on networked banking or outsourced ATM switching must impose control, security, and oversight requirements on both their own systems and third-party service providers.

Chapter IX provides the legal housekeeping: it repeals earlier directions to the extent specified while preserving actions already taken under them, confirms that other applicable laws are not barred, and reserves RBI’s interpretive authority. For a compliance officer, the practical takeaway is that these directions should be treated as the current RBI supervisory baseline for LABs on these topics from the date of issuance, with immediate attention needed to align internal policies on interest charging, dormant/unclaimed deposits, fraud controls, whistleblower handling, vigilance governance, staff rotation, and third-party cyber/ATM arrangements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on July 31, 2026 and effective immediately upon issuance, applies specifically to all Local Area Banks in India. It requires each bank’s Board and Senior Management to formally incorporate data-quality risk identification, assessment, and management into the institution’s overall risk-management framework, and that framework must cover both in-house and outsourced data-related processes as well as policies for data confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk management. The banks must also fully document their risk-data aggregation capabilities and risk-reporting practices and subject them to high validation standards, meaning compliance teams should expect formal governance over how supervisory and risk data are collected, controlled, and reported rather than informal or ad hoc processes.

The Directions define “Supervisory Returns” broadly to include all periodic or ad hoc data submitted to RBI in prescribed formats, regardless of the technology platform, frequency, or submission mode; they also define CIMS as RBI’s online platform for return submission and data dissemination. Operationally, the document establishes that Local Area Banks must follow RBI-prescribed supervisory return formats and procedures, with the specific list of applicable returns, filing timelines, exceptions, penalties, and other instructions set out in Chapter III. Because the text provided cuts off partway through Chapter II, the full return list and exact deadlines are not visible here, but the document clearly anticipates mandatory compliance with RBI filing requirements through CIMS or other prescribed channels.

The Directions were issued under RBI’s powers under Section 27 and Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, along with relevant provisions of the RBI Act, 1934 and other enabling laws. They are intended to replace or sit alongside previous supervisory-return requirements for Local Area Banks, with Chapter IV addressing repeal, saving, and the continued application of other laws unless specifically barred. For a compliance team, the immediate action point is to ensure governance, documentation, validation, and reporting controls are aligned to RBI supervisory-return obligations for Local Area Banks from the date of issuance.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026** take effect **immediately upon issuance** and apply to **all Local Area Banks** in connection with the **appointment and reappointment of statutory auditors**. The directions distinguish between banks that appoint separate **Statutory Branch Auditors (SBAs)**—in which case the term **Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs)** is used—and all other banks, for which the term **Statutory Auditors (SAs)** applies. The document is issued under **Section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and replaces prior RBI instructions on this subject through a new consolidated framework for LAB statutory audits.

For compliance purposes, the core requirement is that LABs must follow RBI’s detailed rules on **governance, auditor eligibility, independence, tenure/rotation, audit fees and expenses, and appointment procedures**. The directions assign responsibilities to the **Board and senior management** for overseeing the appointment process and ensuring compliance with RBI-prescribed criteria. They also set out specific rules for the **number of SCAs/SAs and branch coverage**, meaning banks must determine how many audit firms are needed and which branches or operations each auditor will cover based on RBI’s framework.

The directions further impose detailed **eligibility and independence standards** for auditors, requiring banks to appoint only firms meeting RBI’s prescribed professional and conflict-of-interest criteria. They also include requirements on **professional standards**, **rotation and tenure limits**, and **how audit fees and expenses are to be determined and handled**, so compliance teams will need to ensure proposed auditors are not only qualified but also within applicable rotation/continuity limits and paid in a manner consistent with RBI rules. The appointment process itself is formalized, meaning banks must follow the RBI-mandated steps for selecting, approving, and reappointing auditors rather than relying solely on internal discretion.

A major compliance component is the **Long Form Audit Report (LFAR)** regime, which is specifically addressed for both **Statutory Central Auditors and Statutory Branch Auditors**. The directions prescribe the **procedure and timelines** for LFAR submission and define the **objectives, strategy, scope, and indicative coverage** of the LFAR, so banks must be prepared to coordinate audit planning, information gathering, and reporting within those timelines. Because the document includes annexes and chaptered requirements on governance, appointment, and reporting, a compliance officer should treat it as a full operational framework for LAB statutory audit oversight rather than a narrow reporting update.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI circular, the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026**, applies **only to Local Area Banks (LABs)** and takes effect **immediately upon issuance** on **July 31, 2026**. It replaces a transaction-focused internal audit model with a mandatory **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework, meaning LABs must build their internal audit around evaluation of **risk management systems and internal controls**, while still doing selective transaction testing. The RBI issues these Directions under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they apply to all LABs as “banks” for purposes of the document.

The document states that the internal audit function must be treated as a core part of the bank’s internal control and risk management architecture, not just a checking function. The **Board** is responsible for governance and oversight of the internal audit framework, while **senior management** is expected to implement and support it operationally. Although the excerpt provided stops before the detailed board and management provisions, the document’s structure shows that the Board’s responsibilities, management’s role, and the independence of the audit function are central compliance obligations rather than optional best practices.

The Directions require LABs to maintain a formal **internal audit policy** and to ensure **functional independence** of the internal audit function. They also require a structured **risk assessment** process to determine audit priorities and coverage, a defined **scope** for audits, formal **communication** of audit findings and results, and a mechanism for **performance evaluation** of the internal audit function. The document further contemplates rules on **outsourcing** of internal audit work, indicating that if any part of internal audit is outsourced, it must be done within RBI-prescribed boundaries rather than ad hoc.

The Directions also create a dedicated framework for the **Head of Internal Audit (HIA)**, focusing on the HIA’s **authority, stature, independence, tenure, and reporting line**. In compliance terms, this means LABs must ensure the internal audit head has sufficient seniority and direct access/reporting arrangements to prevent interference from operating management. The final chapter indicates the Directions will also address **repeal and saving provisions**, the extent to which other laws continue to apply, and interpretation issues, so LABs should treat this as a standalone RBI governance regime that supplements other statutory and regulatory requirements rather than displacing them unless expressly stated.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular dated **April 1, 2025** is a **consolidation only** for all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs): it updates the earlier master circular of **January 16, 2024** to reflect instructions issued up to **March 31, 2025**, and expressly states that it **does not contain any new instructions or guidelines**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that banks must continue to follow the operative exposure, statutory, and regulatory restrictions summarized in the circular, including limits on borrower/group exposures, sector exposures, unsecured advances, and restrictions on certain loans and investments.  

On definitions and exposure measurement, the circular says exposure limits are to be fixed using **Tier-I capital as on March 31 of the preceding financial year**, with Tier-I capital defined consistently with the RBI capital adequacy framework for UCBs. “Exposure” covers both **credit exposure** and **investment exposure (Non-SLR securities)**. Credit exposure includes **funded and non-funded limits, underwriting and similar commitments, equipment leasing and hire purchase financing, and ad hoc contingency limits**; it **excludes loans/advances secured against the bank’s own term deposits**. For limit calculation, banks must use the **sanctioned limit or outstanding amount, whichever is higher**; for **fully drawn term loans** with no redrawal facility, the **outstanding** may be used; and for **non-funded limits**, **100% of the limit or outstanding amount, whichever is higher**, must be counted. In consortium/multiple banking/syndication arrangements, each bank’s share is subject to the **single borrower/group exposure** framework.  

The circular also reiterates that UCBs must comply with statutory and regulatory restrictions relating to specific credit/investment activities, including **advances against shares, debentures and bonds** and **investments in shares, debentures and bonds**. It specifically preserves the existing rules on, among other things, **lending to directors and their relatives**, **limits on advances to nominal members**, **advances against fixed deposit receipts issued by other banks**, **bridge loans/interim finance**, **loans against shares/debentures/bonds**, **finance to NBFCs**, **equipment leasing and hire purchase finance**, **agricultural finance**, **SHG/JLG lending**, and **restrictions on advances to defaulters of statutory dues**. The document’s operative compliance message is therefore to continue applying the current RBI exposure ceilings, prohibited/limited transactions, and calculation methodology exactly as consolidated in the annexed master circular and related RBI directions.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs), issued on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/18, is a **consolidation-only update** of all instructions on management of advances issued up to **31 March 2025**; it expressly states that it contains **no new instructions or guidelines** and replaces the earlier master circular dated **25 July 2023**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs must use this circular as the current consolidated reference for advance-related policy, while also noting that their Board-approved credit policies must remain transparent, aligned with RBI’s exposure norms and other applicable guidance, and must be **reviewed by the Board at least once every financial year**.

On working capital assessment, the circular repeats that for borrowers **other than micro and small enterprises** seeking fund-based working capital limits **up to ₹1 crore**, and for **micro and small enterprises** seeking fund-based working capital limits **up to ₹5 crore**, assessment may be based on **projected annual turnover**. The standard approach is that working capital requirement is taken at **25% of projected turnover**, with the borrower funding **5% of turnover as Net Working Capital** and the UCB funding at least **20% of turnover**; “projected turnover” is to be understood as **gross sales including excise duty**. UCBs may instead use the traditional method if they choose, but if the traditional method yields a higher requirement, that higher amount may be sanctioned; actual drawals must be controlled through drawing power after excluding unpaid stocks, and borrowers must submit **monthly stock/receivables statements** with periodic physical verification by the bank. For borrowers above those thresholds—i.e., other than micro and small enterprises with working capital limits **above ₹1 crore**, and MSEs/units with limits **above ₹5 crore**—UCBs may assess needs using their own judgment, turnover method, cash budgeting, or other suitable methods, but **book-debt finance for inland credit sales must not exceed 75% of the sanctioned limit**, leaving at least **25%** to be financed through bills to encourage bill usage.

The circular also restates the loan-system framework for larger working capital accounts: for borrowers enjoying working capital credit limits of **₹10 crore and above** from the banking system, the **loan component should normally be 80%**, with the remaining **20% as cash credit component**. The document is a consolidated master circular and includes references to annexures and sections covering credit administration, credit information reporting/exchange, restructuring, specific lending activities, bill discounting/rediscounting, SHG/JLG lending, and relief measures in natural calamities, but in the text provided the RBI explicitly says these are **existing instructions compiled from earlier circulars** rather than fresh regulatory changes.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular is a consolidation for all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) of the RBI’s instructions on housing finance, updating the earlier circular dated April 2, 2024 to reflect all instructions issued up to March 31, 2025. The RBI explicitly states that this revised circular does **not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it only compiles the existing requirements, with the changes reflected in Annex 3. In other words, compliance teams should treat this as the current consolidated reference for UCB housing finance, but should not expect new substantive policy changes solely from this document.

The circular confirms that UCBs may grant housing finance from their own resources to eligible borrowers, with a focus on supporting housing schemes and weaker sections. Eligible borrowers include individuals, co-operative/group housing societies, housing boards undertaking projects for EWS/LIG/MIG categories, and owners seeking extension, up-gradation, or major repairs of houses/flats. The permitted purposes for finance include construction or purchase of houses/flats, repairs/alterations/additions, housing and hostels for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, slum clearance-related lending either directly to slum dwellers with Government guarantee or through statutory boards, and financing for institutions/centres and shopping/market facilities that form part of a housing project and serve the residents of the settlement or township.

For individual housing loans, UCBs may set margins and approve borrowers based on commercial judgment and prudential considerations, but the circular prescribes ceiling amounts per dwelling unit based on the bank’s tier, subject always to existing single-borrower exposure limits: Tier 1 UCBs up to ₹60 lakh, Tier 2 up to ₹1.40 crore, Tier 3 up to ₹2 crore, and Tier 4 up to ₹3 crore. The text also indicates that prudential exposure limits apply for both single borrower/party and group of connected borrowers/parties, so compliance must ensure loan sizing remains within both the tier-based housing cap and the bank’s general exposure framework. The document says these loans are to be granted based on the bank’s own resources and that bigger banks with surplus funds may undertake larger housing lending as a remunerative deployment of excess liquidity.

The circular also reiterates that, where special permission of the Registrar is otherwise required to finance housing societies, banks should seek general permission instead, subject to prescribed conditions. It contains an outline of further housing-loan rules and related compliance areas—such as interest rate treatment, foreclosure/prepayment, penal charges, key facts statement requirements, security, loan period, graduated instalments, aggregate exposure limits, supplementary finance, lending to housing boards, advances to builders/contractors, priority sector treatment, precautions, and the National Building Code—but the text provided does not include the detailed provisions in those sections. From a compliance standpoint, the key operational point is that this circular is the current consolidated RBI reference as of March 31, 2025 and must be read together with the specific instructions listed in Annex 3 and any applicable exposure/priority-sector norms.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) is dated April 1, 2025 and consolidates all existing instructions on income recognition, asset classification, provisioning, and related prudential matters for advances, updating the prior April 2, 2024 circular to reflect instructions issued through March 31, 2025. RBI expressly states that this version does **not** introduce new instructions or guidelines; its purpose is consolidation only, so compliance teams should treat it as the current single reference for the existing prudential framework. The circular applies to UCBs and reiterates that where State Co-operative Societies Acts/rules or other statutory enactments impose stricter requirements, those stricter requirements continue to apply.

Substantively, the circular requires banks to assess asset quality using objective, recovery-based criteria rather than subjective judgment. A loan or advance must be classified as a non-performing asset (NPA) when, for a term loan, interest and/or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days; for an overdraft/cash credit (including other loan products structured as overdraft facilities, even if not for business purposes and even where interest credits are the only credits), the account is NPA when it becomes “out of order”; and for bills purchased/discounted, when the bill remains overdue for more than 90 days. For direct agricultural advances, the circular points to a separate overdue norm in Annex 1, and for other agricultural loans it applies the general norms unless specifically exempted. Once an account is identified as NPA, the circular requires borrower-wise treatment rather than facility-wise treatment, and it includes detailed instructions on recordkeeping, reporting to the Reserve Bank, consumer education, and income recognition treatment.

The document also consolidates the rules on income recognition, including reversal of accrued income when an account becomes NPA, the treatment of partial recoveries, and accounting entries for accrued interest on both performing assets and NPAs (illustrated in Annex 3). It further consolidates provisioning norms for loans and advances, retirement benefits, fraud accounts, and certain specific cases, along with classification and provisioning treatment for restructuring, project finance, and loan exposures transferred to others. The annexures are operationally important because they include direct finance to farmers for agricultural purposes, proforma/report formats, restructuring concepts and illustrations, guidance for projects under implementation, and a list of all circulars consolidated in this master circular. Since the RBI states the circular is only a consolidation of instructions up to March 31, 2025, compliance officers should use it to verify current prudential requirements and ensure internal policies, asset classification processes, recovery tracking, provisioning, and reporting practices align with the consolidated norms.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) is a consolidation of all instructions on guarantees, co-acceptances, and letters of credit issued up to March 31, 2025; it explicitly states that it does **not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**. The circular replaces the prior version dated April 1, 2024 and is intended as the updated compliance reference for UCBs on these non-fund based exposures.

On **guarantees**, UCBs are directed to keep such business within restricted limits because of the associated risk. As a general rule, banks should issue **financial guarantees rather than performance guarantees**, though scheduled banks may issue performance guarantees with due caution. Guarantees should normally be short-term and **must not exceed 10 years** in any case. The **aggregate outstanding guarantee obligations** at any time must not exceed **10% of the bank’s total owned resources** (paid-up capital, reserves, and deposits). Within that overall ceiling, **unsecured guarantees** outstanding at any time should be capped at the lower of **25% of owned funds** (paid-up capital plus reserves) or **25% of total guarantees** outstanding.

The circular prefers **secured guarantees**, meaning guarantees backed by assets (including cash margin) whose market value is at least equal to the contingent liability, or by counter-guarantees from the **Central Government, State Governments, public sector financial institutions, and/or insurance companies**. Banks are instructed to avoid excessive concentration of unsecured guarantee exposure to any one customer group or trade, and the **Board of Directors must set suitable limits** for unsecured guarantees to any individual constituent so these do not exceed a reasonable proportion of the bank’s total unsecured guarantee commitments or a reasonable multiple of the constituent’s shareholding in the bank. For **deferred payment guarantees**, UCBs should generally require adequate tangible security or counter-guarantees from government entities, public sector financial institutions, insurance companies, or other banks; and where such guarantees are issued for acquisition of capital assets, the bank must ensure that the borrower’s **total credit facilities plus the proposed deferred payment guarantees remain within prescribed exposure ceilings**.

The circular also consolidates requirements on guarantees related to **commodities covered under selective credit controls**, safeguards in issuing guarantees, the **immediate settlement of claims under bank guarantees**, handling of **delays in obtaining certified copies of judgments**, and correspondence with government departments. It further covers **co-acceptance of bills**, including irregularities and required safeguards, and **letters of credit (LCs)**, including guidelines for granting LC facilities, LCs for commodities under selective credit controls, safeguards for opening LCs, and immediate settlement of claims under LCs. Finally, it restates the common rule that **credit exposure norms and statutory/other restrictions on non-fund based limits** continue to apply.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, effective April 1, 2025, consolidates and updates RBI instructions on prudential capital adequacy for all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs), replacing the prior April 1, 2024 circular and incorporating instructions issued through March 31, 2025. It reiterates the statutory minimum under Section 11 of the Banking Regulation Act (AACS) that no co-operative bank may commence or carry on banking unless paid-up capital plus reserves are at least ₹1 lakh, and notes RBI’s separate power under Section 22(3)(d) to prescribe entry-point capital norms for new Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks. The circular states that UCBs must meet minimum net worth requirements of ₹2 crore for Tier 1 UCBs operating in a single district and ₹5 crore for all other UCBs across all tiers; UCBs currently below these levels must reach at least 50% of the applicable minimum by March 31, 2026 and the full minimum by March 31, 2028, with net worth computed as specified in Annex 1.

On capital adequacy, the circular keeps the Tier 1 requirement at a minimum CRAR of 9% of risk-weighted assets on an ongoing basis, while Tier 2 to Tier 4 UCBs must maintain 12% CRAR on an ongoing basis. Tier 1 UCBs are defined as all unit UCBs and salary earners’ UCBs regardless of deposit size, and all other UCBs with deposits up to ₹100 crore; Tier 2 covers deposits above ₹100 crore up to ₹1,000 crore; Tier 3 covers deposits above ₹1,000 crore up to ₹10,000 crore; and Tier 4 covers deposits above ₹10,000 crore. Banks in Tier 2 to Tier 4 that do not yet meet the 12% CRAR requirement must phase it in by reaching at least 10% by March 31, 2024, 11% by March 31, 2025, and 12% by March 31, 2026.

The circular specifies that eligible capital for CRAR includes Tier I and Tier II capital, but Tier II capital is capped at 100% of total Tier I capital for CRAR compliance. Tier I capital includes paid-up share capital from regular voting members, certain contributions from associate/nominal members where the bye-laws allow share allotment and restrict withdrawal similarly to regular members, non-refundable admission fees from nominal and associate members treated separately as reserves, qualifying Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS) under Annex 3, and free reserves from audited accounts, subject to the detailed exclusions and treatment rules in the circular. The document also points to Annex 2 for risk weights used in CRAR computation, Annex 4 for debt capital instruments, and Annex 5 for the return format, meaning compliance teams should treat the annexes as operative requirements rather than background material.

In addition to capital and net worth rules, the circular covers share-linking to borrowings, refund of share capital, protections for investors in regulatory capital instruments, and periodic returns. Compliance teams for UCBs should therefore review both current capital position and phased compliance plans against the specified deadlines, confirm tier classification based on deposits, and ensure any capital instruments issued by the bank meet the relevant annexed regulatory conditions.

rows.summary:
RBI’s April 1, 2025 Master Circular on Board of Directors for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) consolidates and updates all prior RBI instructions on board governance, replacing the earlier April 1, 2024 circular. It applies to UCBs generally under the RBI’s supervisory powers, and it specifically requires boards to be composed of knowledgeable, high-integrity directors, with **at least two professional directors at all times**—meaning persons with suitable banking experience at middle/senior management level or relevant qualifications in **law, accountancy, or finance**. Banks must ensure their bye-laws contain suitable provisions to support this requirement; however, RBI says this specific professional-director expectation will **not be insisted upon for Salary Earners’ Banks** because of their membership structure.

The circular also requires that, for UCBs **other than those with deposit size below ₹100 crore and other than Salary Earners’ Banks**, a **Board of Management (BoM)** must be constituted to strengthen professional management and focus on banking activities, and bye-laws must be amended accordingly in line with the December 31, 2019 RBI guideline referenced in the circular. It reiterates that only persons eligible for membership can become directors (except co-opted and nominated directors), and highlights that persons engaged in money-lending, financing, or investment activities—whether personally or through a proprietary/partnership/employment/directorship role in another concern—as well as persons convicted of criminal offences including moral turpitude, are ineligible, subject to the model bye-law and relevant co-operative society law, BR Act, and co-operative law restrictions.

A notable governance restriction in the 2025 circular is the RBI’s explicit directive that UCBs **must not create any honorary Board-level positions or non-statutory titles** such as “Chairman Emeritus” or “Group Chairman.” RBI’s concern is that such titles can create conflicts of interest, blur accountability, and produce a parallel or shadow authority that interferes with the lawful Board’s independent functioning. The circular also reinforces the core governance split: the Board is responsible for policy formulation, statutory compliance, and overall supervision/control of the bank, while day-to-day administration remains with the Managing Director.

The document further points to the Madhava Das Committee recommendations on UCB boards (reproduced in Annex 1) and a separate set of reviews/matters to be submitted to the Board of Directors of primary UCBs (Annex 2), indicating that compliance teams should review those annexes for board process and oversight obligations. The circular consolidates prior circulars listed in the appendix, so compliance officers should treat this as the operative RBI reference for board constitution, eligibility, bye-law amendments, BoM requirements, and restrictions on board titles as of **April 1, 2025**.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular is a consolidation of RBI instructions on housing finance for **all Scheduled Commercial Banks other than Regional Rural Banks**, issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. RBI states explicitly that this April 1, 2025 circular **does not introduce any new housing-finance rules**; it merely compiles and updates all instructions issued **up to March 31, 2025** and supersedes the earlier consolidated circular dated **April 2, 2024**.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirements remain that housing finance must be used for **genuine housing/construction purposes** and not for **speculation in real estate**. Banks may finance **purchase of plots only if the borrower gives a declaration** that a house will be constructed on the plot, using bank finance or otherwise, within the bank’s stipulated period. Banks may also finance individuals for **purchase or construction of one dwelling unit per family**, **repairs to damaged dwelling units**, and in some cases a **second house** even where the borrower already owns one home, provided the second house is for self-occupation. The circular also permits loans for a house to be let out when the borrower is posted away from headquarters or already has employer-provided accommodation, purchase of an old house currently occupied by the borrower as a tenant, and lending connected with **slum improvement**, including direct lending to slum-dwellers backed by government guarantee, indirect lending through state governments, and finance to slum clearance boards and similar public agencies.

A specific compliance-sensitive requirement is included for **loans used to construct on land already owned by the borrower**: before sanctioning the home loan, banks/FIs must obtain a **copy of the sanctioned building plan** issued by the competent authority **in the applicant’s name**. They must also obtain an **affidavit-cum-undertaking** from the borrower confirming that construction will strictly follow the sanctioned plan and that the borrower is solely responsible for obtaining the **completion certificate within 3 months of completion of construction**; if that certificate is not obtained on time, the bank has the right to **recall the entire loan together with interest, costs, and other usual bank charges**. In addition, an **architect appointed by the bank** must certify the construction at various stages (the excerpt cuts off after this point, but the obligation is clearly that bank-appointed architectural certification is required as part of construction monitoring).

The circular’s scope and classification matter for internal governance: it is a **statutory directive** issued by RBI under **Sections 21 and 35A** of the Banking Regulation Act, so covered banks should treat the consolidated instructions as binding supervisory expectations and ensure their housing-loan policies, documentation checklists, and construction-monitoring procedures align with these requirements. Since RBI confirms there are **no new instructions** in this revision, compliance teams should focus on confirming that existing policies remain aligned with the consolidated text and that staff continue to apply the plan-sanction, undertaking, completion-certificate, and loan-recall provisions where applicable.

rows.summary:
This revised Master Circular, issued by RBI on 1 April 2025 to all Scheduled Commercial Banks other than Regional Rural Banks, consolidates the RBI’s instructions on bank finance to NBFCs as updated through 31 March 2025; it expressly states that it does **not** introduce any new instructions or guidelines, but replaces and consolidates the prior 24 April 2024 circular. It is a statutory guideline issued under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and it applies to banks’ lending and exposure policies for NBFCs, including Housing Finance Companies registered under Section 29A of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987.

The circular clarifies the regulatory scope and definitions that banks must use: “NBFCs” includes RBI-registered NBFCs and HFCs; “current investments” are investments shown as current assets and intended to be held for less than one year; “long term investments” are all other investments; and “unsecured loans” are loans not secured by tangible assets. It explains that while many bank-credit restrictions on NBFC lending have been deregulated, restrictions remain for sensitive NBFC activities, so banks must still avoid financing activities specifically barred in the circular.

For NBFCs that are statutorily registered with RBI and whose principal business is asset financing, loan, factoring, investment, infrastructure financing, equipment leasing, or hire-purchase, the earlier ceiling tying bank credit to the NBFC’s Net Owned Fund (NOF) has been withdrawn. Banks may therefore provide need-based working capital facilities and term loans to these NBFCs, but only subject to the circular’s remaining prohibitions and prudential limits, including the restrictions in paragraph 8. Banks may also finance NBFCs against second-hand assets financed by those NBFCs, reflecting the RBI’s acknowledgment of NBFC experience in that area.

The circular requires each bank to frame its own lending policy for NBFC exposure, with approval from its Board of Directors, and to keep that policy within RBI prudential guidelines and exposure norms. However, even under such board-approved policies, banks are not permitted to finance activities listed as ineligible in paragraphs 4 and 6, meaning the freedom to lend is not unrestricted and must be checked against the specific prohibited uses and financing structures set out in the Master Circular.

rows.summary:
This RBI master circular is a **consolidation only**: it updates the earlier circular dated **April 2, 2024** and incorporates all instructions on prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning for advances issued **through March 31, 2025**. RBI states explicitly that the revised circular **does not introduce any new instructions or guidelines**; it is intended to replace/withdraw the prior consolidated version and serve as the up-to-date reference for **all commercial banks except RRBs**.

For compliance purposes, the practical requirement is to use this document as the governing consolidated source for how banks must recognize income on advances, identify and classify NPAs, and make provisions. It covers the full framework for **non-performing asset definitions**, including “out of order” and “overdue” concepts, **income recognition policy**, reversal of income, appropriation of recoveries in NPAs, interest application, and computation of NPA levels. It also consolidates the rules for **asset classification** into categories of NPAs and the detailed guidelines for classification of assets, as well as the complete **provisioning regime** for loss, doubtful, standard, and substandard assets.

The circular also consolidates special prudential rules relating to **floating provisions**, including when banks may create and use them, and permits **additional provisions at higher-than-prescribed rates** in specified cases. It includes provisions for **leased assets** and other detailed prudential treatment under the bank’s advance portfolio. Because the circular is a consolidation rather than a substantive change notice, the key compliance obligation is to ensure internal policies, monitoring systems, classification triggers, provisioning calculations, and income recognition processes are aligned to the amended master text and its referenced annexures, particularly the instructions listed in **Annex 5**.

The operative date is important for version control: this revised master circular reflects the RBI’s complete instruction set as of **March 31, 2025**, and should be treated as the applicable consolidated guidance from **April 1, 2025** onward for the covered banks. Compliance teams should therefore verify that any local policy documents, accounting treatment manuals, and NPA/provisioning workflows map to this consolidated circular and that any prior references to the April 2, 2024 version are updated accordingly.
