rows.summary:
This revised Master Circular for Guarantees and Co-acceptances is a consolidation of RBI instructions applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks **except Payment Banks and Regional Rural Banks**; it is issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 as a **statutory directive**. It **does not introduce new requirements**: the RBI states it only updates and consolidates all existing instructions on guarantees and co-acceptances issued up to **31 March 2025**, replacing the prior master circular dated **1 April 2024** and incorporating the circulars listed in Annex 2. For compliance purposes, the operative point is that banks must use this consolidated circular as the current reference set for guarantee/co-acceptance business, but the document itself does not alter policy beyond compiling prior directions.

Substantively, the circular reiterates that banks should generally prefer **financial guarantees** over performance guarantees and exercise greater caution with performance guarantees, and should normally confine guarantees to **shorter maturities**. As a rule, no bank guarantee should normally exceed **10 years**, although banks may issue guarantees beyond 10 years where they have extended **long-term loans for periods longer than 10 years** for projects; in that case they must consider the impact on **Asset-Liability Management (ALM)** and may adopt a Board-approved policy for such long-duration guarantees. Banks are also reminded to avoid issuing non-fund-based facilities to, or on behalf of, constituents who do not meet the bank’s normal lending standards, and to ensure guarantees are consistent with prudential credit judgment rather than being used to bypass lending discipline.

The circular consolidates detailed operational controls on guarantee issuance, including precautions against fraud, internal control expectations, and specific restrictions around guarantees issued for various categories of counterparties and transactions. It includes guidance on guarantees on behalf of **banks’ directors**, guarantees under the **Government of India Bank Guarantee Scheme**, guarantees for **share and stock brokers / commodity brokers**, and rules governing **personal guarantees of promoters, directors, other managerial personnel, and shareholders of borrowing companies**. It also covers guarantees of **State Governments**, issuance of **bid bonds and performance guarantees for exports**, unconditional guarantees in favour of **overseas employers/importers** on behalf of Indian exporters, precautions for **project exports** and **export advances**, and conditions for guarantees connected to **overseas investments** involving a foreign entity or its step-down subsidiary.

In addition, the circular reiterates restrictions on guarantees used for **placement of funds with NBFCs or other non-bank entities**, the requirements for **payment when guarantees are invoked**, and safeguards for **co-acceptance of bills**. It also reminds banks to take precautions when issuing or dealing with **letters of credit**, and to ensure compliance with both the **Foreign Exchange Management Act, 2000** and applicable **prudential norms**. Annex 1 provides a **model form of bank guarantee bond**, and Annex 2 lists the circulars that have been consolidated; compliance teams should treat this master circular as the reference compilation of all pre-31 March 2025 RBI instructions on these topics.

rows.summary:
This document is the Reserve Bank of India’s updated Master Circular on Basel III Capital Regulations, issued on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/08 (DOR.CAP.REC.2/21.06.201/2025-26). It applies to all Scheduled Commercial Banks **other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Regional Rural Banks**; the RBI specifically notes that Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks must instead follow their own licensing and operating guidelines for capital adequacy. The circular consolidates and updates the prudential Basel III capital adequacy instructions previously issued up to the date of the 1 April 2024 master circular, and states that the 2025 version incorporates all relevant guidelines issued as of the current date; Annex 26 contains the list of circulars consolidated into this Master Circular.

Substantively, this is a comprehensive Basel III capital regulation compendium rather than a single new rule, but it is the operative consolidated reference for compliance. It covers the full capital framework for affected banks, including minimum capital requirements under Pillar 1, the scope of application of the capital adequacy framework, the composition of regulatory capital, minority interest recognition, deductions and regulatory adjustments, and transitional arrangements. It then sets out the detailed risk-weighted capital treatment for credit risk, including exposures to sovereigns, central banks, PSEs, MDBs/BIS/IMF, banks, primary dealers, corporates/NBFCs, retail portfolios, residential property, commercial real estate, NPAs, specified categories, other assets, off-balance-sheet items, securitisation exposures, and banking book CDS positions, including recognition of third-party CDS hedges and internal hedges.

The circular also restates the approved external credit assessment and credit risk mitigation framework, covering eligible rating agencies, how external ratings are mapped and used for long-term and short-term claims, treatment of unsolicited and multiple ratings, and whether issue ratings can be extended to issuer/other claims. For credit risk mitigation, it addresses collateralised transactions, repo/reverse repo-style transactions, OTC derivatives collateral, on-balance sheet netting, guarantees and counter-guarantees, sovereign and ECGC guarantees, proportional cover, currency mismatches, maturity mismatches, and pooling of CRM techniques, with legal certainty and operational requirements emphasized as conditions for recognition. In the market risk section, it prescribes capital charges for interest rate risk, equity risk, foreign exchange risk, and CDS trading-book exposures, including general market risk, specific risk to the reference entity, counterparty credit risk, treatment below materiality thresholds, aggregation of market risk capital, and illiquid positions.

Finally, the circular sets out the operational risk capital framework, defining operational risk and specifying the measurement methodologies, including the Basic Indicator Approach. Under Pillar 2, it explains the RBI’s Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) and the banks’ Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), including governance expectations, management integration, proportionality, independent review and validation, forward-looking and risk-based assessment, and the use of stress testing/scenario analysis and capital models. The document’s table of contents also shows that Part C addresses market discipline under Pillar 3, indicating that disclosure requirements are part of the consolidated Basel III compliance package, even though the excerpt provided cuts off before the full disclosure section.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, issued on June 16, 2025 and addressed to all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks, consolidates all RBI instructions issued to date on credit facilities for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It does not introduce a single new standalone scheme, but it requires banks to continue and operationalize a set of lending, planning, servicing, and procedural measures intended to increase and improve credit flow to SC/ST borrowers, with special attention at the district and block levels.

Banks are expected to use the District Level Consultative Committees under the Lead Bank Scheme as the main coordination forum, and district credit plans should explicitly link credit to employment and development programmes. Lead banks must also work closely with District Industries Centres, give weightage to SC/STs in block-level credit planning, and prepare special bankable schemes suited to SC/ST self-employment needs; the circular specifically says loan proposals from SC/ST applicants should be considered with “utmost sympathy and understanding.” In formulating Block/District Credit Plans, banks should give special focus to villages with sizeable SC/ST populations and to bastis/localities in towns or villages where these communities are concentrated.

On the operational side, bank staff are instructed to help SC/ST borrowers complete application forms and other formalities so that credit is provided within a stipulated period from receipt of the application. Banks must build awareness of available schemes through brochures, field staff visits, and branch meetings held more frequently and exclusively for SC/ST beneficiaries, so that borrowers understand the features and benefits of the schemes and can have their credit needs reflected in the credit plan. RBI and NABARD circulars relevant to this subject must be circulated internally to staff for compliance.

The circular also sets important lending safeguards for government-sponsored poverty alleviation and self-employment programmes: banks must not insist on deposits from SC/ST borrowers when processing such loan applications, and they must ensure that any applicable subsidy is released upfront rather than being withheld until full repayment of bank dues. RBI explicitly states that withholding subsidy causes under-financing and impairs asset creation and income generation. Banks are also required to provide all necessary institutional support to the National Scheduled Tribes Finance & Development Corporation and the National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation, which operate under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, respectively.

Finally, the circular states that loans sanctioned to State Sponsored Organisations for SC/ST beneficiaries are eligible for priority sector classification when the purpose is purchase and supply of inputs and/or marketing of the beneficiaries’ outputs. If a loan application under a government programme from an SC/ST borrower is rejected, the rejection must be taken up at the next higher level rather than decided at branch level, and the reasons for rejection must be clearly recorded. The circular is framed as a consolidation of existing RBI instructions rather than a fresh policy with a new compliance deadline, so banks should treat it as an updated master reference for ongoing compliance and implementation.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by RBI on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/04 (FIDD.CO.LBS.BC.No.03/02.01.001/2025-26), consolidates all Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) guidelines and instructions issued up to 31 March 2025 and supersedes the need to track the earlier scattered instructions listed in Appendix I. It is addressed to SLBC/UTLBC convenor banks and lead banks, and is the current consolidated reference for compliance with LBS expectations, meeting processes, data flows, and related banking inclusion initiatives. The circular itself does not introduce a single new policy change in the excerpted text; rather, it restates and organizes the operative framework for the scheme and signals that the RBI-hosted version is the authoritative compiled source.

The document explains that the Lead Bank Scheme was created in December 1969 in response to the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee recommendations to address weak rural banking presence through an “area approach.” Under the scheme, RBI assigns one bank as the lead bank for each district to coordinate with credit institutions and government agencies to expand bank finance, especially to the priority sector and the rural economy. The last major review was by the Usha Thorat Committee in 2009, which found the scheme useful for branch expansion, deposit mobilization, and priority-sector lending, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, and recommended continuation of the scheme.

For compliance teams, the structure of obligations in the circular is important: it covers the governance fora under LBS (Block Level Bankers’ Committees, District Consultative Committees, District Level Review Committees, and State Level Bankers’ Committees), plus requirements for meeting conduct, agenda setting, annual calendars of meetings, role of Lead District Managers, quarterly public meetings and grievance redressal, SLBC website standardization, liaison with State Governments, and capacity-building/sensitization programs. It also covers implementation requirements around preparation and monitoring of credit plans, Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs), revised data-flow mechanisms for LBS forum meetings, assignment of lead bank responsibility, and banking penetration initiatives such as the roadmap for unbanked villages, brick-and-mortar branches in villages with population above 5,000 that do not have a scheduled commercial bank branch, alignment with branch authorization policy, and the NSFI 2019–2024 goal of universal access to financial services.

The circular further includes operational policy areas that banks must continue to address through the LBS framework: maintaining and improving Credit Deposit Ratio performance in rural and semi-urban areas, implementing recommendations of the Expert Group on CD Ratio, supporting Direct Benefit Transfer, applying the Service Area Approach including dispensing with the “No Due Certificate,” improving farmers’ income, and expanding and deepening the digital payments ecosystem. In practical compliance terms, this means lead banks and convenor banks must ensure their district/state coordination machinery, reporting, meeting cadence, public grievance processes, website disclosures, and inclusion/planning activities remain aligned with the consolidated RBI instructions as of 31 March 2025.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular dated **April 1, 2025** consolidates and updates all prior instructions on **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)** and **replaces the earlier Master Circular dated April 16, 2024**. It is addressed to **Public Sector Banks and Private Sector Banks, including Small Finance Banks**, and it restates the framework for bank participation in the Government of India’s flagship rural poverty-reduction program, which was originally launched as NRLM on **April 1, 2013** and renamed **DAY-NRLM on March 29, 2016**. The scheme is designed to build strong institutions of the poor, especially women, and help them access financial services and livelihoods through a demand-driven, state-specific approach.

The circular confirms that DAY-NRLM primarily promotes **affinity-based women Self Help Groups (SHGs)**, with an exception allowing **men and women together only for SHGs formed for persons with disabilities and other special categories such as elders and transgenders**. Standard women SHGs must have **10 to 20 members**; however, in difficult areas, groups with disabled persons, and remote tribal areas, the minimum may be **5 members**. Federations of SHGs formed at village, gram panchayat, cluster, or higher levels may be **registered under the relevant state law**. For financial support, the Ministry of Rural Development will provide a **Revolving Fund (RF) of ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 per SHG** to strengthen institutional and financial management capacity and help build internal credit history, but only SHGs that have existed for at least **3/6 months**, follow the “**Panchasutras**” (regular meetings, regular savings, regular internal lending, regular recoveries, and proper books of account), and have **not previously received RF** are eligible. The circular expressly states that **no capital subsidy** will be sanctioned to any SHG under DAY-NRLM. It also notes that **Community Investment Support Fund (CIF)** will be provided to SHGs in all blocks, routed through village- or cluster-level federations and **kept in perpetuity** by those federations; CIF may be used by the federations to make loans to SHGs and/or finance common collective socio-economic activities. In addition, the scheme includes **interest subvention for women SHGs**, with the detailed features set out in **Annex II**.

For banks, the circular makes clear that their role begins with **opening savings/current accounts for all SHGs and SHG federations**, including groups with members who have disabilities. SHGs are eligible to open savings accounts when they are engaged in promoting savings among members. For **KYC of SHG members**, banks must follow the **Master Direction on KYC dated February 25, 2016, as updated from time to time**; for **PAN/Form 60**, banks must follow **Section 33A(b) of the Master Direction on KYC**. The circular also permits **Business Correspondents (BCs)** to open SHG savings accounts, but only if this is done in accordance with existing BC guidelines and the bank’s **Board-approved BC policy**. The excerpt provided ends mid-sentence after beginning a further instruction on opening savings accounts for all members, so any additional account-opening requirement appears to continue beyond the visible text and should be checked in the full circular and annexes before implementation.

rows.title: Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme
rows.desc: RBI/2025-26/01 FIDD.CO.FID.BC.No.4/12.01.033/2025-26 April 01, 2025 The Chairman/ Managing Director/ Chief Executive Officer All Scheduled Commercial Banks Madam/ Dear Sir Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme The Reserve Bank of India has, from time to time, issued a number of guidelines/instructions to banks on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme. The enclosed Master Circular c onsolidates the circulars issued by Reserve Bank on the subject up to March 31, 2025, as indicated in the Appendix. Yours faithfully (Nisha Nambiar) Chief General Manager-in-Charge Encl: As above 2 Master Circular on SHG-Bank Linkage Programme Self Help Groups (SHGs) have the potential to bring together the formal banking structure and the rural poor for mutual benefit. Studies conducted by NABARD in a few states to assess the impact of the linkage project have brought out encouraging and positive features like increase in loan volume of the SHGs, definite shift in the loaning pattern of the members from non-income generating activities to production activities, nearly 100 per cent recovery performance, significant reduction in the transaction costs for both the banks and the borrowers etc., besides leading to a gradual increase in the income level of the SHG members. Another significant feature observed in the linkage project is that about 85 per cent of the groups linked with banks were formed exclusively by women. 2. Recognizing the importance of SHG Bank linkage, banks have been advised to meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, as envisaged in Paragraph 93 of the Union Budget announcement for the year 2008-09, made by the Honorable Finance Minister, wherein it was stated as under: "Banks will be encouraged to embrace the concept of Total Financial Inclusion. rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, dated April 1, 2025, consolidates all prior RBI instructions on the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme up to March 31, 2025 and is addressed to all Scheduled Commercial Banks. It does not announce a wholly new regime, but it restates and consolidates the compliance expectations that banks must follow when opening accounts for, and lending to, Self Help Groups (SHGs), with the goal of supporting “total financial inclusion” and ensuring banks meet the full credit needs of SHG members, including income-generating activity, social needs such as housing/education/marriage, and debt swapping.

Banks must allow both registered and unregistered SHGs that promote savings among members to open savings bank accounts, even if the group has not previously borrowed from a bank. While doing so, banks must apply the simplified customer due diligence (CDD) requirements applicable to SHGs under Chapter VI of the Master Direction on KYC (2016, as updated). The circular also emphasizes that banks should not impose rigid formal structures on SHGs and should keep the process hassle-free, including permitting consumption expenditure as part of the financing approach.

For lending, SHG credit must be built into the bank’s branch, block, district, state, and corporate credit plans, with “utmost priority” in those plans. NABARD operational guidance permits SHG loans generally within a savings-to-loan ratio of 1:1 to 1:4; however, for mature SHGs, banks may lend beyond four times the savings at their discretion. Banks are required to simplify loan applications, procedures, and documentation, eliminate operational bottlenecks, and delegate sufficient sanctioning authority to branch managers so that credit can be sanctioned and disbursed quickly.

On pricing and charges, banks may decide the interest rate on SHG and SHG member loans, but only within the limits of the RBI’s Master Direction on Interest Rate on Advances (March 3, 2016, as updated). The circular also points to the separate RBI priority sector lending instructions for service/processing charges on SHG loans, meaning any applicable charge waivers or restrictions must be followed under those directions. The document’s stated “effective” status is as a consolidation of the extant instructions as of March 31, 2025, so compliance teams should treat it as the current master reference for SHG-bank linkage requirements unless and until superseded.

rows.summary:
On August 12, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued for public comment a draft of the “Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026,” following the policy announcement made on August 5, 2026. The RBI says the draft is intended to replace the current patchwork of interest-rate instructions with a harmonized, principles-based framework for determining interest rates on both fixed-rate and floating-rate loans, with the framework scaled to the nature, complexity, and size of each regulated entity’s operations.

The draft is intended to apply to all regulated entities (REs), but the RBI specifically notes that existing detailed regulatory instructions currently apply mainly to Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks and Local Area Banks, especially for floating-rate lending, internal and external benchmark-based lending frameworks, and spread-setting over benchmarks. For other REs—Non-Banking Financial Companies, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks—the current rules are described as mostly conduct-related rather than a full pricing framework. The RBI also highlights observed inconsistencies in commercial banks’ practices, particularly in how the marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) and its components are determined, and says the present guidance is limited for fixed-rate loans; the draft is meant to address these gaps.

For compliance teams, the key point is that this is a consultation draft, not yet final. The RBI states that, after reviewing feedback, it will issue final Directions separately for each category of regulated entity. Comments from regulated entities and the public are due by September 11, 2026, and may be submitted either through the RBI’s “Connect 2 Regulate” portal or by email using the specified subject line: “Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions).”

CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft Directions on the **Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework** and invited public comments before finalizing them. The draft replaces the RBI’s existing **2011 CVA framework**, which had been based on **2010 Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)** standards, with revised instructions aligned to the **final Basel III CVA framework**. The RBI says the updated framework is intended to make the capital treatment for derivative counterparty credit risk more risk-sensitive and more consistent with current Basel guidance.

The key substantive change is that **banks in India will be permitted to adopt the Basic Approach (BA-CVA)** for calculating the CVA capital charge. Under the draft, eligible banks may choose either the **full BA-CVA** or the **reduced BA-CVA** version. In addition, for banks with an **insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives**, the draft allows an alternative treatment under which the CVA capital charge may be set at **100% of the bank’s counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge**, consistent with BCBS guidance.

The RBI also says the revised instructions would: clarify **which CVA hedges are eligible and how they are recognized**; make the supervisory risk weights for counterparties more sensitive by **sector and credit quality**; and in the **full BA-CVA** calculation, separate **systematic** and **idiosyncratic** CVA risk components to address imperfect matching of indirect CVA hedges. These changes matter for banks that hold derivative portfolios, especially those with non-centrally cleared derivatives exposures and institutions using CVA hedges in their capital calculations.

The draft Directions have been published as the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026**. Comments are invited from **regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties** by **August 28, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section, or sent by email/letter to the **Chief General Manager, Market Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, RBI, 12th Floor, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai 400001**, with the email subject line **“Feedback on Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework.”**

rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released for public comment the draft **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026**. The draft proposes amendments to **Chapter VII: Leverage Ratio framework** of the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025**, with the stated purpose of aligning RBI’s leverage ratio rules with the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s latest **“Leverage Ratio 2017 Standard.”**

For compliance purposes, the material point is that this is a proposed regulatory change affecting **commercial banks** subject to RBI’s capital adequacy framework; the notice does not itself impose the new requirements yet, but it signals forthcoming revisions to the leverage ratio regime once finalized. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent by mail to the **Chief General Manager, Balance Sheet Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, 12th Floor, Central Office Building, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026.”**

No specific numerical leverage ratio, threshold, capital charge, or effective implementation date is stated in the press release itself; the only deadline provided is the **comment submission deadline of August 28, 2026**. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as an advance notice of a likely update to leverage ratio compliance obligations for commercial banks and monitor the final amendment directions for the actual operative requirements and effective date.

The above draft Directions prescribe, inter alia, prudential exposure limits for single/group counterparty, enhanced housing loan limits, and prudential exposure limits on unsecured advances. Additionally, it is proposed to allow flexibility to larger Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) with deposits above ₹1,000 crore in deciding the tenor and moratorium requirements for housing loans, while increasing the ceilings for these parameters in cases of other RCBs. Further, the prescribed prudential sectoral exposure limits, except for real estate sector, are proposed to be withdrawn. 3. rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued draft directions for public comment as part of its review of the concentration risk framework for Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs), following the policy announcement made on August 5, 2026. The proposal has two parts: a new **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2026** that would replace the existing **2025 concentration risk directions**, and a **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Amendment Directions, 2026** that would amend selected provisions of the **2025 Credit Facilities Directions**.

Substantively, the draft rules would continue to prescribe prudential exposure limits for **single and group counterparties** and set **prudential limits for unsecured advances**. They would also **increase housing loan ceilings** and give **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** flexibility to decide the **tenor and moratorium requirements** for housing loans, while **raising the allowed ceilings for those parameters for other RCBs**. In addition, the RBI proposes to **withdraw the sectoral exposure limits** that currently apply, **except for the real estate sector**, meaning the remaining sectoral restriction would continue only for real estate.

The draft directions are currently at the consultation stage, and **comments/feedback must be submitted on or before August 28, 2026**. Submissions may be made either through the RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on the webpage hosting the draft documents, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. This matters for all regulated entities and other stakeholders/public who wish to comment, and for RCB compliance teams that will need to prepare for possible changes to exposure management, housing loan structuring, and sectoral lending policy if the drafts are finalized.

Pursuant thereto, a committee was constituted by the Central Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the extant regulatory framework. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India has prepared a draft of the rationalized Rules. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has released a **draft replacement/rationalization framework** for the current **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (NDI Rules)**, following the **Union Budget 2026–27** announcement that the foreign investment regime would be comprehensively reviewed and modernized. The draft is based on a committee review and stakeholder consultation, and it signals an intended shift toward a **simplified, principle-based, more investor-friendly foreign investment framework** that harmonizes definitions, reduces regulatory complexity, and separates FEMA procedural requirements from **FDI policy and sector-specific conditions** so that policy changes can be updated more efficiently. The RBI also states that the future framework will be **investee-neutral and investor-neutral**, while still preserving regulatory safeguards.

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that this is **not yet final**: the Rules will be finalized only **after wider public consultations**. The RBI has placed the draft **Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026** on its website for comments/feedback from stakeholders. The draft itself is described at a high level in the press release as aiming to streamline procedures, reduce compliance burden, and provide greater operational flexibility, but the press release does **not** set out detailed substantive rule changes, thresholds, sector caps, or new filing requirements beyond the consultation process.

The only explicit deadline in the document is for stakeholder submissions: **comments/feedback must be submitted by August 31, 2026**. Feedback can be filed through the relevant link in the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section or emailed, with the subject line **“Feedback on Draft Foreign Investment Rules”**. Compliance teams with foreign investment, FDI, FEMA, sectoral licensing, or inbound investment governance responsibilities should review the draft, determine whether their current processes depend on the existing NDI Rules, and consider submitting observations before the deadline, especially if they operate in regulated sectors or rely on procedural requirements that may be affected by the proposed rationalization.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at strengthening data governance frameworks at regulated entities because RBI views data as a critical asset and says weak governance can create financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risk. The guidance is expressly applicable to **Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Local Area Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, All India Financial Institutions, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, and Credit Information Companies**.

RBI is inviting comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders **by August 17, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on RBI’s website, or sent by post to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”**

Substantively, the draft guidance does not set out a single numeric capital, reporting, or prudential ratio requirement; instead, it establishes RBI’s expected standards for data governance across the data lifecycle. It identifies broad expectation areas covering **data governance roles, data architecture, metadata and lineage, data quality, and third-party arrangements involving data sharing**. For compliance teams, the immediate action item is to assess whether the institution falls within one of the covered regulated-entity categories and, if so, review current data governance controls against the draft expectations and decide whether to submit comments before the **August 17, 2026** deadline.

rows.summary:
On June 24, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at establishing **holistic regulatory expectations for model risk management across the full model lifecycle** and is intended to address the fact that regulated entities are increasingly using models — including **AI/ML-based models** — across business and decision-making processes, where weak governance, oversight, controls, or risk management can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risk**.

The draft applies to a broad set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies, asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. It also makes clear that the guidance applies to **all models used by these entities**, including **third-party models** and models employing **artificial intelligence / machine learning (AI/ML)**, not just credit models or internally developed tools.

This draft follows RBI’s earlier **August 5, 2024** draft on **“Regulatory Principles for Management of Model Risks in Credit”** and the **August 13, 2025** report of the Committee on Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI). The current draft expands the focus from credit-related model risk to a broader model-risk framework across use cases and lifecycle stages.

RBI has invited **comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders by July 24, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through RBI’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on its website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management.”** For compliance teams, the immediate action item is to review whether the entity uses any models — especially outsourced or AI/ML-enabled models — that would be covered by the draft and to assess whether internal model governance, validation, monitoring, and control processes would need to be upgraded once the guidance is finalized.

On June 10, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued draft amendment directions for public comment as part of a broader effort to harmonize and consolidate instructions on control/assurance functions across multiple regulated sectors. The draft instruments cover 11 separate regulatory frameworks: commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, all India financial institutions, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, non-banking financial companies, credit information companies, and asset reconstruction companies.

Comments can be filed through the RBI’s “Connect 2 Regulate” section via the hyperlink on the page hosting each draft, or by email using the subject line format “Feedback on [full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity)].” The notice does not set out the substantive amended control/assurance requirements themselves, but it clearly signals that all entities in the listed categories should review the draft amendments for potential governance, control-function, or assurance-function impacts and decide whether to respond within the consultation window.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’
rows.desc: June 10, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’ The extant guidelines require the use of the Current Exposure Method (CEM) for the computation of Counterparty Credit Risk (CCR) exposure. In 2016, RBI issued final ‘Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions’ and ‘Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties’, both based on the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR), with an intended implementation date of April 1, 2018. However, the implementation of these guidelines was subsequently deferred. 2. Since then, the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020, has been enacted, while the margining framework has been implemented under the Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also, over time, issued various FAQs providing further clarity on the SA-CCR guidelines. 3. Considering the time elapsed and the recent legal and regulatory developments, the guidelines have been comprehensively reviewed. The key changes between the 2016 guidelines (currently part of the Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025) and the proposed draft Directions include, inter alia, (i) clarification on the scope of CCR across both banking and trading book exposures, (ii) treatment of multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets elaborated in view of the legal / regulatory developments in netting and margining guidelines, (iii) guidance on the treatment of transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI- recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments, (iv) treatment for deferment of option premium, (v) guidance on computation of effective notional for options, and (vi) inclusion of disclosure
rows.summary:
On June 10, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft Amendment Directions on the **Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)** and invited public comments. The draft reflects a comprehensive review of the earlier 2016 SA-CCR-based guidelines, which had originally been intended to take effect on **April 1, 2018** but were later deferred; under the extant framework, banks still compute counterparty credit risk exposure using the **Current Exposure Method (CEM)**. The review was prompted by subsequent legal and regulatory changes, including the enactment of the **Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020**, the implementation of the margining framework under the **Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024**, and additional clarification issued by the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)** through FAQs.

The draft directions make several substantive changes relevant to compliance and risk systems: they clarify the scope of counterparty credit risk across **both banking book and trading book exposures**; expand guidance on **multiple margin agreements** and **multiple netting sets** in light of the new netting and margining regime; address transactions where a bank acts as a **clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges** in the **equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments**; provide treatment for **deferment of option premium**; explain how to compute the **effective notional for options**; and add **disclosure templates** for SA-CCR. RBI states that it has now issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which implies affected institutions should review whether their CCR calculation methodologies, margin/netting documentation handling, and disclosure processes need to be updated once these amendments are implemented.

Comments on the draft are due by **July 1, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Market Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Mumbai 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’”**. The consultation is open to **regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties**.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **revised draft Amendment Directions** on **“Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents”** after receiving substantial stakeholder feedback on the version released for public comment on **February 12, 2026**. The RBI says the earlier draft has been **materially revised** in several key areas based on that feedback, including changes to provisions related to lenders’ proposed use of **technology-based mechanisms to restrict or disable certain functions of financed mobile devices** (such as **mobile phones and tablets**) in order to recover dues from borrowers in default.  

The revised draft is now being issued for **another round of public consultation** and applies across a broad set of RBI-regulated institutions through entity-specific amendment directions, namely: **commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies, and housing finance companies**. The press release does not set out the substantive final rules yet; rather, it announces that these revised drafts have been published and remain open for comment.  

**Comments/feedback must be submitted on or before May 31, 2026.** Regulated entities and other stakeholders may file comments either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website using the hyperlink for each document, or by **email** with the subject line formatted as **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))”**.  

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that RBI is signaling a potential change in how recovery practices and recovery-agent engagement will be regulated, and that the revised drafts may affect debt-recovery procedures, borrower-device restrictions, and related conduct controls once finalized. Organizations in any of the covered entity categories should review the revised drafts promptly and determine whether their current loan-recovery, collections, outsourcing, and technology-enabled recovery practices would need policy, process, legal, customer-notice, or governance updates.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government owned NBFCs in NBFC-UL
rows.desc: April 10, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government owned NBFCs in NBFC-UL The Reserve Bank has issued today the following draft Amendment Directions relating to review of methodology for identification of NBFCs in Upper Layer (NBFC- UL), inclusion of Government owned NBFCs as NBFC-UL and other related aspects. (i) The draft ‘Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Second Amendment Directions, 2026’; and (ii) The draft ‘Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Third Amendment Directions, 2026’ 2. The feedback / comments on the draft Amendment Directions are invited from the NBFCs, members of public and all other relevant stakeholders till May 04, 2026. The feedback / comments may be submitted through the link under the ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ Section available on RBI’s website or may alternatively be forwarded to: Chief General Manager - in - Charge Department of Regulation (SIG-NBFCs) Reserve Bank of India 12 th Floor, Central Office Building Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001 Or by email With the subject line ‘Feedback on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government NBFCs in NBFC-UL’. Background and Objective The Scale Based Regulatory (SBR) Framework for NBFCs prescribes a two- pronged methodology for identification of NBFC-UL viz., top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size and parametric scoring methodology. With a view to adopt a transparent, simple and absolute criteria for identification of NBFC-UL, it is proposed to replace the existing methodology with asset size criteria, which is currently proposed as ₹1,00,000 � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communica
rows.summary:
The RBI has released two draft amendment directions for public comment on changes to the framework for identifying NBFCs in the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) and for related concentration-risk rules: the draft **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Second Amendment Directions, 2026** and the draft **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Third Amendment Directions, 2026**. Comments are invited from **NBFCs, members of the public, and all other relevant stakeholders** by **May 04, 2026**; submissions can be made through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** facility, or sent to the RBI’s **Department of Regulation (SIG-NBFCs)** in Mumbai, or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on the draft Amendment Directions on review of methodology for identification of NBFC-UL and inclusion of Government NBFCs in NBFC-UL.”**

Substantively, the RBI proposes to **replace the current two-pronged NBFC-UL identification method** under the Scale Based Regulatory (SBR) framework—currently based on **the top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size plus a parametric scoring methodology**—with a **single asset-size threshold**. The draft says that threshold is **₹1,00,000 crore and above** (i.e., NBFCs with assets at or above that level would be identified for NBFC-UL consideration under the revised approach), making the framework more “transparent, simple and absolute.”

The RBI also proposes to change how **Government-owned NBFCs** are treated. Under the current SBR framework, such entities are placed in the **Base Layer or Middle Layer**, not the Upper Layer; the draft would instead allow **eligible Government-owned NBFCs** to be considered for inclusion in **NBFC-UL** on the revised criteria, reflecting an **ownership-neutral regulatory regime**. In addition, the RBI proposes to permit **all NBFC-ULs** to use **State Government guarantees as a credit risk transfer instrument without any limit**, but only **subject to specified conditions** in the amended concentration-risk framework.

rows.summary:
This circular from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSE/CML/2026/19 dated August 7, 2026) reminds all listed entities that they must strictly comply with the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, as amended, together with SEBI and stock exchange circulars and SEBI’s FAQs on handling Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI). It is framed as a best-practices/compliance reminder based on observations in certain cases, but it is clearly directed at listed companies and reinforces that their UPSI controls must be fully operational and aligned with the PIT Regulations.

The circular specifically requires listed companies to maintain a structured digital database documenting: the nature of the UPSI; the names and PANs, or any other identifier authorized by law, of the persons who shared the information; and the names and PANs, or other lawful identifiers, of the persons with whom the UPSI was shared. If UPSI is shared with a listed company, intermediary, or fiduciary, the database must also capture the names and identifiers of the individuals actually handling that information. Compliance teams should treat this as a recordkeeping obligation, not just an internal control suggestion.

The circular also says companies must diligently implement and periodically review internal policies designed to prevent UPSI leakage, ensuring those policies match the statutory and regulatory requirements under the PIT Regulations. In addition, listed companies must conduct periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries on the proper manner of handling UPSI, which implies an ongoing compliance and training obligation rather than a one-time exercise. Companies must also ensure that their Code of Conduct under the PIT Regulations is complied with and effectively operationalized in practice.

Finally, the circular advises listed entities to implement any other measures necessary to achieve the objectives of the PIT Regulations, meaning firms should assess whether additional governance, monitoring, escalation, or control mechanisms are needed beyond the expressly listed points. No monetary penalties, thresholds, or new filing deadlines are set out in this circular; the operative change is a heightened emphasis on robust documentation, periodic review, employee/fiduciary training, and practical enforcement of existing insider-trading controls.

rows.summary:
This NSE FAQ explains how listed entities must file and manage corporate action record dates under Regulation 42 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, and it makes clear that the exchange will recognize only a properly filed “Record Date,” not a cut-off date or book closure date. All listed entities may fix a record date for a corporate action under Regulation 42; for InvITs and REITs, the record date must be disclosed under the applicable SEBI regulations at least two working days before the record date, excluding both the date of intimation and the record date itself. The required filing path on NEAPS is specifically NEAPS > COMPLIANCE > Announcements > Corporate Action > Submission, and submissions through any other path will not be taken on record.

The FAQ emphasizes that simply selecting the “Record Date” radio button or uploading a PDF without expressly stating “Record Date” is not enough to satisfy Regulation 42, and any filing that refers only to a cut-off date or book closure date instead of a record date will be rejected and may attract an applicable fine. It also states that a record date does not need to be fixed for an AGM or EGM because the exchange does not treat those meetings as a corporate action for this purpose. If the company needs to change or cancel a previously intimated record date, it may do so only through the same NEAPS path and only if the revised or cancellation submission is made at least two working days before the previously intimated record date; otherwise the change will not be taken on record. The revised intimation must still comply with Regulation 42.

The FAQ also clarifies that the record date under Regulation 42(2) cannot be the same date as the board meeting scheduled to decide the corporate action under Regulation 42(1). Instead, there must be a minimum gap of three working days after board approval or shareholder approval, as applicable, before the record date. For capital reduction, schemes, restructuring, and similar actions, the excerpt indicates that a record date cannot be intimated with only three days’ prior notice, signaling that a longer notice period is required, though the excerpt cuts off before giving the exact minimum period. Overall, the compliance obligation is to file the record date only in the prescribed NEAPS workflow, use the term “Record Date” explicitly, respect the timing rules tied to approval dates and prior intimations, and avoid relying on cut-off/book-closure terminology because such filings may be rejected and penalized.

rows.summary:
This NSE circular (Ref. No. NSE/CML/2026/16, dated June 12, 2026) is a guidance notice to **all listed entities** on the submission of the **Quarterly Integrated Filing – Governance** (formerly the Corporate Governance Report) through the **XBRL utility**. It does not change the underlying law or SEBI/Exchange requirements, but it provides FAQs to help companies file correctly and instructs listed entities to take note and comply accordingly. The circular expressly says the FAQs are for **guidance only** and are **not a substitute for the applicable law, SEBI regulations, or Exchange circulars**.

The filing deadline confirmed in the FAQs is **within 30 days from the end of each quarter**, in line with **Regulation 27(2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. A newly listed entity must begin submitting the Integrated Filing – Governance **from the quarter ending immediately after the date of listing**. The circular also reiterates the basic disclosure standards under Regulation 4: listed entities must provide **adequate and timely information** to the stock exchange(s) and investors, ensure filings are **adequate, accurate, explicit, timely, and in simple language**, and make sure event-based and periodic filings contain **relevant information**.

A key applicability point is the treatment of **SME-listed entities**: under **Regulation 280 of the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018**, as amended on **March 8, 2025**, if a listed SME’s **post-issue paid-up capital exceeds ₹25 crore**, it must comply with the corporate governance provisions under SEBI (LODR), including submission of the **Integrated Filing – Governance Report**. The FAQ also restates the continued-applicability rule under **Regulation 15 of SEBI (LODR)**: once corporate governance provisions in **Regulations 17 to 27**, certain clauses of **Regulation 46(2)**, and **Paras C, D, and E of Schedule V** become applicable, they continue to apply until the entity’s **equity share capital and net worth** both fall below the prescribed thresholds and remain below them for **three consecutive financial years**, even if the entity later falls out of the relevant ranking/category.

For entities that newly enter the **Top 1000/Top 2000 by average market capitalization**, the corporate governance obligations do not begin immediately; they become effective **after three months from December 31 (i.e., April 1) or from the beginning of the immediately next financial year, whichever is later**. The FAQ includes an illustration showing that depending on the quarter in which the entity first enters the Top 1000/2000, the effective date can be **April 1, July 1, October 1, or April 1** (for a December 31 trigger). In the board-composition section, the FAQ specifies that if a director does **not have a DIN**, the company must enter the **dummy DIN “99999999”** and explain the reason in the **remarks** column; the document begins the next FAQ on PAN but the provided excerpt cuts off before the answer.

Attention is invited to the provisions relating to Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (“PPIRP”) under Chapter III-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”). In this regard, as advised by SEBI, it is clarified that, the exemptions available under various SEBI Regulations in respect of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 31 of the IBC are not available in case of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 54L of the IBC under the PPIRP framework. The listed companies are advised to take note of the above and ensure compliance of the same. For and on behalf of National Stock Exchange of India Limited Yukti Sharma Head - Listing
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India’s circular dated **June 1, 2026** clarifies how **Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)** cases under **Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)** are to be treated for SEBI compliance purposes. The key change is that the **regulatory exemptions that are available for a resolution plan approved under Section 31 of the IBC do not apply** when a resolution plan is approved under **Section 54L** in a PPIRP proceeding.

As a result, any **listed entity undergoing PPIRP** must continue to follow **all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements under the relevant SEBI regulations**; the circular does not create a carve-out or relaxation for PPIRP-approved plans. In practical terms, companies in PPIRP should assume they remain fully subject to the ordinary SEBI-regulated compliance process for resolution plans and should not rely on the exemptions tied specifically to Section 31 approvals.

The circular is addressed to **all listed companies**, so it is relevant to any listed issuer that may enter PPIRP. There are **no numerical thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines** stated in the circular; the operative requirement is immediate awareness and full compliance with the applicable SEBI framework for PPIRP cases. Compliance teams should therefore review any current or contemplated PPIRP matter to ensure the company does not incorrectly apply Section 31-based exemptions and instead satisfies the full set of procedural and regulatory obligations under SEBI regulations.

Accordingly, all listed companies, REITs and InvITs are required to submit the aforesaid disclosure only in XBRL format through the revised process as detailed below: To download XBRL utility: NEAPS  Compliance  Download XBRL Utilities For Submission of disclosures: NEAPS  Compliance  Common XBRL Upload  Prohibition of Insider Trading Please note that previously filed disclosures shall continue to be available at the following link: https://www.nseindia.com/companies-listing/corporate-filings-insider-trading-archive-data Further, with reference to Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2026/11 dated May 04, 2026, the said utility will also be available for Single Filing system through API-based integration. rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India has discontinued the old NEAPS filing route for disclosures under Regulation 7(2) and Regulation 7(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, which had been filed under **NEAPS → Compliance → Disclosures → Insider Trading**. Going forward, **all listed companies, REITs, and InvITs must file these disclosures only in XBRL format** using the new utility and revised submission path.

To comply, entities must first download the XBRL utility from **NEAPS → Compliance → Download XBRL Utilities**, and then submit disclosures through **NEAPS → Compliance → Common XBRL Upload → Prohibition of Insider Trading**. The circular does not specify a new substantive disclosure deadline or change the underlying regulatory timing under Regulations 7(2) and 7(3); rather, it changes the **filing format and submission mechanism** and makes the prior filing route unavailable.

The circular also states that previously filed disclosures remain accessible in the NSE archive at **https://www.nseindia.com/companies-listing/corporate-filings-insider-trading-archive-data**. In addition, referencing **Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2026/11 dated May 04, 2026**, NSE notes that the same utility will be available for **Single Filing system submission via API-based integration**, which is relevant for entities using automated filing processes. The circular is effective immediately upon issuance on **May 04, 2026**, and listed entities are instructed to ensure compliance with the new XBRL-only process.

The main change is that the system is being **extended to cover additional XBRL and non-confidential filings**, so listed entities can submit the relevant disclosure once and have it routed through the integrated exchange mechanism. For **XBRL filings**, the single filing/API-based utility is now available for the following disclosures, with the stated effective dates: **Outcome of Board Meeting for dividend, buyback, bonus, and voluntary delisting events** under **Regulation 30 / Schedule III para A part A sub-para 4** effective **April 25, 2026**; **Annual Report – XBRL** under **Regulation 34** effective **April 20, 2026**; **Initiation of forensic audit** under **Regulation 30 / Schedule III para A part A sub-para 17** effective **May 05, 2026**; and **Prohibition of Insider Trading disclosures** under **Regulation 7(2) and 7(3) of the SEBI PIT Regulations, 2015** effective **May 05, 2026**. The XBRL table indicates applicability for **only equity**, **equity + debt**, and, for the PIT disclosure, also **REITs and INVITs**; the table uses check marks to show which entity types are covered, so compliance teams should verify whether their listed entity falls within the applicable columns before relying on the API route.

For **non-confidential filings**, the circular states that the utility now covers a broader set of regulatory disclosures for **only equity** and **equity + debt** listed entities, including: **acquisition/amalgamation/merger/demerger/sale/disposal/other restructuring** under **Regulation 30 / Schedule III para A part A sub-para 1**; **changes in directors, KMPs, senior management, auditor, compliance officer, registrar and share transfer agent** under **Regulation 30 / Schedule III sub-para 7 and 8**; **resignations of statutory auditors** under **sub-para 7A**; **resignation of independent directors, directors, KMPs, SMPs, and compliance officers** under **sub-para 7B and 7C**; **Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report** under **Regulation 34(2)(f)** effective **March 31, 2026**; **prior intimation for board meeting** under **Regulation 29** effective **March 07, 2026**; **closure of trading window** under the **SEBI PIT Regulations**; **fraud/default/arrest** under **Regulation 30 / Schedule III sub-para 6** effective **February 21, 2026**; **corporate debt restructuring** under **Regulation 30 / Schedule III sub-para 9 and 10**; **resolution plans/restructuring relating to bank/FI loans and borrowings and one-time settlement (OTS)**; and **Issue Summary Document (ISD) for buyback via open and tender route** under the SEBI circular on ISD and issue advertisements. The utility also covers **Integrated Filing – Financials** under **Regulation 23(9), Regulation 30 read with Section V-B of the Master Circular, Regulation 32(1), and Regulation 33(3)** effective **January 03, 2026**, **Annual Secretarial Compliance Report** under **Regulation 24A(2)** effective **September 15, 2025**, and **Integrated Filing (Governance)** under **Regulations 13(3), 27(2), and 30** effective **March 01, 2025**; the circular notes that for some of these integrated filing items the applicability for **exclusively debt** entities and **REITs/INVITs** will be **communicated later**.

A specific procedural clarification is included for resignation-related filings: the utility **provides an option to submit the resignation details and the resignation letter(s)** as required under **sub-paras 7A, 7B and 7C of Schedule III, Part A, Para A**, so companies should ensure those supporting documents are attached when using the single-filing route. The circular does not change the underlying disclosure obligations under SEBI regulations; instead, it changes the **filing method** by expanding the set of events that can be submitted through the API-based single filing system. Compliance teams should therefore update filing workflows, confirm the entity-type applicability for each event, and use the new single-filing route from the relevant effective dates onward.

rows.title: XBRL based filing for Violations related to Code of Conduct (CoC) under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/13 Date: May 04, 2026 To, The Company Secretary, All Listed Entities/Intermediaries/Fiduciaries Subject: XBRL based filing for Violations related to Code of Conduct (CoC) under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 SEBI vide Circular No. SEBI/HO/ISD/ISD/CIR/P/2020/135 dated July 23, 2020, prescribed the format for reporting violations of the Code of Conduct under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. To enhance accuracy and efficiency in disclosures, the Exchange has introduced an XBRL utility for reporting such violations through NEAPS with effect from May 05, 2026. All Listed Companies/Intermediaries/Fiduciaries shall submit the reporting through the following paths: To download XBRL utility: NEAPS  Compliance  Download XBRL Utilities For Submissions: NEAPS  Compliance  Common XBRL Upload  Violation of Code of Conduct under SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 It may be noted that reporting by listed entities shall be made only in XBRL mode without submission of any PDF. Further, any unlisted entity reporting in the capacity of Intermediary or Fiduciary shall continue to submit the disclosures through email at pit_coc@nse.co.in, as per Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2020/44 dated August 26, 2020. The disclosure pertaining to violations of the Code of Conduct shall not be disseminated on the Exchange website. All listed entities are advised to mandatorily submit the reporting through NEAPS only. Submission through any other mode shall not be taken on record and shall be considered invalid. Listed entities, Intermediaries and Fiduciaries are advised to take note of the above and comply accordingly. Yours faithfully, For National Stock Exchange of India Limited Harshad Dharod Chief Manager-Listing Compliance
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) has introduced a new **XBRL-based filing process** for reporting **violations of the Code of Conduct (CoC)** under the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**, replacing the prior non-XBRL reporting approach for listed entities. This change is intended to improve the accuracy and efficiency of disclosures and becomes **effective from May 5, 2026**.

For **all listed companies, intermediaries, and fiduciaries**, the filing must be handled through **NEAPS**. The circular specifies the workflow: users should download the XBRL utility via **NEAPS → Compliance → Download XBRL Utilities**, and submit filings via **NEAPS → Compliance → Common XBRL Upload → Violation of Code of Conduct under SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015**. For **listed entities**, reporting must be made **only in XBRL mode** and **no PDF submission is permitted**; any submission through another mode will **not be taken on record and will be treated as invalid**.

The circular also preserves the existing treatment for **unlisted entities acting as intermediaries or fiduciaries**: they must continue to submit disclosures **by email to pit_coc@nse.co.in**, in line with **NSE Circular No. NSE/CML/2020/44 dated August 26, 2020**. In addition, the disclosure relating to CoC violations **will not be disseminated on the Exchange website**. Compliance teams should ensure that listed entities switch to the NEAPS XBRL-only process immediately from the effective date and that any non-listed intermediary/fiduciary reporting remains on the email route.

rows.summary:
NSE has updated its “single filing system” through API-based integration between stock exchanges, originally introduced under Circular NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024. Effective March 07, 2026, the single-filing mechanism is expanded to cover additional XBRL filings for specified disclosures, but only to the extent expressly listed in the circular and only for the listed entity categories shown in the table.

For **equity-listed entities** and **equity + debt listed entities**, the new single-filing coverage now includes XBRL submissions for: prior intimation of board meeting under Regulation 29 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015; closure of trading window under the SEBI PIT Regulations; fraud/default/arrest disclosures under Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR and sub-para 6 of Part A of Schedule III; corporate debt restructuring disclosures under Regulation 30 and sub-para 9 and 10 of Part A of Schedule III; resolution plans/restructuring related to bank/financial institution borrowings, inter-creditors agreements, and one-time settlement (OTS); issue summary document (ISD) for buyback via open and tender route; integrated filing–financials under Regulations 23(9), 30 read with Section V-B of the Master Circular, and Regulations 32(1) and 33(3) (effective January 03, 2026); annual secretarial compliance report under Regulation 24A(2) (effective September 15, 2025); integrated filing–governance under Regulations 13(3), 27(2), and 30 (effective March 01, 2025); meetings of shareholders and voting results under Regulation 44(3) (effective December 28, 2024); reconciliation of share capital audit report under Regulation 76 (effective November 15, 2024); corporate governance report under Regulation 27(2) (effective October 26, 2024), which has been merged into Integrated Filing–Governance pursuant to the SEBI circular dated December 31, 2024; and investor grievance report under Regulation 13(3) (effective October 01, 2024).  

The circular makes an important limitation clear: **for Regulation 29, Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR, and trading window disclosures, listed entities must continue filing PDF submissions at both exchanges and these are not yet covered by single filing except for the XBRL events specifically listed in the table**. Likewise, for all other Regulation 29 and Regulation 30 events not included in the table, entities must continue to make submissions separately on all exchanges, in PDF and XBRL where applicable. NSE also instructs listed entities to avoid duplicate filings of the same disclosure on both exchanges, because the objective is to move toward a true single-filing process. If an exchange later asks for clarification after submission, the listed entity must respond only to the exchange that requested it.  

In practical compliance terms, affected listed entities should update their disclosure workflows from March 07, 2026 to route the newly covered XBRL filings through the single-filing/API process for the exact events identified above, while continuing legacy dual filing where the circular expressly says single filing does not yet apply. Questions are to be directed through NEAPS at **NEAPS > Help > Contact Us > Listing Compliance** or by email to **takeover@nse.co.in**.

rows.title: Seeking of comments / feedback on the XBRL being introduced for filing Qualified Institutional Placements (“QIP”)  applications with the Exchange.
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: LISTING Circular Ref. BACKGROUND: Listed entities are required to seek approval from the Stock Exchange(s) for issuance of securities through “QIP” as laid down in SEBI LODR Regulations, 2015 and SEBI ICDR Regulation 2018 and various applicable relevant provisions, circulars, guidance note, etc. as amended from time to time. . Accordingly, companies are required to submit applications for in-principle approval, post-allotment approval, and trading approval to the Stock Exchange(s). Over a period of time, Stock Exchanges, in a phased manner, have undertaken initiatives to migrate filings made under the SEBI Act, Regulations and circulars from document-based formats to XBRL- based reporting, with an objective to standardize securities market data and enhance regulatory efficiency. It has been deliberated that implementation of an XBRL-based filing mechanism for QIP applications covering “In-Principle approval and Post-Allotment Listing Approval” which would enable submission of standardised, consistent, and homogeneous compliance data to ease the filing process for listed entities as well as facilitate efficient data analysis and monitoring by the Stock Exchange. Accordingly, in this regard, filing of QIP-related information would require listed entities to file the aforesaid applications in XBRL exclusively, formats of which are made ava
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India Limited is seeking comments on a proposed move to **XBRL-only filing** for certain **Qualified Institutional Placement (QIP)** applications, replacing the current **application-based process** where companies manually enter data and upload PDFs. The change is aimed at standardizing securities-market data and improving regulatory efficiency, and it would apply to listed entities seeking **QIP approvals** under the SEBI LODR Regulations, 2015 and SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, specifically for **in-principle approval** and **post-allotment listing approval** (the circular also references trading approval in the background, though the proposed XBRL framework described is for in-principle and post-allotment filings).

The circular does not immediately impose a final compliance obligation; rather, it **invites listed entities to comment, suggest additions, or propose modifications** to the draft XBRL fields and format. Comments must be emailed to **DL-FI@nse.co.in** **no later than February 11, 2026**, and the email subject must read **“Comments / Feedback on the XBRL being introduced QIP applications with the Exchange.”** The reply format requested by NSE includes the **name of entity/person, contact number and email address, event name (“XBRL filing for QIP”), the field/heading, comments/suggestions, and detailed rationale**.

The draft Annexure A shows the substantive data points that would have to be captured in XBRL for **Qualified Institutions Placement XBRL for Regulation 28(1) – In Principle Approval (Pre Allotment)**. For the issue details, the filing would require disclosure of the **symbol/BSE code/MSEI symbol**, the **exchange(s) where the issuer is listed** (NSE/BSE/MSEI/others, with the specific exchange required if “others” is chosen), the **board resolution date approving the specified securities issue**, the **date of notice to shareholders**, the **date of shareholders’ approval for QIBs**, the **type of security** (dropdown options: **Equity, Non-Convertible Debt and Warrants, Convertible Securities, Units**), the **number of securities and/or amount in INR crores**, the **lead manager**, and the **objects of the issue**. The draft specifies that **either the number of securities or the issue amount must be mandatory**, and the number-of-securities field changes based on the security type selected: for **Equity**, one row for “No. of Equity Securities”; for **Non-Convertible Debt and Warrants**, separate rows for “No. of Non-Convertible Debt Securities” and “No. of Warrants”; for **Convertible Securities**, one row for “No. of Convertible Securities”; and for **Units**, one row for “No. of Units.”

The draft objects-of-issue table indicates the system will require categorization of proceeds by stated purposes such as **capital expenditure, repayment of loan, conversion of loan, working capital requirement, acquisition of the entity, unidentified acquisition, investment in subsidiary/associates/others, and augmentation of capital base of the company**. Overall, the compliance impact for listed entities is that QIP-related approvals would move from narrative/PDF-based submissions to a **structured electronic XBRL data submission**, with the expectation of standardized field-level disclosure once the framework is implemented after this consultation.
