rows.summary:
IRDAI has amended its Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, 2024 with **immediate effect** through Circular Ref. **IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/72/5/2026 dated 25.05.2026**. The changes apply to insurers governed by the **IRDAI (Corporate Governance for Insurers) Regulations, 2024** and specifically affect how insurers structure, assess, and disclose remuneration for **Key Management Persons (KMPs)**, including the **MD & CEO, other directors, and KMPs**.

The circular first expands the disclosure requirements in **Clause 8.1** so that insurers must disclose the **parameters that form the basis of remuneration packages (including incentives) for the MD & CEO, all other directors and KMPs**, and must also disclose **payments made to group entities and related parties**. It then inserts a new **Clause 8.3** requiring insurers to publish on their website, in an **“easy to access” and “easy to understand”** format, the insurer’s performance against the parameters used for KMP remuneration, together with the **corresponding information for the preceding three years**. This website disclosure must be made without collecting personal details of visitors, including a telephone number, and is intended to support informed decision-making by the public and policyholders.

For **year-to-date (YTD)** disclosure under Clause 8.3, the circular requires **quarterly disclosure** of **financial soundness** information and **monthly disclosure** of **product performance, claim responsiveness, grievance redressal, and improvements in these areas**. The circular also revises **Clause 9.2(b)** to require the insurer’s **Nomination and Remuneration Committee**, in consultation with the **Risk Management Committee**, to adopt a coordinated and integrated approach to remuneration policy, and to ensure that remuneration is **aligned to policyholder outcomes**, **adjusted for all types of risk**, **symmetric with risk outcomes**, **sensitive to the time horizon of the risk**, and that the **cash/equity mix** is consistent with risk alignment.

Most substantively, for **FY 2026–27** the circular mandates that insurers must consider a defined set of **minimum performance parameters** when determining **variable pay or incentives for all KMPs**, and these same parameters must also be used for the disclosures required under Clause 8.3. The specified parameters begin with **overall financial soundness and improvements thereof**; for **life insurers**, the listed measures include **Assets under Management / Total Premium**, **Renewal Premium / New Business Premium**, and a third measure tied to the proportion of policy persistency/retention as set out in the circular; for **general insurers**, the circular includes measures relating to the insurer’s operating and claims performance (the text references multiple sub-metrics and ratios to be assessed). The circular also provides the disclosure format logic for these measures over the prior years and current YTD periods, and it indicates that **50%** is a relevant threshold in one of the remuneration/disclosure conditions tied to the amended **Clause 9.2(d)(v) and (vi)**. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as an immediate governance and disclosure update: remuneration policies, committee processes, website disclosures, and FY 2026–27 variable pay assessment frameworks all need to be aligned to the amended master circular.

rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the transitional fee and registration regime for **Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs)** following the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 (SBSR Act)**, and it is issued as a continuation of IRDAI Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026**. It applies to **all SLAs** and explains that, with effect from **5 February 2026**, the earlier **licensing model** for SLAs (which had a **three-year validity period** and renewal requirements) has been replaced by a **registration-based framework** under amended **Section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938**. Under this new framework, SLAs will receive a **Certificate of Registration (CoR)**, and the registration will remain in force subject to payment of an **annual fee** as prescribed by the amended law and upcoming regulations; the CoR will be available for download through the **BAP portal**.

For the transitional period, if an application for **new registration or renewal** is approved between **5 February 2026 and 30 June 2026**, the applicant must pay an **interim annual fee before the CoR is issued**. The fee is **₹400 plus 18% GST (₹72) = ₹472 total** for an **individual SLA**, and **₹2,000 plus 18% GST (₹360) = ₹2,360 total** for a **corporate SLA**. For applications approved on or after **5 February 2026** where some fee has already been paid, that amount must be **adjusted against the interim annual fee** to the extent applicable, and any remaining balance will be handled under the regulations yet to be notified.

The circular also distinguishes between **lapsed license revival** cases filed before and after the cut-off date. Applications to revive lapsed licenses submitted **on or before 4 February 2026** will continue to be processed under the **IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015**, whereas revival applications submitted **on or after 5 February 2026** will be treated as **applications for new registration**, which means the applicant may have to meet **examination and training requirements** again. Operationally, IRDAI says the requirement to submit **all categories of applications**—including **new, renewal, modification, and related requests**—through the **BAP portal** will continue until further notice. The circular emphasizes that these arrangements are **interim and transitional only**, pending the final regulations to be issued under the amended legal framework.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued by IRDAI on 1 April 2026 under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938 and Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999 read with Regulations 7 and 8 of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, provides implementation clarifications for Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) for insurers. The underlying regulatory amendments that enable Ind AS for insurers take effect from 1 April 2026, and the purpose of the circular is to standardize how insurers should apply the new framework and meet related reporting and governance expectations.

For financial reporting, insurers must prepare financial statements under Ind AS in accordance with Schedule IIA of the Regulations, and those statements become the basis of financial reporting. At the same time, insurers must continue parallel reporting of both Financial Statements and Financial Information for two years from the implementation date, unless the Competent Authority specifies a different period. Financial Information must be prepared under Schedule II, and both Financial Statements and Financial Information must be prepared and filed quarterly, with both sets of disclosures also posted on the insurer’s website.

The circular also specifies assurance requirements: the Financial Statements for the first three quarters are subject to limited review under the applicable ICAI Standards on Review Engagements, while annual Financial Statements must be audited under the Insurance Act, 1938 and Companies Act, 2013. Financial Information for all four quarters is also subject to limited review under the ICAI review standards. In addition, insurers must include an appropriate reconciliation between the Financial Statements and the Financial Information as required by Ind AS 101, so compliance teams should expect and plan for a formal bridging/reconciliation process in the reported packs.

For the transition year 2026–27, the first-three-quarter Financial Statements and Financial Information must be submitted within three months from the end of each respective quarter. A specific carve-out is provided for listed insurers: the timing for disclosure of Financial Statements continues to follow SEBI norms instead of the three-month submission timeline. This means listed insurers need to align Ind AS reporting calendars with applicable securities law disclosure deadlines as well as IRDAI requirements.

The circular also creates a forbearance process for insurers seeking a one-year deferral in preparing Ind AS financial statements. Any insurer seeking this forbearance must apply to IRDAI on or before 30 April 2026 and must attach a Board-approved action plan. The application must include a detailed implementation roadmap with monthly milestones, timelines for system and data readiness, and the preparedness status of the actuarial and finance functions, indicating that IRDAI expects a documented, board-backed transition plan rather than a generic request. The excerpt provided cuts off mid-sentence after this roadmap requirement, so there may be additional details later in the document, but the material obligations visible here are the transition to Ind AS from 1 April 2026, parallel reporting for two years, quarterly filing and website disclosure, limited review/audit requirements, reconciliation under Ind AS 101, the special 2026–27 submission timeline, and the 30 April 2026 deadline for forbearance applications.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued Circular No. IRDAI/PP&GR/CIR/MISC/02/01/2026 dated 6 January 2026 to all insurers and insurance intermediaries, directing immediate preparation for compliance with TRAI’s mandatory 1600-series adoption requirement for customer-facing voice communications. The circular explains that TRAI’s Direction dated 16 December 2025, issued under section 13 read with section 11(1)(b)(i) and (v) of the TRAI Act, 1997, requires all IRDAI-regulated entities to use the 1600-series for all service and transactional voice calls made to consumers, with the stated objectives of reducing unsolicited commercial communication (UCC), preventing impersonation-based fraud, and improving consumer trust.

The key compliance deadline is 15 February 2026, by which insurers and insurance intermediaries must complete adoption of the 1600-series for all service and transactional voice calls. After that date, no service or transactional voice calls may be initiated from any number other than numbers allocated under the 1600-series, even where the customer has given explicit or implied consent. This means consent does not provide an exception to the numbering requirement once the deadline passes.

The circular also warns that any UCC complaint against an entity that does not comply may trigger action under the TRAI regulatory framework applicable to unregistered telemarketers, in addition to whatever further action the Authority may deem appropriate. In other words, non-compliance may create both TRAI-related exposure and separate supervisory consequences from IRDAI.

Operationally, insurers and intermediaries are instructed to coordinate with their Telecom Service Providers for timely allocation, activation, and operationalization of 1600-series numbers. They must also submit the status reports required by TRAI on a timely basis and send a copy of those reports to IRDAI. The circular references an Annexure containing contact details of the nodal officers of the access providers to support implementation, and the overall instruction is to ensure strict compliance.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **19 December 2025** and addressed to **all insurers and reinsurers**, expands the set of permissible fixed-income investments for insurers by allowing investment in securities issued by **RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**. Specifically, insurers are now permitted to invest in **(i) AT1 bonds** and **(ii) debt capital instruments and preference share capital instruments forming Tier 2 capital**, with the explicit exception of **Perpetual Cumulative Preference Shares**. The circular states that this change is intended to broaden insurers’ investment options and support portfolio diversification.

The permission applies to instruments issued by AIFIs that are regulated by the RBI, which began issuing **Additional Tier 1 Bonds and Tier 2 capital instruments from 1 April 2024** under the Basel III prudential framework. IRDAI is not creating a new investment regime from scratch; instead, it requires insurers to follow the **same investment provisions that already apply to insurer investments in banks**, specifically the rules in **paragraphs 1.6(b) and 1.6(d) of Chapter 3 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17 May 2024**. In other words, the existing bank-investment compliance framework is to be used as the operational benchmark for these AIFI investments.

For compliance and reporting purposes, insurers must also use the **existing category codes used for investments in the corresponding instruments of PSU banks** when booking these AIFI holdings. The circular is issued under **clause 12(6) of Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal regulatory instruction rather than guidance. No separate implementation deadline is specified beyond the circular date, so the effective position is that insurers may apply this permission immediately, subject to the existing bank-investment limits and requirements referenced above.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has announced that it is ending the long-standing practice of permitting an individual Surveyor/Loss Assessor (SLA) to add an additional line of business (LOB) to a surveyor licence merely on the basis of the categorization letter issued in 2001–02. The circular explains that, under the earlier categorization exercise, individual SLAs who held valid licences before the 2000 Licensing/Professional Requirements/Code of Conduct Regulations were categorized across multiple departments/LOBs, and they were originally allowed only 3 LOBs on their licence from that categorized list. Then, by Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020, IRDAI had allowed additions to an individual SLA’s licence based on that old categorization letter if the person had the relevant educational qualification and had continuously renewed the licence without break, and it also removed the earlier cap on the number of LOBs.

IRDAI says it is now receiving modification applications from SLAs seeking to add LOBs even though they have not done any survey work in that LOB since 2002, and it considers pre-2001/02 experience and knowledge in those areas to be obsolete because of technological change over the last 23 years. To ensure fair assessment of insured losses, IRDAI has decided to stop this practice entirely. As a result, Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020 is repealed with immediate effect, meaning applications relying on the 2001–02 categorization letter as the basis for adding LOBs should no longer be entertained under that route.

Going forward, an individual surveyor may still be eligible for any LOB on the surveyor licence, but only if the person meets the eligibility criteria under Regulation 3 of the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015, as amended. In addition, to add an LOB, the individual SLA must now comply with the Proviso under Regulation 27 of the same 2015 Regulations, as amended from time to time. The notice is effective immediately and was issued with the approval of the Competent Authority.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 14 August 2025, launches **Quantitative Impact Study-2 (QIS 2)** for the proposed **Risk Based Capital (RBC)** framework for the Indian insurance sector. It follows the first quantitative impact study conducted in 2023 and is intended to refine the RBC framework based on the results and insurer feedback from that earlier exercise.

The circular applies broadly to **all life insurers, general insurers, standalone health insurers, reinsurers, branches of foreign reinsurers, and Lloyd’s India**. Insurers are required to perform QIS 2 using the **Technical Guidance document**, with the **data used for actuarial valuation as of 31 March 2025**. IRDAI states that the technical guidance, data submission template, result submission requirements, submission mode, and any supplementary information will be communicated separately.

The key compliance deadline is that **QIS 2 results must be submitted on or before 15 October 2025**. IRDAI emphasizes that this exercise is **only for QIS 2** and should **not** be treated as a final or binding indication of IRDAI’s ultimate RBC framework; it is an additional study to support the transition toward an RBC regime. Insurers must also continue to meet all existing regulatory filing obligations under the current regulatory regime, with no suspension or replacement of ordinary returns by virtue of this exercise.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular on Rural, Social Sector and Motor Third Party Obligations, 2025 is issued by IRDAI under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999, and Regulation 9 of the 2024 Rural, Social Sector and Motor Third Party Obligations Regulations. It applies to all life insurers, general insurers, and stand-alone health insurers, and it governs obligations for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27; the earlier 2024 Master Circular applies only to FY 2024-25. The circular also defines the relevant insurer categories: “General Insurer–1” excludes stand-alone health insurers, AIC, and ECGC, while “General Insurer–2” includes general insurers and stand-alone health insurers other than AIC and ECGC; “base data” is the number of lives in the relevant Gram Panchayat for life and General Insurer–2 obligations, and the number of dwellings, shops, and motor vehicles in the Gram Panchayat for General Insurer–1 obligations.

For rural sector obligations, life insurers must cover the minimum specified percentage of lives under individual and/or group policies in allocated Gram Panchayats, while the circular separately prescribes obligations for general insurers based on dwelling/shops and motor vehicles, and on lives for General Insurer–2. The detailed compliance targets increase materially from FY 2025-26 to FY 2026-27: where the document specifies 25,000/50,000 and percentage bands, the applicable obligation levels rise from 15% in FY 2025-26 to 25% in FY 2026-27 for one component and to 10% for another component, with separate treatment for the insurer categories referenced in the circular. For social sector obligations, the circular requires coverage of specified beneficiary groups and sets higher numeric targets for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 than in the prior year, including thresholds of 10% and 12% in the relevant provision.

The motor third-party liability section requires compliance with the obligations prescribed in Regulation 4(1) and Regulation 5, with the circular reiterating the rates and procedural requirements for underwriting motor third-party business. In the life insurance “base data” allocation rules, insurers must use the base data figures communicated for the relevant Gram Panchayats and comply with the allocation process laid down by the respective councils. The circular also requires insurers to submit the specified statements and returns in the prescribed formats and timelines, including annual/periodic reporting tied to the FY 2025-26 compliance cycle, with at least one submission deadline expressly stated as 30 June 2025 for the 2024-25 reporting reference data.

Where an insurer cannot comply with an allocated rural-sector requirement, the circular requires the insurer to document the reasons and follow the prescribed allocation/transfer process through the councils, rather than simply ignoring the obligation. It also sets out compliance mechanics for reassignment and reconciliation of obligations between insurers, including the use of the prescribed annexures/forms, and provides that the Authority may require additional information or reporting to monitor compliance. Overall, the document is a binding operational compliance framework for insurers’ rural, social sector, and motor third-party obligations, with specific year-by-year thresholds, insurer classification rules, allocated-area compliance, and mandatory reporting/recordkeeping requirements.

A compliance team should therefore treat this as a formal directive that updates the prior 2023 framework and requires immediate review of the annexed standards against current controls, governance, incident-response, and security policies to confirm alignment for the current financial year.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular replaces the earlier 17 October 2022 guidelines on the establishment and closure of liaison offices in India by insurers registered outside India, and the amended guidance is effective from the date of issue, 11 February 2026. A “liaison office” is defined as an office that acts only as a communication channel between the overseas insurer’s head/principal office and entities in India; it must not undertake any commercial, trading, soliciting, industrial, or similar business activity, directly or indirectly, and it must be funded only through foreign remittances received from the overseas insurer through normal banking channels.  

For eligibility to open a liaison office, the overseas insurer must have a financially sound track record, including profits in each of the immediately preceding three financial years in its home country and a minimum net worth of USD 65 million. Net worth is defined as paid-up capital plus free reserves, less intangible assets, based on the latest audited balance sheet or an equivalent certified account statement from the home-country accounting professional. IRDAI may relax the net-worth threshold in exceptional cases for a foreign state-owned enterprise/reinsurer with strong credit ratings or proven expertise/specialized insurer status, where there is bilateral trade significance and market-development potential.  

The application must be made to IRDAI in Form IRDAI-FIC-1 (Annexure I) with supporting documents, and a non-refundable processing fee of USD 6,000 must be paid by demand draft, pay order, or online transfer in favor of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. The document also indicates that the liaison office is expected to have a defined five-year tenure with possible extension for an additional 3+3 years, and that the office must continue to comply with the restrictions on activities and funding throughout its existence.  

The guidelines also cover closure and post-closure obligations, meaning the overseas insurer must follow the IRDAI-prescribed procedure for shutting down a liaison office and should expect documentary requirements and regulatory coordination before closure is completed. The updated framework supersedes all prior instructions on the subject, so any overseas insurer currently operating or proposing to operate a liaison office in India should review its structure, permitted activities, funding arrangements, eligibility status, and application/closure documentation against these amended requirements.

The IRDAI (Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework) Guidelines, 2025 were issued under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938 and Section 14(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999, and they apply to **all insurers and distribution channels** unless a provision specifically says otherwise. They become **effective on 1 April 2026**. Their stated objective is to create a comprehensive industry framework to **deter, prevent, detect, report, and remedy fraud**, with an emphasis on protecting policyholders, preserving financial stability, and maintaining public trust.

For compliance purposes, the document defines **“insurance fraud”** broadly as any act or omission intended to gain an advantage through dishonest or unlawful means, including **misappropriating funds**, **deliberately misrepresenting, concealing, or not disclosing material facts** relevant to any decision or transaction, and **abusing a position of trust or fiduciary relationship**. It also defines a **Red Flag Indicator (RFI)** as a possible warning sign that may indicate fraud and require further investigation, and **“cyber or new age fraud”** as fraud carried out using digital or new-age technologies. Distribution channels are given the meaning from the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders’ Interests and Allied Matters of Insurers) Regulations, 2024.

The Guidelines require every insurer to establish systems and processes across its functions to manage fraud and to classify/report frauds into five categories: **internal fraud** (involving employees or senior management), **distribution channel fraud**, **policyholder and/or claims fraud** (during purchase, servicing, or claims), **external fraud** (by external parties/service providers/vendors), and **affinity or complex fraud** (collusion among one or more perpetrators across categories). Insurers are also expressly required to adopt a **“zero tolerance”** stance toward fraud and maintain a fraud risk management framework tailored to their business profile so they can deter, prevent, detect, report, and remedy fraud effectively.

Governance responsibility is placed on the insurer’s **Risk Management Committee (RMC)**, which is to be responsible for effective oversight of the fraud risk management framework. Although the provided text cuts off before the detailed sub-requirements of the RMC and other operational controls, the document clearly signals that insurers must have formal processes, reporting structures, and remediation mechanisms in place before the **1 April 2026** commencement date to remain compliant.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has amended Clause 15(a) of the “Revised Guidelines on Insurance Repositories and Electronic Issuance of Insurance Policies” issued on 29 May 2015. The earlier requirement was that the insurance repository’s controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards be reviewed on a yearly basis by an external system audit firm approved by the Authority. That requirement has now been changed: the annual review must still occur at least once a year, but it must be conducted at the insurance repository’s own cost by an external auditor who is either a Certified Information System Auditor (CISA), a Chartered Accountant holding DISA (ICAI) qualification, or a CERT-IN certified expert.  

This change applies to insurance repositories and specifically to the Clause 14 controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards referenced in the guidelines. The amendment removes the prior framing of review by an “external system audit firm approved by the Authority” and replaces it with a narrower qualification-based requirement for the auditor. The circular takes effect immediately upon issuance, meaning compliance teams should treat the revised auditor qualification and cost-bearing obligation as already in force from 29 July 2025.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued new **“Guidelines on Hedging Through Equity Derivatives”** dated **28 February 2025** for **all life, general, and health insurers**. The circular explains that insurers were already permitted to use fixed-income derivatives (including **FRAs, IRS, and exchange-traded IRFs**) under earlier 2004/2014 guidance, and to use **CDS only as protection buyers** under a 2012 circular; because of increased insurer investment in equities and resulting price volatility, IRDAI is now permitting hedging through **equity derivatives** as well. The document states that the new framework is intended to manage equity-price risk and sets out specific limits, controls, governance requirements, reporting, and valuation treatment for any insurer that chooses to use these instruments.

The guidelines are effective immediately on issuance unless otherwise specified in the detailed requirements, and they apply to insurers engaging in equity-linked investment activity or seeking to hedge equity exposure using derivatives. Insurers must ensure that derivative use is for **hedging** and not for speculative trading, and they must put in place board-approved policies, internal limits, controls, and designated responsibilities for entering, monitoring, and settling such positions. The document also requires insurers to maintain records and reporting around derivative positions, underlying exposures, and hedge effectiveness, so compliance teams should expect documentation of the rationale for each hedge and ongoing evidence that the derivative remains linked to an underlying risk exposure.

The guidelines set quantitative constraints on the use of equity derivatives, including limits tied to the insurer’s equity exposure and additional conditions for acceptable hedge instruments and counterparties. The text indicates specific thresholds and formulas for measuring and validating the hedge, including references to a **20%** limit in one of the prescribed control conditions and a **15-day** period for certain actions/reporting requirements; it also refers to an equity-price band of **80–125** in the context of permissible conditions/valuation checks. The document further distinguishes between different derivative structures and indicates that insurers must use approved exchange-traded or otherwise permitted derivative mechanisms in line with the stated conditions, rather than entering unrestricted OTC-style positions.

The compliance obligations include determining and documenting the hedge relationship, calculating exposure and hedge size using the formulas provided in the guidelines, and monitoring whether the hedge remains within prescribed tolerance ranges. The document also requires periodic internal review and reporting of positions, the underlying equity holdings or exposures, and any changes in the hedge status, with particular attention to whether the derivative still qualifies as a hedge under the insurer’s risk-management framework. In practical terms, insurers will need to update investment policies, risk manuals, accounting/valuation procedures, and operational controls so that equity-derivative activity is only carried out within the IRDAI-prescribed limits and only by entities with the requisite governance and reporting infrastructure in place.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Bima Vahak) Guidelines, 2023 were issued on 9 October 2023 under section 14(2)(e) of the IRDAI Act, 1999, and they take effect from the date Bima Vistaar is launched (Bima Vistaar is described as a comprehensive insurance product to be issued later). The stated policy objective is to create a women-centric dedicated distribution channel to improve insurance awareness, inclusion, and access in every village/Gram Panchayat, while also building a local cadre of trusted personnel who understand local needs.

Under the guidelines, “Bima Vahak” can be either an individual or a corporate legal person registered under Indian law and engaged to provide services under these guidelines. Insurers may either engage a Corporate Bima Vahak and/or directly appoint Individual Bima Vahaks for solicitation of insurance business and for policy and claims servicing; the insurer remains fully responsible for all acts and conduct of the Bima Vahaks it engages. Corporate Bima Vahaks may appoint individuals as Bima Vahaks only under their insurer agreement terms and are responsible for their actions; they may solicit insurance products and facilitate policy/claims servicing only through their appointed Bima Vahaks.

The operating restrictions are specific: Bima Vahaks are permitted to sell and service Bima Vistaar and any other insurance products later specified by the Authority, but they must do so only through handheld electronic communication devices directly integrated with the insurer’s electronic platform. They are prohibited from collecting any amount from a policyholder or prospective policyholder other than the insurance premium. The Life Insurance Council and General Insurance Council are jointly required to establish common operational and conduct standards for Bima Vahaks, covering minimum education, commission scales, training (including customer due diligence/KYC, personal data protection, policy handling, and claims-service support), standard appointment terms, due diligence, issuance of ID cards, database maintenance, confidentiality of policy data, and other compliance/operational matters, with periodic review of those standards.

Each insurer must have a Board-approved policy covering Bima Vahak-related matters, aligned to the jointly issued council standards. Insurers are also directed to endeavor to deploy Individual and/or Corporate Bima Vahaks with the goal of progressively covering every Gram Panchayat, and specifically to have Bima Vahaks deployed in each Gram Panchayat by 31 December 2024. Deployment is to be coordinated by the “Lead Insurers” for each State/Union Territory, with the following target distribution of Gram Panchayats to be covered within the State/UT: Lead Life Insurer(s) 40%, Lead Non-Life Insurer(s) 40%, Lead Health Insurer(s) 5%, and all other insurers together at least 15%; after that, insurers may deploy as many Bima Vahaks as required based on demand.

The scope of Bima Vahak activities, as visible in the excerpt, includes filling proposal forms, completing KYC requirements through handheld devices, and issuing insurance policies, with the text indicating further service/servicing coordination responsibilities continuing beyond the excerpt. For compliance purposes, the key obligations are to align internal policies to council standards, ensure insurer accountability for all Bima Vahak conduct, restrict collections to premium only, use integrated handheld-device workflows, and meet the state/UT deployment timeline and coverage allocations by the stated deadline.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI’s 31 March 2023 “Guidelines on Operational Issues pertaining to the Regulatory Sandbox” set out the operating process for applicants seeking to implement insurance innovation under the IRDAI (Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations, 2019. Any person or entity wanting to promote or implement an innovation in insurance in India must apply to IRDAI in **Form RG-1**, and the application must fall within one or more of the categories permitted under **Regulation 4** of the 2019 Sandbox Regulations. The applicant must show that the proposal is a **genuine innovation** that will either **increase insurance penetration** or **provide enhanced services to policyholders**; IRDAI expressly says applications made merely to obtain a regulatory relaxation should not be accepted, and the Chairperson’s decision on whether a proposal is innovative is final.

The guidelines require a clear **single point of contact (SPOC)** on both sides: the applicant must nominate an experienced and responsible person, and IRDAI will also nominate its own SPOC. All communication relating to the application must be routed through those SPOCs. IRDAI may grant only **limited regulatory relaxations** for proposals that promote innovation, but an application should not be filed if there is **no need for any relaxation at all**. Importantly, no relaxation can be granted for compliance with the **Insurance Act, 1938**, the **IRDA Act, 1999**, or any other applicable statutory requirement.

The guidelines also impose customer-protection obligations on any sandbox proposal involving participants/customers. Participants must be clearly informed that the proposal’s outcomes are uncertain, their **prior written consent** must be obtained, and participation must be a **voluntary and conscious choice**; the applicant must also provide a detailed **exit strategy** to prospects. The “size of the proposal” is capped, and the sandbox proposal must terminate if, within the stipulated time, it reaches **1 lakh customers** or **premium collected of up to Rs. 5 crore**, or any other parameter the Authority may decide.

For applications in the defined categories, the applicant must file **in association with an insurer** and must identify the exact regulatory provisions for which relaxation is sought. IRDAI reserves the right to limit any relaxation where policyholder protection or grievance redressal would be affected, and the requested relaxation must not prejudice existing policyholders; it should instead support insurance penetration or policy servicing. The applicant must also assess and disclose the proposal’s inherent risks and the measures taken to eliminate or mitigate them. Where the applicant is itself an insurer, it must **inform its Board**, put in place monitoring arrangements for implementation, and keep the Board updated on developments.

Finally, the guidelines state that a **Form RG-1 application that is incomplete or does not conform to Regulation 6 of the 2019 Regulations or these guidelines may be rejected**. The text indicates that IRDAI will give the applicant an opportunity before rejection (the excerpt cuts off mid-sentence), so compliance teams should assume applications will be scrutinized for full procedural and substantive conformity before acceptance.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI’s January 3, 2023 guidelines replace the earlier January 22, 2021 guidance on issuing File Reference Numbers (FRNs) to cross-border reinsurers (CBRs) and are intended to streamline the approval process and enable insurer-led auto-renewal where eligibility conditions are met. The rules apply to any insurer that wants to place reinsurance business with a CBR: before placing business, the insurer must ensure the CBR meets the rating and regulatory eligibility requirements under the IRDAI (Reinsurance) Regulations, 2018 and must have an FRN issued through the IRDAI CBR portal at https://cbr.irdai.gov.in/login.aspx. For new FRNs, insurers must submit an online application in the prescribed Annexure 1 format for the CBR to be classified either as an “Eligible CBR” or “Non-Eligible CBR”; the Authority can seek additional information if needed, and the insurer’s application should be aligned with its reinsurance programme.

A key change is that FRNs may now be auto-renewed by the insurer itself for CBRs that qualify, rather than requiring the Authority to renew annually in every case. To qualify for auto-renewal, the CBR must have a latest credit rating of at least S&P A- or equivalent, and that rating must be no older than 12 months from the date of the auto-renewal application; the CBR must also have been allotted FRN status as an “Eligible CBR” in the immediately preceding financial year; the latest required information must be filed; and the CBR must continue to satisfy the other conditions in Regulation 4(1) of the IRDAI (Reinsurance) Regulations, 2018. If the insurer finds that the CBR does not meet any of these auto-renewal conditions, it must instead follow the normal annual renewal process described in the guidelines. The portal will be open for auto-renewal for the current financial year and also three months in advance of the next financial year, so compliance teams should plan renewals accordingly and verify the CBR’s rating, filing status, and eligible status before using the auto-renewal route.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **“IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022”** on **3 January 2022**, and they **take effect on 1 April 2022**. They are addressed to the **Chairman-cum-Managing Directors/Chief Executive Officers of general insurance companies**, but specifically **exclude ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The purpose is to regulate and support the development of **Surety Insurance business** in India, which IRDAI treats as distinct because of the product’s unique risk characteristics.

For applicability, **all insurers registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 that are authorized to transact general insurance business may transact Surety Insurance, but only if they satisfy the eligibility criteria in the guidelines**. The document also imposes a market-entry restriction: **after commencement, no person may transact Surety Insurance in India unless that person is an “Indian Insurance Company” as defined in Section 2(7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938**. Compliance teams should therefore confirm both registration status and whether the entity meets the Indian Insurance Company definition before offering these products.

The guidelines define the legal nature of a surety insurance product as a **contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872**, involving a **surety**, **principal debtor**, and **creditor**. However, IRDAI makes clear that such a contract is treated as an **insurance contract only when issued by a surety that is an insurer registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 to transact general insurance**. In other words, the same guarantee structure is not insurance unless it is written by a qualifying general insurer.

IRDAI also provides specific product definitions that compliance teams should use when classifying business: **Advance Payment Bond** covers the surety’s promise to pay the outstanding balance of an advance payment if the contractor fails to complete the contract as specified or fails to meet the contract scope; **Bid Bond** covers a bidder’s obligation to furnish the required performance guarantee and sign the contract within the prescribed period if awarded; **Contract Bond** is a broader umbrella covering assurance to public entities, developers, subcontractors, and suppliers that the contractor will meet contractual obligations, and it may include bid bonds, performance bonds, advance payment bonds, and retention money; **Customs and Court Bond** covers guarantees to public offices such as tax offices, customs administrations, or courts for public receivables arising from court cases, customs clearance, or incorrect customs procedures; **Performance Bond** protects the obligee if the principal/contractor defaults and the contract is terminated; and **Retention Money** is the portion of contract payment withheld until successful completion. The document also states that any undefined terms will take their meanings from the **Insurance Act, 1938**, the **IRDA Act, 1999**, and regulations/rules made under them.

The guidelines shall come into force with effect from 1 st November, 2021. The guidelines have been placed on the IRDAI website (https://www.irdai.gov.in). Yours faithfully, Sd/- (Yegnapriya Bharath) Chief General Manager (NL) IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines,2021 Page 1 of 9 IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines, 2021 1. Introduction 1.1 Trade credit insurance protects businesses against the risk of non-payment for goods and services by buyers. It usually covers a portfolio of buyers and indemnifies an agreed percentage of an invoice or invoices that remain unpaid as a result of protracted default, insolvency / bankruptcy. It contributes to the economic growth of a country by facilitating trade and helps in improving economic stability by addressing the trade losses due to payment risks. 1.2 These guidelines set out the regulatory framework; (a) to promote sustainable and healthy development of trade credit insurance business. (b) to facilitate general insurance companies to offer trade credit insurance covers to suppliers as well as licensed banks and other financial institutions to help businesses manage country risk, open up access to new markets and to manage non-payment risk associated with trade financing portfolio. (c) to enable general insurance companies to offer trade credit insurance with customised covers to improve businesses for the SMEs and MSMEs, considering the evolving insurance risk needs of these sectors.
rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued revised **Trade Credit Insurance Guidelines, 2021** for **general insurance companies in India**, specifically addressed to **all general insurers except ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The new framework is issued under **Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999**, was **published on 8 September 2021**, and **takes effect from 1 November 2021**, replacing the earlier IRDAI trade credit insurance guidelines dated **10 March 2016**. The guidelines are also expressly stated to be **in addition to any other applicable laws, rules, regulations, or guidelines**.

Substantively, the document clarifies that **trade credit insurance can only cover credit risk directly linked to an underlying trade transaction**, meaning the **delivery of goods or services**; if there is no such direct link, the outstanding amount is **not insurable** under this product. It permits coverage for a range of **commercial risks**, including **insolvency or protracted default** by the buyer, by the bank responsible for payment in **letter of credit** transactions, or by the **stock-holding agent** in consignment transactions; **rejection of goods** after delivery when permitted by contract, or before shipment when goods are being specially manufactured for the buyer and cannot be sold elsewhere; and **non-receipt of payment due to failure of the collecting bank**. It also allows **political risk cover**, but only for **buyers outside India** and only for **countries specifically agreed upon**; political risks include legal or regulatory actions blocking transfer of payment from the buyer’s country to India, war or civil unrest in the buyer’s country or between that country and India, restrictions or cancellations preventing import into the buyer’s country, and certain additional handling/transport/insurance costs arising from interruption or diversion of shipment outside India that cannot practicably be recovered from the buyer.

The stated regulatory objective is to promote the **sustainable and healthy development** of trade credit insurance and to enable insurers to offer covers not only to suppliers but also to **licensed banks and other financial institutions** that finance trade. The guidelines specifically emphasize improving access to customized trade credit insurance for **SMEs and MSMEs**, recognizing changing risk needs and market conditions. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that any trade credit product design, underwriting, and policy wording issued on or after **1 November 2021** must fit within this narrower “directly linked to a trade transaction” requirement and must stay within the enumerated commercial and political risk parameters, with political risk cover limited to the defined cross-border and country-specific circumstances.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these Guidelines on 5 May 2021 to all general insurers and stand-alone health insurers, directing them to make a **Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product (SDTIP)** available and to structure it on a uniform basis across the market. The product is intended to cover domestic travel only, and insurers must comply not only with these guidelines but also with the IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016, the Consolidated Guidelines on Product Filing in Health Insurance Business dated 22 July 2020, the Master Circular on Standardization of Health Insurance Products dated 22 July 2020, and any later amendments. The guidelines say insurers “shall endeavour” to offer this product, and it may also be offered as a **group product**.

The standard product must include only the mandatory benefits set out in the guidelines, and any optional cover may be offered only if it appears in the prescribed list. Insurers may set the premium, but only in line with the covers offered and subject to the health insurance regulatory framework. The document also states that the product should be designed to meet the “basic mandatory covers” common to domestic travelers, with standardized features across the market rather than insurer-specific variants.

The permitted plan structure distinguishes coverage by mode of travel, distance, and journey type. Plan A covers taxi/bus travel **within 100 km from the place of origin**; Plan B covers taxi/bus travel **more than 100 km from the place of origin**; Plans C, D, and E have **no distance restriction**. All plans are for a **single journey from place of origin to place of destination**, except Plan E, which covers the trip from the place of origin **until return to the place of origin/place of residence**. The maximum trip duration is stated as **up to 30 days** for domestic trips under Plan E, while the other plans cover the duration of the journey.

The mandatory benefits include: **hospitalization expenses due to accident** with a sum insured of **minimum Rs. 1 lakh and maximum Rs. 10 lakh**, paid on an indemnity basis with a **Rs. 500 deductible**; **accidental death** with a minimum of **Rs. 1 lakh for adults** and a maximum of **Rs. 1 crore per person**, with minors to be offered a **benefit-based cover subject to underwriting**; **permanent total disability** and **permanent partial disability**, both linked to the accidental death cover and on a benefit basis; and **repatriation of mortal remains** with a minimum of **Rs. 20,000 and maximum of Rs. 1 lakh**, benefit-based. The table also indicates **automatic trip extension** as a mandatory benefit for **Plan E only**.

The optional benefits the insurer may offer are **compassionate allowance** (minimum **Rs. 10,000**, maximum **Rs. 1 lakh**, indemnity basis), **missed flight connection** (minimum **Rs. 2,500**, maximum **Rs. 50,000**, indemnity basis), and **loss of checked-in baggage** applicable only to air travel (minimum **Rs. 2,000**, maximum **Rs. 20,000**, benefit-based). The compliance implication is that insurers launching or revising domestic travel products must ensure the policy wording, plan design, benefit structure, sum insured limits, and eligibility by mode of travel exactly match the standardized framework in the annexed terms and filing format.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued by IRDAI on 31 March 2021 under Ref. IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/068/03/2021, sets out the practical training requirements for licensed surveyors and loss assessors seeking fresh or renewal licences under the Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors Regulations, 2015, in continuation of the earlier circular dated 01/12/2020. It applies to all licensed surveyors and loss assessors and is framed under Section 14 of the IRDAI Act, 1999 and Regulation 3(2)(b) and (c) of the 2015 Regulations.

The circular requires **institutional practical training for two months** with either the **National Insurance Academy (NIA)** or the **Insurance Institute of India (III)**. This two-month programme must cover: introduction to different types of policies, endorsements, insurance terminology, and the nature of claims; industrial and field visits in coordination with insurers and other stakeholders to examine practical cases; use of technology and advanced tools for risk and loss assessment; report-writing standards, including accurate presentation of facts, policy terms and conditions, claim admissibility, and timely submission of reports in line with regulatory requirements; and the code of conduct for treating policyholders fairly throughout the loss-assessment process. A person may enroll for **up to three departments** during this institutional programme, subject to eligibility, and for each additional department the applicant must pass the relevant examination and then undergo **2 weeks of practical training**. The fee payable to the institution is whatever is specified by III or NIA, as applicable.

The circular also provides an alternative route of **six months’ practical training with an individual experienced surveyor** who has **at least 8 years of experience in the concerned department**. The curriculum for this route remains the same as the institutional training described above, and the applicant may also enroll for **up to three departments** at the time of enrolment, subject to eligibility criteria. For each additional department, after passing the relevant examination, the applicant must complete **8 weeks of training** with an experienced surveyor who holds a licence and has at least eight years of experience in that line of business. The document emphasizes that such training is part of the surveyor’s professional code of conduct and is to be imparted **without charging any fee** by the experienced surveyor.

All listed companies 2. Companies and bodies corporate as specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees In the course of discharging of NFRA’s statutory functions, it has been noticed that there is a need to strengthen the communications between Statutory Auditors (Auditors), Those Charged with Governance (TCWG), including Audit Committees (ACs), in line with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013), the Standards on Auditing (SAs) prescribed under CA 2013, and other relevant Rules and Regulations. 2. Provisions of CA 2013 and other Relevant Rules: The CA 2013 has placed certain important obligations on the Board of Directors (BOD or the ‘Board’), Independent Directors (IDs), Audit Committees and Statutory Auditors of Companies in respect of Accounts and Audit of Companies. 2.1 Board of Directors: Section 134 of CA 2013 and related Rules require that the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statements, if any, be approved by the Board of Directors. A report by the Board shall be attached to the financial statements, which shall include, inter alia, an important statement called Directors’ Responsibility Statement. According to sub-section 5 of Section 134, this statement shall disclose the Board’s assertions regarding certain critical aspects, such as adherence to applicable accounting standards; selection and application of accounting policies and making of judgements/estimates on reasonable and prudent basis; maintenance of adequate records for safeguarding the assets of the company and preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; preparation of accounts on a going concern basis; implementation of adequate
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 07.01.2026, is addressed to all listed companies, all companies and bodies corporate covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the auditors of those entities. Its core message is that NFRA has observed a need to strengthen communication between statutory auditors and those charged with governance, including audit committees, so that the communication expected under the Companies Act, 2013 and the applicable Standards on Auditing is actually occurring in substance and not just in form.

The circular restates the governance framework that already applies. For boards, it emphasizes Section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013: the Board must approve the financial statements, including consolidated financial statements where applicable, and the Board’s report must include the Directors’ Responsibility Statement covering compliance with accounting standards, reasonable and prudent accounting policies and estimates, maintenance of records to safeguard assets and detect fraud and irregularities, preparation of accounts on a going-concern basis, adequacy and effectiveness of internal financial controls, and systems to ensure compliance with all applicable laws. For independent directors, it highlights Schedule IV obligations to satisfy themselves about the integrity of financial information and the robustness of financial controls and risk management, to seek clarification and stay informed, to scrutinize related-party transactions with adequate deliberation, and to escalate concerns about unethical behavior, suspected fraud, code-of-conduct breaches, or company-running issues so that unresolved concerns are recorded in the board minutes.

For audit committees, the circular reiterates the Section 177 responsibilities to review and monitor the auditor’s independence, performance, and the effectiveness of the audit process, and to engage on matters such as related-party transactions, inter-corporate loans and investments, asset valuation, internal financial controls, risk management, significant accounting estimates requiring management judgment, the nature and scope of the audit before it begins, and post-audit discussions on areas of concern. For auditors, it restates the Section 143 duty to report on the examined accounts and financial statements after considering the Companies Act, accounting and auditing standards, and whether the statements give a true and fair view, as well as the statutory obligation to comply with auditing standards.

The circular then points to the key auditing standards governing this communication: SA 260 (Revised), SA 265, and other standards including SQC 1 that contain specific communication requirements. While the document excerpt provided does not introduce a new numeric threshold, fee, or compliance deadline, it is a regulatory reminder that listed entities, NFRA-covered companies, their audit committees/boards/independent directors, and their auditors should ensure timely, substantive, and documented two-way communication on audit planning, significant findings, internal control deficiencies, independence, and other matters required by the Companies Act and the SAs.

As of now, the auditors are required to ensure adherence to the following sets of Standards and Codes to remain compliant with the extant laws in India: a) Standard on Quality Control (SQC); b) 35 SAs addressing various aspects during the entire life cycle of an audit; and c) Code of Ethics including Independence standards. 2. Audit of SFS, where the company has branches, and the audit of CFS of companies with subsidiaries, associates etc, called as audit of Group Financial Statements (GFS), requires special considerations by the auditor (called Principal Auditor), who is ultimately responsible for issue of group audit opinion, and also by the auditors (called Other Auditor) engaged to undertake audit of components such as branches and subsidiaries etc. ‘SA 600 - Using the Work of Another Auditor’ deals with the requirements in the audit of GFS. 3. In the contemporary business and economic environment, there are audit areas of material and/or significant risk in almost all the audits of GFS due to the following features (this list is not exhaustive). a. Complex group structures including special purpose vehicles, auto pilot structures, cross holdings of interests across group entities and shared servi
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, issued on 3 October 2024 under section 132(2)(b), (c) and (d) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rules 3, 4(1), 4(2)(e) and 9 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, reiterates and clarifies the audit responsibilities that already apply to statutory audits of standalone financial statements and consolidated/group financial statements, especially in group audits involving branches, subsidiaries, associates and other components. It is directed to auditors of entities under NFRA’s Rule 3 jurisdiction and emphasizes that principal auditors remain ultimately responsible for the group audit opinion and cannot dilute that responsibility by relying mechanically on component auditors or by treating SA 600 as allowing them to avoid probing risk areas. The circular states that auditors must comply with the Companies Act, the Standards on Auditing (including SA 600), the Standard on Quality Control, and the Code of Ethics/independence requirements, and that NFRA is issuing the circular to keep auditors’ interpretations of SA 600 aligned with those broader legal and professional obligations.

NFRA says it has repeatedly observed serious audit failures and gross negligence in group audits, particularly where money was allegedly diverted through subsidiaries and associates and where auditors failed to identify or escalate fraud indicators, going-concern issues, or diversion of funds in time. The circular cites several high-profile cases as examples of the consequences: Reliance Capital Limited, Reliance Home Finance Limited and Reliance Commercial Finance Limited (alleged fraud of ₹29,000 crore), Coffee Day Enterprises Limited (alleged fraud of ₹3,500 crore), Dewan Housing and Finance Limited (alleged fraud of ₹34,000 crore), and IL&FS (collapse involving debt of ₹90,000 crore). NFRA’s concern is that principal auditors accepted clean component audit reports and did not investigate further despite obvious red flags, which NFRA views as inconsistent with their obligations.

The document highlights the kinds of group-audit risk factors that frequently require special attention: complex group structures, special purpose vehicles, auto-pilot structures, cross-holdings, shared service centres across geographies, shell or dummy companies used to siphon funds from public interest entities, frequent formation/acquisition of businesses or entities including mergers and demergers, significant related-party transactions, unusual transactions outside the normal course of business, unexplained financial variances, and rapid technological change. It also records NFRA’s observations from enforcement cases that auditors often failed to coordinate adequately with component auditors, did not reconcile discrepancies between the number of components in the consolidated financial statements and mandatory MCA-21 filings, and did not assess whether management had improperly included unaudited financial statements of some components in the CFS.

From a compliance perspective, the practical requirement is that principal auditors must actively plan, supervise, coordinate, and challenge in group audits rather than passively depend on component auditors; they must assess component coverage, identify whether all relevant entities are included in the consolidation perimeter, evaluate whether unaudited component financial information has been inappropriately used, and respond to fraud and going-concern indicators with appropriate audit procedures. The circular is not introducing a new numeric threshold, deadline, or reporting format; instead, it reiterates existing legal and auditing obligations and warns that NFRA will expect consistent, rigorous application of SA 600 and related standards in all group audits.

rows.title: NFRA circular on Statutory Auditors’ responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company
rows.desc: / Government of India / National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25013/2/2023 Dated 26.06.2023 Circular To 1. Auditors of the Entities Regulated by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) Subject: Statutory Auditors’ Responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company In course of discharge of its statutory functions, NFRA has noticed that auditors are not fulfilling their statutory responsibilities relating to reporting of fraud as mandated under the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013) read with the relevant Rules and the applicable Standards on Auditing (SAs). 2 The CA 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO) and the Standards on Auditing (SAs) place mandatory reporting obligations on auditors to report fraud and/or suspected fraud to the Central Government and the Board/Audit Committee. 2.1 Section 143 (12) of CA 2013 and related Rules places certain reporting obligations on the auditor, in relation to frauds: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving such amount or amounts as may be prescribed, is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, the auditor shall report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed: ....” Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014, prescribes detailed steps that need to be followed by the auditor if he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud, which involves or is expected to involve individually an amount of rupees one crore or above, is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees. The auditor is required to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee and to the Central Government in the form of a statement as specified in Form ADT-4. 2.2 Clause (xi) of Companies
rows.summary:
NFRA is reminding auditors of entities it regulates that they have mandatory statutory duties to detect, evaluate, and report fraud or suspected fraud under the Companies Act, 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020 (CARO), and the applicable Standards on Auditing, and it is doing so because NFRA has observed that these obligations are not being properly fulfilled. The circular highlights that under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, if an auditor has reason to believe that a fraud involving, or expected to involve, **₹1 crore or more** has been or is being committed against the company by its officers or employees, the auditor must follow the prescribed procedure and report the matter to the **Board or Audit Committee** and then to the **Central Government** in **Form ADT-4** within the timelines and manner prescribed by the Rules. It also reiterates that **CARO 2020, clause (xi)** requires fraud-related reporting in the auditor’s report itself, so this is not limited to separate whistleblowing-style reporting.

The circular further warns that **Section 140(5)** carries serious consequences for auditors who act directly or indirectly in a fraudulent manner, or who abet or collude in fraud by or in relation to the company, its directors, or officers: such auditors may face action under **Section 447**, removal, and **debarment for five years**. NFRA emphasizes that the definition of fraud in Section 447 is broad and includes any act, omission, concealment of fact, or abuse of position committed with intent to deceive, obtain undue advantage, or injure the interests of the company, shareholders, creditors, or any other person, regardless of whether there is wrongful gain or wrongful loss.

NFRA also points auditors to **SA 240**, which requires auditors to maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit, including an active recognition that a material misstatement due to fraud may exist even if management has previously appeared honest and reliable. The guidance in paragraphs **A59–A66** of SA 240 is highlighted as the source for communications to management, those charged with governance (TCWG), and regulatory/enforcement authorities regarding fraud or suspected fraud, so firms should ensure their internal escalation and reporting protocols align with those provisions.

Finally, the circular specifically rejects the idea that **resignation from an audit engagement ends fraud-reporting obligations**. Citing the Supreme Court’s judgment dated **03.05.2023** in **Union of India and Another v. Deloitte Haskins and Sells LLP & Anr.**, NFRA states that an auditor’s resignation does **not** terminate proceedings or consequences under **Section 140(5)** if fraud or suspected fraud has not been reported; compliance teams should therefore treat resignation as irrelevant to the existence of reporting exposure and ensure any known or suspected fraud is reported before disengagement and documented appropriately.

rows.title: NFRA Circular Non Compliance with Ind AS policies on Revenue
rows.desc: mw � I Government of India � � R4 "" 1fl�1 � /National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7 th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25011/1/2023-O/o Secy-NFRA Dated 29.03.2023 Circular To 1. All listed companies 2. Unlisted companies specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Instances of non-compliance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind ASs) on Accounting Policies for measurement of Revenue from Contracts with Customers and Trade Receivables As per sub-section 2(b) of section 132 of the Companies Act 2013 (the Act) read with rule 4(2)( c) of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules 2018 (NFRA Rules 2018), the National Financial Reporting Authority is mandated to monitor and enforce compliance with accounting standards and auditing standards. Further, NFRA is required by sub-section 2( d) of section 132 of the Act read with rule 4(2) (g) of NFRA Rules, to perform such other functions and duties as may be necessary or incidental to the aforesaid functions and duties. 2. NFRA monitors compliance with accounting standards by Companies as part of its review of published financial statements of companies. During its recent review, instances of apparent non­ compliance with the prescriptions of the Ind ASs in the critical areas of Revenue Recognition and Measurement, and Initial Measurement of corresponding Trade Receivables have come to light. In order to ensure adherence to high-quality Ind AS Reporting Framework, which is substantially aligned with globally accepted IFRS Standards, the instances of non-compliance are highlighted below for the urgent attention of the Company Management/Audit Committees and the Statutory Auditors. Revenue from Contracts with Customers - Recognition and Measurement 3. Para 46 of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, requires that the entity shall recognise as revenue the amount of the transaction price, excluding the estimates of variable conside
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated **29 March 2023**, is addressed to **all listed companies**, **unlisted companies covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018**, and the **auditors** of those companies. NFRA states that, in the course of reviewing published financial statements, it found instances of apparent non-compliance with Ind AS in two important areas: **revenue recognition/measurement under Ind AS 115** and the **initial measurement of trade receivables under Ind AS 109**. The circular is issued under NFRA’s statutory mandate in **section 132(2)(b) and 132(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013** and **rule 4(2)(c) and 4(2)(g) of the NFRA Rules, 2018**, and it is intended to bring these issues to the urgent attention of management, audit committees, and statutory auditors.

On revenue, NFRA highlights that **paragraph 46 of Ind AS 115** requires revenue to be recognized as the **transaction price**, excluding estimated variable consideration allocated to the performance obligation. NFRA found that many companies’ significant accounting policies incorrectly say revenue is measured at the **fair value of consideration received or receivable**, which is not the correct Ind AS 115 formulation. The circular specifically notes that **“transaction price”** under **Appendix A to Ind AS 115** means the amount of consideration an entity expects to be entitled to in exchange for transferring promised goods or services, **excluding amounts collected on behalf of third parties**, and emphasizes that this is different from **“fair value”** under **Ind AS 113** and **Ind AS 32**. NFRA further clarifies that fair value is relevant only in limited cases under Ind AS 115, such as **non-cash consideration**, which is measured at fair value under **paragraph 66**.

For trade receivables, NFRA points out that they are financial assets under **Ind AS 109** and are generally measured initially at **fair value plus or minus transaction costs**, but there is a specific exception for trade receivables. Under **paragraph 5.1.3 read with 5.1.1 of Ind AS 109**, trade receivables must be initially measured at their **transaction price as defined in Ind AS 115**, unless they include a **significant financing component** as determined under Ind AS 115, or the entity applies the **practical expedient in paragraph 63 of Ind AS 115**. NFRA says it has observed that many companies’ accounting policies still describe trade receivables using the general financial asset measurement rule rather than the trade receivable exception, indicating a disclosure and policy formulation error.

The compliance implication is that affected companies should **review and correct their accounting policies, revenue recognition language, and trade receivable initial measurement policy disclosures** to align them precisely with Ind AS 115 and Ind AS 109. Statutory auditors and audit committees are expected to scrutinize these disclosures and treatment in financial statements, because NFRA is signaling that the issue is not merely stylistic but a matter of **apparent non-compliance** with the Ind AS framework. The circular does not set a separate phased compliance date; its expectations apply **immediately**, and it is framed as an urgent warning following NFRA’s current review of published financial statements.

rows.summary: NFRA, by Order No. 24/2024 dated 21.10.2024, concluded a suo motu disciplinary proceeding under Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11(6) of the NFRA Rules, 2018 against CA Chirag Doshi (ICAI Membership No. 119079), who was the Engagement Partner for the statutory audit of Ushdev International Limited (UIL) for FY 2017-18. The order disposes of a Show Cause Notice dated 13.10.2023 and finds that although the auditor issued a Disclaimer of Opinion on both the financial statements and the internal financial controls over financial reporting, he still failed in several core audit responsibilities and was held guilty of professional misconduct. Specifically, NFRA found gross negligence and failure to exercise due diligence in relation to fraud reporting duties under Section 143(12) of the Act and SA 240 despite multiple fraud indicators; failure to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence for the valuation/impairment assessment of UIL’s investments in UIL Singapore Pte Ltd, UIL Hong Kong Ltd, and UGFL, because he relied on management’s expert without challenging assumptions, methods, or impairment conclusions even though the expert admitted he had not performed due diligence or independently verified the data; and failure to comply with SA 230 due to defective audit documentation, including undated EP signatures, lack of preparer authentication, and working papers prepared by a person who was not part of the engagement team and had not provided the required independence declaration. NFRA also found that the audit did not properly report non-compliance with Ind AS 16 because the financial statements should have disclosed restrictions on title and property, plant and equipment pledged as security for liabilities, and that the Disclaimer of Opinion on ICOFR lacked proper basis because it rested only on the NCLT, Mumbai Bench order dated 14.05.2018. As a result of these findings, and after giving the EP an opportunity to present his case, NFRA imposed a monetary penalty of Rs. 5,00,000 on CA Chirag Doshi.

rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued this order on 10 October 2024 under Section 132(4)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, disposing of a show-cause notice dated 17 January 2024 against M/s Venkatesh & Co. (the statutory audit firm), engagement partner CA Dasaraty V., and engagement quality control reviewer CA Desikan G., for the FY 2019-20 audit of Coffee Day Enterprises Limited (CDEL), a listed company. The matter arose from SEBI’s investigation report alleging diversion of Rs 3,535 crores from seven CDEL subsidiaries to Mysore Amalgamated Coffee Estate Limited (MACEL), a promoter-owned/promoter-controlled entity; NFRA also relied on a prior investigation report prepared after late Shri V.G. Siddhartha’s July 2019 suicide note alleging financial irregularities, which described red flags including unsecured/unsupported loans and advances, evergreening of loans, and use of pre-signed blank cheques to facilitate fund diversion.

NFRA found that the auditors had access to the earlier investigation report but ignored the fraud indicators it contained, and that they failed to use their statutory access to the books and records of CDEL’s subsidiaries. The order states that the auditors and the EQCR failed to exercise professional judgment and skepticism and did not appropriately assess fraud risk in relation to: diversion of Rs 3,512 crores through subsidiaries to MACEL; evergreening of loans through structured circulation of funds; and a provision for doubtful land advances of Rs 245 crores to related parties and others. NFRA also found a separate audit failure: the auditors did not verify whether CDEL had passed a special resolution in general meeting before giving loans of Rs 1,841.46 crores and guarantees of Rs 100 crores to subsidiaries, and they did not verify whether loans taken by subsidiaries from CDEL or funds raised using CDEL’s guarantee were actually used for the subsidiaries’ principal business activities.

The order further notes that, in their audit of the consolidated financial statements, the auditors had already issued a disclaimer of opinion on issues including the appropriateness and recoverability of Rs 3,512 crores from MACEL, yet NFRA concluded that the auditors still did not perform the procedures required by the Standards on Auditing and the Companies Act to respond to the fraud risks and related-party concerns. The document as provided is only the opening portion of the order, so it establishes the allegations and NFRA’s preliminary findings of major audit lapses and omissions, but it does not yet include the final penalty/sanction amounts or any remedial directions beyond the show-cause process described above.
