EXECUTIVE SUMMARY NFRA suo moto examined the professional conduct of the statutory auditors of Coffee Day Enterprises Limited under Section 132(4) of the Companies Act 2013 (‘the Act’ hereafter), pursuant to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI’ hereafter) investigation report regarding diversion of funds worth Rs 3,535 crores from seven subsidiary companies of Co
rows.summary:
NFRA (National Financial Reporting Authority) issued Order No. 020/2024 dated 19 August 2024 in the matter of Coffee Day Enterprises Ltd. (CDEL) for FY 2018-19, disposing of Show Cause Notice No. NF-23/14/2022 dated 17 January 2024 issued to M/s BSR & Associates LLP, CA Aravind Maiya (Engagement Partner) and CA Amit Somani (Engagement Quality Control Reviewer). The case arose from SEBI’s investigation report alleging diversion of Rs 3,535 crore from seven CDEL subsidiaries to Mysore Amalgamated Coffee Estate Limited (MACEL), an entity owned and controlled by CDEL’s promoters, and NFRA examined whether the statutory auditors complied with the Companies Act, Standards on Auditing (SA), and Standards on Quality Control.

For the consolidated financial statements (CFS), NFRA found the principal auditors did not properly comply with SA 600 when a substantial portion of the CFS was audited by other auditors: they failed to make sure their own work and participation were sufficient to act as principal auditor and did not perform, or ensure others performed, adequate additional audit procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The Order specifically highlights gross negligence in assessing the business rationale and audit implications of Rs 2,226 crore of loans/advances to MACEL, despite this being an important audit area; similarly, the auditors were found grossly negligent in evaluating recoverability and impairment for Rs 842.49 crore receivable from MACEL, a related party with minimal business activity, in a context where funds were allegedly routed through intra-group circular transactions with MACEL as the main conduit. NFRA also states the CFS contained false/erroneous balances that understated receivables through book entries showing repayment by cheques that had been received but not encashed as of the balance sheet date, and that the auditors failed to apply due professional judgment and skepticism in relation to these items.

The Order further records a major lapse in the audit of the standalone financial statements (SFS), concluding that the auditors did not detect or address material misstatements and did not carry out adequate procedures over related-party transactions and fund movements. NFRA also found violations of SQC 1 and SA 230, meaning the audit documentation and quality-control processes were deficient and did not properly evidence planning, execution, supervision, review, or conclusions reached. Overall, NFRA concluded there was omission and commission by the audit firm and professional misconduct by the auditors under section 132(4)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, and the Order imposes penalties/sanctions accordingly; the document is a final enforcement action rather than a forward-looking rule change, so the key compliance takeaway is that auditors of listed companies must rigorously apply SA 600, thoroughly verify related-party exposures and recoverability, and maintain complete audit documentation showing skeptical, evidence-based work.

rows.title: Request for public comments – Draft SA 600 (Revised)
rows.desc: SA 600 (REVISED) Request for Public Comments by 30.10.2024 (Refer accompanying note on NFRA website) SA 600 (Revised), SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS—AUDITS OF GROUP FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (INCLUDING THE WORK OF COMPONENT AUDITORS) (Applicable to PIEs under Rule 3 of NFRA Rules 2018 except PSUs, PSBs and PSIs and their branches) Introduction Scope of this SA 1. The Standards on Auditing (SAs) apply to an audit of group financial statements (a group audit). This SA deals with special considerations that apply to a group audit, including in those circumstances when component auditors are involved. The requirements and guidance in this SA refer to, or expand on, the application of other relevant SAs to a group audit, in particular SA 220 (Revised), 1 SA 230, 2 SA 300, 3 SA 315 (Revised), 4 and SA 330. 5 (Ref: Para. A1–A2) 2. Group financial statements include the financial information of more than one entity or business unit through a consolidation process, as described in paragraph 14(k). The term consolidation process as used in this SA refers not only to the preparation of consolidated financial statements in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, but also to the presentation of combined financial statements, and to the aggregation of the financial information of entities or business units such as branches or divisions. (Ref: Para. A3–A5, A27) 3. As explained in SA 220 (Revised), 6 this SA, adapted as necessary in the circumstances, may also be useful in an audit of financial statements other than a group audit when the engagement team includes individuals from another firm. For example, this SA may be useful when involving such an individual to attend a physical inventory count, inspect property, plant and equipment, or perform audit procedures at a shared service center at a remote location. Groups and Components 4. A group may be organized in various ways. For example, a group may be organized by legal or other entities (e.g., a parent and one or mor
rows.summary:
NFRA is seeking public comments on the draft revised Standard on Auditing 600 (“SA 600 (Revised)”) by **30.10.2024**. The revised standard applies to **Public Interest Entities (PIEs) under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018**, **except** PSUs, PSBs, PSIs and their branches. It governs **audits of group financial statements**, meaning audits where financial information from more than one entity or business unit is brought together through a consolidation process; the document makes clear that “consolidation process” is used broadly and includes not only consolidated financial statements under the applicable reporting framework, but also **combined financial statements** and the **aggregation of information from branches, divisions, and other business units**.

The draft reiterates that group audits require special attention because the group auditor may need to rely on **component auditors**. It explains that the group auditor must determine the **nature, timing, and extent** of component auditor involvement, and that component auditors may be involved in all phases of the group audit because they often have stronger local knowledge of the component’s business, laws and regulations, language, culture, and operating environment. The standard also clarifies that component auditors can be used to provide information or perform audit work needed to meet the requirements of the standard, and that component auditors may be particularly useful where work can be performed centrally, through **shared service centers**, or using common information systems and internal controls.

The document states that the group auditor must use professional judgment to identify the components at which audit work will be performed, based on an understanding of the group and its environment and on how the group is organized — whether by legal entities, geography, branches/divisions, functions, or business activities. It also ties the revised standard to other SAs, especially **SA 220 (Revised)**, **SA 230**, **SA 300**, **SA 315 (Revised)**, and **SA 330**, indicating that SA 600 expands or adapts those standards for the group audit context. In addition, it notes that although SA 600 is directed at group audits, it may also be useful in non-group audits when the engagement team includes individuals from another firm, such as for inventory counts, PPE inspections, or work at remote shared service centers.

A key compliance point in the draft is that **detection risk in a group audit expressly includes the risk that a component auditor fails to detect a misstatement** in a component’s financial information that could affect the group financial statements. This means the group auditor’s responsibilities do not end with delegating work to component auditors; the group auditor must ensure appropriate planning, supervision, and resource allocation, consistent with SA 220 (Revised), which requires sufficient and appropriate resources to be assigned or made available in a timely manner. In short, for covered PIE group audits, firms should expect enhanced coordination, documentation, and oversight obligations around component auditor use, component selection, and the evaluation of risks arising at the group and component levels.

rows.summary:
NFRA is proposing a revision to SA 600, the standard dealing with audits of group financial statements and the work of component auditors, and is inviting public comments before finalizing it. The proposed revision is aimed at audits of Public Interest Entities (PIEs) that fall under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, but it expressly excludes Public Sector Enterprises, Public Sector Banks, Public Sector Insurance Companies, and their respective branches. NFRA says the change is being made on the lines of the updated international standard ISA 600 issued by IAASB, and it was approved for consultation following decisions taken in NFRA’s 17th meeting on 26 August 2024.

The document explains that SA 600 is especially important where a holding company is audited by a principal auditor while subsidiaries, associates, branches, joint ventures, or other components are audited by “other” or “component” auditors. NFRA’s stated concern is that audit quality for consolidated financial statements depends heavily on how effectively the principal auditor oversees and relies on the work of component auditors, particularly for large listed or publicly important groups with significant exposure to investors, creditors, and capital markets. The consultation note emphasizes that the revisions are intended to strengthen the audit framework for group audits because these statements are relied on by a wide range of stakeholders.

NFRA is requesting comments on all aspects of the proposal and specifically asks respondents to identify the issue or question being addressed, provide rationale and, where possible, empirical data. If a commenter disagrees with any proposal, NFRA asks them to suggest alternatives with supporting reasoning and data. Comments should be clearly captioned “Comments on proposed SA 600 (Revised)” for ease of reference, and can be submitted by email to nfra-comments@nfra.gov.in or by post to the Secretary, National Financial Reporting Authority, 7th-8th Floor, Hindustan Times House, 18-20, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi 110001.

The deadline for receiving comments is 30 October 2024. The note also provides access to the draft proposed SA 600 (Revised) through the listed PDF link, and indicates that the consultation is supported by NFRA’s background analysis, including enforcement experience, references to judicial and parliamentary commentary on convergence with global standards, and consultation with SEBI, RBI, and CAG, which it says have given in-principle agreement.

Audit of financial reports of PIEs by Independent Auditor enhances the credibility and integrity of the general purpose financial reports of PIEs. Therefore, the need for high-quality comprehensive financial information covering both financial and non-financial aspects of PIEs cannot be overemphasised. 2. The role and responsibilities of the independent auditors of such entities have also evolved significantly with focus on the need to build commensurate professional and operating capabilities within the auditing profession. In this backdrop, Regulators and Oversight Authorities in some overseas jurisdictions 1 require audit firms carrying out audit of PIEs to prepare and publish information in the form of Transparency Reports on annual basis. Accordingly, the audit firms in those jurisdictions have been publishing the Transparency Reports 2 4. Indian companies have become significant constituents of the global economy and India has evolved
rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA), in a 16 January 2023 invitation for public comment, proposed to require statutory auditors/audit firms of NFRA-regulated public interest entities (PIEs) to publish an Annual Transparency Report (ATR) on an annual basis. NFRA says the ATR should contain “critical information” about the auditor’s operational activities, management, governance, ownership structure, and the policies and procedures used to deliver high-quality audits; the stated regulatory purpose is to improve audit quality, transparency, and accountability in line with expectations already seen in some overseas jurisdictions.

The notice explains that the requirement is grounded in Rule 8(2) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, which empowers NFRA to require an auditor to report on governance practices and internal processes designed to promote audit quality, protect reputation, and reduce risks, including failure risk. NFRA also cites a 2018 Committee of Experts report (constituted pursuant to Supreme Court direction) that recommended a similar transparency requirement for auditors and firms operating in India, especially those that are part of international networks.

NFRA said the ATR requirement would be rolled out gradually across the audit profession for PIE audits under NFRA’s purview, beginning with auditors/audit firms that audit the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation. The initial implementation point identified in the notice is the financial year ending 31 March 2023, so compliance planning should start with that year for the first affected cohort.

This document is not the final rule itself but a public consultation on the proposed ATR contents. NFRA requested stakeholder comments on the annexed reporting requirements and set 16 February 2023 as the deadline for submissions, to be emailed to nfra-comments@nfra.gov.in. Compliance teams at affected audit firms should treat this as an advance warning that annual public transparency reporting is likely to become a formal recurring obligation, initially for auditors of the largest listed entities and potentially expanding beyond that first group.

rows.summary:
NFRA issued this consultation paper on 29 September 2021 to seek stakeholder comments on possible changes to the statutory audit and auditing-standard framework for micro, small and medium companies (MSMCs), which NFRA is using as a research category for companies with net worth below Rs. 250 crores. The paper’s stated policy concern is that financial reporting and audit regulation should be proportionate and should not impose undue compliance burden or cost on smaller companies, and NFRA is relying on MCA-21 filing data and analysis of the financial statements and likely users of those statements to assess that burden. It also notes that the Rs. 250 crore net-worth level is a significant dividing line between companies applying Accounting Standards (AS) and those applying Ind AS, so that threshold is central to the analysis.

For compliance purposes, the immediate operative requirement in the document is the request for written public comments on the consultation paper. The original deadline for comments was 10 November 2021, and the document title indicates that this was later extended to 30 November 2021. Comments were to be submitted either by email to comments-tac.paper@nfra.gov.in or by post to NFRA at its New Delhi address. This is a consultation, not a final rule, so the paper itself does not yet impose new audit obligations; it is seeking input before any recommendation is made to the Central Government under section 132(2)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013.

The paper frames the issue around whether audit and reporting requirements for smaller companies should be adjusted in light of the scale and risk profile of MSMCs. It emphasizes that a large proportion of these companies are likely to be micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises in economic terms, and that the regulatory framework should be calibrated to company size and type. The table of contents shows that NFRA is examining not only the context and its own research findings, but also issues related to the audit of MSMCs and possible audit exemption thresholds, including international comparisons and cost estimates using a standard cost model approach.

The document also identifies the broader audit and reporting ecosystem that may be relevant to any eventual changes, including statutory audit, Standards on Auditing (SAs), Companies’ Auditor’s Report Order (CARO) 2020, internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR), and the distinction between AS and Ind AS reporting regimes. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this paper signals a possible policy review of audit intensity, audit scope, or exemption thresholds for smaller companies, but the document excerpt provided does not itself announce any binding change in law or standard beyond the consultation deadline and submission process.

NFRA’s 29 September 2021 consultation paper does **not itself change law immediately**; it is a **request for stakeholder comments** on possible reforms to statutory audit and auditing standards for smaller companies. Comments were due by **10 November 2021** and had to be submitted **in writing** either by **email to comments-tac.paper@nfra.gov.in** or by **post**. The paper is issued under NFRA’s function in **section 132(2)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013** to recommend accounting and auditing policies and standards to the Central Government.

Substantively, the paper says current financial reporting and audit regulation should be **proportionate to the size and type of the entity** and should not impose unnecessary burden or cost on smaller businesses. For its analysis, NFRA examined companies registered in India that filed on MCA-21 and focused on entities with **net worth below ₹250 crore**, which NFRA labels **“Micro, Small and Medium companies (MSMCs)”** for purposes of the consultation. NFRA notes that this label is **for research purposes**, not necessarily a legal classification, and that the **₹250 crore net worth threshold** is treated as a key dividing line because it separates companies applying **Accounting Standards (AS)** from those applying **Ind AS**.

The document explains that NFRA studied the financial characteristics of these MSMCs, the likely primary users of their general purpose financial statements, and the compliance burden created by existing audit requirements. It specifically signals a review of whether audit and reporting rules should be redesigned so that obligations better match the needs and size of smaller companies. The consultation paper also references comparison data and analysis of **global audit exemption thresholds**, implying NFRA is considering international practice when evaluating possible changes for India.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this paper is an early-stage policy consultation affecting **companies with net worth under ₹250 crore**, and potentially their auditors, because NFRA is examining whether their statutory audit and auditing standards should be revised or tailored. No final requirement is imposed in the paper itself, but it is a precursor to possible future recommendations to the Central Government that could alter audit scope, reporting burden, or exemption thresholds for smaller companies.

rows.summary:
This document is a cover letter from NFRA dated 28 September 2021 to ICAI regarding ICAI’s recommendations to revise the existing Accounting Standards under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013. NFRA records that ICAI has submitted an Approach Paper for revising the current standards and draft text for 18 of the 32 revised Accounting Standards expected to emerge from the project. The revision exercise is being undertaken because India has already implemented Ind AS for certain “Public Interest Entities,” and ICAI had earlier developed, and then revised in 2020, a proposal for a second set of accounting standards for companies that are not required to adopt Ind AS.

The key compliance point is that the revised Accounting Standards would apply to companies for which Ind AS is not mandatory, which means they would become mandatory for a very large universe of mostly micro, small, and medium-sized companies, replacing the existing Accounting Standards originally notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006 and re-notified in 2021 under the Companies Act, 2013. NFRA notes that implementation is planned in two phases beginning with the accounting year 2023–24. The letter emphasizes that the affected population is not uniform: it will include very small companies with net worth in the “few lakhs” range as well as medium-sized companies with net worth up to ₹250 crores.

NFRA’s main message is not approval of the draft standards themselves, but that a robust and comprehensive Regulatory Impact Assessment must be undertaken before finalizing the revision. The reason given is that although alignment with high-quality Ind AS/IFRS-style recognition and measurement is desirable, the impact on the large and diverse set of non-Ind AS companies could be significant and must be assessed carefully before implementation. For compliance teams, the practical implication is to monitor the final revised standards and the two-phase rollout tied to FY 2023–24, because the new framework is intended to replace the current AS regime for all companies outside the mandatory Ind AS population.

This document is a compilation of public comments received by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) on its consultation paper based on the Technical Advisory Committee’s report on enhancing stakeholder engagement. It is not itself a rule change or enforcement notice; rather, it records stakeholder responses and positions on proposed NFRA initiatives such as stakeholder consultation mechanisms, inspection policy, communication/advocacy, NFRA’s roadmap, and regulatory capacity-building. The listed respondents include major industry bodies, research/academia, audit firms, individuals, and ICAI, with one non-relevant comment letter excluded.

The excerpted substantive comment begins with CII strongly supporting NFRA’s role as India’s independent accounting and auditing regulator and welcoming the creation of a Technical Advisory Committee to improve engagement with users, preparers, and auditors of financial statements. CII states that NFRA’s initiative is intended to strengthen trust, improve awareness of accounting and auditing compliance, and align NFRA’s processes with global regulatory best practices. CII also notes that the consultation topics include stakeholder engagement, inspection policy, communication and advocacy, NFRA’s future roadmap, and building regulatory capacity, and says it consulted relevant stakeholders before submitting its comments.

On the specific question of forming Stakeholder Consultation and Advisory Groups, CII supports creating a single Stakeholders Advisory Group to maintain dialogue with corporates, investors, auditors, and other stakeholders and to give them a meaningful role in helping NFRA achieve its mission. CII references Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, which empowers NFRA to make recommendations on the contents of professional standards, including accounting and auditing standards, as the legal basis for such engagement. The excerpt ends mid-comment, so no final positions, deadlines, numeric thresholds, or implementation dates are provided in the visible text; the document as shown is primarily a collection of stakeholder feedback rather than a finalized compliance requirement.

This document is a **NFRA press release and consultation paper notice**, not a final rule or enforcement order. The only operative change announced in the press release dated **9 July 2021** is an **extension of the deadline for public comments** on NFRA’s consultation paper titled **“Enhancing Engagement with Stakeholders: Report of Technical Advisory Committee (March 2021)”**: the due date moved from **10 July 2021 to 30 July 2021**. Comments were to be submitted **in writing**, either **by email or by post**, and the consultation paper was made available on NFRA’s website at **https://nfra.gov.in/consultation_papers**.

Substantively, the consultation paper explains NFRA’s role as India’s independent regulator for accounting and auditing (established in **October 2018**) and states that NFRA’s responsibility is to protect the public interest and the interests of investors, creditors, and others associated with **Public Interest Entities (PIEs)** within its jurisdiction. NFRA says its remit covers financial reporting of PIEs end-to-end, including **standard-setting** and **monitoring/enforcing compliance** with those standards. The paper also states that NFRA’s institutional charter emphasizes **objectivity, integrity, impartiality, independence, fairness, and transparency**.

The paper further notes that NFRA has formed a **Technical Advisory Committee (TAC)** to provide input from the perspectives of users, preparers, and auditors, and this consultation is intended to gather stakeholder views on the TAC’s March 2021 report. For compliance teams, the practical obligation in this document is not a regulated filing requirement but an opportunity to review the consultation material and, if relevant, submit written comments by the extended deadline of **30 July 2021**. The document includes a standard disclaimer that NFRA assumes no liability for use of the consultation paper’s contents, and it reserves rights against reproduction or circulation except for the purpose of making comments on the consultation paper.

rows.title: M/s CNK & Associates LLP – Inspection Report No.132.2-2024-09
rows.summary:
NFRA’s Inspection Report 2024 for M/s CNK & Associates LLP (Firm Registration No. 101961 W/W - 100036) summarizes an audit-quality inspection conducted under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, which empowers NFRA to monitor compliance with Auditing Standards and oversee service quality. NFRA initiated the inspection in March 2025, performed the on-site work in October/November 2025, and issued the final report on March 27, 2026; the report covers both firm-wide quality controls and selected audit files for the statutory audit of financial statements for the year ended 31.03.2024. The inspection reviewed the firm’s compliance with SQC-1 and focused on two recurring risk areas across engagements—Revenue Recognition and Loans and Advances—plus one additional engagement-specific risk area per audit file; NFRA reviewed policies, procedures, and audit documentation, shared prima facie observations with the firm, and then considered the firm’s written responses before issuing the final public version.

The principal firm-wide issue identified is that the firm needs proper documentation for the appointment/nomination of leaders responsible for key functional areas such as Independence, Audit Quality, HR, and Monitoring, along with documented assessment that those individuals are suitable for those roles and evidence that the appointments were communicated to the relevant person and others in the organization. More broadly, the report indicates weaknesses in the firm’s quality control system documentation and governance around leadership responsibilities for quality, independence requirements, audit documentation, monitoring, engagement performance, and human resources. For compliance purposes, this means the firm should have formal records showing who owns each quality-control function, how those individuals were evaluated as fit for the role, and how the firm ensures those responsibilities are known and operationalized internally.

The report also covers inspection of individual audit engagement files and specifically examines audit work on Revenue, Loans & Advances, Provisions, Going Concern, and Trade Receivables, indicating that NFRA assessed whether the audit evidence and documentation in those areas were adequate for the year-end 31.03.2024 statutory audits. Because the report is an inspection report rather than a rulemaking document, it does not set a new statutory threshold or rate; instead, it identifies required corrective attention in the firm’s quality-control and audit-file practices. The public version notes that confidential or proprietary information has been excluded, and the firm’s response is included in an appendix, so the report should be read as an enforcement/oversight finding that may inform remediation, enhanced documentation, and future inspection readiness rather than as a change in law.

rows.title: M/s B D G & CO LLP – Inspection Report No. 132.2-2024-08
rows.summary:
NFRA’s Inspection Report No. 132.2-2024-08, issued on March 27, 2026, records the results of an audit quality inspection of M/s B D G & CO LLP (Firm Registration No. 119739W/W100900) under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013. NFRA states that its mandate includes monitoring compliance with Auditing Standards, overseeing the quality of services of auditors, and suggesting improvements, and that this inspection was carried out in October 2025, including an on-site visit and follow-up review of the firm’s submissions and documents. The inspection covered the firm’s quality control system and three selected audit engagements for the year ended 31 March 2024, with focused testing in the areas of Revenue from Operations, Loans & Advances (for all selected files), and entity-specific areas including Investments (Company A), Property, Plant & Equipment (Company B), and Borrowings (Company C).

The report says the inspection findings are based on policy documents and tested samples, and that certain aspects of the firm’s system of quality control (SQC) need strengthening. Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the detailed findings, the report structure shows NFRA reviewed four firm-wide areas: independence requirements, client acceptance and continuance policy, engagement performance, and monitoring. For the engagement-level review, NFRA examined selected audit files against the above risk areas, indicating that compliance expectations were not limited to generic policy documentation but extended to how the firm applied those policies in actual audits.

For a compliance team, the key significance is that NFRA has already completed a full inspection cycle: it performed the on-site inspection, issued prima facie observations, received the firm’s replies, circulated a draft report, and then finalized this report after reviewing the firm’s response and supporting documents. The report therefore reflects finalized regulatory observations rather than preliminary comments. Because the scope included both firm-wide controls and specific audit workpapers for the year ended 31 March 2024, any compliance remediation would need to address both policy design and operating effectiveness across independence, acceptance/continuance, engagement execution, and monitoring, as well as substantive audit work on the named financial statement areas.

rows.title: Deloitte Haskins & Sells & Affiliates – Inspection Report No.132.2-2024-05
rows.summary:
NFRA’s Inspection Report No. 132.2-2024-05 covers three Deloitte Haskins & Sells entities—Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP (FRN 117366W/W100018), Deloitte Haskins & Sells (FRN 008072S), and Deloitte Haskins & Sells (FRN 015125N)—and is issued under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, which empowers NFRA to monitor audit-standard compliance and the quality of audit services. The inspection was conducted during 2025–26 and included a review of how the firms addressed prior-year deficiencies, plus a focused review of consultation, monitoring, and human resources under SQC-1; NFRA also reviewed five selected audit engagements for the year ended 31 March 2024, with primary attention to Revenue Recognition and Loans & Advances, and a third engagement-specific focus area. The inspection process involved virtual walkthroughs with engagement teams, onsite review of quality-control policies and documents from 5 January 2026 to 9 January 2026, and follow-up in-person interactions with firm leadership, remaining engagement teams, and other personnel.  

The report makes clear that the inspection was not limited to general quality-control governance: NFRA examined whether remedial actions from the prior inspection were actually implemented, and reviewed how the firms performed in two major audit-risk areas on selected files. The report structure also indicates specific findings on independence policy and practices, firm-wide audit quality control compliance with previous inspection observations, and individual engagement areas such as loans and advances, arm’s-length evaluation, audit committee review and end-use verification, expected credit loss/impairment, extension of credit period to a related party, and whether a draft CARO was included in the management representation letter (MRL).  

From a compliance perspective, the key dates to note are the inspection fieldwork period of 5–9 January 2026 and the report date of 27 March 2026, with the underlying audited financial statements relating to the year ended 31 March 2024. The document is an inspection report, not a new rulemaking instrument, so it does not itself establish numeric thresholds, rates, or statutory deadlines; instead, it records NFRA’s oversight focus and the areas of likely deficiency or required remediation for the inspected firms. For a corporate compliance team using Deloitte or reviewing auditor oversight, the practical takeaway is that NFRA is actively scrutinizing whether auditors are properly documenting and testing loan-related matters, related-party and credit-period changes, impairment/ECL judgments, independence controls, and compliance with audit committee review and end-use verification requirements, and that prior inspection findings are expected to have been remediated and demonstrably addressed.

rows.title: M/s Singhi & Co. – Inspection Report No.132.2-2024-10
rows.summary:
This is the National Financial Reporting Authority’s inspection report on the audit firm M/s Singhi & Co. (Firm Registration No. 302049E), issued on March 27, 2026 as Inspection Report No. 132.2-2024-10. It is not a rulemaking or a new law, but an oversight finding on the firm’s audit quality control system and selected audit engagements, and it identifies areas where the firm’s practices were reviewed and where compliance weaknesses may have been noted. The report’s structure shows that NFRA examined firm-wide quality controls first and then reviewed individual engagement files, with particular attention to personal independence, audit documentation, consultations, human resources/performance evaluation, engagement performance, use of technology, and uniformity of practices.

At the firm-wide level, the inspection specifically reviewed whether the audit firm maintained adequate controls for auditor independence, documentation, consultation processes, staffing and performance evaluation, and overall engagement execution. The report also indicates that the inspection considered whether the firm uses appropriate technology and whether its audit practices are consistent across engagements. For compliance purposes, this means the report is focused on whether the firm’s internal systems are strong enough to support audit quality and regulatory compliance, rather than on a single client issue.

The engagement-level review focused on selected audit areas that are typically higher-risk or more judgmental: revenue from operations, other operating income, loans and advances, information technology controls, capital work-in-progress (CWIP), audit opinion formation, and audit documentation. Within revenue, NFRA examined substantive testing, how contradictory evidence was documented and addressed, and the effectiveness of controls over revenue recognition. For loans and advances, it reviewed substantive procedures, controls over lending/advances, and the use of external confirmations. It also reviewed IT controls and CWIP, which suggests the inspection looked at whether the firm appropriately addressed system-related reliance and capitalization of long-term project costs.

The report’s table of contents shows that the inspection also includes an Executive Summary, an Inspection Overview, an Audit Quality Inspection Approach, Inspection Methodology, the firm profile, and an acknowledgement section, followed by a chronology of events and an appendix containing the audit firm’s response to the inspection report. That means the final report likely includes both NFRA’s observations and the firm’s formal replies or remedial position, which a compliance team should review to understand whether deficiencies were admitted, explained, or contested. Because the content provided is only the report’s front matter and section outline, it does not disclose the specific findings, penalties, or corrective actions in the body of the report; however, the existence of the inspection itself and the detailed review areas make clear that Singhi & Co.’s independence, documentation discipline, consultation controls, engagement execution, and selected audit procedures were under regulatory scrutiny as of March 27, 2026.

rows.summary:
NFRA inspected M/s Walker Chandiok & Co. LLP (WCCL) under section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, as part of its mandate to monitor compliance with auditing standards and audit quality. The inspection began in September 2025, the on-site work was conducted in December 2025, and NFRA issued a draft report to the firm on 17 March 2026 before finalizing this public report dated 27 March 2026. The review covered firm-wide quality controls required by SQC 1—specifically independence, human resources, consultations, and monitoring—plus selected audit documentation for the statutory audit of financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2024, with focused testing of Revenue Recognition and Loans & Advances and at least one additional risk-based area for each selected engagement.

The most material firm-wide issue remains independence. NFRA says this is the third time independence concerns have been raised in prior inspections, and it criticizes WCCL’s position that it is not accepting that it is part of the GTIL network, because that stance may undermine compliance with the Companies Act and SQC 1 independence requirements. NFRA also notes that the firm’s current self-imposed embargo, which since 1 April 2025 applies only to NFRA-governed entities and to “recognized firms” in India, is too narrow and does not ensure full compliance with section 144 of the Act. In addition, NFRA flags that WCCL’s code of conduct under SEBI’s PIT Regulations, 2015 does not define “immediate relative,” which creates a risk that disclosures and insider-trading compliance for employees’ immediate relatives may be incomplete or missed.

NFRA also identifies a control weakness in how independence confirmations are handled: it says there is a need for systemic improvement so that every team member’s independence declaration is obtained and documented in the audit tool before the engagement is signed off. The report further indicates concerns around the firm’s procedures for mandated compliance with audit-quality requirements, including follow-up from earlier inspections, though the excerpt provided cuts off before the full detail of those observations. Overall, the report is significant for a compliance team because it points to recurring independence and governance deficiencies, possible gaps in insider-trading policy definitions, and the need for tighter evidence-backed sign-off procedures across audits subject to Indian regulatory oversight.

rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) conducted an audit-quality inspection of the B S R & Affiliates Network of audit firms, identified as Network Registration No. NRN/W/00011, covering B S R & Co. LLP, B S R & Associates LLP, B S R and Co, and B S R S & Co (formerly B S R and Associates). The scope of the review included the firm-wide quality control system—specifically independence, human resources, consultations, and monitoring—to assess compliance with SQC-1, along with follow-up on prior inspection findings, and review of selected audit documentation for statutory audits of financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2024.  

NFRA’s field inspection was conducted on-site in November 2025, and the report is dated 16 March 2026. During the inspection, the team discussed matters with firm personnel, reviewed policies and procedures, and examined documents to form a prima facie view of compliance and audit quality. The engagement-level review focused on two standard risk areas in each audit file—Revenue Recognition and Loans and Advances—plus one additional engagement-specific area selected based on risk for each audit engagement.  

For a compliance team, the key point is that the report is not announcing a new rule or deadline; rather, it is an enforcement/oversight inspection under an existing statutory mandate, with findings tied to the firm’s compliance with SQC-1 and auditing standards for FY 2023-24 audits. The report implies continuing obligations for the network firms to maintain effective firm-wide quality control, independence safeguards, monitoring, and documentation practices, and NFRA’s review specifically tested whether those systems were functioning adequately in practice. If your organization is part of, works with, or relies on any B S R network audit firm, the report signals heightened attention to audit quality in the areas inspected and the importance of robust support for revenue recognition judgments, loan and advance testing, and complete audit documentation.

rows.title: M/s SRBC & Co. LLP – Inspection Report No.132.2-2024-02
rows.summary:
This NFRA inspection report covers the audit firm M/s S R B C & Co. LLP (firm registration no. 324982E/E300003) and its network firms under M/s S.R. Batliboi & Affiliates, following an audit quality inspection initiated in March 2025 and including an on-site visit in December 2025. The inspection looked at the firm’s follow-up on deficiencies from the prior inspection report, its firm-wide quality control under SQC 1 with particular attention to human resources, consultation, and monitoring, and five selected audit engagements for financial years ending 31 March 2024. The engagement testing focused mainly on Property, Plant & Equipment and Shares & Investments, with one additional engagement-specific area. The firm provided an Action Taken Report on the earlier report dated 27 March 2025, responded to draft observations, and this final report reflects that process.

At the firm-wide level, NFRA says the eligibility/appointment letters used by the firm are not fully compliant with section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 because the engagement partner’s independence declaration uses the term “immediate family member” rather than the statutory term “relative.” The report states the firm assured NFRA it would take remedial action. NFRA also found that although the firm has policies and tools intended to ensure firm-wide independence, including a policy that EY network firms will generally not provide non-audit services to NFRA-regulated audit clients (subject to some exceptions), the firm still needs a better monitoring mechanism to verify that these independence policies are operating effectively in practice and are actually being complied with.

For the individual engagement reviews, NFRA identified audit deficiencies in Property, Plant & Equipment in two of the three selected engagements: one or more required audit procedures were not properly performed in relation to the annual review of asset retirement obligations. The report also notes additional findings in the selected engagements involving Shares & Investments, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the detailed description of those issues. Overall, the report indicates that NFRA issued written observations, reviewed the firm’s replies, and finalized the inspection report after considering the firm’s response. The compliance takeaway is that the firm must align appointment documentation with section 141(3) terminology, strengthen real-time monitoring of independence controls across the network, and correct audit execution failures in the tested engagement areas, especially procedures tied to asset retirement obligations within PPE audits.

rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule, set to become effective on December 15, 2026.
rows.desc: At September 9 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Adopting Amendments to Quality Control Standard WASHINGTON, Sep. 3, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule set to become effective on December 15, 2026. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. The public may also view the meeting via a livestream on the PCAOB’s event page, and a recording will be available after the meeting concludes.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. Related Topics About the PCAOB
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that it will hold an open meeting on **Wednesday, September 9, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. ET** to consider whether to **adopt proposed amendments to QC 1000, “A Firm’s System of Quality Control,”** along with **related amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule**. If adopted, the changes are currently stated to become **effective on December 15, 2026**.

The notice does not describe the substance of the proposed QC 1000 amendments in detail, but it makes clear that the action concerns the PCAOB’s **quality control framework for audit firms**, meaning the requirements would be directed at firms subject to PCAOB oversight. Those affected would include firms whose audits fall under PCAOB jurisdiction, particularly firms auditing **public companies** and firms overseeing audits of **SEC-registered brokers and dealers**, because the PCAOB’s core mandate covers those activities.

The meeting will be **open to the public** and held in the PCAOB’s **Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC**. The public may also **watch via livestream on the PCAOB event page**, and the PCAOB said a **recording will be posted after the meeting**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the PCAOB is signaling an imminent finalization step on quality-control rule changes with a stated effective date of **December 15, 2026**, so firms should monitor the meeting outcome and any final adopting release for the exact compliance obligations once adopted.

rows.title: The PCAOB posted select materials shared for discussion purposes with the Inspections Modernization Council for its meetings in July and August 2026.
rows.desc: PCAOB Posts Discussion Materials From Summer 2026 Meetings of the Inspections Modernization Council WASHINGTON, Aug. 24, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today posted select materials shared for discussion purposes with the Inspections Modernization Council (IMC) for its meetings in July and August 2026. The discussion materials – which address topics including the development of a QC-informed inspection approach, use of technology, inspection reporting, and remediation – are available at the IMC’s page on the PCAOB website.Launched in May 2026, the IMC is a resource group composed of outside parties with capital markets expertise and knowledge of the PCAOB’s inspection activities. The IMC’s objective is to provide perspectives to inform the PCAOB’s efforts to modernize its inspection program, as part of the PCAOB’s continued efforts to improve audit quality.“The PCAOB’s inspection program has contributed meaningfully to improving audit quality over time, and, to build on these accomplishments, we need to continue to evolve,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “Since its formation, the IMC has provided us with excellent input to inform our work in this area, and we thank all IMC members for sharing their time and perspectives.”The PCAOB is posting the IMC discussion materials as part of its commitment to transparency and stakeholder engagement as it works on inspections modernization. Stakeholders with questions or ideas regarding the PCAOB’s inspections modernization efforts are encouraged to contact the PCAOB at [email protected].Note: the materials posted today were prepared by PCAOB staff for discussion purposes. rows.summary:
The PCAOB has opened a public comment process on draft goals and objectives for its 2026–2030 Strategic Plan, which will guide the Board’s work over the next five years and also serve as the basis for the PCAOB’s annual budgets. This is not a rulemaking or an immediate compliance requirement for audit firms; rather, it is a planning document that signals the PCAOB’s strategic direction in standard setting, inspections, enforcement, and internal operations. The Board says it began the strategic planning process in early 2026, first solicited comments on strategic priorities on March 31, 2026, and used that feedback to develop the draft goals and objectives now out for comment.

The draft plan is organized around three core priorities: advancing audit quality and investor protection, clarifying expectations and the bases for PCAOB decisions, and transforming how oversight is delivered. Substantively, the PCAOB says it intends to focus oversight on the areas with the greatest effect on audit quality, including promoting a high-quality standard-setting approach, modernizing inspections through a quality control–focused approach, and targeting enforcement toward conduct that creates meaningful risk to investors. It also emphasizes more transparent and consistent decision-making so standards, inspections, and enforcement produce clearer and more predictable outcomes aligned with investor protection.

The document specifically says the PCAOB wants to modernize its standard-setting process so standards are more effective, implementable, and aligned with the public interest. It also signals operational changes inside the PCAOB: greater use of technology and data capabilities, stronger internal coordination and governance, and investment in personnel to make oversight more effective and efficient. One stated objective is to “clarify what constitutes a high-quality standard,” and the first listed goal is “Modernize Standard Setting and Implementation,” with an objective to establish a framework for high-quality standard setting.

For compliance teams, the practical significance is that the PCAOB is telegraphing likely future shifts in inspection focus, standard-setting philosophy, and enforcement targeting, especially toward quality-control systems and meaningful investor-risk conduct. No numeric thresholds, rates, or substantive legal obligations are imposed in this release. The only deadline in the document is the comment deadline: written comments must reference PCAOB Release No. 2026-006 and be received by September 4, 2026, and may be submitted by email to comments@pcaobus.org, through the PCAOB website, or by mail to the Office of the Secretary at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. All comments will be made public, and commenters may, but are not required to, provide their name and professional affiliation.

rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George Kostolampros as General Counsel.

Prior to his appointment as General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. Before returning to private practice, he served as Senior Counsel in the Division of Enforcement at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Kostolampros received his J.D., magna cum laude, from Widener University School of Law and his B.A. from Syracuse University. “I am honored to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the talented OGC staff to advance the PCAOB’s priorities and mission,” said Mr. Kostolampros. rows.summary:

OERA is the PCAOB office that performs independent economic and risk analysis to support the Board’s oversight work, including inspections, investigations, rulemaking, standard setting, and post-implementation reviews. This is a leadership appointment rather than a new rule or compliance requirement, so the document does not impose any new obligations, deadlines, filings, or thresholds on registrants, auditors, brokers, or dealers.

Dr. Compton is coming to the PCAOB from PwC International Limited, where she was a managing director advising the Global Assurance Leadership Team, and previously served as chief of staff to the PwC US Assurance Leader. rows.title: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB after more than 17 years of service.
rows.desc: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich to Depart the PCAOB WASHINGTON, Jun. 26, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB on July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. “I have greatly valued Barb’s expert advice – her accomplishments at the PCAOB have been extraordinary,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We thank her for her leadership and dedication, and we wish her well as she embarks on a new professional opportunity.” Ms. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009. After serving in several roles at the PCAOB – including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor – she was named Chief Auditor in October 2022. During her tenure as Chief Auditor, the PCAOB adopted several new standards that represented important milestones in the PCAOB’s work to improve audit quality and protect investors. Most notably, the PCAOB in May 2024 adopted QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control. The standard, which will become effective December 15, 2026, features a risk-based approach designed to drive continuous improvement in audit quality. Additionally, Ms. Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, the creation of resources to help audit firms with implementation of new standards, the launch of the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process through which registered public accounting firms can submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. “It has been an honor to advance the PCAOB’s investor-protection mission, together with my talented colleagues in the Office of the Chief Auditor and so many others across the PCAOB,” said Ms. Vanich. The PCAOB is beginning a search to fill the Chief Auditor
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced on June 26, 2026 that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will depart the organization effective July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009 and served in multiple leadership roles before becoming Chief Auditor in October 2022.

For compliance teams, the substantive regulatory item highlighted in the announcement is the PCAOB’s adoption of QC 1000, “A Firm’s System of Quality Control,” which was adopted in May 2024 and is scheduled to become effective on December 15, 2026. The standard uses a risk-based approach intended to drive continuous improvement in audit quality, so firms subject to PCAOB oversight should be tracking implementation readiness against that effective date.

The announcement also notes several related PCAOB initiatives led during Vanich’s tenure that may affect audit firms’ compliance planning and engagement with the PCAOB: development of other major standard-setting projects, creation of implementation resources for firms adopting new standards, launch of the Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first request for comment on future standard-setting priorities, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process. Under that process, registered public accounting firms may submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views, creating a formal channel for interpretive consultation. The PCAOB said it has begun searching for a new Chief Auditor and will solicit applications from qualified candidates soon; no other immediate compliance deadline is announced beyond the January 15, 2026 departure date and the December 15, 2026 QC 1000 effective date.

rows.summary:
On June 25, 2026, the PCAOB announced a new **Firm Consultation Process** administered by the Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA) to give registered public accounting firms a more direct way to obtain **informal staff views** on how PCAOB requirements should be interpreted and applied. The process is intended to improve the **timeliness and consistency** of PCAOB guidance, particularly for questions involving the **implementation of new standards** and the **application of existing standards**.

The process is available to **registered public accounting firms** and covers questions about PCAOB **auditing, attestation, and quality control standards**, as well as related **rules and forms**, and PCAOB **ethics and independence** standards and rules. If a firm wants to use the process, it must submit a request by completing the **Consultation Intake Form**. The PCAOB stated that it does **not plan to make individual consultation requests public**, although it may later issue **public guidance** if it receives questions that are asked frequently or that would be broadly useful. There are no specific compliance deadlines, numerical thresholds, or effective-date phase-ins stated beyond the announcement date itself; the key operational change is the availability of this new consultation channel for firms seeking interpretive guidance.

rows.summary:

The Board says the purpose of the request is to improve transparency and ensure its priorities reflect stakeholder views, and it is specifically asking commenters to address the need for, priority of, and possible scope of any reconsideration of its standard-setting approach.

This is not a rule change itself, but a consultation that may influence future PCAOB standards and research projects affecting audits of public companies and registered broker-dealers. The document states that the PCAOB uses this process to identify current and emerging audit issues and decide whether to undertake standard setting or research on standards-related topics, in support of its mission to protect investors and promote informative, accurate, independent audit reports. It also highlights two specific topic areas within its agenda-setting work: data and technology, including artificial intelligence and digital assets, indicating these are active focus areas for potential future standard-setting or research.

For compliance teams, the immediate obligation is to decide whether to submit comments and, if so, prepare them by the deadline. Comments must be submitted by August 7, 2026, and can be sent by email to comments@pcaobus.org, through the PCAOB website, or by postal mail to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street, NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. Submissions must reference “Request for Public Comment on PCAOB Standard Setting” in the subject or reference line, and all comments received will be publicly posted on the PCAOB website.

The release is dated June 23, 2026 (PCAOB Release No. 2026-005). rows.summary: The PCAOB announced on June 15, 2026 that George G. Demos has been appointed Director of its Division of Enforcement and Investigations (DEI). rows.title: The PCAOB has published its annual report on broker-dealer audits.

Overseeing the audits of these SEC-registered broker-dealers 1 is a key component of our mission to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. This Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers (“Annual Report”) provides: yInformation about our 2025 inspections approach; and yA summary of our 2025 inspections observations. The information in this Annual Report is provided under the requirements of PCAOB Rule 4020T, Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers, which addresses, among other things, reporting under the interim inspection program. Under Rule 17a-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”), broker-dealers registered with the SEC are generally required to file the following documents annually with the SEC: 1. Financial Report: A financial report inclu
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s **Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers** (PCAOB Release No. **2026-003**, dated **June 11, 2026**) summarizes the Board’s **2025 inspections approach** and **2025 inspection observations** for auditors of SEC-registered broker-dealers. The report is issued under **PCAOB Rule 4020T**, which governs the interim inspection program for broker-dealer audits and related reporting.

For compliance purposes, the document restates the core broker-dealer annual reporting framework under **Exchange Act Rule 17a-5**: broker-dealers registered with the SEC generally must file annually with the SEC a **financial report** (financial statements plus supporting schedules/supplemental information), either a **compliance report** or an **exemption report** depending on whether they claim an exemption from the **Customer Protection Rule (Exchange Act Rule 15c3-3)**, and the related **independent public accountant reports**. If the broker-dealer does **not** claim an exemption from the Customer Protection Rule, it must file a **compliance report** and its auditor must issue an **examination report** under **PCAOB Attestation Standard No. 1 (AT No. 1)**. If the broker-dealer **does** claim an exemption, or is otherwise eligible to do so under SEC rules, it must file an **exemption report** and the auditor must issue a **review report** under **PCAOB Attestation Standard No. 2 (AT No. 2)**. The report emphasizes that these AT No. 1 and AT No. 2 engagements are collectively referred to as **attestation engagements**.

The report also clarifies which broker-dealers are typically in each bucket. Broker-dealers that **carry customer accounts, maintain custody or control of customer cash or securities, or clear securities transactions for customers** generally **cannot** use the exemption and therefore must file **compliance reports**. By contrast, **most broker-dealers, including introducing broker-dealers**, file **exemption reports**. The document notes that broker-dealer audit attestation engagements are complex and involve professional judgment, and that any deficiency described in the annual report reflects information communicated to the PCAOB by the inspection team rather than a final Board determination that the firm committed sanctionable conduct.

From a compliance-team perspective, this document does **not** announce a new rule or deadline change; rather, it is an annual PCAOB inspection report that reinforces the existing filing and auditor-reporting structure and signals how the PCAOB is supervising broker-dealer audit work. The most important operational takeaway is that a broker-dealer must ensure it has correctly determined whether it is required to file a **compliance report** or an **exemption report**, because that decision drives the type of auditor engagement and the required PCAOB report under the relevant attestation standard.

rows.title: The PCAOB today issued for public comment a proposal regarding narrow, targeted amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control.
rows.desc: PCAOB Release No. 2026-002 June 9, 2026 PCAOB Rulemaking Docket Matter No. 057 Summary: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“PCAOB” or the “Board”) is issuing a supplemental request for comment on potential amendments to certain provisions of QC 1000 and related amendments to the QC reporting rule and PCAOB forms. This supplemental request for comment seeks commenters’ views on proposed amendments and other matters discussed in this release. Public Comment: Interested persons may submit written comments to the Board. Comments should be sent by e-mail to comments@pcaobus.org or through the Board’s website at pcaobus.org. Comments also may be sent to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street, NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. All comments should refer to PCAOB Rulemaking Docket Matter No. 057 in the subject or reference line and should be received by the Board no later than July 9, 2026. Board Contacts: Barbara Vanich, Chief Auditor, Office of the Chief Auditor (202/207-9363, vanichb@pcaobus.org); Jessica Watts, Senior Associate Chief Auditor, Office of the Chief Auditor (202/207-9376, wattsj@pcaobus.org); Karen Wiedemann, Senior Associate, Chief Counsel, Office of the Chief Auditor (202/591-4411, wiedemannk@pcaobus.org). SUPPLEMENTAL REQUEST FOR COMMENT: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO QC 1000, A FIRM’S SYSTEM OF QUALITY CONTROL, AND RELATED RULE AND FORMS PCAOB Release No. 2026-002 June 9, 2026 Page 2 Staff Contributors: Ekaterina Dizna, Associate Chief Auditor; Linnette Klinedinst, Assistant Chief Auditor; Schuyler Simms, Assistant Chief Auditor; David Ellam, Assistant Chief Auditor; Carla Del Monico, Assistant Chief Auditor; Kevin Lombardi, Associate Chief Counsel; Erik Durbin, Acting Director and Chief Economist, Office of Economic and Risk Analysis; Nick Galunic, Assistant Director, Economic Analysis; Zhoudan (Zoey) Xie, Financial Economist. PCAOB Release No. 2026-002 June 9, 2026 Page 3 TABLE OF CONTENTS I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY .............................
rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued this June 9, 2026 supplemental request for comment on targeted amendments to QC 1000, the standard governing a firm’s system of quality control, plus conforming changes to the QC reporting rule and PCAOB forms. This is not yet a final rule: it is a public-comment release seeking views on specific proposed revisions and related issues, with comments due by July 9, 2026 and submitted by email, web portal, or mail, referencing PCAOB Rulemaking Docket Matter No. 057. The release applies to PCAOB-registered firms and, where relevant, to the persons responsible for firm quality control governance, including firms that will need to design, implement, operate, evaluate, and document a QC system under QC 1000.

The supplemental request indicates the Board is considering amendments in several areas of QC 1000, including the requirement to design, implement, and operate the QC system, roles and responsibilities, the use of an external QC function, information and communication processes, monitoring and remediation, evaluation and reporting on the QC system, and documentation. It also proposes related changes to Rule 2203A and Form QC, as well as amendments to other PCAOB forms to align reporting and filing requirements with the revised QC framework. Because this is a proposal, no new compliance deadline is imposed yet beyond the comment deadline, but firms should review whether the proposed changes would require new governance, escalation, monitoring, and recordkeeping procedures if adopted.

The document’s operative compliance point at this stage is to identify whether a firm’s existing QC program would need redesign or enhancement under the proposed amendments, especially in the areas of accountability, use of outside QC resources, communications within the firm, remediation of QC deficiencies, and formal evaluation/reporting of QC effectiveness. The Board also flags “implementation support efforts” and “recent rulemaking history,” suggesting the proposal is part of a broader QC 1000 rollout and refinement process. For a compliance team, the immediate action item is to assess the proposal against current internal QC policies and, if desired, submit comments before July 9, 2026.

rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider issuing proposed amendments related to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, for public comment.
rows.desc: At June 9 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Issuing Proposed Quality Control Related Amendments for Public Comment WASHINGTON, Jun. 3, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Tuesday, June 9, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider issuing for public comment proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control, the PCAOB’s quality control standard that is set to become effective on December 15, 2026, and related amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. The public may also view the meeting via a livestream on the PCAOB’s event page, and a recording will be available after the meeting concludes. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that it will hold an open meeting on **Tuesday, June 9, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. ET** to consider whether to **issue proposed amendments for public comment** relating to **QC 1000, “A Firm’s System of Quality Control,”** which is the PCAOB’s quality control standard. The notice also says the Board will consider related amendments to **PCAOB forms** and the **QC reporting rule**.

For compliance purposes, the key timing point is that **QC 1000 is currently set to become effective on December 15, 2026**, and the Board is now considering whether to modify that framework before the effective date. The announcement does **not** itself adopt any new requirements or change any obligations yet; it only signals that proposed amendments may be released for public comment after Board consideration at the meeting.

The meeting is **open to the public** and will be held at the PCAOB’s **Multi-Purpose Room (301), 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC**. It will also be available via **livestream on the PCAOB’s event page**, and a **recording will be posted after the meeting**.

The PCAOB’s oversight scope, as restated in the notice, includes audits of **public companies** and audits of **brokers and dealers registered with the SEC**, including compliance reports filed under federal securities laws. No filing deadline, transition date, or quantitative threshold is stated in this notice beyond the December 15, 2026 effective date for QC 1000.

rows.title: The PCAOB is seeking investors, audit committee members, auditors, financial executives, and other experts to serve on a new advisory body: the Inspections Modernization Council. Applications are due on June 15, 2026.

For the Inspections Modernization Council, the Board seeks participants with capital markets expertise and knowledge of the PCAOB’s inspection program, including investors, audit committee members, financial executives at public companies, academics, technologists, other regulators, and practitioners from public accounting firms of varying sizes. The application period will close on June 15, 2026. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interes
rows.summary:

Interested individuals can find application materials and additional information on the Inspections Modernization Council page. The notice also reiterates the PCAOB’s statutory role: it oversees audits of public companies to protect investors and further the public interest, and it also oversees audits of SEC-registered brokers and dealers, including related compliance reports filed under federal securities laws.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s January 13, 2026 Order censures Zwick CPA, PLLC and its owner Jack Zwick after finding violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with one issuer audit. The Board revoked the Firm’s PCAOB registration, barred Zwick from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a joint and several civil money penalty of $50,000 on the Firm and Zwick. In addition, the Firm cannot reapply for PCAOB registration for three years from the date of the Order, and Zwick cannot petition for Board consent to associate with a registered firm for three years from the date of the Order.

The Order also imposes forward-looking compliance conditions on any future registration effort by the Firm: before submitting any future registration application, the Firm must undertake specified remedial measures concerning its quality-control system and must provide evidence of those measures with the application. Zwick must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education focused on PCAOB auditing standards, and this requirement is in addition to any CPE needed to maintain any professional license. The settlement was entered under PCAOB Rule 5205, with Respondents consenting to the Order without admitting or denying the findings, except that PCAOB jurisdiction over them and the matter was admitted.

From a compliance perspective, the document matters because it shows the PCAOB will treat serious audit-performance failures as grounds for firm-level registration revocation, individual bars, monetary sanctions, and mandatory remediation/CPE tied to future reinstatement or re-association. The Board expressly found that the conduct met the Act’s sanction threshold under Section 105(c)(5), which allows sanctions for intentional/knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct, that violates statutory, regulatory, or professional standards. The only audit context described is an issuer-client audit performed by the Firm, with Zwick serving as engagement partner and Jeffrey Hoskow as audit manager.

rows.summary:
PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-038, issued December 18, 2025, imposes sanctions on Jennifer A. Crofoot, CPA, for PCAOB-rule violations in connection with audits of four issuer clients. The Board censured Crofoot, barred her from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education focused on PCAOB auditing standards before she may seek Board consent to re-associate with a registered firm; this CPE is in addition to any CPE required for her professional license. Crofoot may not petition for Board consent until three years after the date of the Order. The Board accepted her settlement offer without a civil money penalty because of her financial resources, but stated that it otherwise would have imposed a $50,000 civil penalty.

The Order states that the sanctions are based on findings that Crofoot, while an audit partner and engagement partner at Fruci & Associates II, PLLC, violated PCAOB rules and standards in audits of issuer financial statements. Crofoot is a Washington State CPA (license no. 30844) and, at the relevant times, was an associated person of a registered public accounting firm under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB rules. The proceedings were brought under Section 105(c) of the Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the Order was entered pursuant to Crofoot’s settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205; she admitted the Board’s jurisdiction but neither admitted nor denied the substantive findings.

The document identifies the affected issuers, which were public companies subject to PCAOB audit requirements: Clean Vision Corp. (Nevada corporation with principal executive office in Manhattan Beach, California, focused on recycling plastic waste for clean energy solutions) and Hammer Fiber Optics Holdings Corp. (Nevada corporation with principal executive office in Sarasota, Florida, engaged in acquisition and exploration of mineral properties). The excerpt indicates there were four issuer audits in total, but the text provided here cuts off before naming the remaining issuers and before describing the specific audit-evidence or quality-control deficiencies. For compliance purposes, the key operational consequences are that Crofoot is currently barred from registered-firm association, any future reinstatement requires Board consent after a three-year waiting period, and her return to practice before the PCAOB would also require the specified 40 hours of PCAOB-auditing-standards CPE.
