rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s December 4, 2025 order censures Beckles & Co. Inc., a Florida-licensed and PCAOB-registered public accounting firm, imposes a civil money penalty of $35,000, and requires the firm to comply with its own policies and procedures designed to ensure compliance with PCAOB audit participant reporting rules. The Board found that Beckles repeatedly failed to timely file required Form APs under PCAOB Rule 3211, which requires a registered firm to disclose engagement partners and other accounting firms participating in issuer audits for each audit report issued, with the Form AP due by the 35th day after the audit report is first included in an SEC filing.

The violations involved multiple issuer audits across 2023–2024 and into 2025. For OpGen, Inc., the firm issued an audit report dated June 3, 2024, included the same day in OpGen’s Form 10-K, and did not timely file the corresponding Form AP. For Token Communities, Ltd., Beckles issued audit reports dated August 2, 2024 (included in a Form 10-K/A filed August 5, 2024) and December 31, 2024 (included in a Form 10-K filed the same day), again failing timely Form AP filing obligations. For UbuyHoldings, Inc., the firm issued audit reports dated March 7, 2024 (included in a Form 10-K the same day) and June 6, 2025 (included in a Form 10-K the same day), and for Vestiage, Inc., it issued audit reports dated April 16, 2024 (included in a Form 10-K the same day) and April 15, 2025 (included in a Form 10-K the same day); these filings likewise were not timely made under Rule 3211.

The order was entered as a settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205 and Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, with Beckles consenting without admitting or denying the findings, except for jurisdiction. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB is enforcing the 35-day Form AP deadline strictly and has expressly tied sanctions not only to a monetary penalty but also to an affirmative obligation to strengthen internal procedures aimed at ensuring audit participant reporting is completed on time for every issuer audit report.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s December 4, 2025 order sanctions TPS Thayer LLC, a registered U.S. public accounting firm headquartered in Sugar Land, Texas, for deficiencies tied to its use of audit work performed in a substantial role by an unregistered Beijing-based firm, “Firm A,” on five issuer audits. The Board censured TPS Thayer, imposed a $100,000 civil money penalty, and required additional contingent remedial actions described later in the order. The conduct involved audits of Huadi International Group Co., Ltd. and Ostin Technology Group Co., Ltd., both foreign private issuers organized in the Cayman Islands with principal places of business in China; Huadi’s subsidiaries manufacture and sell steel products, and Ostin’s subsidiaries supply display modules and polarizers for consumer electronics, LCDs, and automotive displays.

The PCAOB found that TPS Thayer failed to properly plan the five audits and failed to reasonably supervise Firm A, even though Firm A was a public accounting firm and associated person for PCAOB purposes but was not registered with the Board at any relevant time. The order says TPS Thayer improperly allowed the unregistered firm to play a substantial role in the audits, which is significant because PCAOB registration and supervision requirements were not met despite the firm’s participation in the issuer engagements. The Board also found disclosure failures: TPS Thayer did not properly disclose Firm A’s participation in Form AP filings submitted to the PCAOB or in communications to the issuers’ audit committees.

Procedurally, the PCAOB instituted disciplinary proceedings under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) and (2), and the matter was resolved through a settlement offer accepted by the Board under PCAOB Rule 5205, with TPS Thayer neither admitting nor denying the findings except as to the Board’s jurisdiction. The order notes that TPS Thayer had filed a Form 1-WD on April 7, 2025, seeking withdrawal from PCAOB registration, and that request would be handled separately under PCAOB Rule 2107. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that PCAOB-registered firms must ensure any non-U.S. or other outside audit firm used in a substantial role is properly assessed for registration status, supervised to PCAOB standards, accurately disclosed in Form AP, and communicated to audit committees; failure to do so can result in censure, monetary penalties, and remedial obligations.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s October 7, 2025 Order in Release No. 105-2025-035 sanctions former audit partner Daniel Carpio Diaz for violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with his work on the audit of Gilat Satellite Networks Ltd.’s 2020 financial statements and 2020 internal control over financial reporting. The Board found that Carpio, while a partner at EY Peru in Lima and the engagement partner for the relevant audit, was an associated person of a registered public accounting firm and that his conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

The sanctions are: a censure, a bar from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, a civil money penalty of $50,000, and a requirement that he complete 40 hours of continuing professional education before he can file any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The Order also states that Carpio may not even petition for Board consent until three years from the date of the Order, meaning the earliest petition date is October 7, 2028.

The proceeding was resolved through a settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205, with Carpio consenting to the Order without admitting or denying the findings, except that he admitted the Board’s jurisdiction over him and the subject matter. The Order notes that EY Peru removed Carpio from all PCAOB-covered audit work in March 2021 and transferred him to a non-PCAOB-registered EY Peru affiliate. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the audit-partner misconduct as serious enough to trigger both a firm-association bar and a monetary penalty, and it expressly tied any future return to PCAOB-regulated audit practice to a three-year waiting period plus completion of 40 hours of CPE.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s September 23, 2025 Order censure​s Marcum Asia CPAs LLP (formerly Marcum Bernstein & Pinchuk LLP), imposes a $100,000 civil money penalty, and requires the firm to complete training on communications between predecessor and successor auditors. The sanctions arise from the Board’s finding that MarcumBP violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards governing such communications when it transferred draft work papers to Haoxin, the successor auditor, in connection with Gridsum Holding Inc.’s audit.

The proceeding was instituted on October 23, 2024 under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1). The PCAOB determined there was good cause to make the hearing public under Section 105(c)(2) and Rule 5203, although MarcumBP did not consent; MarcumBP then submitted an Offer of Settlement under Rule 5205, which the Board accepted. The findings in the Order are based on that settlement and are binding only on MarcumBP for these proceedings, not on other persons or entities.

MarcumBP is a PCAOB-registered public accounting firm headquartered in New York, New York, with licenses in New York (license no. 093038), Texas (license no. P05632), and California (out-of-state license no. OFR1004). It served as Gridsum Holding Inc.’s external auditor from June 28, 2018 until Gridsum dismissed it on January 6, 2019, but it did not issue any audit reports on Gridsum’s financial statements. Gridsum was a Cayman Islands issuer with headquarters in Beijing, China, whose American Depositary Shares were listed on Nasdaq and which was therefore an “issuer” under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 1001(i)(iii).

Haoxin, a PCAOB-registered firm headquartered in Weifang City, Shandong Province, China, and licensed by the China Ministry of Finance (license no. 37060025), succeeded MarcumBP as Gridsum’s auditor on January 6, 2019 and continued until Gridsum terminated its SEC registration in April 2021. The PCAOB had previously sanctioned Haoxin on November 30, 2023 for conduct connected to audits of Gridsum’s 2015–2017 financial statements. The Order specifically identifies the misconduct here as MarcumBP’s improper handling of the auditor transition, namely its transfer of draft work papers to the successor auditor, which the Board found violated the PCAOB’s predecessor-successor communication requirements.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s July 22, 2025 Order permanently revokes the PCAOB registration of Hong Kong accounting firm Centurion ZD CPA & Co. and permanently bars its owner/managing partner, CHAN Kam Fuk (Dominic), from being an associated person of any PCAOB-registered public accounting firm. The Board also censured both respondents and imposed a joint-and-several civil money penalty of $75,000. The action was brought under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the sanctions were accepted pursuant to settlement offers under Rule 5205; the respondents did not admit or deny the findings, except that PCAOB jurisdiction was admitted.

The order states that the sanctions were based on multiple categories of misconduct tied to audit work: violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with audits of the 2021 financial statements of two issuer clients and audit procedures for subsidiaries of a third issuer; audit-reporting violations in the two issuer audits; inaccurate and/or untimely Forms AP; violations of PCAOB quality control standards; and Chan’s direct and substantial contribution to the Firm’s audit-reporting violations. The conduct was found sufficient to meet Section 105(c)(5)’s standards for sanctions because it involved intentional, knowing, or reckless conduct, and/or repeated negligent conduct resulting in violations of applicable standards.

Centurion was a Hong Kong public accounting firm registered with the PCAOB since September 6, 2006, through predecessor firms, but it had already canceled its Hong Kong accounting license in December 2024 and its business registration in March 2025. Chan was the firm’s managing partner and sole equity partner, and served as engagement partner on the affected issuer audits; he was not registered to practice in Hong Kong since August 2023. The order identifies one of the issuers as Luckin Coffee Inc., a Cayman Islands company headquartered in Xiamen, Fujian, China, indicating that the affected audit work involved Chinese-related issuer audit engagements.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaways are that the firm can no longer perform PCAOB-registered audit work, Chan can no longer act in any capacity as an associated person of a PCAOB-registered firm, and the matter reflects PCAOB enforcement for audit quality, reporting, and Form AP compliance failures. The order also underscores that failures in audit reporting and quality control, not just substantive audit procedures, can trigger severe registration and personnel sanctions.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB sanctioned PWR CPA LLP in a July 8, 2025 order because the firm failed to perform required fraud-risk inquiries in an issuer audit and also repeatedly failed to comply with PCAOB reporting requirements. The order censures the firm, imposes a $60,000 civil money penalty, and requires PWR to complete remedial actions before it can submit any future PCAOB registration application; the firm must also provide evidence of those remedial steps with any future application. The Board tied the sanctions to violations of PCAOB rules and standards in an audit of one issuer, plus repeated reporting noncompliance, and stated the action was necessary to protect investors and the public interest in accurate, independent audit reports.

The order is also significant because PWR filed a Form 1-WD on January 17, 2025 seeking withdrawal from PCAOB registration, but the Board states that the withdrawal will not be processed until PWR first establishes, revises, or supplements its policies and procedures as required by Paragraph IV.C.1 and submits the written certification required by Paragraph IV.C.2. In other words, PWR cannot exit PCAOB registration immediately; it must first complete specified remediation steps and certify them.

The affected firm is PWR CPA LLP, a Houston, Texas public accounting firm licensed in Texas (license number P05877) and formerly registered with the PCAOB under Section 102 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB rules. The order identifies the issuers involved in the underlying matters as Ainos, Inc.; ADM Endeavors, Inc. (ADMQ); Rapid Therapeutic Science Laboratories, Inc.; and Reliant Holdings, Inc., each of which was an issuer during the relevant period. Ainos was described as a Texas company headquartered in San Diego focused on medical technologies; ADMQ as a Nevada company headquartered in Haltom City, Texas operating through Just Right Products Inc. in screen-printing, embroidery, digital production, import wholesale sourcing, and uniforms; Rapid Therapeutic as a Nevada biotech company headquartered in Dallas developing aerosol-delivered natural relief products including non-psychoactive cannabinoids; and Reliant Holdings as a Nevada company headquartered in Austin with multiple subsidiaries across various businesses.

From a compliance perspective, the key takeaways are that PCAOB-registered firms must maintain and evidence proper fraud-risk inquiry procedures in audits and must meet PCAOB reporting obligations consistently; failures can trigger censure, monetary penalties, and remedial conditions tied to future registration activity or withdrawal processing. The order does not provide the detailed remedial steps in the excerpt, but it clearly makes future PCAOB registration relief contingent on completing those steps and documenting compliance.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB sanctioned Goldman & Company, CPA’s, P.C., a registered public accounting firm headquartered in Marietta, Georgia, for violating audit documentation rules in connection with its audit of Broker-Dealer A, a Georgia broker-dealer registered with the SEC. In the Order dated July 8, 2025, the PCAOB censured the firm, imposed a $25,000 civil money penalty, and required remedial actions described later in the Order; the firm accepted the settlement without admitting or denying the findings, other than PCAOB jurisdiction.

The violation centered on AS 1215’s audit documentation completion requirement. Goldman issued its audit report on Broker-Dealer A’s 2022 financial statements on March 30, 2023, which made the documentation completion deadline May 14, 2023—no later than 45 days after report release. After the PCAOB’s Division of Registration and Inspections notified the firm on May 31, 2023 that the audit would be inspected, firm personnel then changed 28 work papers and added 4 new work papers between June 6 and June 22, 2023, weeks after the documentation completion date.

The added and altered work papers related to multiple core audit areas, including risk assessment, cash, notes payable, prepaids and other assets, income statements, income taxes, equity, investments, and review of the system and organization controls report. Based on those post-deadline changes, the PCAOB found the firm did not assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation by the required deadline, which is a breach of PCAOB audit documentation standards. This matter is important for compliance teams because it shows that audit files must be complete and final within 45 days of report release, and any substantive additions or alterations after that deadline can trigger enforcement action, especially once an inspection has been announced.

The Order states that the sanctions were imposed under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and that the proceeding was instituted to protect investors and promote informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The document also notes that the findings apply only to the firm in this proceeding and are not binding on others.

rows.summary:
PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-026, issued July 8, 2025, sanctions Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C., an Illinois-licensed public accounting firm registered with the PCAOB and also licensed in Connecticut, New Jersey, Georgia, and North Carolina. The PCAOB censured the firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required remedial actions because the firm repeatedly violated PCAOB standards on 17 broker and/or dealer engagements by failing to obtain a required engagement quality review from a qualified engagement quality reviewer before issuance of the engagement reports.  

The violation concerned PCAOB AS 1220, Engagement Quality Review, which requires an engagement quality review for all audits and for broker-dealer attestation engagements under Attestation Standard No. 1 (examinations of compliance reports of brokers and dealers) and No. 2 (reviews of exemption reports of brokers and dealers). The Order also cites failure to comply with QC Section 20.01 because the firm did not maintain a system of quality control that provided reasonable assurance that engagement quality reviews would be performed on all audits in accordance with PCAOB standards. The Board found that the firm was not ensuring the required “concurring approval of issuance” by a qualified engagement quality reviewer before allowing clients to use the engagement reports, and that the reviewer had to be a partner or equivalent at the issuing firm.  

The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the firm settled under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to PCAOB jurisdiction. The practical compliance takeaway is that registered firms performing broker-dealer audit or attestation work must have controls in place to ensure every covered engagement receives a properly qualified engagement quality review and formal approval of issuance before the report is released; failure to do so can result in PCAOB censure, monetary penalties, and mandated remedial measures.

(“Deloitte Netherlands,” the “Firm,” or “Respondent”). The Board is: (1) censuring the Firm; (2) imposing a civil money penalty in the amount of $3,000,000 on Deloitte Netherlands; and (3) requiring Deloitte Netherlands to undertake certain remedial actions as described in Section IV of this Order. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that Deloitte Netherlands violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards over several years in connection with the Firm’s internal training program. I. The Board deems it necessary and appropriate, for the protection of investors and to further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, that disciplinary proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, as amended (“Act”), and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) against Respondent. Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Deloitte Accountants B.V., Respondent. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-023 June 24, 2025 2 II. In anticipation of the institution of these proceedings, and pursuant to PCAOB Rule 5205, Respondent has submitted an Offer of Settlement (the “Offer”) that the Board has determined to accept. Solely for the purpose of these proceedings and any other proceeding brought by or on behalf of the Board, or to which the Board is a party, and without admitting or denying the findings contained herein, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction over Respondent and the subject matter of this proceeding, which is admitted, Respondent consents to the
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 Order against Deloitte Accountants B.V. (“Deloitte Netherlands”) censures the firm, imposes a $3.0 million civil money penalty, and requires remedial actions under Section IV of the Order. The Board found that, from at least 2018 through 2022, Deloitte Netherlands failed to establish and maintain adequate policies and procedures to administer and oversee its internal training exams, violating PCAOB rules and quality control standards tied to integrity and personnel management. Those failures allowed the firm to miss widespread misconduct involving hundreds of personnel who improperly shared answers or access to test questions and answers, or received such access without reporting it, in mandatory online training courses covering subjects such as U.S. auditing standards, U.S. GAAP, and professional ethics.

The misconduct occurred through unauthorized methods including electronic communications and joint test-taking, and most of the involved personnel worked in the firm’s Audit & Assurance practice. Deloitte Netherlands is a Rotterdam-headquartered affiliate within the Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited network, registered with the Dutch Authority for the Financial Markets and, at the relevant times, registered with the PCAOB. The settlement was entered under PCAOB Rule 5205; the firm consented without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the PCAOB treated weak controls over mandatory internal training assessments as a quality control failure serious enough to support sanctions under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The Order indicates that firms must have effective systems to govern training exam administration, monitoring, and escalation/reporting of improper answer sharing, not merely policies on paper. The Board found the conduct satisfied the statutory sanction standard because it involved intentional/knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct, over multiple years.

rows.title: The PCAOB has permanently barred Michael T. Studer, CPA, and permanently revoked the PCAOB registration of his firm, Michael T. Studer CPA P.C.
rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-022 June 24, 2025 By this Order Making Findings and Imposing Sanctions (“Order”), the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“Board” or “PCAOB”) is: (1) censuring Michael T. Studer CPA P.C. (“Firm”) and Michael T. Studer, CPA (“Studer”) (collectively, “Respondents”); (2) revoking the Firm’s registration; (3) barring Studer from being an associated person of a registered public accounting firm; and (4) imposing a civil money penalty in the amount of $20,000, jointly and severally, on the Firm and Studer. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that: (a) Respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with performing the audit of the financial statements of an issuer client; (b) Studer failed to properly supervise the work of the engagement team on that audit; (c) the Firm violated PCAOB standards by failing to obtain an engagement quality review (“EQR”) in connection with that audit; (d) the Firm violated PCAOB quality control standards; and (e) Studer directly and substantially contributed to the Firm’s EQR and quality control violations. I. On June 20, 2024, the Board instituted disciplinary proceedings against Respondents pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, as amended (the “Act”), and Order Making Findings and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Michael T. Studer CPA P.C. and Michael T. Studer, CPA, Respondents. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-022 June 24, 2025 2 PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1). The Board determined, under Section 105(c)(2) of the Act and PCAOB Rule 5203, that good cause was shown to make the hearing in this proceeding public, and the Division of Enforcement and Investigations consented to making the hearing public. As permitted by Section 105(c)(2) of the Act and PCAOB Rule 5203, Respondents did not consent to make the hearing in this proceeding public. II. In response
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 order permanently bars Michael T. Studer, CPA from being associated with any registered public accounting firm and permanently revokes the PCAOB registration of his firm, Michael T. Studer CPA P.C.; the order also censures both Studer and the firm and imposes a joint-and-several civil money penalty of $20,000. These sanctions arise from PCAOB findings that, in connection with audits of issuer financial statements, the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards, Studer failed to properly supervise the engagement team, the firm failed to obtain an engagement quality review (“EQR”), the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards, and Studer directly and substantially contributed to the EQR and quality control violations.

The proceedings were instituted on June 20, 2024 under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1); the Board determined there was good cause to make the hearing public under Section 105(c)(2) and PCAOB Rule 5203, although the respondents did not consent to a public hearing. The respondents submitted settlement offers under PCAOB Rule 5205, which the Board accepted; they neither admitted nor denied the findings, except they admitted the Board’s jurisdiction over them and the subject matter.

The firm was registered with the PCAOB on November 5, 2003 and is located in Freeport, New York. The misconduct related to three audits on which the firm issued unqualified opinions with going-concern explanatory paragraphs: JMU Limited’s fiscal year ended December 31, 2018 audit report issued June 28, 2019; UBI Blockchain Internet Ltd.’s fiscal year ended August 31, 2018 audit report issued December 5, 2018; and The Greater Cannabis Company, Inc.’s fiscal year ended December 31, 2018 audit report issued April 15, 2019. Studer, a New York-licensed CPA (license no. 033662), is the firm’s founder, sole stockholder, and president, and served as the engagement partner on each of the three audits.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as sufficiently serious to warrant the most severe firm/person sanctions available in this proceeding: permanent firm registration revocation, a permanent bar on Studer as an associated person of any registered firm, and a monetary penalty. The order also confirms that intentional, knowing, reckless, or repeated negligent conduct can support these sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Act.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a settlement order on June 12, 2025 against Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) and its partner Kristofer Heaton, CPA, for audit documentation and quality-control failures tied to five issuer audits. The Board found that the firm did not timely assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation for retention on those five audits, and that Heaton did not adequately perform the required engagement quality reviews (“EQRs”) for those same five issuer audits; the Board also found that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards and that Heaton directly and substantially contributed to those quality-control violations. The sanctions are severe: the firm is censured, its PCAOB registration is revoked, Heaton is barred from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, and both respondents must pay civil penalties—$35,000 for the firm and $25,000 for Heaton.

The order also imposes forward-looking compliance conditions. If the firm seeks to reapply for PCAOB registration in the future, it must first complete remedial measures required by the order before submitting any new application. Heaton must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, in addition to any CPE required for his state or other professional licenses, before he may file any petition seeking PCAOB consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The order states that both the firm and Heaton may reapply/petition only after two years from the date of the order, meaning no earlier than June 12, 2027.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as serious enough to warrant registration revocation and a bar, not merely a reprimand, because the conduct involved repeated audit-documentation breakdowns and deficient EQR performance across multiple issuer engagements. The order was entered pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the respondents settled without admitting or denying the findings except as to PCAOB jurisdiction.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s April 22, 2025 Order (Release No. 105-2025-020) censures Adeptus Partners LLC, a registered public accounting firm, and Howard S. Krant, CPA, for audit-related failures tied to supervision, review, and quality control. Krant is suspended for one year from acting as an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and he must pay a $50,000 civil money penalty; Adeptus must pay a $75,000 civil money penalty. In addition, the firm is required to engage an independent consultant to review Adeptus’s system of quality control and make recommendations, with the consultant work to be performed under the conditions specified in Section IV of the Order.

The sanctions were imposed because the PCAOB found that Krant violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audits of two issuers—Blockchain of Things, Inc. and Applied UV, Inc.—and that Adeptus violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards. Krant was the engagement partner for both audits, so the misconduct directly implicates engagement-level supervision and review responsibilities. Adeptus is headquartered in New York, New York, and is registered with the PCAOB; it is also licensed in New Jersey and Maryland, which may matter for broader state practice oversight, though the PCAOB action itself is under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB rules.

The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the respondents resolved it through settlement offers under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the PCAOB’s jurisdiction. The Board stated that the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions because it involved intentional or knowing conduct, including reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct resulting in violations of applicable standards. The order is aimed at protecting investors and promoting informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, so the key compliance takeaway for audit firms is that deficient engagement supervision, review, and quality control can lead not only to firm censure and monetary penalties, but also to individual suspension and mandated third-party quality-control remediation.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 25, 2025 order against James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner, Yu-Ching James Pai, resolves disciplinary proceedings over audit failures in two issuer audits and imposes both firm-level and individual sanctions. The Board censured both respondents, revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, barred Pai from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $40,000 civil money penalty jointly and severally on the firm and Pai. The order states that the firm may reapply for PCAOB registration only after three years from the date of the order, and Pai may seek PCAOB consent to associate with a registered firm only after three years from the date of the order.

The sanctions are based on findings that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with two audits of one issuer client’s financial statements; that the firm failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR) for those audits; that the firm filed inaccurate PCAOB Form APs in connection with one of the audits; and that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards. The PCAOB also found that Pai directly and substantially contributed to the EQR, Form AP, and quality control violations, and that the conduct met the statutory standard for sanctions under Section 105(c)(5) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act because it involved intentional or knowing, reckless, or repeated negligent conduct. These findings were made pursuant to settlement offers, which the respondents submitted without admitting or denying the findings, except for the Board’s jurisdiction.

Beyond the monetary penalty and prohibitions, the order requires the firm to undertake specific remedial actions to its system of quality control before it can submit any future PCAOB registration application, and to provide evidence of those remedial measures with any future application. Pai is also required to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, in addition to any CPE required for licensure, before filing any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that PCAOB registration status, public-company audit eligibility, and future association rights are restricted for at least three years, and any re-entry effort must be supported by documented quality-control remediation and Pai’s additional education completion.

rows.summary:

The Board found that Sellers, acting as engagement partner on BF Borgers CPA PC’s audits of NetSol Technologies, Inc. (NTI) for fiscal years ended June 30, 2021 and June 30, 2022, repeatedly violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards by failing to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in areas she had identified as significant risks, including revenue recognition and accounting estimates. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated these as serious, repeated audit-quality failures involving core audit areas and independence compliance. The matter involved an issuer audit, a registered public accounting firm, and an associated person under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), so firms should view this as a reminder that engagement partners must ensure adequate evidence for significant-risk areas and strict adherence to independence rules before audit reports are issued, including where critical audit matters are described in the report.

rows.title: The PCAOB has sanctioned PwC Singapore for violations of PCAOB rules and quality control standards.
rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-018 March 11, 2025 By this Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions (“Order”), the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“Board” or “PCAOB”) is : (1) censuring PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (“PwC Singapore,” the “Firm,” or “Respondent”); (2) imposing a civil money penalty in the amount of $1,500,000 on PwC Singapore; and (3) requiring the Firm to undertake certain remedial actions as described in Section IV of this Order. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that in connection with the Firm’s administration of Personal Independence Compliance Testing (“PICT”), the Firm violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards over approximately two years. I. The Board deems it necessary and appropriate, for the protection of investors and to further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, that disciplinary proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, as amended (“Act”), and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) against Respondent. II. In anticipation of the institution of these proceedings, and pursuant to PCAOB Rule 5205, Respondent has submitted an Offer of Settlement (“Offer”) that the Board has determined to accept. Solely for purposes of these proceedings and any other proceedings brought by or on behalf of the Board, or to which the Board is a party, and without admitting or Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, Respondent. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-018 March 11, 2025 2 denying the findings herein, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction over Respondent and the subject matter of these proceedings, which is admitted, Respondent consents to entry of this Order as set forth below. 1 III
rows.summary:
The PCAOB, in Release No. 105-2025-018 dated March 11, 2025, sanctioned PwC Singapore (PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, a PCAOB-registered public accounting firm in Singapore) for violations of PCAOB rules and quality control standards connected to the firm’s Personal Independence Compliance Testing (PICT) process. The Board found that, from 2022 through mid-2024, the firm failed to establish and implement adequate policies and procedures governing PICT and failed to foster an ethical culture within its Independence Office, which undermined the integrity of its quality control system. While those weaknesses existed, personnel in the Independence Office created and used methods to influence the PICT results reported to the PCAOB’s Division of Registration and Inspections and to understate the rate at which firm personnel failed to timely report financial interests and relationships.

As sanctions, the PCAOB censured PwC Singapore, imposed a civil money penalty of $1,500,000, and required the firm to undertake remedial actions described later in the Order. The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the Board accepted PwC Singapore’s settlement offer under Rule 5205; the firm did not admit the findings except for the PCAOB’s jurisdiction. The document makes clear that the Board viewed the conduct as intentional/knowing or at least reckless, or alternatively as repeated negligent conduct, meeting the statutory conditions for sanctions.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirement is that PCAOB-registered firms must maintain and properly operate a system of quality control with documented policies and procedures that provide reasonable assurance that personnel perform professional responsibilities with integrity, and that responsibility assignments and documentation are adequate to make the system effective. This order signals that misleading internal compliance-testing results, especially where they affect reported independence-deficiency rates, can itself be treated as a serious PCAOB violation even if the underlying issue is within an internal independence or quality-control function rather than an audit engagement. The remedial actions referenced in Section IV are part of the enforcement outcome and should be reviewed as compliance obligations imposed on the firm, though the excerpt provided does not specify those steps.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a settled disciplinary order on March 11, 2025, against KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda. (KPMG Brazil), a PCAOB-registered public accounting firm headquartered in São Paulo and a member of the KPMG International network. The Board censured the firm, imposed a $700,000 civil money penalty, and required remedial actions, all under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1); KPMG Brazil accepted the settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205 without admitting or denying the findings, except as to jurisdiction.

The Order says the violations occurred between 2020 and 2023 and involved repeated compliance failures tied to issuer audits. First, KPMG Brazil failed to make required communications to the relevant audit committee or audit committee equivalent in connection with 38 issuer audits for fiscal years between 2019 and 2022, violating AS 1301.10d, which governs communications with audit committees. Second, it failed to report on PCAOB Form 2 the audit reports or consents it issued in connection with six issuer audits, violating PCAOB Rule 2200 (Annual Report). Third, it filed two inaccurate Form APs, violating PCAOB Rule 3211(a), which requires accurate disclosure of audit participants.

The PCAOB also found that KPMG Brazil violated PCAOB quality control standards, specifically in the areas of engagement performance and monitoring. The Order notes that KPMG Brazil served as principal auditor for between 10 and 14 issuer clients annually during the relevant period, and that KPMG Assurance Services Ltda., an unregistered São Paulo-based affiliate, performed audit procedures in connection with numerous issuer audits conducted by KPMG Brazil. The Order’s summary indicates that the remedial requirements are set out in Section V, so compliance teams should review that section for any mandated enhancements to controls, communications, reporting, or quality-control remediation.

From a compliance perspective, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB treated the failures as repeated and systemic rather than isolated: audit committee communications, Form 2 reporting, and Form AP accuracy are all directly implicated, along with broader quality control obligations. Firms in a network structure, or those using affiliated non-registered entities in audit work, should treat this as a reminder that PCAOB obligations apply at the engagement and firm level, and that failures in reporting or communications can lead to censure, monetary penalties, and mandated remedial actions.

The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that Murphy: (1) failed to cooperate with the PCAOB’s 2022 inspection of Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) (“Heaton & Co.” or the “Firm”) by providing misleading information to PCAOB inspectors in connection with two issuer audits; (2) failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two issuer audits; and (3) failed to timely assemble for retention a complete and final set of audit documentation in a total of five issuer audits. 1 Murphy may file a petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm after five years from the date of this Order. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s February 25, 2025 Order (Release No. 105-2025-006) resolves disciplinary proceedings against Natalie Murphy, CPA, a former partner and engagement partner at Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah), a PCAOB-registered firm. The Board found that, in connection with the firm’s 2022 inspection, Murphy failed to cooperate by giving PCAOB inspectors misleading information about two issuer audits; failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two audits; and failed to timely assemble and retain a complete, final audit file for a total of five issuer audits. The conduct was treated as meeting the Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 105(c)(5)(A) standard for sanctions based on intentional/knowing or repeated negligent violations.

As a result, PCAOB censured Murphy, barred her from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education before she can file any petition asking the Board to consent to her re-association with a registered firm. The bar is not permanent: she may petition for Board consent to associate again only after five years from the date of the Order, subject to Board approval. The 40 CPE hours are in addition to any continuing education already required for any professional license she holds.

The proceeding was brought under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and Murphy consented to the Order through a settlement offer under PCAOB Rule 5205 while neither admitting nor denying the findings, except as to PCAOB jurisdiction. The Order identifies Murphy as a Utah-licensed CPA (license no. 7388678-2601) and confirms that at all relevant times she was an “associated person of a registered public accounting firm.” The firm involved, Heaton & Co., was PCAOB-registered at the time and located in Farmington, Utah. The Order also references one of the affected issuers, Issuer A, a Wyoming-incorporated mobile application company with a principal executive office in New York, whose 2021 Form 10-K included an audit report dated March 31, 2022, issued by Heaton & Co.

rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report, issued July 22, 2026 for Ernst & Young LLP’s 2025 inspection, evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional requirements in audits of issuers. The PCAOB reviewed 64 issuer audits with fiscal years generally ending in 2024 and also evaluated elements of EY’s system of quality control; the report is a partial review of those audits, not a full re-audit of the issuers’ financial statements.

The most consequential findings are in Part I.A: three of the 64 audits were identified as having deficiencies so significant that the PCAOB believes EY, at the time it issued its audit reports, had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinions on the financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The deficiencies in those unsupported-opinion matters related to testing controls over, and/or substantive testing of, revenue and related accounts, income taxes, and insurance-related assets and liabilities, including insurance reserves. The report says the most common Part I.A issues involved testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing.

Part I.B captures other PCAOB non-compliance not rising to the level of unsupported opinions. For 2025, these included deficiencies involving retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, audit planning, management communications, and Form AP filings. Part I.C covers apparent independence violations; the report identifies issues tied to financial relationships, employment relationships, non-audit services, and tax services involving persons in a financial reporting oversight role.

The report also makes clear that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that a material weakness in ICFR exists, or that the firm has not already remedied the issue. Likewise, an independence deficiency does not necessarily mean the Board concluded EY failed to remain objective and impartial throughout the audit and engagement period. The report includes a separate Part II on quality control observations and an appendix with EY’s response to the draft report, but the excerpt provided does not include the substance of those sections.

rows.summary:
This PCAOB inspection report covers PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP’s 2025 inspection, issued June 12, 2026, and evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable regulatory/professional requirements for issuer audits. The PCAOB reviewed 64 issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2024, and also assessed elements of PwC’s system of quality control. The report is organized into three types of findings: Part I.A deficiencies, which were serious enough that the PCAOB believes PwC had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its audit opinion(s) on certain financial statements and/or ICFR; Part I.B deficiencies, which are other PCAOB non-compliance issues not tied to sufficient audit evidence; and Part I.C deficiencies, which are apparent independence-rule violations.

The report states that 6 of the 64 audits reviewed were included in Part I.A. Those deficiencies were concentrated in testing controls and/or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts and long-lived assets. The most common Part I.A issues were failures in evaluating the appropriateness of the issuer’s accounting method or disclosure, testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing, and testing estimates. The report also notes that inclusion of a Part I.A deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated or that an undisclosed material weakness in ICFR existed, but it does mean the PCAOB found the audit evidence insufficient for the opinion issued in those engagements.

For Part I.B, the report identifies deficiencies involving audit committee communications, management communications, critical audit matters, the firm’s audit report, and Form AP. These are compliance problems with PCAOB requirements other than the “unsupported opinion” issues discussed above. For Part I.C, the report identifies apparent independence-related noncompliance, with the most common issues involving audit committee pre-approval, unpaid fees, financial relationships, and non-audit services. The report emphasizes that a Part I.C finding does not necessarily mean the Board concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the audit and engagement period.

No specific remediation deadline or effective-date change is announced in the excerpted text, but the report is a public inspection report and serves as a compliance signal for issuers, audit committees, and the firm that these categories of deficiencies were found in the 2025 cycle. The document also indicates there is a Part II section on quality control observations and an appendix containing the firm’s response to the draft report, which may contain further firm-level remediation or explanations beyond the executive summary.
